title: Fast and Accurate: An Adaptive VLA Inference Framework through Environment-aware Model Selection
summary: Embodied intelligence demands both long-horizon reasoning and real-time closed-loop responsiveness. Recent dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures combine fast reactive control with slow deliberative reasoning to balance inference speed and task success rate. However, existing dual-process VLAs tightly couple the fast module to intermediate representations of the slow module, necessitating end-to-end joint training and limiting modularity, extensibility and flexible system switching. In this paper, we propose Environment-aware Model Selection (EMS), an adaptive VLA inference framework that switches between two fully decoupled systems of different scales through environment-aware model selection. The large-scale deliberative system provides globally consistent trajectory planning to ensure task success, while a lightweight reactive system enables high-frequency closed-loop control. A reinforcement-learning-based switching policy dynamically selects which system to invoke based on real-time feedback, enabling sparse use of the slow system and thereby balancing pretrained knowledge utilisation with runtime efficiency. Our design offers three key advantages over prior hierarchical VLA frameworks: (1) a fully decoupled and modular dual-system architecture that supports plug-and-play model replacement; (2) an adaptive, environment-aware switching strategy; (3) high-frequency inference for responsive closed-loop control. We extensively evaluate EMS in both simulation and real-world environments. On the LIBERO benchmark, EMS achieves success rates comparable to the large-scale baseline while increasing the effective action frequency to 93.4 Hz. The framework further demonstrates strong extensibility in real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks, where it accelerates task completion while maintaining robust performance.

AI.tldr: EMS introduces a fully decoupled dual-system VLA framework that uses RL-based environment-aware switching to balance speed and task success. It maintains modular plug-and-play components, enabling high-frequency reactive control while leveraging a large deliberative system for planning. Evaluated on LIBERO with 93.4 Hz action frequency and strong real-world extensibility.
AI.motivation: Current dual-process VLA models tightly couple fast and slow modules, forcing end-to-end training and limiting modularity, extensibility, and flexible system switching. There is a need for a modular, environment-aware mechanism to switch between systems with minimal overhead to balance inference speed and success rate.
AI.method: EMS employs two fully decoupled systems: a large-scale deliberative module for global trajectory planning and a lightweight reactive module for high-frequency closed-loop control. An RL-based switching policy selects which system to invoke based on real-time feedback, enabling sparse use of the slow module. The framework emphasizes plug-and-play modularity for model replacement and environment-aware adaptation.
AI.result: On LIBERO benchmark, EMS achieves success rates comparable to the large-scale baseline while boosting effective action frequency to 93.4 Hz. Real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks demonstrate improved task completion speed with robust performance, illustrating extensibility and practical gains.
AI.conclusion: EMS offers a modular, adaptive dual-system VLA framework with environment-aware switching and high-frequency closed-loop control, achieving comparable task success to large-scale planning while significantly increasing throughput and enabling easy model replacement in both simulation and real-world settings.

title: LyEvO: Lyapunov-Guided Evolutionary Optimization for Safe and Robust Sim-to-Real Policy Learning
summary: Training controllers that are safe and robust in simulation, and systematically assessing their readiness for real-world deployment, remain key challenges in sim-to-real transfer. To address this, we propose LyEvO, a physics-grounded framework that combines constrained Evolutionary Optimization and Statistical Model Checking (SMC)-based verification with Lyapunov-based stability analysis. Leveraging prior knowledge of the system dynamics, LyEvO uses Lyapunov analysis to compute an initial candidate stability region. An iterative loop then uses operational scenarios drawn from this region to jointly optimize and statistically verify a policy, and subsequently expands the region's boundaries based on the verification outcome. This integrated procedure provides a practical criterion for assessing deployment readiness. We evaluate LyEvO on Cartpole and 3D Quadrotor benchmarks through extensive simulations and targeted real-world experiments, demonstrating safe and robust sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: LyEvO is a physics-grounded framework that fuses Lyapunov stability analysis with constrained Evolutionary Optimization and Statistical Model Checking to iteratively enlarge a safe stability region for a policy, providing a practical readiness criterion for sim-to-real transfer; validated on Cartpole and 3D quadrotor with simulations and targeted real-world tests.
AI.motivation: Sim-to-real transfer suffers from safety/robustness gaps and deployment unreliability. A verifiable, dynamics-informed approach is needed to certify readiness and guide policy optimization.
AI.method: 1) Use Lyapunov analysis to compute an initial stability region from known system dynamics. 2) Within this region, apply constrained Evolutionary Optimization to jointly optimize policy parameters. 3) Use Statistical Model Checking to verify stability/performance on operational scenarios sampled from the region. 4) If verification passes, expand the region boundaries and repeat, iterating until deployment readiness is demonstrated.
AI.result: Evaluated on Cartpole and 3D quadrotor benchmarks with extensive simulations and targeted real-world experiments, showing safe and robust sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: The integrated LyEvO loop yields a practical criterion for deployment readiness by coupling physics-based guarantees with data-driven optimization and probabilistic verification. It can generalize to other dynamics with known models, though computational cost and modeling fidelity are potential limitations.

title: A Disturbance in the Force: Force Actuation on the RAVEN II Surgical Robot with Parallel Motor-Cable Units
summary: Difficulty in haptic feedback for surgical robots has been a long-term problem for decades. In recent years, learning-based force estimation from robot states suggests desirable accuracy without the necessity of extra sensors. However, challenges remain in obtaining representative training data in which the robot moves in the workspace under various external forces. In this work, a parallel motor-cable system is developed. With six motor-cable units installed around the robot workspace, cables with controllable tension connected to the robot end-effector can provide the desired external force without interfering with the movement of the surgical robot. The development of the system includes motor-unit hardware, control software, sensor drivers, simulations, and more. Preliminary experiments suggest an accuracy of force actuation with errors less than 1 N.

AI.tldr: A parallel motor-cable system is proposed to enable controllable external forces on a surgical robot's end-effector, addressing haptic feedback challenges and training data limitations for learning-based force estimation.
AI.motivation: Haptic feedback in surgical robotics remains difficult; learning-based force estimation requires representative training data under varying external forces, which is hard to obtain in practice.
AI.method: Develop a parallel system: six motor-cable units positioned around the workspace; cables with controllable tension connect to the end-effector to apply external forces without hindering motion; encompasses hardware, control software, sensor drivers, and simulations.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments indicate force actuation accuracy with errors < 1 N.
AI.conclusion: The proposed motor-cable system can apply controllable external forces without impeding robot motion, potentially improving data collection for learning-based force estimation and advancing haptic feedback in surgical robotics.

title: SyncSBC: Decentralized Swarm Behavior Prediction for Synchronized Autonomous Control
summary: Robot swarms utilize many independent limited-sensing agents to produce complex emergent behaviors without requiring centralized control. However, little research explores how agents can infer swarm-level behavior from purely local perception, a capability critical for detecting faults and behavior changes. In this paper, we introduce Synchronized Swarm Behavior Classification (SyncSBC), which combines improvements in machine learning and distributed consensus to classify collective swarm behavior and synchronize swarm decision-making in an entirely decentralized manner. We show that SyncSBC achieves high classification accuracy and low synchronization delay, making it suitable for real-world deployment. Finally, we use SyncSBC to demonstrate two promising swarm applications on real robots where we show that swarms utilizing SyncSBC can accurately identify anomalies in robot behavior and autonomously coordinate collective changes in swarm behavior. Videos, code and supplemental experiments are available at https://sites.google.com/view/sync-sbc/home.

AI.tldr: A decentralized framework that classifies swarm behavior from local observations and synchronizes decisions using machine learning and distributed consensus.
AI.motivation: Detect faults and behavior changes in robot swarms by inferring swarm-level states from local perception; existing work lacks effective decentralized sensing/decision synchronization.
AI.method: Integrates ML-based behavior classification with distributed consensus in a fully decentralized pipeline (no central controller) to both classify collective behavior and synchronize swarm decision-making.
AI.result: High classification accuracy and low synchronization delay on simulations and real robots; demonstrated anomaly detection and coordinated behavior changes; potential for real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: SyncSBC enables robust, decentralized swarm monitoring and control, facilitating fault detection and adaptive coordination without centralized infrastructure.

title: UAV3DCrop: Benchmarking 3D Reconstruction in Repeated Multi-Angle UAV Crop Surveys
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Dataset and project page: https://link-dev.github.io/UAV3DCrop/
summary: Accurate 3D crop monitoring underpins data-driven precision agriculture by enabling field-scale analysis of plant structure, growth dynamics, and management response. Modern 3D reconstruction methods perform strongly on generic benchmarks, but rendered appearance may not translate into metrically and agronomically useful geometry in crop fields. We introduce UAV3DCrop, a public benchmark of repeated multi-angle unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) crop surveys. It contains 88,830 RGB images at $5280 \times 3956$ pixels, with a ground sampling distance of 3.6-5.8 mm, from 91 scenes spanning corn, soybean, wheat, and oat. Track A evaluates seven scene-optimized methods -- Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) variants -- on held-out views, photogrammetry-referenced depth, and canopy-height recovery. Track B tests four pretrained feed-forward models on zero-shot camera-pose and geometry estimation. The scene-optimized methods rank differently across the three targets: Splatfacto-big leads appearance, whereas Scaffold-GS leads depth and is statistically tied with Splatfacto for canopy height. Among feed-forward models, MapAnything leads on seven of the eight metrics, while the remaining models vary more across crops and fail severely on absolute scale in a way that alignment conceals. Repeated acquisitions reveal further sensitivities that differ by output type and by model, associated with position within the acquisition sequence and with tie-point multiplicity. Current 3D reconstruction methods are therefore not yet interchangeable for agronomic use: no single method wins on appearance, geometry, and canopy height at once, and only one of four feed-forward models recovers usable metric scale. The dataset is publicly available at https://link-dev.github.io/UAV3DCrop/

AI.tldr: UAV3DCrop provides a large UAV-based 3D crop dataset to benchmark appearance, geometry, and canopy-height reconstruction; results show no single method excels across all targets and only one feed-forward model recovers metric scale, highlighting current limitations for agronomic use.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between photorealistic 3D reconstructions and agronomically useful geometry in crop fields; enable evaluation of metric-scale depth and canopy-height accuracy across multiple crops.
AI.method: Track A evaluates scene-optimized methods (NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting variants) on held-out views, photogrammetry-referenced depth, and canopy-height recovery. Track B tests four pretrained feed-forward models for zero-shot camera-pose and geometry estimation. Dataset comprises 88,830 RGB images (5280×3956) with 3.6–5.8 mm GSD from 91 scenes of corn, soybean, wheat, and oat; repeated multi-angle UAV surveys.
AI.result: Scene-optimized methods rank differently by target: Splatfacto-big for appearance, Scaffold-GS for depth (tied with Splatfacto for canopy height). Among feed-forward models, MapAnything leads on seven of eight metrics; others vary by crop and largely fail to recover absolute scale. Repeated acquisitions reveal sensitivities to acquisition order and tie-point multiplicity; no method dominates appearance, geometry, and canopy height simultaneously; only one feed-forward model yields usable metric scale.
AI.conclusion: Current 3D reconstruction methods are not interchangeable for agronomic use; no single method wins across appearance, geometry, and canopy height, and metric-scale recovery remains elusive for most feed-forward models. The dataset provides a public benchmark to drive development toward agronomically useful, metric-scale 3D crop reconstructions.

title: Towards Multi-Label Graph Foundation Models: from Single-Vector Representation Learning to Multi-Semantic Basis Learning
summary: Multi-label node classification is an important yet challenging task in graph learning, where nodes exhibit multiple semantics simultaneously. Existing methods for multi-label node classification can effectively model multiple labels, while only considering in-domain scenarios where the model needs to be trained and tested within the same graph domain, resulting in limited cross-domain generalization. Recently, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable graph representations across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks. However, existing GFMs are built upon single-label assumption, where all nodes are arbitrarily regarded as containing only one class of semantic and embedded into a single representation. For multi-label nodes, such a representation essentially approximates multiple semantics with a single point in the representation space, inevitably leading to semantic entanglement and making simultaneous discrimination of multiple labels difficult. To address these limitations, we propose a Multi-Semantic Basis Graph Foundation Model (MSB-GFM), a framework for cross-domain multi-label node classification. Specifically, we introduce a multi-semantic basis representation learning paradigm that models each multi-label node as an adaptive composition of semantic bases, thereby enabling flexible representational capacity for modeling multiple semantics. Furthermore, we develop a semantic-structure dual-channel architecture with domain adversarial training for effective cross-domain knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

AI.tldr: Proposes MSB-GFM for cross-domain multi-label node classification using adaptive multi-semantic basis representations and a dual-channel architecture with domain adversarial training.
AI.motivation: Addresses semantic entanglement and poor cross-domain generalization of single-label Graph Foundation Models when applied to multi-label nodes; aims to enable transferable modeling of multiple semantics across graph domains.
AI.method: Introduces an adaptive composition of semantic bases to represent multi-label nodes; develops a semantic-structure dual-channel architecture with domain adversarial training to transfer knowledge across domains.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.
AI.conclusion: MSB-GFM enables flexible cross-domain modeling of multi-label semantics on graphs and mitigates semantic entanglement by decomposing representations into semantic bases with adversarial domain alignment.

title: Latent Fact-Checking: Detecting Misinformation through Activation Engineering
summary: The proliferation of misinformation online has driven demand for scalable detection systems. While most existing approaches rely on surface-level linguistic features or external knowledge retrieval, we examine truthfulness as a geometric property of a language model's representation space. We introduce a misinformation detection framework grounded in activation engineering, which leverages the latent geometry of transformer models. Our approach elicits a misinformation direction in the residual stream by contrasting activations from paired truthful and false statements, following the difference-in-means principle of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). At inference time, the last-token activation of an unseen claim is projected onto this direction, and the projected representation is fed to an Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) for classification. The procedure requires no fine-tuning of the backbone model, no external evidence retrieval, and no task-specific supervision beyond the contrastive pairs used to estimate the direction. We evaluate the method across 11 models from the Gemma, Llama, and Qwen families, ranging from 270M to 12B parameters, on three fact-checking benchmarks: AVeriTeC, LIAR, and FACTors. The falsehood direction is recoverable across model scales and architectural families, and last-token projection matches or surpasses zero-shot and few-shot prompting baselines on LIAR and FACTors, with the largest gains observed for smaller models. Performance on AVeriTeC is more limited, which we attribute to its evidence-grounded labeling scheme. These findings provide evidence that truthfulness is a structured, linearly separable concept in the latent space of pretrained language models, and point toward interpretability-driven misinformation detection as a practical complement to retrieval-based pipelines. The code is available on https://github.com/Malta-Lab/LaFaCt.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot/few-shot compatible misinformation detector that uses activation-based direction in transformer residual streams to separate truthful vs false statements, requiring no fine-tuning or external retrieval, evaluated across multiple models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To move beyond surface linguistic cues and external retrieval by exploring the latent geometry of language-model representations, treating truthfulness as a linearly separable property in the model's latent space.
AI.method: Construct a misinformation direction by contrasting activations from paired truthful and false statements (difference-in-means in the residual stream, via Contrastive Activation Addition). At inference, project the last-token activation of a claim onto this direction, then classify with an MLP. No backbone fine-tuning or external evidence retrieval; uses contrastive pairs to estimate the direction. Evaluated on 11 models (Gemma, Llama, Qwen, 270M–12B) across AVeriTeC, LIAR, FACTors.
AI.result: The misinformation direction is recoverable across model scales and architectures. Last-token projection matches or surpasses zero-shot/few-shot prompting baselines on LIAR and FACTors, with larger gains for smaller models. AVeriTeC performance is weaker due to its evidence-grounded labeling scheme. The approach suggests truthfulness is a structured, linearly separable concept in LM latent space, offering a practical interpretability-driven complement to retrieval-based pipelines; code available at the referenced GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Truthfulness in pretrained LMs can be captured as a linear direction in latent space, enabling efficient, non-fine-tuned misinformation detection that complements retrieval-based methods, with particular strength for smaller models.

title: The Reeb Structure of Bend Distance in Grid Domains: Cycle Bounds with Holes, Exact Sector Geometry on Disks, and the Two-Port Constant $c_2^\square=3$
comment: 32 pages, 5 figures. Ancillary Python script verifies all finite examples
summary: The fixed-parameter algorithm for coordinated motion planning on discretized simple polygons (ICALP 2026) rests on a single-port sector decomposition: grid vertices are labelled by the minimum number of bends needed to reach an oriented terminal. We develop the structure theory of this decomposition on grid domains with holes. Once its endpoint convention is made precise, bend distance extends to a canonical piecewise-affine function on the domain, and the sector graph is the parallel-edge shadow of the Reeb multigraph of that function. For a finite pure planar cubical domain with $h$ holes this yields $β_1(Γ_p) \le β_1(R_{f_p}) \le h$, together with a linear-time computable feedback set of at most $h$ sector vertices; coordinate-level one-hole examples show that the finer hole-free geometry -- unique predecessors and straight baselines -- fails. On hole-free cubical disks the machinery is exact: every positive sector is the one-sided extrusion of a unique straight parent interface, and the two-port common refinement has treewidth exactly $c_2^\square=3$, although sector count, cycle rank, and feedback number are unbounded already there. The endpoint precision is necessary rather than cosmetic: under the literal reading of the source's definition, one hole-free unit square has sector graph $C_3$, falsifying the single-port tree lemma; the augmented convention used here is exactly the metric computed by the source's own layering procedure. We do not obtain an $f(k,h)n^{O(1)}$ algorithm; the paper supplies the structural first step and a falsification tool for that program.

AI.tldr: A structure-theoretic study of single-port sector decompositions on grid domains with holes, connecting bend-distance to the Reeb multigraph; yields topological bounds and a linear-time feedback set, demonstrates the necessity of endpoint conventions, and shows limits: no general f(k,h)n^O(1) algorithm yet; hole-free cases have partial exactness.
AI.motivation: To understand the structure of bend-distance sector decompositions to inform fixed-parameter algorithms for coordinated motion planning on discretized polygons.
AI.method: Define single-port sector decomposition; label grid vertices by minimum bends to an oriented terminal; extend bend-distance to a canonical piecewise-affine function; show sector graph is the parallel-edge shadow of the Reeb multigraph of that function; analyze finite pure planar cubical domains with h holes to bound β1 and provide a linear-time office (feedback set) of size ≤ h; examine hole-free cubical disks, proving exactness for certain properties (treewidth 3 for two-port common refinement) but with unbounded sector counts; demonstrate endpoint-precision necessity with counterexamples; present augmented endpoint convention aligned with layering procedure.
AI.result: β1(Γ_p) ≤ β1(R_{f_p}) ≤ h with a linear-time computable feedback set of at most h sector vertices; hole-free disks yield exact treewidth 3 for the two-port common refinement, but sector count and other invariants can be unbounded; one-hole counterexamples show that finer hole-free geometry fails under naive definitions; endpoint precision is essential; no f(k,h)n^O(1) algorithm obtained; provides a structural first step and a falsification tool for such algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint precision is essential; the work offers a foundational structural framework and a practical falsification tool for pursuing fixed-parameter tractable approaches, while also highlighting inherent geometric limitations in current models and the need for refined endpoint conventions and further methodological development.

title: Plan-and-Avoid: Real-Time Aircraft Trajectory Coordination in a Multi-Agent Environment
summary: This paper presents a real-time Plan-and-Avoid (PAA framework for coordinating cooperative multi-agent airspace operations around a declared priority trajectory. The priority trajectory represents an aircraft flight plan that must be preserved because of constrained maneuverability, an emergency, a mission-critical task, or assigned operational priority. The framework predicts uncertainty-aware, well-clear separation violations with surrounding traffic and, when the priority plan alone cannot maintain separation, generates vehicle-constrained unilateral advisories that modify nearby aircraft trajectories to maintain well-clear separation for all traffic. The approach is applicable to any declared priority trajectory. This paper demonstrates the Plan component using a contingency landing planner to generate candidate priority trajectories. PAA then identifies nearby aircraft passing too close to this priority trajectory and issues Avoid resolution advisories to these aircraft. The framework is tested using real-world Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) traffic from the Washington, D.C., airspace across more than 900 forced-landing cases, totaling over 140 hours of simulated flight. The PAA framework generates feasible cooperative advisories for all 575 unique conflict encounters, with a worst-case end-to-end response time of 5.7 s on a personal computer, including priority trajectory planning, advisory generation, and 1 s two-way datalink delay. In total, 93.5% of generated advisories satisfy the 35 s RTCA DO-365 Detect-and-Avoid temporal threshold. These results demonstrate low-latency coordination for preserving priority trajectories while maintaining well-clear separation through real-time automated advisory generation. Future work will quantify advisory-induced delays and their operational impacts.

AI.tldr: Real-time Plan-and-Avoid (PAA) framework coordinates cooperative multi-agent airspace operations around a priority trajectory to preserve the trajectory while maintaining well-clear separation; it predicts potential violations and issues unilateral Avoid advisories when needed; demonstrates low-latency performance using ADS-B data with 900 forced-landing cases.
AI.motivation: Need to preserve critical priority trajectories under constraints while ensuring safety in dynamic, mixed air traffic; achieve real-time, automated advisory generation.
AI.method: Plan component uses contingency landing planner to generate candidate priority trajectories; identifies nearby conflicts with the trajectory and issues Avoid resolution advisories; 1 s datalink; tested with ADS-B data in DC airspace; end-to-end latency up to 5.7 s; RTCA DO-365 threshold 35 s.
AI.result: Feasible cooperative advisories for 575 unique conflicts; 93.5% meet 35 s threshold; tested across 900 forced-landing cases, >140 hours; demonstrates low-latency coordination.
AI.conclusion: PAA enables real-time preservation of priority trajectories while maintaining well-clear separation; future work includes quantifying advisory-induced delays and operational impacts.

title: Deep Evidential Regression for Sparse Forest Height Estimation from Multimodal Satellite Imagery
summary: Accurate estimation of forest height from satellite imagery is essential for applications such as carbon accounting, biodiversity monitoring, and ecosystem management. While recent deep learning approaches provide accurate predictions, they typically do not quantify predictive uncertainty. This limitation is particularly relevant in geospatial settings characterized by sparse supervision and geographic distribution shift. In this work, we investigate Deep Evidential Regression (DER) for forest height estimation on the TreeUQ benchmark, a large-scale dataset designed for the joint estimation of tree count and average tree height at 10 m resolution, based on Sentinel-1/-2 data as well as tree inventory data over the federal state of Bavaria. To account for the extreme label sparsity of the tree inventory data, we introduce a masked evidential loss for dense geospatial prediction. Using a U-Net architecture with multimodal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 inputs, the proposed approach jointly predicts tree height and associated uncertainty estimates in a single forward pass. Experimental results show that DER achieves predictive performance comparable to a deterministic U-Net while additionally providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. These findings demonstrate the potential of evidential learning as an efficient framework for uncertainty-aware forest structure estimation from Earth observation data.

AI.tldr: Deep Evidential Regression (DER) yields uncertainty-aware forest height estimates on TreeUQ with performance comparable to a deterministic U-Net, while providing well-calibrated predictive uncertainties via a masked evidential loss to handle extreme label sparsity.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification is critical for EO-based forest height estimation, especially under sparse supervision and geographic distribution shift. Conventional DL approaches offer point estimates but not calibrated uncertainty, risking unreliable decisions in carbon accounting and ecosystem management.
AI.method: Propose a Deep Evidential Regression framework trained with a masked evidential loss to address label sparsity. Use a U-Net with multimodal inputs from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 to jointly predict tree height and associated uncertainty in a single forward pass, on the TreeUQ benchmark (forest height and tree count at 10 m resolution over Bavaria).
AI.result: DER achieves predictive performance on par with a deterministic U-Net while yielding well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. The approach demonstrates the efficiency and effectiveness of evidential learning for uncertainty-aware forest structure estimation from EO data.
AI.conclusion: Evidential learning is a viable framework for uncertainty-aware forest height estimation in Earth observation data, capable of handling sparse supervision and distribution shifts without sacrificing accuracy.

title: EntropyMoE: Entropy-Aware Sparse Expert Routing for Tokenizer-Free LLMs
summary: Recent byte-level large language models (LLMs) have made tokenizer-free modeling increasingly competitive by grouping bytes into dynamically sized patches. However, existing byte-patch architectures still apply the same dense feed-forward computation to every patch. This uniform computation cannot adapt model capacity to variations in patch semantics and granularity. We address this limitation with EntropyMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture designed for dynamic byte patches. EntropyMoE replaces the dense feed-forward modules in the global patch Transformer with Top-K expert layers. Each dynamic patch serves as the basic unit of expert routing, and its byte coverage determines its contribution to workload accounting. The router selects experts directly from patch entropy, using the same granularity signal that underlies dynamic patch construction to organize sparse computation. Patch entropy and length jointly define the feature space for regulating expert specialization. Experiments show that EntropyMoE achieves the lowest held-out bits-per-byte among matched dense and sparse baselines while maintaining comparable downstream accuracy. These results establish patch entropy as an effective routing coordinate for sparse conditional computation and extend Mixture-of-Experts modeling beyond tokenizer-based representations.

AI.tldr: EntropyMoE applies Top-K expert routing to dynamic byte patches in a tokenizer-free model, using patch entropy as the routing coordinate to achieve sparse computation with lower bits-per-byte while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tokenizer-free byte-level models with dynamically sized patches suffer from uniform dense computation; patch semantics and granularity vary, making fixed capacity inefficient. A conditional, sparse mechanism that adapts to patch entropy and length can improve efficiency and enable Mixture-of-Experts in tokenizer-free settings.
AI.method: Replace dense feed-forward networks in the global patch Transformer with Top-K experts (EntropyMoE). Use each dynamic patch as the routing unit; workload is determined by the patch's byte coverage. The router selects experts based on patch entropy, leveraging the same granularity signal used to construct patches. Patch entropy and length define the feature space guiding expert specialization and routing. This supports dynamic, sparse conditional computation in tokenizer-free representations.
AI.result: Empirically, EntropyMoE achieves the lowest held-out bits-per-byte among matched dense and sparse baselines and maintains comparable downstream accuracy. Patch entropy serves as an effective routing coordinate for sparse computation and extends Mixture-of-Experts modeling beyond tokenizer-based representations.
AI.conclusion: Patch entropy is a viable and effective routing signal for sparse conditional computation in tokenizer-free byte models, enabling dynamic, capacity-aware mixture-of-experts with competitive efficiency and accuracy.

title: Risk-Aware Decision Policies for Agents Under Noisy Perception
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to the 2026 Conference on Artificial Life (ALIFE2026)
summary: Perception in biological systems is inherently noisy, requiring organisms to make decisions under uncertainty where misclassification can be costly or fatal. We present an Artificial Life predator-prey model of foraging under noisy perception, and compare agent performance when using various policies that take into account their noisy predictions. Through controlled experiments under both symmetric and asymmetric perceptual noise, we show that blindly trusting perceptual labels leads to catastrophic failure as noise increases, while uncertainty-aware strategies significantly improve survival and reduce fatal errors. We further observe qualitative regime shifts in behaviour, with agents transitioning from exploratory to conservative strategies as uncertainty increases. Our model links risk-sensitive foraging, ecological information use, and Artificial Life by showing that explicit information gathering can improve robustness when perception is unreliable. These results highlight the importance of uncertainty-aware decision-making and provide an interpretable artificial life analogue to robust learning with noisy labels.

AI.tldr: Uncertainty-aware decision-making in an artificial life predator-prey model improves robustness under perceptual noise, preventing catastrophic failures that occur when blindly trusting noisy predictions; agents transition from exploration to conservatism as uncertainty rises and explicit information gathering boosts survival.
AI.motivation: Understand how perceptual uncertainty affects foraging strategies and survival, linking risk-sensitive foraging, ecological information use, and robust learning with noisy labels.
AI.method: Develop an Artificial Life predator-prey simulation with symmetric and asymmetric perceptual noise. Compare policies that blindly trust noisy perceptual labels against uncertainty-aware strategies that explicitly account for prediction uncertainty. Evaluate survival, fatal errors, and behavioral regime shifts.
AI.result: Uncertainty-aware strategies significantly outperform naïve labeling under noise, increasing survival and reducing fatal errors. Higher noise amplifies benefits, with agents exhibiting regime shifts from exploratory to conservative behavior and benefiting from explicit information gathering.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly handling perception uncertainty yields robust performance in noisy environments and provides an interpretable artificial-life analogue to robust learning with noisy labels, highlighting the role of uncertainty-aware information use in risk-sensitive foraging.

title: Exact Computation of Trait-induced Merge Trees for Bivariate Fields
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, To appear in an IEEE VGTC workshop "TopoInVis Connect 2026 - Topology meets Artificial Intelligence"
summary: Trait-induced merge trees (TIMTs) provide a robust topology-based method for selecting and browsing feature level sets in multivariate data by analyzing the distance field induced by a user-specified trait in attribute space. Existing TIMT computations typically sample this distance field at mesh vertices and assume piecewise-linear interpolation, although the Euclidean distance-to-trait function is generally not piecewise linear on the original mesh. As a result, the resulting merge tree may miss zero-valued features and may perturb the locations and values of minima and merge events. We study the exact computation of TIMTs for piecewise-linear bivariate fields, focusing first on point traits. We show that the restricted sublevel sets inside each tetrahedron are convex and therefore have trivial local merge-tree structure, implying that global topological changes arise only through gluing across simplex boundaries. Based on this observation, we construct a weighted graph whose merge tree is isomorphic to the exact merge tree of the induced distance field. We further relate TIMTs to Jacobi sets, showing how nonzero edge events of the TIMT are localized by the singular structure of the underlying bivariate map. We establish a theoretical upper bound on the error of the vertex-sampled linear interpolation, expressed in terms of the maximum length of projected mesh edges in the range. We discuss extensions to line, line-segment, and finite point-set traits, and implement the method robustly using CGAL and VTK, demonstrating results on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: Exact TIMT computation for piecewise-linear bivariate fields via a graph isomorphism, with convex per-tetrahedron sublevel sets, error bounds for vertex sampling, and extensions to various traits; implemented with CGAL/VTK and validated on synthetic/real data.
AI.motivation: Current TIMT computations rely on sampling the distance field at mesh vertices with piecewise-linear interpolation, which can miss zero-valued features and perturb minima/merge events. An exact, topology-preserving method for TIMTs on piecewise-linear bivariate fields is needed.
AI.method: Prove that restricted sublevel sets inside each tetrahedron are convex for point traits, implying trivial local merge-tree structure; construct a weighted graph whose merge tree is isomorphic to the exact TIMT; relate TIMTs to Jacobi sets to localize nonzero edge events; derive an error bound for vertex-sampled linear interpolation based on maximum projected edge length; discuss extensions to line/segment/point-set traits; implement robustly using CGAL and VTK.
AI.result: Established a graph-based method that yields an exact TIMT for piecewise-linear bivariate fields by exploiting convex sublevel sets within tetrahedra and gluing across boundaries; demonstrated isomorphism between the graph merge tree and the exact TIMT; linked TIMT features to Jacobi set structure for localization of nonzero edge events; provided a theoretical upper bound on interpolation error; implemented the approach with CGAL/VTK and validated on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an exact, scalable approach to TIMTs for PL bivariate fields, overcoming inaccuracies of vertex sampling, and offers insights via Jacobi-set connections; it supports extensions to diverse trait geometries and has practical applicability with robust software implementation.

title: SoRoMoX: Fast, Differentiable, and Parallelizable Soft Robot Models
summary: Reduced-order models based on Cosserat-rod theory are now well established, and modeling theory is no longer the primary bottleneck in soft-robot control. Their implementations, however, do not support the differentiable, GPU-parallel, and control-oriented workflows that underpin advanced rigid-robotics applications. Here, we fill this gap with SoRoMoX (Soft Robot Models in JAX), a fully numerical, JIT-compilable Python/JAX framework. SoRoMoX implements articulated, Piecewise Constant Strain, and Variable Strain models through a unified, control-ready interface that provides inertia matrices, gravitational and elastic forces, Jacobians, and their derivatives. To our knowledge, it is the first rod/strain-based soft-robot modeling framework that runs directly on GPUs and is end-to-end differentiable with respect to states, inputs, and parameters. Sequential CPU rollouts are up to 18.1x faster than state-of-the-art alternatives, while GPU-parallel rollouts increase throughput by up to 234.6x. This performance enables workflows that were previously impractical or impossible: static-equilibrium system identification with 66% lower marker RMSE; residual-force learning with a further 64% reduction; computed-torque tracking with RMSE reduced by a factor of approximately 500 relative to model-free PD; control-gain optimization with up to 62% lower loss than untuned gains; safety-constrained control using high-order control barrier functions to keep the peak contact force within a prescribed 5 N bound, compared with 33.5 N without the safety constraint; and reinforcement-learning policy training up to 7x faster than a CPU PyElastica discrete-rod baseline through massively parallel rollouts.

AI.tldr: A differentiable, GPU-accelerated Cosserat-rod framework (SoRoMoX) in JAX enabling end-to-end control-oriented workflows with fast CPU and GPU rollouts and improved performance across identification, learning, and control tasks.
AI.motivation: Current soft-robot modeling lags in differentiable, parallelizable, GPU-accelerated workflows needed for advanced control; existing rod models (Cosserat/PCSM) lack end-to-end differentiability and fast rollouts for optimization and learning.
AI.method: Introduce SoRoMoX implementing articulated, Piecewise Constant Strain, and Variable Strain Cosserat-rod models in a unified JAX framework; provide inertia, gravity, elastic forces, Jacobians, and derivatives; end-to-end differentiable w.r.t states, inputs, parameters; CPU and GPU rollouts with JIT; ability to run on GPUs with parallelization.
AI.result: CPU rollouts up to 18.1x faster than state-of-the-art; GPU-parallel rollouts up to 234.6x; improved static-equilibrium identification (66% lower marker RMSE); residual-force learning (64% reduction); computed-torque tracking RMSE improvement ~500x; control-gain optimization with 62% lower loss; safety-constrained control with high-order control barrier functions keeping contact force within 5 N bound (vs 33.5 N without); RL policy training up to 7x faster than CPU PyElastica baseline.
AI.conclusion: SoRoMoX delivers a fully differentiable, GPU-enabled, control-ready soft-robot modeling framework, enabling efficient optimization, learning, and real-time control workflows for Cosserat-rod based soft robots.

title: TransSLR: A Lightweight Transformer for Sign Language Recognition
comment: This paper has been accepted for oral presentation at Deep Learning Indaba 2026 which will be hosted on the IJCAI hosting platform. paper link: https://chairingtool.com/conferences/dli2026/main-track/submissions/356
summary:
Automated Sign Language Recognition for under-represented languages remains a largely unsolved problem. Central African Sign Language (CASL) exemplifies this gap: the only available bench-mark, CASL-W60, has a best reported accuracy of 69.93%, and we show that the common heuristic of fine-tuning high-resource models fails to close it. This failure stems from two compounding factors: the limited scale of available CASL data and the significant lexical and visual domain gap between CASL and large-scale corpora such as WLASL, which renders pre-trained representations largely uninformative.
  To address this, we propose TransSLR, a lightweight Temporal Transformer Encoder trained from scratch on 64-frame normalized pose sequences, with average pooling and a classification head. By operating on geometric keypoint representations rather than raw RGB, TransSLR achieves signer-independent generalization without relying on visual appearance. On the CASL-W60 benchmark, TransSLR establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 80.39%, surpassing the prior best by +10.46%. Beyond accuracy, our encoder-only design significantly reduces computational overhead, making deployment feasible in resource-constrained environments. We conduct extensive experiments on the CASL-W60 benchmark, comparing against RGB-based and multimodal baselines, and demonstrate that TransSLR achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: TransSLR is a lightweight, encoder-only Temporal Transformer trained from scratch on 64-frame pose sequences for CASL-W60, achieving 80.39% accuracy and improving the previous best by 10.46 points, by focusing on geometric keypoints instead of RGB to enable signer-independent generalization and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Under-represented sign languages like Central African Sign Language (CASL) suffer from scarce data and a large domain gap to high-resource datasets. Fine-tuning high-resource models often fails due to limited data and lexical/visual mismatch, necessitating a geometry-based, efficient approach.
AI.method: Develop TransSLR, an encoder-only Temporal Transformer trained from scratch on 64-frame normalized pose sequences (geometric keypoints). Uses average pooling and a classification head, operating on pose geometry rather than RGB, to achieve signer-independent generalization with reduced computational overhead.
AI.result: On CASL-W60, TransSLR achieves 80.39% accuracy, the new state-of-the-art, surpassing the previous best by +10.46%. Outperforms RGB-based and multimodal baselines and demonstrates strong generalization with lower compute.
AI.conclusion: Pose-based, encoder-only architectures can attain state-of-the-art performance for CASL-W60 with improved generalization and efficiency, highlighting the viability of geometry-based representations for under-represented sign languages and resource-constrained deployment.

title: Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast
summary: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of interpretation methods for MoE reward models.

AI.tldr: CoCo introduces response-level interpretability for sparse MoE reward models by using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts to jointly reveal routing and preference, yielding more faithful and specialized interpretations while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy; claims novelty as the first systematic MoE reward interpretation study.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE reward models use routing weights to explain which prompts reach which experts, but do not reveal how experts judge responses; there is a need for a faithful, joint interpretation of routing and judgment to improve interpretability and trust in MoE reward models.
AI.method: Identify response pairs with the largest contribution contrast between chosen and rejected responses; compute and analyze contributions to reward predictions to characterize expert roles; compare CoCo to router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based baselines; validate with automatic metrics and human evaluations.
AI.result: CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than baselines, while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy; represents the first systematic study of interpretation methods for MoE reward models.
AI.conclusion: CoCo advances the interpretability of MoE reward models by faithfully capturing how routing and preference combine to form predictions, offering a practical and more trustworthy approach with potential applicability to other MoE settings.

title: Sharding Prevents LLM Oversight Failures and Adversarial Exploitation
summary: Giving an LLM judge more compute does not necessarily make it check more requirements. When one call must return many verdicts, some decisions become weakly grounded in the evidence, even when that call receives the same token or tool budget as a panel of separate calls. Across expert-graded research replications, legal work, and clinical-trial assessments, agreement with experts falls as the number of verdicts per call grows. We identify sharding as the intervention that mitigates this failure in model-based oversight. Sharding partitions the requirements into smaller groups, assigns each group to a separate call, and aggregates the verdicts. Against a single call with the panel's full budget, sharding improves agreement while holding the model, evidence, total budget, and per-decision budget fixed. Overall, we find that a sharded weaker judge can outperform a more capable holistic judge and match that judge even when the latter receives the panel's full budget. Additionally, we find that sharding exhibits robustness against adversaries. A best-of-N adversary can hold the underlying work fixed, vary only its presentation, and increase an overloaded judge's acceptance of genuinely unmet criteria severalfold. Wherever sharding reduces baseline error, it removes this adversarial advantage, keeping over-acceptance low even as the adversary's search widens. Sharding does not address attacks that persuade the judge separately on each criterion rather than exploiting overload. In that setting, we find that debate-style opposition on top of sharding withstands such adaptive re-optimization.

AI.tldr: Sharding—partition verdict criteria into smaller groups and aggregate results—improves agreement with experts under fixed budgets, can outperform a single holistic judge, and offers robustness to adversarial framing, though it doesn't defend against attacks that persuade on each criterion; debate-style opposition helps in that case.
AI.motivation: LLM-based oversight struggles to stay aligned with expert judgments when each call must generate many verdicts; increasing compute per call does not guarantee better checking, so scalable, robust methods are needed.
AI.method: Partition the requirements into smaller shards, assign each shard to a separate call, and aggregate the verdicts. Compare against a single holistic call with the panel’s full budget across domains (expert-graded replications, legal work, clinical-trial assessments). Test robustness with adversarial settings, including best-of-N adversaries and debate-style opposition.
AI.result: Sharding improves agreement relative to a single call with the same total budget. A weaker sharded judge can outperform a stronger holistic judge and match it even when the holistic judge has the full panel budget. Sharding also reduces susceptibility to an adversary that varies presentation to overload the judge. Debate-style opposition on top of sharding further resists attacks that focus on per-criterion persuasion.
AI.conclusion: Sharding is a practical intervention to improve model-based oversight under fixed budgets, balancing efficiency and reliability. It mitigates some adversarial risks, but attacks targeting per-criterion persuasion remain, where debate can provide additional robustness.

title: CrossTracer: Cross-Embodiment Navigation via VLA Model Reasoning and Trace Residuals Adapting
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide strong semantic priors for robot navigation, but they often ignore embodiment-specific mobility constraints. A path that is semantically plausible for one robot may be physically infeasible for another. We propose CrossTracer, a hierarchical framework for cross-embodiment navigation through adaptive trace residuals. CrossTracer represents navigation plans as normalized image-plane waypoints, forming a unified pixel-space interface between semantic reasoning and physical grounding. First, Vision-Language Trace Proposer (VL-Tracer) adapts a pretrained VLA model to predict an initial navigation trace from egocentric observations and flexible goal specifications. Second, CE-Adapter refines this trace by predicting embodiment-conditioned residual corrections from visual traversability cues, robot identity, and the initial trace. To train the refinement module without costly manual annotation, Cross-Embodiment RRT* (CE-RRT*) converts panoptic segmentation into robot-conditioned traversability cost maps and generates cost-minimizing pixel-space traces. We evaluate CrossTracer on the NaviTrace benchmark, which tests whether a model can generate embodiment-consistent navigation traces from egocentric observations, language instructions, and robot embodiment types. CrossTracer achieves a total score of 45.68, outperforming the strongest evaluated general-purpose baseline, Gemini-2.5-Pro, by 10.01 points, corresponding to a 28.1% relative improvement. Real-world deployment on wheeled and legged robots further shows improved navigation success and execution efficiency.

AI.tldr: CrossTracer is a hierarchical framework that adapts vision-language navigation to different robot embodiments by predicting pixel-space traces and refining them with embodiment-conditioned residuals. It unifies semantic reasoning with physical grounding through a two-stage planner (VL-Tracer and CE-Adapter) trained with CE-RRT* cost maps.
AI.motivation: Vision-language navigation often neglects embodiment constraints, leading to semantically plausible but physically infeasible paths for a given robot.
AI.method: VL-Tracer predicts an initial image-plane navigation trace from egocentric observations and flexible goals. CE-Adapter adds embodiment-conditioned residuals using visual traversability cues, robot identity, and the initial trace. CE-RRT* converts panoptic segmentation into robot-conditioned traversability cost maps to train the refinement module by generating cost-minimizing pixel-space traces. The navigation traces are represented in a normalized image-plane, forming a unified interface between semantic planning and physical grounding.
AI.result: On NaviTrace, CrossTracer achieves 45.68, outperforming the strongest baseline Gemini-2.5-Pro by 10.01 points (28.1% relative). Real-world deployments on wheeled and legged robots show improved navigation success and execution efficiency.
AI.conclusion: CrossTracer enables embodiment-consistent navigation by aligning semantic traces with physical constraints via a two-stage trace prediction and residual refinement framework, validated on a standard benchmark and real robots.

title: Test-Time Adaptation with Online Personalized Energy-Based Cache for Fine-Grained Video Expression Recognition
summary: Facial expression recognition (FER) in videos is challenging because models must identify subtle, temporally evolving affective states that vary across individuals. Although vision-language models provide transferable visual-semantic representations, models trained on subject-independent data often degrade under subject-specific distribution shifts at inference time. Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods commonly update model parameters during inference, increasing computational cost and latency. Cache-based methods avoid parameter updates, but they usually require enough target samples to form reliable class prototypes, which is difficult early in adaptation and for rarely observed classes. We introduce Energy-Based Cache Personalization (EB-CaP), a subject-based online TTA method for video FER that generates class-specific prototypes personalized to each target video. EB-CaP uses a lightweight energy-based model to sample prototypes from the current unlabeled video and populate a personalized cache online, without accumulating large amounts of target data or storing diverse source prototypes. Its energy function relies only on pretrained CLIP: similarities between the target video embedding and class text embeddings guide prototype sampling. In parallel, positive and negative caches store reliable and uncertain target embeddings. An adaptive entropy gate controls cache updates according to the evolving confidence distribution, while a diversity gate limits redundant samples. Final predictions combine cache-derived scores with the current CLIP scores. Experiments on BioVid, StressID, and BAH show that EB-CaP outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods while maintaining low computational and memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/MasoumehSharafi/EB-CaP.

AI.tldr: Energy-Based Cache Personalization (EB-CaP) enables subject-specific online test-time adaptation for video facial expression recognition by sampling class prototypes from unlabeled target videos via an energy-based model using CLIP, maintaining positive/negative caches with adaptive entropy and diversity gates, and combining cache scores with CLIP predictions to improve performance with low overhead.
AI.motivation: FER in videos is challenged by subject-specific distribution shifts and limited target data, making online adaptation desirable but expensive. Existing TTA methods are heavy; cache methods struggle early in adaptation and for rare classes. A lightweight, per-video personalization that does not rely on abundant target samples is needed.
AI.method: An energy-based prototype sampler samples class-specific prototypes from the current unlabeled video using the CLIP similarity between the video embedding and class text embeddings. Positive and negative caches store reliable vs uncertain target embeddings. Adaptive entropy gate regulates cache updates by tracking confidence evolution, while a diversity gate reduces redundant samples. Final predictions combine cache-derived scores with current CLIP-based scores.
AI.result: On BioVid, StressID, and BAH datasets, EB-CaP outperforms state-of-the-art test-time adaptation methods while keeping low computational and memory overhead, demonstrating effective subject-specific online personalization for video FER.
AI.conclusion: EB-CaP provides a practical, efficient approach for subject-based online TTA in video FER by personalizing prototypes on-the-fly using an energy-based sampler guided by CLIP, with constrained caches that adapt to the target video and complement CLIP predictions.

title: Interpretable Unsupervised Community Detection with LLM-Symbolized Structured Processes
summary: Community detection is a fundamental task in graph analytics that aims to identify cohesive groups of entities with similar behaviors or interests. Classic objective-driven methods struggle with complex graph structures, while deep-learning approaches improve performance at the expense of interpretability and rely on labeled data and training. Large language models (LLMs), with strong reasoning capabilities and world knowledge, are promising for interpretable, label-free community detection. To leverage these strengths, we propose LUCID, an LLM-guided, interpretable, training-free, and unsupervised community detection method. Inspired by phase-transition kinetics in natural systems, where complex structures emerge through initialization, merging, refinement, and selection, LUCID is designed as a four-stage pipeline. Within this pipeline, the LLM induces formal rules that translate implicit knowledge into explicit and interpretable logical structures. Specifically, (1) the Local-View Community Initialization stage encodes local graph structures using k-ego contexts and unsupervised node roles; (2) the Multi-factor Community Merge stage uses LLM-induced rules to iteratively merge local communities; (3) the Multi-grain Community Refinement stage applies LLM-induced coarse-to-fine rules in parallel to reduce boundary noise; and (4) the Global-view Community Selection stage identifies high-quality communities based on topological compactness and boundary clarity. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that LUCID, as an unsupervised approach, achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms leading unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines.

AI.tldr: LUCID is a training-free, unsupervised community detection method that uses an LLM-guided four-stage pipeline to produce interpretable, rule-based community structures without labels, achieving state-of-the-art performance against unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome the lack of interpretability in deep-learning-based community detection and the label-dependence of supervised methods, by leveraging LLMs to induce explicit, verifiable rules that govern community formation.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline guided by LLMs: (1) Local-View Initialization using k-ego contexts and unsupervised node roles to encode local graph structure; (2) Multi-factor Merge applying LLM-induced rules to iteratively merge local communities; (3) Multi-grain Refinement applying coarse-to-fine LLM rules in parallel to reduce boundary noise; (4) Global-view Selection identifying high-quality communities by topological compactness and boundary clarity. The LLM translates implicit knowledge into explicit logical structures, enabling interpretability without training data or labels.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world datasets shows LUCID achieves state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised methods and outperforms leading unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines.
AI.conclusion: LUCID demonstrates that LLM-driven, training-free, unsupervised community detection can achieve strong performance while yielding interpretable, rule-based partitions, validating the utility of LLMs for interpretable graph analytics without labeled data.

title: Adversarial Causal Intervention Falsification
summary: Generative models can reproduce an observational distribution while encoding an incorrect causal structure. We study a sequential game in which a structural causal generator proposes observational and interventional distributions, while an adversarial experimentalist selects interventions intended to maximally falsify the generator. The discriminator is therefore not merely a real-versus-synthetic classifier: it is indexed by an intervention and tests whether the generator reproduces the corresponding post-intervention law. We introduce Adversarial Causal Intervention Falsification (ACIF), formulate oracle and implementable versions of the game, and distinguish three objects that are often conflated: observational fit, interventional equivalence over an admissible query class, and point identification of a structural causal model. For finite model and intervention classes, we prove: (i) an exact reduction of the adversarial objective to a worst-intervention integral probability metric; (ii) identification up to interventional equivalence, with point identification under a separating intervention family; (iii) existence of mixed-strategy equilibria; (iv) finite-sample uniform convergence and margin-based model-selection guarantees; and (v) a logarithmic elimination guarantee for a disagreement-driven sequential design under a balanced-separation condition. We also give a complete linear-Gaussian example in which two observationally indistinguishable causal directions are separated by a single well-chosen intervention. The framework clarifies what an adversarial causal discriminator can and cannot certify, and provides a principled bridge between causal generative modeling, active causal discovery, and experimental design.

AI.tldr: ACIF frames causal model falsification as an adversarial game where a generator proposes observational and interventional distributions and a discriminator tests if post-interventional laws match, yielding identification under certain intervention families and establishing equilibria, finite-sample guarantees, and an actionable linear-Gaussian example.
AI.motivation: To separate observational fit from interventional identifiability, quantify what an adversarial discriminator can certify about a causal model, and connect causal modeling with active discovery and experimental design.
AI.method: Define ACIF with a structural causal generator and an intervention-indexed discriminator. Formalize oracle and implementable versions, reduce the objective to a worst-intervention IPM, prove identifiability up to interventional equivalence, existence of mixed equilibria, finite-sample uniform convergence with margin-based model selection, and a disagreement-driven sequential design with a logarithmic elimination bound. Provide a complete linear-Gaussian example where two causal directions are separated by a single intervention.
AI.result: Establishes theoretical foundations for adversarial causal falsification: reduction to a worst-intervention IPM, identifiability under separating interventions, equilibria existence, finite-sample guarantees, and a constructive linear-Gaussian case illustrating practical separability of directions with minimal intervention.
AI.conclusion: The framework clarifies the capabilities and limits of adversarial causal discriminators and offers a principled bridge among causal generative modeling, active causal discovery, and experimental design, with concrete results on identifiability, equilibria, and sample-efficiency.

title: Hoverflie: An empirical investigation of rotor shrouds to transform micro air vehicles into multi-modal hovercraft
summary: Small rotorcraft intended for use indoors or around the built environment have extremely limited flight duration. This paper presents the design and experimental characterization of a custom shroud system that transforms a Crazyflie 2.1 micro air vehicle into a multi-modal robot capable of operating as a high-efficiency hovercraft or a free-flying drone. A custom experimental platform was developed for precise control of hover height and rotor duty cycle, and automated data logging of lift forces. Parametric testing of duct, intake, and nozzle geometries was performed to investigate the impact of shroud configuration on in-ground-effect and free-flight performance. An empirical model is developed which, unlike typical models for ground effect in rotorcraft, captures the suckdown effect that reduces force at intermediate height. It is shown that, through proper design of the shroud, beneficial ground effects can be increased while diminishing negative effects both close to the ground and in free flight. An optimized configuration exhibited nearly three times higher in-ground-effect force while maintaining comparable out-of-ground-effect aerodynamic thrust, although the added shroud mass reduces free-flight control authority. Lightweight shrouds are manufactured using thin-film thermoformed components, and total single-charge flight time is shown to increase by 60% in-ground-effect while decreasing by only 30% in free-flight as compared to the stock drone. Finally, controlled flight in the air, hovering close to the ground, and hover-to-flight transitions are demonstrated using a simple mode-switching controller, with tracking errors reported to quantify performance. This work provides an experimentally-validated and easily adoptable foundation for future research into lightweight ground-effect vehicles and hybrid drone-hovercraft systems.

AI.tldr: A lightweight shroud for Crazyflie 2.1 enables a hybrid hovercraft/drone by leveraging ground effects, with experimentally characterized performance improvements and trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Indoor micro aerial vehicles suffer from short flight durations; exploiting ground effects through a shroud can increase lift and endurance while enabling hovercraft-like operation.
AI.method: Developed a custom experimental platform to control hover height and rotor duty cycle; automated lift-force logging; parametric testing of duct, intake, and nozzle geometries; created an empirical model capturing suckdown; manufactured lightweight thermoformed shrouds; demonstrated mode-switching control for hover-to-flight.
AI.result: Optimized shroud configuration achieved ~3x higher in-ground-effect lift with similar thrust in free flight; added mass reduces free-flight control authority; total single-charge flight time increases ~60% in-ground-effect and decreases ~30% in free-flight; hover near ground and hover-to-flight transitions demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Provides an experimentally-validated, easily adoptable foundation for lightweight ground-effect vehicles and hybrid drone-hovercraft systems, balancing ground-effect gains against free-flight penalties.

title: InsertFuse: A Unified Framework for Multi-Category Reference-Guided Image Insertion
summary: We present InsertFuse, a unified framework for multi-category reference-guided image insertion. Its key idea is to decouple category-specific expertise learning from cross-category capability consolidation. InsertFuse first trains specialized experts for different insertion categories and then introduces Insertion On-Policy Distillation (IOPD) to consolidate their capabilities into a single student. By querying the matched expert at states visited by the student, IOPD preserves category-specific insertion behavior while mitigating the cross-category interference caused by direct joint training. To improve spatial control, we propose Token-Aligned Geometry Conditioning (TAGC), which maps mask-derived geometric cues to the visual token grid, and Region-Balanced Flow Matching, which separately normalizes prediction errors inside and outside the insertion region to prevent background-dominated and scale-dependent supervision. We further introduce Reference CFG to isolate and strengthen the guidance induced by the visual reference under fixed scene and geometry conditions, with IOPD transferring this enhanced supervision into the unified student. Extensive experiments on the public AnyInsertion benchmark and our multi-category test set demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on most metrics, showing strong reference fidelity and generation quality across diverse insertion categories.

AI.tldr: A unified multi-category reference-guided image insertion framework (InsertFuse) that decouples category-specific expertise from cross-category learning, using on-policy distillation (IOPD), geometry-aware token conditioning (TAGC), region-balanced flow matching, and Reference CFG to deliver state-of-the-art results across diverse insertion categories.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, high-fidelity multi-category image insertion by preserving category-specific behavior while preventing interference when learning multiple tasks jointly.
AI.method: 1) Train specialized experts per insertion category. 2) Apply Insertion On-Policy Distillation (IOPD) to distill capabilities into a single student by querying the matched expert at student states. 3) Introduce Token-Aligned Geometry Conditioning (TAGC) to map mask-derived geometry to token grids. 4) Use Region-Balanced Flow Matching to normalize errors inside/outside insertion regions. 5) Introduce Reference CFG to strengthen guidance from the visual reference under fixed scene/geometry, with IOPD transferring supervision to the student.
AI.result: Empirical results on the AnyInsertion benchmark and a multi-category test set show state-of-the-art performance on most metrics, with strong reference fidelity and generation quality across diverse categories.
AI.conclusion: InsertFuse effectively decouples category expertise and cross-category learning to deliver a unified, high-fidelity multi-category insertion model, validating its design with comprehensive experiments.

title: ADIAS: Automated Design of Interactive Agentic Systems
summary: Automated agent design improves agent harnesses through iterative revision, evaluation, and feedback summarization. Existing methods are largely candidate-centric: cross-round experience is organized around candidate agents, which leaves the repair progress implicit. This causes inefficient repair targeting, slow consolidation of partial progress, and propagation of ineffective interventions across rounds. Therefore, we formulate issue-centric agent optimization, in which repair progress is carried forward as an explicit persistent issue state to guide optimization, rather than re-derived from candidate history in each round. We instantiate the formulation in ADIAS, a framework for automated full-code agent design with two mechanisms. A persistent issue state maintains stable issue identities, lifecycle status, supporting evidence, and intervention-outcome histories. Issue-guided optimization uses this state to jointly propose repair targets and revision directions for subsequent focused full-code modification. Across five interactive benchmarks, ADIAS outperforms the strongest baseline by 25.2% on average and achieves consistent gains across four backbone models. Controlled ablations further show that removing persistent issue state or replacing issue-centric revision with candidate-centric policies leads to performance drops of up to 40.7%.

AI.tldr: ADIAS introduces an issue-centric optimization paradigm with a persistent issue state for automated full-code agent design, leading to significant performance gains over candidate-centric baselines and robust across backbone models.
AI.motivation: Current automated agent design methods are largely candidate-centric, with repair progress implicit in candidate history, causing inefficient repair targeting and slow consolidation. There is a need to carry repair progress forward as explicit, persistent issue state to guide optimization.
AI.method: ADIAS comprises two mechanisms: (1) a persistent issue state that tracks stable issue identities, lifecycle status, evidence, and intervention histories; (2) issue-guided optimization that uses this state to jointly propose repair targets and revision directions for subsequent full-code modifications across rounds.
AI.result: In five interactive benchmarks, ADIAS outperforms the strongest baseline by 25.2% on average and shows consistent gains across four backbone models. Ablation studies show that removing the persistent issue state or replacing issue-centric revision with candidate-centric policies can cause performance drops up to 40.7%.
AI.conclusion: Issue-centric optimization with a persistent issue state substantially improves automated full-code agent design, reducing inefficiencies in repair and enhancing cross-round progress, with results robust across models and ablations.

title: Fixed and Adaptive Topological DeepONets: Functional Measurements on Hausdorff Locally Convex Spaces
summary: Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets; arXiv:1910.03193) typically encode an input function through point values on a fixed discretization. Building on the Topological DeepONet framework of Ismailov (arXiv:2603.11972), we replace point samples by continuous linear functionals drawn from the continuous dual of a Hausdorff locally convex space $({V},\{p_α\}_{α\in A})$, whose topology is generated by a point-separating family of seminorms rather than a single norm, and develop fixed and adaptive functional measurement systems. Measurements are combined with the coefficient-space Two-Step procedure of Lee and Shin (arXiv:2309.01020), while a training-only decoder and regularization stabilize the adaptive coordinates. We derive a discrete error decomposition separating measurement, output-basis, and neural-approximation errors, together with a Barron-rate refinement. The framework is evaluated on the antiderivative operator, a non-normable locally convex input space, heterogeneous Darcy flow, a controlled operator, and fixed-time and time-evolving Navier-Stokes vorticity operators. In the heterogeneous Darcy problem, the functional models retain nearly resolution-independent errors of 5.5-5.6% on unseen grids, while in the controlled problem adaptive measurements reduce the mean error below 1.2%. For the fixed-time Navier-Stokes problem, the Adaptive Topological DeepONet is the most accurate DeepONet-based model, attaining a mean relative $L^2$ error of 1.685% +/- 0.017% using 128 functional coordinates. A comparably sized Fourier neural operator (FNO; arXiv:2010.08895) achieves the lower error 0.832% +/- 0.172%, but requires the full 64x64 input field, twice the training time, and 10.7x greater peak GPU memory. The formulation provides compact, interpretable, and discretization-portable coordinates in the continuous dual $V'$, including for non-normable input spaces.

AI.tldr: Extends DeepONets by using continuous linear functionals from a Hausdorff locally convex dual space to encode inputs, introducing adaptive functional measurements and a training-only decoder; provides a discrete error decomposition with Barron-rate refinements; demonstrates competitive performance on several operators with discretization-portable, interpretable coordinates in the dual space, including non-normable spaces.
AI.motivation: Overcome fixed discretization limits of pointwise DeepONets by exploiting topology-driven input representations via the continuous dual, enabling adaptable measurements and interpretability, and establishing an error analysis framework.
AI.method: Builds on the Topological DeepONet framework by replacing point samples with continuous linear functionals from the continuous dual V' of a locally convex space (topology generated by a family of seminorms). Combines measurements with the coefficient-space Two-Step procedure, adds a training-only decoder and regularization, derives a discrete error decomposition and Barron-rate refinement, and evaluates on multiple operators using fixed-time/time-evolving problems.
AI.result: Heterogeneous Darcy: functional models achieve 5.5–5.6% error on unseen grids. Controlled problem: mean error below 1.2%.
