Fixed-time Navier–Stokes: Adaptive Topological DeepONet attains mean relative L2 error 1.685% ± 0.017% with 128 coordinates; a Fourier Neural Operator of similar size achieves 0.832% ± 0.172% but requires the full 64×64 input, longer training, and 10.7× more peak memory. Non-normable input spaces are supported; coordinates in the continuous dual V' are compact, interpretable, and discretization-portable.
AI.conclusion: The framework yields compact, interpretable coordinates in the continuous dual, supports non-normable input spaces, and offers competitive accuracy with advantageous discretization-portability and measurement adaptivity, albeit with trade-offs in absolute error versus large, dense-input baselines like FNO.

title: AtlasVLA: Persistent World-Ego State Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced embodied AI, their fundamentally reactive paradigm severely limits performance in partially observable and long-horizon tasks. When restricted to a single wrist-mounted camera, they inevitably suffer from perception forgetting as objects exit the field of view, and temporal task-progress forgetting} during multi-step execution. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose AtlasVLA, a novel framework that transitions from direct reactive manipulation to proactive reasoning through a persistent world-ego state. AtlasVLA features a dual-memory architecture: a 4D Persistent World State Memory that lifts transient 2D observations into a globally updated, voxel-hashed spatial state to resolve visual blind spots, and an Ego-Working State Memory that tracks historical ego state and task progress. By conditioning a diffusion transformer (DiT) on this joint World-Ego state, AtlasVLA enables robust spatial reasoning. Extensive evaluations across LIBERO, RLBench, and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that AtlasVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance using solely a wrist camera. Remarkably, it decisively outperforms multi-view baselines, yielding absolute success rate improvements of 9.4% on LIBERO-Long and 17.5% in real-world long-horizon tasks.

AI.tldr: AtlasVLA transitions from reactive to proactive manipulation by maintaining a persistent world-ego state, using a 4D world memory and an ego memory to condition a diffusion transformer, yielding state-of-the-art performance with wrist cameras and outperforming multi-view baselines on long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Reactive VLA agents suffer perception forgetting (objects leaving FOV) and temporal task-progress forgetting in partially observable, long-horizon tasks when restricted to a single wrist camera. A persistent world-ego representation can support robust spatial reasoning and long-horizon planning.
AI.method: Introduce a dual-memory architecture: (1) a 4D Persistent World State Memory that lifts 2D observations into a globally updated voxel-hashed spatial state, reducing visual blind spots; (2) an Ego-Working State Memory that tracks historical ego state and task progress. A diffusion transformer is conditioned on the joint World-Ego state to perform robust spatial reasoning for manipulation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across LIBERO, RLBench, and real-world benchmarks shows AtlasVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance using only a wrist camera and outperforms multi-view baselines. Notably, it achieves absolute success rate gains of 9.4% on LIBERO-Long and 17.5% on real-world long-horizon tasks.
AI.conclusion: Proactive world-ego reasoning with a persistent world state enables robust spatial reasoning and long-horizon manipulation under partial observability, surpassing reactive VLA baselines and multi-view approaches on varied benchmarks.

title: Improving Low-Resolution Face Recognition under Limited Data: How Synthetic Data Generation Can Close the Domain Gap
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB) 2026, Focus Session on Generative AI for Fair and Secure Biometrics under Limited Data
summary: Face Recognition (FR) systems in surveillance settings often encounter Low Resolution (LR) faces, those whose face region falls below the standard 112 $\times$ 112 input size. While labelled High Resolution (HR) training data is abundant, labelled native-LR data, and above all paired native LR/HR data, is scarce. One workaround is to synthesize LR data from the available HR faces, but how much synthesis effort is repaid in recognition accuracy remains unclear. We present a study of simple synthetic generation strategies for a compact, edge device-oriented face recognition system, spanning interpolation-based degradation, knowledge distillation, a Prepended Domain Transformer (PDT), Real ESRGAN-style degradation, and a learned Super Resolution (SR) front-end with an identity-aware loss. We evaluate these strategies on synthetic cross-resolution face benchmarks (LFW, CFP-FP, AgeDB-30) and on TinyFace, a real-world native LR dataset, and expose a synthetic-real gap: the degradation setting that is optimal on synthetic benchmarks is not the one that is optimal on real LR. We find that more synthesis effort does not help monotonically: the learned SR front-end does not surpass a direct feed of the aligned LR image into a strong backbone, while simple interpolation augmentation of a compact backbone is the only synthesis that improves over its own baseline. We conclude that generative methods for LR face recognition must be validated on real LR and against a direct-feed baseline, and release our pipeline at https://idiap.ch/paper/synth-lrfr

AI.tldr: Synthetic LR generation strategies for face recognition on edge devices were evaluated; findings reveal a real-LR degradation gap between synthetic benchmarks and real LR, with simple interpolation augmentation on a compact backbone improving performance, while complex generative methods do not consistently outperform direct LR input.
AI.motivation: LR face recognition suffers from scarce native LR and paired LR/HR data. The study seeks to understand whether synthesizing LR data from HR can meaningfully boost recognition on compact, edge-device pipelines, and which synthesis strategies transfer from synthetic benchmarks to real LR.
AI.method: Evaluate five strategies for LR degradation/synthesis: (1) interpolation-based degradation, (2) knowledge distillation, (3) Prepended Domain Transformer (PDT), (4) Real ESRGAN-style degradation, (5) learned super-resolution (SR) front-end with an identity-aware loss. Assess on synthetic cross-resolution benchmarks (LFW, CFP-FP, AgeDB-30) and on TinyFace, a real native-LR dataset; compare to a direct feed of aligned LR into a strong backbone.
AI.result: A synthetic-real gap is observed: the degradation setting optimal for synthetic benchmarks does not yield best performance on real LR. More synthesis is not monotonically beneficial; the learned SR front-end underperforms compared to directly feeding the LR into a strong backbone. The only synthesis that offers improvement over its own baseline is simple interpolation augmentation of a compact backbone.
AI.conclusion: Generative methods for LR face recognition must be validated on real LR data and against a direct-feed baseline. The study emphasizes careful evaluation against real LR and provides a practical pipeline for LR-FR on edge devices.

title: Learning to Predict Middle-Layer Attention in MLLMs for Visual Token Prunin
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance across diverse vision-language tasks, but their efficiency is limited by the cost of processing numerous visual tokens. Visual token pruning can reduce this cost, but requires accurate token importance estimates. Recent studies have demonstrated that text-to-vision attention from middle language model layers can effectively guide visual token pruning, typically using attention from a predefined middle layer to select the visual tokens to retain. Two problems therefore remain. First, our analysis shows that the layer whose attention is most responsive to the question varies substantially across samples, making a fixed layer suboptimal. Second, obtaining attention from the appropriate middle layer requires processing numerous visual tokens through several language model layers, by which point considerable computation has already been spent. To address both problems, we propose Middle-layer Attention Prediction (MAP), which uses Question Contrastive Teacher Selection to identify a sample-specific teacher layer by contrasting attention under the original and reference questions, and distills attention from the selected layer into a lightweight predictor that estimates visual token importance from multi-modal input features. During inference, MAP combines the predicted importance scores with a diversity criterion to prune visual tokens before the first language model layer. Thus, MAP requires no attention maps for pruning and remains compatible with existing inference acceleration techniques. Across ten benchmarks on LLaVA-NeXT-7B, MAP retains 97.5% of the unpruned model performance with only 5.56% of the visual tokens, yielding a 3.09x end-to-end speedup.

AI.tldr: MAP adaptively selects a sample-specific middle-layer attention source via Question Contrastive Teacher Selection and distills it into a lightweight visual-token-importance predictor to prune tokens before the first LLM layer, achieving 3.09x end-to-end speedup with 97.5% of unpruned performance using 5.56% tokens on LLaVA-NeXT-7B across ten benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs incur high compute from processing numerous visual tokens; a fixed middle-layer attention source is suboptimal since the most responsive layer varies across samples; existing attention-based pruning also requires processing through multiple layers, adding cost.
AI.method: 1) Question Contrastive Teacher Selection identifies a sample-specific teacher layer by contrasting attention patterns under the original and a reference question. 2) Distill attention from the selected layer into a lightweight predictor that maps multi-modal features to visual token importance. 3) At inference, combine predicted importance with a diversity criterion to prune tokens before the first LLM layer. No attention maps are needed at inference, and the method remains compatible with existing acceleration techniques.
AI.result: Empirical results on ten benchmarks with LLaVA-NeXT-7B show MAP preserves 97.5% of unpruned performance while using only 5.56% of visual tokens, achieving a 3.09x end-to-end speedup.
AI.conclusion: MAP effectively resolves both issues—layer-variability and computational cost—by selecting a sample-specific teacher layer and pruning tokens via a lightweight predictor, yielding substantial speedups with minimal accuracy loss and remaining compatible with standard inference acceleration.

title: MiGHT-EHR: A Multi-task Graph Transformer for Heterogeneous Temporal Electronic Health Records
summary: Learning from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has gained significant attention due to its potential to improve clinical prediction. However, effective learning remains challenging because EHRs encode heterogeneous, temporally ordered clinical interactions. In particular, EHRs contain: (i) heterogeneous clinical entities, including patients, visits, diagnoses, prescriptions, and procedures, together with their heterogeneous interactions, (ii) longitudinal patient trajectories across hospital visits and (iii) shared statistical dependencies across related clinical prediction tasks. Existing EHR learning methods capture only a subset of these properties. To bridge this gap, we propose Multi-task Graph transformer for Heterogeneous Temporal EHRs (MiGHT-EHR), which jointly models all three within a unified representation learning method. MiGHT-EHR constructs a heterogeneous graph from EHRs in which nodes represent clinical entities and edges connect statistically associated entities identified via normalized point-wise mutual information. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets, MiGHT-EHR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on average across four tasks: drug recommendation, prediction of length-of-stay, mortality, and readmission, with particularly strong improvements in mortality and readmission prediction. Furthermore, a post-hoc analysis of the learned representations reveals that patient neighborhoods are organized by clinical outcomes, salient medical concepts are recoverable as linear directions in the representation space, and task probabilities are well calibrated. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MiGHT-EHR representations support diverse prediction tasks while preserving clinically interpretable structure.

AI.tldr: MiGHT-EHR is a multi-task graph-transformer framework for heterogeneous temporal EHRs that builds a PMI-based heterogeneous graph over clinical entities (patients, visits, diagnoses, prescriptions, procedures) and jointly learns four tasks (drug recommendation, length-of-stay, mortality, readmission). It outperforms state-of-the-art on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV and yields interpretable representations.
AI.motivation: EHR data are heterogeneous, temporally ordered, and predictive signals are shared across tasks. Existing methods capture only subsets of these properties. A unified representation that models heterogeneity, temporal dynamics, and cross-task structure is needed.
AI.method: Construct a heterogeneous graph where nodes are clinical entities (patients, visits, diagnoses, prescriptions, procedures) and edges connect statistically associated entities identified via normalized point-wise mutual information (PMI). Apply a graph transformer to learn unified representations and perform multi-task learning for four prediction tasks. Post-hoc analysis checks interpretability, including neighborhood structure and linear directions corresponding to medical concepts.
AI.result: MiGHT-EHR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on average across four tasks on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, with strong improvements in mortality and readmission prediction. Post-hoc analyses show patient neighborhoods organize by clinical outcomes, salient medical concepts are recoverable as linear directions in representation space, and task probabilities are well calibrated.
AI.conclusion: A unified, interpretable representation for heterogeneous temporal EHRs is feasible and effective for diverse prediction tasks. The approach demonstrates strong predictive performance while maintaining clinically meaningful structure, suggesting broad applicability to EHR analytics.

title: Is Forward Prediction Enough? Physical State Grounding for JEPA World Models
summary: Learning structured and control-relevant latent representations remains a key challenge for world models. Recent JEPA-based world models learn action-conditioned predictive latent dynamics from observation sequences. However, their forward-prediction objectives do not explicitly enforce reliable identifiability of robot-centric physical state from individual latents or state changes from latent pairs, which can limit downstream planning and policy performance. We propose PSG-JEPA, a physically grounded JEPA world model that shapes its latent space with two complementary grounding objectives beyond forward prediction: grounding individual latents in robot proprioceptive state, and grounding latent pairs in multi-horizon joint-angle changes. Both objectives are applied only during training, leaving the inference architecture and computational cost unchanged. To comprehensively evaluate PSG-JEPA, we conduct experiments at three levels: (1) latent identifiability via probing, (2) goal-conditioned planning on frozen latents, and (3) policy learning in simulation and on a real robot. Experiments demonstrate that our PSG-JEPA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art latent world-model baselines at all three levels.

AI.tldr: PSG-JEPA adds physically grounded training objectives to a JEPA-based world model to improve identifiability and planning, with two latent-grounding losses (proprioceptive mapping and multi-horizon joint-angle change) that operate during training only, yielding better latent identifiability, planning on frozen latents, and policy learning in simulation and on real robots.
AI.motivation: Address the weak identifiability of robot-centric physical state and changes from latent representations in JEPA-based world models, which can hinder planning and policy performance.
AI.method: Introduce two training-only grounding losses: (1) ground individual latents to robot proprioceptive state, and (2) ground latent pairs to multi-horizon joint-angle changes; keep inference architecture and compute unchanged; evaluate with latent identifiability probes, goal-conditioned planning on frozen latents, and policy learning in sim and on a real robot.
AI.result: PSG-JEPA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art latent world-model baselines across three evaluation levels: latent identifiability, planning on frozen latents, and policy learning in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: Integrating physical grounding objectives into JEPA-based world models enhances latent identifiability and downstream task performance without altering the inference pipeline or cost, offering a practical improvement for robot control with latent models.

title: Toward surface-based registration of a virtual preoperative cutting guide onto the mandible for reconstruction surgery
summary: Mandibular reconstruction restores facial continuity and oral function after segmental resection. Patient-specific cutting guides transfer a computed tomography (CT)-based plan to the operating room with three-dimensional information, but printed guides add cost and lead time, cannot adapt after fabrication, and may interrupt surgery if sterility is lost. We investigate a markerless augmented reality (AR) alternative that registers a virtual cutting guide to the exposed mandible from surface geometry. The method extends surface-based registration for the transoral setting, where teeth form the most distinctive visible surface. After camera calibration, a HoloLens 2 time-of-flight camera captures a partial intraoperative point cloud. The user supplies a rough head-based alignment only to crop the region of interest. A teeth-weighted global stage computes correspondences and solves a truncated least-squares rigid alignment. An asymmetric point-to-plane iterative closest point (ICP) stage refines the complete CT mandible against the partial depth cloud target. The guide-to-mandible transform places the guide in the HoloLens world frame, while pose updates and interpolation follow target motion. We define a blinded phantom protocol with 30 target registration error (TRE) points under full, intermediate, and teeth-only exposure, plus a motion-to-display latency test. Our median TRE is 4.05, 6.10, and 7.10 mm respectively, and median latency is 0.805 s. These values support the feasibility of using AR to replace physical prints. The workflow removes mounted fiducials and manual landmark selection and provides a testable path toward transoral cutting guidance.

AI.tldr: Markerless AR using HoloLens for transoral mandibular cutting guidance shows feasibility with mm-range localization but accuracy depends on tooth exposure (TRE 4.05–7.10 mm) and ~0.8 s latency; avoids fiducials and printed guides.
AI.motivation: Replace costly, time-consuming, and rigid patient-specific cutting guides with a markerless AR approach to improve intraoperative workflow, sterility, and adaptability in transoral mandibular procedures.
AI.method: Extend surface-based registration to a transoral setting using a partial intraoperative point cloud captured by a HoloLens 2 time-of-flight camera. Start with rough head-based alignment to crop ROI. Use a teeth-weighted global stage for correspondences and a truncated least-squares rigid alignment. Refine with an asymmetric point-to-plane ICP to align the full CT mandible to the partial depth cloud. Place the guide in the HoloLens world frame and update pose with target motion. Evaluate with a blinded phantom protocol (30 TRE points) under full, intermediate, and teeth-only exposure; measure motion-to-display latency.
AI.result: Median TRE: 4.05 mm (full), 6.10 mm (intermediate), 7.10 mm (teeth-only). Median latency: 0.805 s. Findings support feasibility of AR-guided transoral cutting without physical guides, though accuracy decreases with reduced tooth exposure.
AI.conclusion: Markerless AR for transoral mandibular cutting is feasible and can replace physical guides in principle, offering workflow advantages and sterilization benefits, but accuracy currently falls short of typical clinical requirements under limited tooth visibility; further improvements are needed to reduce TRE and ensure robust real-time tracking.

title: WebGrader: Training LLMs for Web Development with Self-Evolving Programmatic Grader
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material is included in the main PDF
summary: Large language models increasingly generate complete websites from natural-language descriptions, and reinforcement learning has become a central approach to closing their remaining functional gap. This training regime is bottlenecked by reward design. Hand-authored browser scripts are executable yet costly to write for open-ended requirements, while VLM and GUI-agent graders scale but may issue verdicts before observing the decisive state. We propose WebGrader, a self-evolving programmatic grader that autonomously derives the required interaction flows from each website request, represents each flow as an executable Flow Contract, and uses its execution outcome as an RL reward. WebGrader materializes the generated project in a live browser, grounds target actions against the source code and live DOM, and collects visual, DOM, response, and persistent-state evidence along the same browser trajectory. A residual-driven offline loop then discovers reusable verifier skills, screens them on disjoint validation pages, and freezes the promoted skill graph before policy training. By separating test planning, action grounding, evidence collection, and semantic judgment, WebGrader issues a Pass verdict only after observing the requested transition. On WebGen-Bench, WebGrader trains an 8B policy to a 52.01% functional success rate, outperforming a matched appearance-plus-script reward by 7.88 points and surpassing o4-mini and DeepSeek-v4-flash. On WG-core-250, the policy reaches a Full Score of 44.953 and surpasses Qwen3-Coder-480B.

AI.tldr: Self-evolving programmatic grader WebGrader grounds web interactions in live browsers to generate RL rewards, achieving notable improvements over baselines on WebGen-Bench and WG-core-250.
AI.motivation: Address reward design bottleneck in RL-based web generation; reduce reliance on hand-crafted scripts; enable scalable, verifiable evaluation and learning of web automation policies.
AI.method: Autonomously derive interaction flows and represent them as Flow Contracts; execute in live browser; ground actions to source code and live DOM; collect visual, DOM, response, and persistent-state evidence along a single trajectory; offline residual loop discovers reusable verifier skills, validating and freezing a skill graph; separate test planning, action grounding, evidence collection, and semantic judgment to issue a Pass verdict only after observing the requested transition.
AI.result: WebGen-Bench: 8B policy reaches 52.01% functional success, +7.88 points over appearance-plus-script reward; surpasses o4-mini and DeepSeek-v4-flash. WG-core-250: Full Score 44.953, surpassing Qwen3-Coder-480B.
AI.conclusion: Separating planning, grounding, evidence collection, and semantic judgment enables reliable Pass verdicts and scalable improvements in web-automation RL for large models.

title: SNI-GNN: SmartNIC-Assisted Full-Graph GNN Training with In-Network Embedding Prediction
comment: Camera-ready version accepted at ICDE 2026. 14 pages, 18 figures
summary: Full-graph GNN training delivers high accuracy but scales poorly on multi-server clusters due to heavy, irregular inter-node embedding exchanges. We present SNI-GNN, a SmartNIC-assisted full-graph training system that reduces communication while preserving accuracy by predicting remote embeddings in-network. SNI-GNN deploys a lightweight linear-trend predictor on SmartNICs to refine cached historical embeddings, coupled with an importance-based boundary-node sampling policy and an asynchronous DPU--GPU data pipeline with intermediate-result reuse. We provide error and convergence bounds showing that predictor bias remains controlled under bounded second-order dynamics and yields standard non-convex convergence with inexact gradients. Implemented on NVIDIA BlueField-3, SNI-GNN integrates with state-of-the-art full-graph systems, cuts communication by 21--45\%, achieves 1.3--3.6$\times$ end-to-end speedups over BNS-GCN and up to 1.29$\times$ over baseline SANCUS, with accuracy loss $\leq 0.01$, and scales efficiently to 16 GPUs on graphs with up to tens of millions of edges. These results indicate SmartNIC-based in-network prediction is a practical complement to partitioning and compression techniques for communication-efficient full-graph GNN training at scale.

AI.tldr: SNI-GNN: SmartNIC-assisted full-graph GNN training reduces inter-node communication by in-network prediction of remote embeddings using a lightweight linear-trend predictor on SmartNICs, boundary-node sampling, and asynchronous DPU–GPU data pipelines; achieving substantial communication reductions and speedups with minimal accuracy loss, scalable to large graphs.
AI.motivation: Full-graph GNN training achieves high accuracy but scales poorly on multi-server clusters due to heavy, irregular inter-node embedding exchanges.
AI.method: Deploy a lightweight linear-trend predictor on SmartNICs to refine cached historical embeddings; apply an importance-based boundary-node sampling policy; use an asynchronous DPU–GPU data pipeline with intermediate-result reuse; provide error and convergence bounds; integrate on NVIDIA BlueField-3 to work with existing full-graph systems.
AI.result: Reduces communication by 21–45%, achieves 1.3–3.6× end-to-end speedups over BNS-GCN and up to 1.29× over baseline SANCUS, with accuracy loss ≤ 0.01, and scales to 16 GPUs on graphs with tens of millions of edges.
AI.conclusion: SmartNIC-based in-network prediction is a practical complement to partitioning and compression techniques for communication-efficient full-graph GNN training at scale.

title: R2S-EGO: Dual-Proxy Refinement for Sparse-Capture Real-to-Sim
summary:
Real-to-sim (R2S) depends on scene representations that render observations along robot ego trajectories, yet dense multi-view capture limits per-environment real-image capture-count efficiency, and sparse human capture can
  leave behavior-scoped robot views under-supported. Camera-controlled synthesis can fill missing views, but its use in R2S requires behavior-admissible queries and capture-anchored structural conditioning. We present R2S-EGO,
  which couples a simulator-derived robot proxy that represents the behavior-scoped executable query domain with a capture-anchored geometry proxy that supplies scene-specific structural conditions. Within this domain, fixed-
  budget selection targets current support deficits for which geometry support is available. The generated observations are assimilated as pseudo-observations to refine the visual asset, while real captures remain anchors. The
  fused geometry proxy also supplies the scene collision surface, which is refreshed between rounds. Together, these updates refine the existing simulation scene while its robot dynamics and control stack stay fixed. Across 48
  frozen Unitree G1 ego views in three Replica scenes, six-view R2S-EGO reaches 19.062 dB PSNR, compared with 14.226 dB for the strongest reported R2S baseline. Across five paired policy-training seeds, R2S-EGO achieves 82.5%
  +/- 6.8% real-G1 sitting success, compared with 10.0% +/- 10.5% for GaussGym.

AI.tldr: R2S-EGO fuses a simulator robot proxy with a capture-anchored geometry proxy to fill missing views in real-to-sim for robotics, using pseudo-observations and fixed robot dynamics to improve scene assets; yields higher PSNR and policy success vs GaussGym.
AI.motivation: Dense real-image capture is costly and sparse coverage leaves behavior-specific robot views under-supported; targeted, behavior-admissible view synthesis and geometry-conditioned conditioning are needed to improve R2S.
AI.method: Introduce R2S-EGO: a two-proxy framework consisting of a simulator-derived robot proxy (behavior-scoped executable queries) and a capture-anchored geometry proxy (scene-specific structural conditioning). Operate under fixed-budget view synthesis to address support deficits, use generated observations as pseudo-observations to refine visual assets while real captures anchor the data, and refresh the scene collision surface between rounds. Maintain fixed robot dynamics/control stack while refining the simulation scene.
AI.result: Empirical gains: on 48 frozen Unitree G1 ego views across three Replica scenes with six-view R2S-EGO, PSNR improves to 19.062 dB vs 14.226 dB baseline; policy-wise, across five seeds, real-G1 sitting success is 82.5% ± 6.8% vs 10.0% ± 10.5% for GaussGym.
AI.conclusion: R2S-EGO effectively addresses data-efficiency and coverage gaps in real-to-sim by tightly coupling behavior-driven simulation proxies with capture-anchored geometry, using pseudo-observations to refine visuals while preserving dynamics, leading to substantial improvements in both perceptual fidelity (PSNR) and real-world policy success.

title: SLED: Scalable Location Encoding via Distillation
summary: The plethora of readily available geospatial data offers exciting opportunities to learn high quality representations of the planet, but the sheer size of the Earth Observations (EO), differing modalities, and different sensor types pose significant challenges in doing so. Location encoders have emerged as an efficient way of compressing EOs into location-specific embeddings. However, current state-of-the-art location encoders rely on computationally expensive CLIP-style frameworks that require large batch sizes in the 16K--32K range, suffer from false negative samples, and scale poorly with additional modalities. We introduce the Scalable Location Encoder via Distillation (SLED), a distillation-based location encoder that uses geospatial location as a binding modality to pretrain location encoders with any modality of geospatial data. The resulting location encoder framework is lightweight, modular, and can flexibly incorporate multiple modes, while eliminating the need for spatiotemporal coregistration of samples. SLED is performant with batch sizes as small as 128, enabling pretraining at a fraction of the runtime and compute costs of current state-of-the-art models. We demonstrate our approach by pretraining unimodal and multimodal SLED models on Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat imagery. We show that both unimodal and multimodal SLED models keep pace with or outperform existing approaches on a diverse set of 19 human-centric benchmark tasks and explore the benefits of using additional modes in pretraining.

AI.tldr: SLED introduces a scalable, distillation-based location encoder for geospatial data that uses location as a binding modality to pretrain encoders with any modality, enabling small batch-size training and modular multimodal fusion. It demonstrates on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery and matches or surpasses baselines on 19 human-centric benchmarks while reducing compute and avoiding spatiotemporal coregistration.
AI.motivation: The abundance of geospatial data across multiple modalities and sensors offers rich representations but poses scale and cross-modality integration challenges. State-of-the-art CLIP-like location encoders require massive batch sizes and suffer from false negatives and poor scalability with more modalities. A lightweight, scalable alternative is needed to efficiently leverage diverse geospatial data without heavy coregistration.
AI.method: Propose Scalable Location Encoder via Distillation (SLED), a distillation-based pretraining framework that uses geospatial location as a binding modality. It pretrains location encoders with unimodal and multimodal geospatial data, is lightweight and modular, does not require spatiotemporal coregistration, and supports small batch sizes (as low as 128). Demonstrates pretraining on Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat imagery and evaluates on multiple human-centric tasks, including exploring benefits of adding more modalities.
AI.result: SLED achieves competitive performance with substantially reduced compute—able to pretrain with batch sizes as small as 128 and faster runtime than CLIP-style methods. Both unimodal and multimodal SLED models match or exceed existing baselines across 19 human-centric benchmarks and show tangible gains from incorporating additional data modalities during pretraining.
AI.conclusion: SLED provides a scalable, modular alternative for geospatial representation learning by distilling across modalities and using location as a binding modality. It eliminates the need for spatiotemporal coregistration, supports multiple modalities, and delivers competitive or superior results with significantly lower compute requirements.

title: Can MLLMs Decode the Creative Leap? Introducing C4 for Cross-Concept Understanding
summary: Creative capabilities of MLLMs matter in design, communication, education, and human--AI collaboration, yet remain difficult to evaluate because explicit targets and reward signals are scarce compared with accuracy-oriented tasks. Cross-concept understanding is a core cognitive capacity underlying receptive creativity. It enables a perceiver to recover intended meaning from non-obvious but meaningful conceptual relations. We operationalize item construction as cross-concept encoding and model inference as cross-concept decoding. We introduce C4, a cognition-inspired evaluation framework for Chengyu (Chinese idiom)-based Cross-Concept Creativity. Its encoding component maps target slots to imageable substitute concepts along bridge paths in a manually annotated and third-party-reviewed cross-concept network, enabling batch generation with explicit structure, difficulty indexed by bridge count and depth, and exact answers. Using this framework, we instantiate the C4 Evaluation Set (C4-Eval), comprising 184 synthetic items and 37 human-created cross-concept chengyu figures collected from online sources. We manually construct and review cross-concept relations, bridge paths, and reasoning processes for the collected figures. Each C4-Eval item is instantiated in five task settings, yielding 884 primary answer-recovery cases. Across ten evaluated MLLMs, the strongest closed models reach 50.7% and 48.0% primary accuracy, while open-source models remain substantially lower. Candidate constraints improve accuracy sharply, but bridge hints and explanation requests provide only modest gains. These results expose a substantial gap in how current MLLMs decode creatively encoded meaning through cross-concept relations. The code is in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: A cognition-inspired cross-concept evaluation framework (C4) for Chengyu-based cross-concept creativity in multilingual LLMs, using structured encoding/decoding to derive exact answers; introduces C4-Eval with synthetic and human-generated items; reveals current LLMs struggle to decode cross-concept meaning.
AI.motivation: Evaluate creative capabilities of LLMs when explicit targets/rewards are scarce; cross-concept understanding underlies receptive creativity; need structured benchmarks beyond accuracy.
AI.method: Encode target slots to imageable substitute concepts along annotated cross-concept bridge paths; batch generation with explicit structure; difficulty indexed by bridge count and depth; five task settings; manual annotation/review of cross-concept relations, bridge paths, and reasoning; evaluate across ten LLMs; analyze effects of candidate constraints, bridge hints, and explanations.
AI.result: Strongest closed models reach about 50.7% and 48.0% primary accuracy; open-source models substantially lower; candidate constraints improve accuracy sharply; bridge hints and explanation requests provide only modest gains; reveals a substantial gap in decoding creatively encoded meaning through cross-concept relations.
AI.conclusion: C4 offers a cognition-inspired, structured evaluation for cross-concept creativity; demonstrates current LLMs' limitations in cross-concept decoding; underscores need for improved cross-concept reasoning and evaluation protocols; code/data likely available in supplementary materials.

title: ED-CSP: Crystal Structure Prediction from Electron Diffraction
summary:
Recovering a periodic 3D crystal structure from sparse, unindexed electron diffraction (ED) observations is a challenging generative inverse problem. Existing ED-based learning methods mainly predict crystallographic labels, reconstruct structures from indexed reflections, or retrieve candidates from finite structure libraries. Here, we introduce ED-CSP, a machine learning framework that predicts crystal structures from chemical composition, atom count, and multiple detector-plane ED spot sets. ED-CSP combines a relational set encoder, permutation-invariant multi-view aggregation, and a periodic flow generator to jointly predict lattice parameters and fractional atomic coordinates.
  To train the model, we construct ED-CS, a dataset of 4.85 million simulated multi-view ED crystal structures, deduplicated across seven materials repositories and filtered to exclude CHILI-100K overlaps. On 2,075 held-out CHILI-100K materials, ED-CSP trained only on CHILI achieves a structural match rate of 57.49% MR@5, outperforming PXRDGen (52.92%), a state-of-the-art crystal structure prediction model conditioned on powder X-ray diffraction. Scaling training data further improves performance: initializing from a one-million-structure precursor raises MR@5 to 66.27%. On 1,024 compositions absent from the training retrieval library, the model still achieves 53.52% MR@5, demonstrating true generative capability beyond exact-formula retrieval. Replacing target ED observations with diffraction from non-isomorphic structures of identical composition decreases MR@5 by 22.09 percentage points, confirming that predictions depend on the input diffraction patterns rather than composition alone. ED-CSP and ED-CS establish a benchmark for generative crystal structure prediction from sparse ED observations and provide a foundation for future transfer to experimental data.

AI.tldr: ED-CSP is a machine learning framework that predicts 3D crystal structures from sparse, unindexed electron diffraction (ED) observations, using a relational set encoder, permutation-invariant multi-view aggregation, and a periodic flow generator. Trained on a large simulated ED dataset (ED-CS), it achieves strong MR@5 performance, scales with more data to near 66% MR@5, and demonstrates generative capability beyond exact-formula retrieval, with true dependence on input ED patterns.
AI.motivation: Recover accurate crystal structures from sparse ED data, addressing the bottleneck of structure prediction beyond simple label prediction or library retrieval; aim to outperform existing ED-based and PXRD-based baselines.
AI.method: Relational set encoder to capture composition/atom counts; permutation-invariant multi-view aggregation over multiple detector-plane ED spot sets; periodic flow generator to predict lattice parameters and fractional atomic coordinates; training on ED-CS (4.85M simulated structures) deduplicated across seven repositories and filtered to avoid CHILI-100K overlaps; evaluation on held-out materials and compositions.
AI.result: MR@5 on 2,075 CHILI-100K holdout materials: 57.49% (ED-CSP trained on CHILI); PXRDGen: 52.92%. Scaling data by initializing from a 1M-structure precursor raises MR@5 to 66.27%. For compositions absent from training, MR@5 remains 53.52%, indicating true generative capability beyond exact-formula retrieval. Replacing target ED with non-isomorphic diffracted patterns reduces MR@5 by 22.09 percentage points, demonstrating dependence on input diffraction patterns rather than composition alone.
AI.conclusion: ED-CSP and ED-CS establish a benchmark for generative crystal structure prediction from sparse ED observations and lay groundwork for transfer to experimental data.

title: When Coordination Becomes a Threat: Communication Attacks in LLM-Controlled Multi-Robot Systems
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as high-level planners in embodied multi-robot systems, enabling robots to interpret natural language instructions and coordinate executable actions. Yet, this growing reliance on LLM planners also raises security concerns. Prior work has focused mainly on individual robots, while communication risks in multi-robot collaboration remain insufficiently understood. Existing multi-robot studies are further limited to preliminary analysis under the Decentralized Multi-agent System (DMAS) architecture, so it remains unclear whether these risks persist across other common communication architectures and how attacker access settings shape their propagation. To fill this gap, we formulate two communication attacks corresponding to distinct attacker access settings: the External Entry Point Attack and the Privileged In-System Attack. We evaluate both attacks across DMAS, HMAS-1, and HMAS-2 using three LLMs and five embodied multi-robot tasks. Results show that unsafe information can turn into unsafe actions across all three architectures: DMAS reaches a 96.7\% entry endorsement rate and a 100\% post endorsement activation rate, HMAS-1 reaches a 97.8\% unsafe action success rate, and HMAS-2 triggers 88.3\% of task defined unsafe action slots. To mitigate risks from trusted information flow, we introduce the Claim Provenance and Verification (CPV) Gate, which verifies communicated claims before downstream reuse and reduces the violation rate from 70.0\% to 36.6\%.

AI.tldr: Unsafe information in LLM-driven multi-robot systems can propagate to unsafe actions across DMAS, HMAS-1, and HMAS-2; a CPV Gate mitigates violations.
AI.motivation: Understand security risks of inter-robot communication with LLM planners beyond DMAS; evaluate attacker settings and architectures.
AI.method: Formulate External Entry Point Attack and Privileged In-System Attack; evaluate across DMAS, HMAS-1, HMAS-2 with three LLMs and five tasks; measure endorsement and activation rates; propose CPV Gate.
AI.result: Unsafe information leads to unsafe actions across architectures: DMAS (96.7% entry endorsement; 100% post endorsement activation), HMAS-1 (97.8% unsafe action success), HMAS-2 (88.3% of unsafe action slots). CPV Gate reduces violation rate from 70.0% to 36.6%.
AI.conclusion: CPV Gate improves safety by verifying claims before reuse; however, security risks persist across architectures; need robust defense for LLM-based planning in multi-robot systems.

title: Do 3D Medical Foundation Models See Through MRI Artifacts? A Controlled Study of Representation Robustness
comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Artificial Intelligence for Medical 3D Vision (AI4M3D)
summary: Self-supervised 3D medical foundation models are increasingly used as general-purpose feature extractors, yet their sensitivity to MRI artifacts remains poorly understood. We present a controlled evaluation of representation robustness across five pretrained 3D encoders spanning different architectures, objectives, pretraining domains, and dataset scales. Using BraTS-Africa cases with four MRI sequences, we generate seven frequency- and image-domain artifacts at five predefined corruption settings. Robustness is assessed using linear centered kernel alignment (CKA), RankMe, and UMAP, complemented by an independent segmentation-consistency analysis. We find that robustness is strongly model- and artifact-dependent. 3DINO exhibits the most consistently stable representations, while BrainIAC is highly sensitive to several corruptions; NeuroVFM, BrainFM, and Neuro-SimCLR show intermediate but distinct artifact-specific profiles. Across many conditions, CKA decreases substantially while RankMe remains comparatively stable, indicating that artifacts often distort representation geometry without causing dimensional collapse. Segmentation consistency also degrades under corruption, particularly for ghosting and Rician noise, but aligns only partially with representation-level robustness. These findings show that larger-scale or domain-specific pretraining alone does not guarantee artifact invariance and motivate explicit robustness evaluation before deploying 3D foundation models in heterogeneous MRI settings.

AI.tldr: Across five pretrained 3D encoders on BraTS-Africa MRI with seven artifacts across five corruption settings, artifact robustness is model- and artifact-dependent; 3DINO is most stable, BrainIAC is highly sensitive; RankMe remains stable while CKA shows geometry distortion; segmentation degrades under ghosting/Rician noise, only partially aligning with representation robustness; large-scale pretraining alone does not guarantee artifact invariance.
AI.motivation: To quantify how self-supervised 3D medical foundation models generalize under MRI artifacts and whether larger-scale/domain-specific pretraining yields artifact invariance.
AI.method: Evaluate five pretrained 3D encoders (varying architectures/objectives/domain/scale) using BraTS-Africa data with four MRI sequences. Introduce seven frequency- and image-domain artifacts across five corruption levels. Assess representations with linear CKA, RankMe, and UMAP; perform segmentation-consistency analysis as an independent check.
AI.result: Robustness is strongly model- and artifact-dependent. 3DINO is most consistently stable; BrainIAC is highly sensitive to several corruptions; NeuroVFM, BrainFM, and Neuro-SimCLR show intermediate but artifact-specific profiles. Across conditions, CKA decreases under corruption while RankMe remains comparatively stable, indicating artifacts distort representation geometry without causing dimensional collapse. Segmentation consistency degrades under corruption, especially ghosting and Rician noise, but aligns only partially with representation-level robustness.
AI.conclusion: Larger-scale or domain-specific pretraining alone does not guarantee artifact invariance; explicit robustness evaluation is necessary before deploying 3D foundation models in heterogeneous MRI settings.

title: KNOWPLAN: Knowledge-Driven AI Agents for Smart Degree Pathway Planning
summary: Planning a degree from official university sources requires solving two problems in order. The institution's curriculum must first be reconstructed from catalogs, departmental pages, JSON endpoints, and PDFs that share no schema, and only then can a student-specific path be optimized under prerequisite logic and overlapping requirement constraints. Coupling the two lets each failure mode hide the other, because a planner that drives its own crawling never learns facts its current plan does not need. We present KnowPlan, which enforces an extraction-first boundary and measures the interface between the stages rather than assuming it. CatalogBrowse explores with no access to any user profile. It scores legal actions by lower-confidence expected marginal gain over a finite set of atomic catalog obligations per unit of source access, parses deterministically through platform adapters with a span-constrained clause-to-AST model fallback, and terminates on a closure certificate over index, schema, provenance, and reference completeness instead of a reward threshold. Its output contract is three provenance-linked JSON documents. DegreeMap consumes only those documents. It compiles them into a typed requirement hypergraph and optimizes lexicographically with CP-SAT over hard feasibility, completion horizon, load and risk, personalized utility, and option value, so that each stage optimizes inside the previous stage's proven optimum and stays certifiable within the solver budget. Across a 100-university broad track and a six-school dense track, CatalogBrowse reaches 96.2% inventory recall and 88.7% masked-source recovery at 47% less source access than an exhaustive crawler, DegreeMap holds 100.0% hard feasibility while improving personalized utility by +0.066 over the strongest baseline, and the full pipeline certifies 99.5% of requests with a utility gap to the privileged gold graph of 0.015.

AI.tldr: KnowPlan is an extraction-first two-stage planning pipeline that reconstructs degree curricula from heterogeneous sources and optimizes student paths, achieving high recall, feasibility, and certifiability with reduced data access.
AI.motivation: Reconstruct curricula from inconsistent sources before pathway optimization; coupling causes hidden failure modes; absence of extraction-first boundary leads planners to optimize on incomplete facts.
AI.method: Propose KnowPlan enforcing extraction-first boundary; CatalogBrowse parses catalogs without user profiles, returns three provenance-linked JSON documents; DegreeMap consumes these, builds a typed requirement hypergraph, and optimizes lexicographically via CP-SAT over hard feasibility, horizon, load, risk, personalized utility, and option value; includes certifiability checks.
AI.result: CatalogBrowse: 96.2% inventory recall, 88.7% masked-source recovery, 47% less source access; DegreeMap: 100% hard feasibility and +0.066 personalized utility; full pipeline certifies 99.5% of requests with utility gap to gold graph 0.015.
AI.conclusion: Extraction-first pipeline yields high empirical performance and certifiability across large-scale university data, with efficiency gains and predictable interface between stages.

title: Beyond Attention: Signed Integrated Gradients Attribution in a BiomeGPT-Style Microbiome Transformer
summary:
In a feature-tokenized transformer (arXiv:2106.11959) such as BiomeGPT (doi:10.64898/2026.01.05.697599), each input token is built by fusing a fixed identity with a sample-specific measurement: a fixed species and a variable abundance, T = S + A. To interpret downstream classification in such models, prior work inspects the attention weights of the special [CLS] token (arXiv:2106.11959, arXiv:1810.04805, BiomeGPT) to rank sample tokens by importance. These weights have two critical limitations: they are nonnegative, so they cannot separate disease-supporting from health-supporting evidence (arXiv:2201.12114), and they act after token fusion, obscuring how the input sources S and A each affect the output.
  To address this we use Integrated Gradients (arXiv:1703.01365), a signed, fusion-aware attribution method, and propose a source-derived baseline T' = S + A_0 for feature-tokenized models such as BiomeGPT, which preserves species identity as a fixed biological coordinate while isolating the effect of abundance variation. Applied to a disease-versus-health decision margin, it yields polarity that explicitly separates pathogenic from protective microbial signals. We show that this gradient-based approach uncovers species-abundance directional relationships and sensitivity diagnostics entirely obscured by unsigned [CLS] attention weights. We further recommend second-order Integrated Hessians (arXiv:2002.04138) to expose microbiome community interaction rules: how a perturbation in one member alters the model's sensitivity to another, and which other species drive ambiguous cases toward disease or health at a given abundance level. This provides a principled approach to explainability in BiomeGPT that generalizes to other smooth and differentiable feature-tokenized transformers. Code is available at https://github.com/nohren/token-source-attribution

AI.tldr: Integrated Gradients with a source-derived baseline for feature-tokenized transformers (e.g., BiomeGPT) yields signed, fusion-aware attributions; reveals disease vs health polarity in species-abundance signals and uncovers interaction rules via second-order Hessians, addressing limitations of [CLS] attention.
AI.motivation: Limitation of unsigned, post-fusion [CLS] attention in feature-tokenized models; need to disentangle species (S) and abundance (A) contributions and reveal interactions for microbiome-based disease decisions.
AI.method: Adopt Integrated Gradients with a source-derived baseline T' = S + A0; apply to disease-vs-health margin to obtain polarity; propose second-order Integrated Hessians to quantify interactions among species and drive ambiguous cases toward disease/health; generalize to smooth differentiable tokenized transformers.
AI.result: Gradient-based attributions show directional S-A effects; separate pathogenic vs protective signals; reveal microbiome interaction patterns hidden by [CLS] attention; provide a principled explainability framework; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Provides signed, fusion-aware explainability for feature-tokenized transformers, enabling interpretation of S and A contributions and interaction effects; applicable beyond BiomeGPT.

title: Unordered Landmark Visual Navigation
summary: Image-goal navigation is a fundamental capability for embodied AI, yet its practical deployment is strained by strong prior assumptions. Existing methods predominantly rely on temporally ordered video streams or auxiliary sensors (e.g., depth, LiDAR) to maintain spatial consistency. These sequential and multimodal dependencies severely restrict scalability, especially when deploying robots using crowd-sourced or pre-recorded unordered image collections. When temporal priors are removed, current methods struggle with severe perceptual aliasing, noisy associations, and catastrophic mapping failures. To address this underexplored challenge, we propose Unordered Landmark Visual Navigation (ULVN), a unified RGB-only framework free from temporal and odometric priors. ULVN systematically mitigates error accumulation by integrating mapping, localization, and planning. Specifically, it constructs a robust 2D topological map directly from unstructured images via calibrated geometric verification and maximum spanning forest refinement. For closed-loop execution, ULVN abandons sequential heuristics, utilizing a graph-based belief propagation filter with entropy-adaptive fusion for global localization and dynamic subgoal planning. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world deployments demonstrate that ULVN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: Unordered Landmark Visual Navigation (ULVN) enables robust image-goal navigation without temporal or odometric priors by building a 2D topological map from unordered RGB images and using graph-based localization and planning; it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both simulation and real-world tests.
AI.motivation: Address scalability and robustness of image-goal navigation when temporal priors and auxiliary sensors are unavailable, such as with crowd-sourced or pre-recorded unordered image collections, and mitigate severe perceptual aliasing and mapping failures.
AI.method: ULVN constructs a robust 2D topological map directly from unstructured RGB images via calibrated geometric verification and maximum spanning forest refinement. For closed-loop execution, it replaces sequential heuristics with a graph-based belief propagation filter that uses entropy-adaptive fusion for global localization and dynamic subgoal planning, all without temporal or odometric priors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world deployments show that ULVN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: ULVN demonstrates the viability of RGB-only unordered image-goal navigation by effectively integrating mapping, localization, and planning to mitigate error accumulation, enabling scalable deployment from unordered image collections.

title: When Semantics Saturate or Emerge: Adaptation-Conditional Semantic Utility in Source-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning
summary: Language descriptions in source-free cross-domain few-shot learning (SF-CDFSL) are often selected according to zero-shot accuracy obtained with a frozen vision--language model. This paper asks whether that ranking remains valid after target-domain visual adaptation. Under a strictly paired protocol, we compare a generic class-name template with fixed detailed class descriptions before and after visual Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on EuroSAT, CropDisease, ISIC, and ChestX. Let $\deltazero$ and $\deltalora$ denote the Detailed-minus-Base accuracy before and after adaptation, respectively. Two recurring regimes emerge. In \emph{semantic saturation}, $\deltazero>0$ but $0<\deltalora\ll\deltazero$: on EuroSAT and CropDisease, initial gains of 8.13--21.54 percentage points contract to 0.69--2.96 points after LoRA. In \emph{semantic emergence}, $\deltazero\leq0$ but $\deltalora>0$: on ISIC and ChestX, detailed descriptions become more useful only after the visual representation is updated. Training trajectories and sample-level decomposition show that saturation is driven mainly by Base-LoRA recovering errors already solved by detailed semantics, whereas emergence is associated with prediction turnover and newly formed Detailed-only correct decisions. Fixed-point-free shuffled-semantic controls, a second CLIP backbone, and multiple random seeds support the broad pattern while identifying ChestX 1-shot as a weak boundary case. These findings establish that zero-shot prompt quality is an incomplete proxy for adaptation-anchor quality and motivate evaluating language on both sides of the adaptation boundary.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot prompt quality is not a reliable proxy for adaptation performance in source-free cross-domain few-shot learning (SF-CDFSL); after visual adaptation with LoRA, the usefulness of detailed language shifts, revealing semantic saturation and semantic emergence regimes across datasets.
AI.motivation: To test whether the ranking of zero-shot prompts (generic class-name templates vs detailed descriptions) established on frozen vision-language models persists after target-domain visual adaptation, and to understand how detailed language interacts with adaptation.
AI.method: Strictly paired protocol: compare a generic class-name template with fixed detailed class descriptions, before and after visual adaptation with LoRA, on EuroSAT, CropDisease, ISIC, ChestX. Define deltazero (Detailed−Base accuracy before adaptation) and deltaloRA (after adaptation). Analyze training trajectories and sample-level decomposition. Include controls: fixed-point-free shuffled semantics, a second CLIP backbone, and multiple random seeds; identify boundary cases (e.g., ChestX 1-shot).
AI.result: Two recurrent regimes emerge: semantic saturation (deltazero>0 but 0<deltaloRA<<deltazero) on EuroSAT/CropDisease; gains from 8.13–21.54 points shrink to 0.69–2.96 after LoRA. Semantic emergence (deltazero≤0 but deltaloRA>0) on ISIC/ChestX, where detailed descriptions become useful only after adaptation. Training trajectories show base-LoRA recovers errors solved by detailed semantics; emergence associates with prediction turnover and new Detailed-only correct decisions. Controls and multiple seeds confirm the pattern; ChestX 1-shot is a weak boundary case. The broad pattern holds across backbones and controls.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot prompt quality is an incomplete proxy for adaptation-anchor quality. Effective evaluation should consider language usefulness on both sides of the adaptation boundary, as language can become more or less advantageous depending on the state of visual adaptation.

title: TaskSense: Focusing on What Matters in World Models
summary: World models for visual control typically learn compact latent states by reconstructing observations, implicitly encouraging representations to preserve information across the entire visual input. However, task-relevant content often occupies only a small fraction of the observation, while background clutter and distractors consume valuable representational capacity. This mismatch between visual reconstruction and control objectives biases latent representations to model task-irrelevant visual content, diluting learning signals for control-relevant features and severely degrading downstream performance under visual distractions. We introduce TaskSense, a task-centric world modeling framework that enforces task relevance before latent encoding through a differentiable stochastic spatial attention mechanism conditioned on the previous latent state. To steer attention toward control-relevant regions, we augment training with an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective. Rather than reconstructing the full observation, the world model reconstructs only the attended regions, encouraging latent representations to preserve task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant visual content. The decoder is further conditioned on the sampled attention map, enabling consistent reconstruction despite stochastic attention. Compared with the DreamerV3 baseline, TaskSense maintains competitive performance on the DeepMind Control Suite while consistently outperforming DreamerV3 on the Distracting Control Suite, demonstrating substantially improved robustness to visual distractions. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the learned attention, guided by inverse-dynamics supervision, consistently localizes control-relevant regions while suppressing irrelevant visual content.

AI.tldr: TaskSense uses a task-centric world model with stochastic spatial attention and inverse-dynamics supervision to reconstruct only attended regions, yielding robust control under distractions with competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Reconstruction-based world models waste capacity modeling background content; emphasize task-relevant regions to improve robustness when distractors are present.
AI.method: Differentiable stochastic spatial attention conditioned on the previous latent state; auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective; reconstruct only attended regions; decoder conditioned on attended map for consistent reconstruction; evaluation against DreamerV3 on DeepMind Control Suite and Distracting Control Suite.
AI.result: Maintained competitive performance on standard DM Control; outperformed DreamerV3 on Distracting Control Suite; qualitative analysis shows attention localizes control-relevant regions and suppresses distractions.
AI.conclusion: TaskSense demonstrates that task-centric latent representations with attention and inverse-dynamics guidance improve robustness to visual distractions without sacrificing performance.

title: Toward Reliable Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents: An Empirical Study of Execution Instability
summary: Recurrent context compression controls context growth in long-horizon agents, but its behavioral effects remain poorly understood. In this preliminary empirical study, we show that compression can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability across runs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce TRACE, a verifier-guided framework that evaluates individual compaction events through paired closed-loop continuations from the same environment state and uses summary preferences to optimize a natural-language compression prompt while keeping all models frozen. Initial results on AppWorld show improvements over existing compression baselines in task performance, multi-run reliability, and context--execution efficiency. These findings provide early evidence for boundary-local evaluation as a promising direction for reliable agent context compression.

AI.tldr: Compression in recurrent agents reduces influence of recent interactions, causing more exploration, blocked actions, and instability; TRACE is a verifier-guided framework that evaluates compaction events via paired closed-loop continuations, optimizing a natural-language compression prompt while keeping models frozen; AppWorld experiments indicate improved task performance, reliability, and efficiency over compression baselines; boundary-local evaluation is a promising direction for reliable context compression.
AI.motivation: To understand how context compression shapes agent behavior and to develop a reliable, model-agnostic compression method that can be optimized via prompts while keeping the underlying models fixed.
AI.method: Empirical study of recurrent context compression; use of paired closed-loop continuations from the same environment state to assess individual compaction events; optimization of a natural-language compression prompt via summary preferences, with all models frozen; verifier-guided framework TRACE; evaluation on AppWorld platform.
AI.result: Compression weakens the influence of recent interactions, leading to more blocked actions, repeated exploration, and cross-run instability. TRACE improves task performance, multi-run reliability, and context–execution efficiency relative to existing compression baselines on AppWorld.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-local evaluation offers a promising path for reliable agent context compression. TRACE demonstrates how verifier guidance and natural-language prompting can optimize compression without altering model parameters, though the approach is early-stage and requires broader validation.

title: Are Visual Place Recognition Models Recognizing Places or Conditions? Distractor-Augmented Evaluation and Condition Suppression
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Long-term Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is typically evaluated by matching queries from one condition against a database from another. Crowdsourced map databases, however, may mix conditions and include images that resemble the query in condition but depict different places. In the presence of these distractors, a method may retrieve by condition similarity rather than place identity. We argue that this susceptibility arises because the discriminability of VPR methods allows them to encode information such as illumination, weather, and seasonal appearance in their descriptors. We therefore introduce Distractor-Augmented Recall (DAR) to isolate and quantify the effect of distractors, and propose condition suppression to remove condition information from VPR descriptors. Across eleven methods and six datasets, method rankings under DAR@1 differ from those under Recall@1 (R@1), while applying INLP and LEACE as condition suppression methods generally improves DAR@1 without reducing R@1. Thus, distractor robustness is distinct from standard retrieval performance and can be improved by suppressing condition information.

AI.tldr: A new evaluation framework (Distractor-Augmented Recall, DAR) isolates the impact of distractors in long-term Visual Place Recognition (VPR) and shows that condition information degrades place-identity retrieval. The study proposes condition suppression (via INLP and LEACE) to remove condition cues from descriptors, improving distractor robustness (DAR@1) without harming standard Recall@1 (R@1).
AI.motivation: Long-term VPR performance is hindered by distractors in crowdsourced databases where images with similar conditions may depict different places. Discriminability of VPR descriptors can encode non-geometric condition cues (illumination, weather, season), causing retrieval by condition rather than place identity.
AI.method: Introduce Distractor-Augmented Recall (DAR) to quantify distractor effects. Propose condition suppression to remove condition information from VPR descriptors. Evaluate across eleven methods and six datasets; apply INLP and LEACE to suppress condition cues and measure effects on DAR@1 and Recall@1 (R@1).
AI.result: DAR@1 rankings differ from Recall@1 rankings, indicating distractor influence. Condition suppression with INLP and LEACE generally improves DAR@1 without reducing Recall@1, suggesting improved robustness to distractors without harming standard place-identification performance.
AI.conclusion: Distractor robustness is a distinct aspect of VPR not captured by conventional retrieval metrics. Suppressing condition information is an effective strategy to mitigate distractor effects and enhance place-identity retrieval in the presence of confounding conditions.

title: Corrupting Attention: Evasion-Based Adversarial Attacks on Encoder Attention in Detection Transformers
summary: Adversarial vulnerabilities remain a major concern for the safe deployment of neural networks, particularly in object detection, a core task embedded in many safety-critical systems. Detection transformers have emerged as leading object detectors, yet their adversarial robustness remains comparatively underexplored. Most existing attacks target the detection output rather than the attention mechanism that makes these models distinctive. In this paper, we introduce the first attack that directly optimizes an encoder-attention objective under an imperceptible, bounded $\ell_\infty$ perturbation. Rather than introducing an attacker-owned sink token through a visible patch, it drives the model's own attention toward a corrupted target. We argue that encoder attention concentrates the model's spatial reasoning, so corrupting it propagates through the detection pipeline more disruptively than perturbing the detection output alone. Our attack reduces DETR-R50 mAP on COCO from 42.1 to 0.97, a $\sim 4\times$ reduction in resulting mAP over the strongest existing attack under an identical perturbation budget and iteration count. We further show that this vulnerability is not specific to a particular corruption objective: across four qualitatively distinct targets, dispersion, re-ranking, permutation, and peak-suppression, detection consistently drops below 3 mAP, suggesting that the weakness arises from disrupting the attention structure itself rather than from any single target. Finally, we demonstrate that the attack generalizes across attention formulations, reducing DINO-Swin-L from 56.8 to 1.44 mAP against 7.3 for the strongest prior attack, establishing state-of-the-art on both dense and deformable attention.

AI.tldr: First adversarial attack on detection transformers that optimizes an encoder-attention objective under bounded L_infty perturbations; causes dramatic drops in mAP and outperforms output-focused attacks; generalizes across attention types.
AI.motivation: Test robustness of detection transformers by attacking the attention mechanism, which drives spatial reasoning. Prior work targets detection outputs; understanding attention vulnerability reveals fundamental weaknesses in transformer-based detectors.
AI.method: Optimize an encoder-attention objective under imperceptible bounded L_infinity perturbations to steer the model's attention toward a corrupted target, avoiding attacker-owned sink patches. Evaluate across four targets (dispersion, re-ranking, permutation, peak-suppression) on DETR-R50 COCO, and test cross-attention formulations (dense and deformable) including DINO-Swin-L.
AI.result: DETR-R50 mAP decreases from 42.1 to 0.97; about 4x stronger than the strongest prior attack under the same budget/iterations. Across four targets, mAP drops below 3.0. Generalizes to different attention formulations: DINO-Swin-L drops from 56.8 to 1.44 (vs 7.3 for prior attack).
AI.conclusion: Disrupting encoder attention is a potent and general adversarial vulnerability in detection transformers, suggesting the need for attention-focused defenses and robustness strategies beyond output-targeted attacks.

title: Divergent Response Modes in Frontier Language Models Under Steering Pressure
summary: Frontier language models are trained using distinct data, objectives, and safety pipelines. Whether these differences produce measurably different behaviors under explicit steering pressure remains underexplored. This study evaluates behavioral steerability across six frontier models from six developers using 300 paired base and steered items over three categories: values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression (plus 40 validation items). All six models act as blind peer judges and classify every response based on fixed behavioral rubrics. The resulting 24,480 judgments are scored by leave-one-out consensus. We find that models differ not just in how much steering shifts their behavior but in what kind (mode) of response they give, and some response modes appear in only one or two of them. GPT-5 deflects requests to disclose its reasoning while leaving its answer intact (99% vs. 0% for all other models). Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression instructions and in different ways. Using Llama as the open-weight model, we trace the largest behavioral split to its internals. A linear probe decodes the behavior from the residual stream at 0.87 held-out accuracy while injecting that direction during generation drives the behavior from 0% to 86% across an intervention sweep. Every finding holds under both a token-budget remediation and a control experiment with a hypothesis-blind judgment prompt.

AI.tldr: Systematic, cross-model study of steering behavior in frontier language models using blind peer judgments across six models, revealing model-specific steering modes, internal correlates of steerability, and distinct deflection/suppression patterns; findings show high misalignment between steering instructions and responses, with internal representations traceable and perturbable.
AI.motivation: Address whether differences in training data, objectives, and safety pipelines across frontier LMs lead to qualitatively different steerability, including the modes of response and their internal bases.
AI.method: Six frontier models from six developers evaluated with 300 paired base/steered items plus 40 validation items across values-conflict, reasoning-elicitation, and reasoning-suppression. Models act as blind peer judges, classifying responses via fixed rubrics. 24,480 judgments scored by leave-one-out consensus. Internal representations probed with a linear classifier on the residual stream (0.87 accuracy). Intervention by injecting steering direction during generation and evaluating behavior sweep (0% to 86%). Controls include token-budget remediation and hypothesis-blind judgment prompts.
AI.result: Models differ in both the magnitude and mode of steering; some response modes appear in only one or two models. GPT-5 deflects requests to reveal reasoning while keeping answers; Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5 resist explicit suppression prompts in distinct ways. Internal splits traced to Llama internals; steering direction decodes from residuals and can be injected to steer behavior substantially (0%→86%). Findings robust under controls.
AI.conclusion: Steerability is model-specific and not merely a function of steering strength. Internal representations encode steering directions, enabling both detection and perturbation. Implications for safety pipelines, model evaluation, and potential vulnerabilities to steering manipulation.

title: Unmasking Removal-Budget Confounding: A Matched Operating-Point Evaluation Framework for Adaptive Data Cleaning
summary: Adaptive data-cleaning methods replace manual filtering thresholds with data-driven partitions. However, changing the partition granularity, the number of groups used to segment samples by estimated corruption risk, can implicitly shift the decision boundary and alter the overall number of removed samples. This creates a bias known as removal-budget confounding, where apparent gains in metrics like precision or false-positive rate reflect a smaller removal budget rather than superior corruption discrimination. To address this evaluation bias, we introduce an operating-point-aware evaluation framework that evaluates methods using matched-budget and matched-recall controls alongside threshold-independent metrics (AUROC and AUPRC). We test this framework on a multi-cue adaptive cleaner redesign featuring a reweighted learning-difficulty cue, an auxiliary Euclidean-distance cue, and increased partition granularity intended to isolate clean-but-difficult samples. While naive evaluations (assessing configurations at their own induced operating points) suggest substantial performance improvements for the redesign, these gains disappear once operating points are equalized. False-positive decomposition reveals that clean-but-difficult samples primarily drive error counts at low corruption rates, become threshold-dependent at moderate corruption, and contribute negligibly under severe corruption. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 demonstrate that most performance differences observed in naive evaluation shrink or vanish at low-to-moderate corruption when operating points are matched. True ranking advantages only remain in specific low-prevalence settings and in high-recall regions under severe corruption. These findings highlight that adaptive cleaning methods must be benchmarked at matched operating points to ensure performance gains reflect genuine corruption discrimination.

AI.tldr: Adaptive data-cleaning methods exhibit removal-budget confounding due to partition granularity; an operating-point-aware evaluation with matched budgets/recall and threshold-independent metrics shows naive gains vanish, with true advantages confined to specific low-prevalence or high-recall regimes.
AI.motivation: Mitigate evaluation bias caused by varying partition granularity in adaptive cleaners, which changes the number of samples removed and shifts decision boundaries, leading to misleading performance claims.
AI.method: Propose an operating-point-aware evaluation framework using matched-budget and matched-recall controls plus AUROC/AUPRC; redesign a multi-cue adaptive cleaner (reweighted learning-difficulty cue, Euclidean-distance cue, higher granularity) to isolate clean-but-difficult samples; perform false-positive decomposition; validate on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100.
AI.result: Under matched operating points, gains from the redesign largely disappear; false positives are driven by clean-but-difficult samples at low corruption, become threshold-dependent at medium corruption, and are negligible at high corruption; naive evaluations exaggerate improvements.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark adaptive data-cleaning methods at matched operating points to reveal genuine discrimination capabilities; most observed gains are artifacts of removal-budget effects, with true advantages limited to certain regimes (low prevalence or high recall under severe corruption).

title: How Should I Pick a Foundation Model for My Robot? In Favor of a Community Evaluation Framework for Social Robots
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the FoRMA workshop (Foundation Models in the RO-MAN Age: Responsible Development for Social Robotics) at IEEE RO-MAN 2026, Kitakyushu, Japan. Workshop homepage: https://sites.google.com/cam.ac.uk/forma/
summary: Researchers who seek to build social robot applications on foundation models are faced with a difficult question: how should we pick a model? Public leaderboards offer little guidance: the demands of real-time, embodied social interaction lie largely outside their focus.
