And direct evaluation is impractical at scale: each embodied study requires scarce participant, robot, and experimenter time. In this paper, we identify five evaluation dimensions for foundation models in social robots: (i) conversational competence, (ii) user safety, (iii) embodied character, (iv) target scene effectiveness, and (v) audience appropriateness. To make model selection cheaper and better informed, we propose a three-tiered evaluation funnel paradigm that first filters with general metrics, then extends to simulated interactions, and terminates in more expensive, robot-specific evaluation. We map all five dimensions across all three tiers, chart where applicable evaluation methods exist and are missing, and close with a call to action: let's build the evaluation framework together as a community.

AI.tldr: Proposes a three-tier evaluation funnel for foundation models in social robots across five dimensions, maps existing methods and gaps, and calls for community-driven framework development.
AI.motivation: Selecting suitable foundation models for socially interactive robots is hard due to real-time, embodied interaction demands that existing leaderboards do not capture and because direct large-scale evaluation is impractical.
AI.method: 1) Define five evaluation dimensions: conversational competence, user safety, embodied character, target scene effectiveness, audience appropriateness. 2) Propose a three-tier funnel: Tier 1 general metrics, Tier 2 simulated interactions, Tier 3 robot-specific, expensive evaluations. 3) Map dimensions across tiers to assess method availability and gaps. 4) Present a community call to build the framework.
AI.result: A structured evaluation framework outline that identifies where evaluation methods exist or are missing across three tiers for five dimensions, enabling cheaper-to-expensive model assessment.
AI.conclusion: Encourage collaborative development of a shared evaluation framework to improve model selection for social robots.

title: CoDAT: Collaborative Dual-Attention Transformer with Low-Cost Temporal Modeling for Efficient Edge Action Recognition
summary: Real-time human action recognition on Internet-of-Things (IoT) edge devices requires models that capture rich spatio-temporal cues within strict latency, memory, and power envelopes. Current 3D CNNs, video transformers, and shift-based ViT deliver high accuracy but come at computational costs that preclude edge IoT deployment. This paper proposes CoDAT, a Collaborative Dual-Attention Transformer that replaces conventional multi-head attention with a lightweight dual-branch module: Spatial Convolutional Attention (SCA) for local aggregation and Strided Single-Head Attention (SSHA) for global context. SSHA jointly compresses the spatial resolution and channel dimensions of the query, key, and value tensors via stride-based sparse projection, then fuses the resulting global and local features at a markedly reduced cost. To enable temporal communication across frames, a parameter-free TShift module is embedded in each block. Extensive experiments on Jetson AGX Orin and Raspberry Pi 5 demonstrate that CoDAT achieves an energy-accuracy balance in both image and action recognition. On ImageNet-1K, CoDAT-M runs 2x faster than EfficientViT384 and FastViT-S12 at comparable accuracy, and CoDAT-L matches ViT-S with 3x fewer parameters at 2x higher throughput. On Kinetics-400 and MA-52, CoDAT achieves competitive Top-1 accuracy against state-of-the-art CNN, transformer, and hybrid baselines while running up to 2.9x faster than VSwin-T, 2x faster than ViT-Temporal-Shift variants, and 5x faster than UniFormer-B. On UCF-101, CoDAT-S384 matches TokShift and LAPS while being 6x faster and requiring up to 13x fewer FLOPs, establishing an efficiency-accuracy balance for real-time action recognition in edge IoT perception systems. Code is available at https://github.com/novendrastywn/CoDAT .

AI.tldr: CoDAT introduces a lightweight dual-attention Transformer with local spatial attention and global strided attention, achieving real-time action recognition on edge IoT devices with strong energy efficiency and competitive accuracy across image and video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Edge IoT constraints (low latency, limited memory and power) require efficient spatio-temporal modeling. Standard 3D CNNs, video transformers, and shift-based ViTs are too computationally heavy for deployment on devices like Jetson and Raspberry Pi.
AI.method: Replace standard multi-head attention with two branches: Spatial Convolutional Attention (local) and Strided Single-Head Attention (global). SSHA uses stride-based sparse projection to compress Q/K/V, enabling global context at reduced cost. A parameter-free TShift module enables temporal communication across frames within each block.
AI.result: Empirical results show CoDAT delivers strong energy-accuracy balance on edge hardware. On ImageNet-1K, CoDAT-M is ~2x faster than EfficientViT384 and FastViT-S12 at similar accuracy; CoDAT-L matches ViT-S with 3x fewer parameters and 2x higher throughput. On Kinetics-400 and MA-52, CoDAT is competitive with CNNs, transformers, and hybrids, while running up to 2.9x faster than VSwin-T, 2x faster than ViT-Temporal-Shift variants, and 5x faster than UniFormer-B. On UCF-101, CoDAT-S384 matches TokShift and LAPS with ~6x speedup and up to 13x fewer FLOPs. Code available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: CoDAT demonstrates an efficient, edge-friendly architecture for real-time action recognition, achieving favorable energy-accuracy trade-offs and enabling deployment on resource-constrained IoT devices; the dual-attention design and strided attention mechanism contribute to reduced computation without sacrificing performance.

title: Automated item evaluation: Predicting item acceptance and rejection using LLM-generated critiques
summary: Automated item evaluation (AIE) refers to the use of computational methods to assess item quality without requiring manual expert review or field testing of the items under evaluation. We aimed to build a near-comprehensive AIE model by predicting item acceptance and rejection from item text using historical rejection data from a large-scale standardized testing program. The dataset contained 52,759 English language arts (ELA) and mathematics items with 34% permanently rejected from future operational use. Rejection reasons included poor psychometric properties, content issues, bias and sensitivity concerns, and non-content issues. We fine-tuned a DeBERTaV3-large classifier on raw item text, a second DeBERTa classifier on Qwen3-generated item critiques, and a fusion model combining representations from both. The fusion model achieved the strongest overall performance (Accuracy = .75, F1 = .64, AUC = .80, Sensitivity = .64, Specificity = .81). Prediction for math (F1 = .73, AUC = .86) was considerably more accurate than ELA (F1 = .51, AUC = .72). Lowering the decision threshold from .5 to .25 raised average sensitivity for ELA and math to .88 and .91, while reducing specificity to .31 and .56, respectively, which may be preferable in automated item generation contexts where generating items is cheaper than evaluating them. Incorporating item critiques alongside raw item text improved performance across most rejection reasons. The model assigned higher rejection probabilities to more difficult items. However, the fusion model struggled to identify items flagged for bias, sensitivity, fairness, or accessibility, especially for ELA. These findings suggest that text-based AIE is feasible in some areas and may offer a practical tool for reducing the burden of manual review and field testing, while also underscoring the importance of human review for items with fairness concerns.

AI.tldr: Text-based automated item evaluation (AIE) using DeBERTaV3 and critiques predicts item rejection; fusion model outperforms single models; math items more predictable than ELA; lowering threshold increases sensitivity; human review still needed for fairness concerns.
AI.motivation: Reduce manual item review and field testing burden by predicting item acceptance/rejection from item text using historical rejection data from a large-scale standardized testing program; aim for near-comprehensive coverage.
AI.method: Fine-tuned DeBERTaV3-large on raw item text; second DeBERTa on Qwen3-generated critiques; fusion model combining representations; evaluated on 52,759 items with 34% permanently rejected; analyzed rejection reasons; threshold tuning from 0.5 to 0.25; measured accuracy, F1, AUC, sensitivity, specificity.
AI.result: Fusion model achieved strongest overall performance: Accuracy 0.75, F1 0.64, AUC 0.80, Sensitivity 0.64, Specificity 0.81; Math: F1 0.73, AUC 0.86; ELA: F1 0.51, AUC 0.72. Lower threshold improved sensitivity to 0.88 (ELA) and 0.91 (math) but reduced specificity to 0.31 and 0.56. Critiques improved performance across most rejection reasons; model assigned higher rejection probabilities to more difficult items; fusion struggled to identify items flagged for bias, sensitivity, fairness, or accessibility, especially for ELA.
AI.conclusion: Text-based AIE is feasible in some areas and may reduce manual review burden, but human review remains essential for fairness concerns; performance varies by subject and rejection reason; indicates value for automated item generation contexts but with caution regarding bias/fairness.

title: Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation: Experimental Design for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects under Population Shift
summary: Randomized experiments are often run in one population to guide decisions in another. Allocating by experimental proportions wastes budget on groups that rarely appear in deployment, whereas allocating by deployment proportions under-samples groups that are hard to measure precisely. We propose \textbf{TWNA} (Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation), a two-stage stratified design that uses pilot estimates of group--arm outcome variances to allocate final-stage sample sizes and treatment probabilities for target-weighted group average treatment effect (GATE) precision. The oracle rule has a closed form and balances deployment importance with statistical difficulty; the plug-in rule recovers it as pilot variance estimates stabilize. We also extend TWNA to handle uncertainty about deployment composition, remaining robust whether the target mix is roughly known or entirely unknown. Finally, we distinguish this weight robustness from a pilot-robust variant for skewed, rare-event, or contaminated outcomes. Simulations and real-covariate benchmarks show the largest gains when groups are both deployment-important and difficult to measure.

AI.tldr: Two-stage Target-Weighted Neyman Allocation (TWNA) selects final-stage sample sizes and treatment allocations across deployment-relevant groups to minimize error in estimating a target-weighted GATE, using pilot variances; contains an oracle closed-form rule, a plug-in estimator that converges, and extensions to deployment-uncertainty with robustness properties; showing gains when deployment importance and measurement difficulty align.
AI.motivation: Improve efficiency of randomized experiments when results are applied to a deployment population, by balancing deployment importance against statistical difficulty of estimating group-specific effects.
AI.method: Two-stage stratified design. Use pilot estimates of group–arm variances to compute deployment-weighted precision for each group; derive an oracle allocation rule with closed form; implement a plug-in rule that uses stabilized pilot variances; extend to uncertain deployment composition with robustness guarantees; compare to pilot-robust variants for skewed/rare outcomes.
AI.result: Simulations and real-covariate benchmarks show largest gains when groups are both deployment-important and difficult to measure; TWNA improves precision efficiency for GATE under target mix; robustness to deployment composition uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: TWNA provides an efficient, robust framework for cross-population experimentation by targeting precision through a weight-aware Neyman allocation, with practical plug-in estimators and extensions to composition uncertainty.

title: Spatiotemporal Agility: Time-Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Guided Dynamic Quadrupedal Interception
summary: Legged robots require robust agility to perceive and interact with complex and dynamic environments within a constrained time. However, most existing quadruped locomotion works rely on velocity-tracking policy, which struggle to reach precise targets within strict temporal constraints. Moreover, integrating real-time perception with agile locomotion for highly dynamic targets remains challenging due to sensor latency and processing delays. To concretely study and benchmark such agility in dynamic settings, we introduce a challenging ball-catching task for legged robots. This paper proposes an integrated framework that combines a vision module for landing point and time prediction with a direct position and time conditioned RL locomotion policy, instead of intermediate velocity commands. Beyond the method design, this work presents a system-level contribution that completes real-time robotic interception system that integrates multi-camera perception, online trajectory prediction, low-latency target communication, and sim-to-real locomotion control into a closed-loop deployment pipeline. By explicitly predicting the future spatial-temporal target, our approach mitigates perception latency during dynamic interception. We conducted extensive ball-catching experiments for the legged robot. Through comparative experiments against a velocity-tracking baseline, our direct target-conditioned approach achieves a higher success rate in catching balls with predicted landing spots within 2 meters and flight times between 0.8 and 1.2 seconds. This shows that the robot has successfully completed the dynamic ball-catching task under our tested setup. Furthermore, our policy exhibits a smaller performance gap after deployment, suggesting improved sim-to-real behavior in these trials.

AI.tldr: Direct target-conditioned RL locomotion paired with a vision-based landing-point/time predictor outperforms velocity-tracking baselines in real-time ball-catching tasks for legged robots, demonstrating improved sim-to-real transfer within a closed-loop, multi-camera system.
AI.motivation: Address latency and precision issues in dynamic interception where traditional velocity-tracking policies fail under strict temporal constraints; enable tight perception–action coupling for agile legged locomotion.
AI.method: Integrate a vision module that predicts landing point and time with a direct position-and-time conditioned RL policy (no velocity commands). Build a system-level pipeline with multi-camera perception, online trajectory prediction, low-latency communication, and sim-to-real deployment in a closed loop.
AI.result: In experiments, the direct target-conditioned approach achieves higher catching success within 2 m predicted landing spots and 0.8–1.2 s flight times, outperforming a velocity-tracking baseline, and shows a reduced performance gap post-deployment, indicating better sim-to-real robustness.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly predicting future spatial-temporal targets and conditioning the policy on position/time improves dynamic interception for legged robots, with strong system integration enabling real-time operation under perception latency.

title: Suppress and Diversify: Refining Robust Pathways for Corruption Robustness
summary: Model robustness against natural image corruptions is essential for safety-critical applications. While existing methods primarily focus on implicit representation learning, we provide the first systematic exploration of computational pathways to explicitly characterize internal robustness. We identify a progressive decay of robust features across network layers and establish a functional dependency between the prevalence of these features and model performance. To exploit these insights, we propose Suppress and Diversify (S\&D), a non-intrusive refinement approach that enhances robustness by dynamically selecting robust pathways and diversifying them through symmetry-preserving transformations. S\&D is architecture-agnostic, parameter-free, and incurs zero test-time overhead. Extensive evaluations across eight benchmarks demonstrate that S\&D consistently improves performance across multiple vision tasks, diverse backbones, and complex real-world scenarios, highlighting its broad efficacy and scalability.

AI.tldr: A non-intrusive, architecture-agnostic refinement (S&D) that enhances robustness to natural image corruptions by suppressing non-robust pathways and diversifying robust ones via symmetry-preserving transformations, achieving zero test-time overhead and improvements across eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To move beyond implicit robustness analysis, the authors systematically study how robust features decay across layers and how their prevalence correlates with performance, aiming to explicitly characterize internal robustness and guide refinement.
AI.method: Identify robust feature pathways and implement Suppress and Diversify: dynamically select robust pathways (suppress non-robust) and apply symmetry-preserving transformations to diversify robust ones; the approach is non-intrusive, architecture-agnostic, parameter-free, and incurs no test-time cost.
AI.result: S&D yields consistent performance gains across various vision tasks, backbones, and real-world scenarios in eight benchmarks, demonstrating broad efficacy and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Explicit robustness characterization plus S&D offers a practical, scalable strategy for improving model robustness without sacrificing efficiency, applicable across architectures.

title: NxN E-valuation: Hypothesis Certification via a Conformal CRT Null
summary: We propose NxN E-valuation, a handy, e-value-based hypothesis-certification algorithm that lets a hypothesis be verified without building any case-specific certification procedure---such as constructing a dedicated null hypothesis---as long as a large enough dataset is available. The method is especially suited to LLM-based exploration systems, where LLMs are remarkably good at proposing hypotheses but suffer badly from hallucination; this hallucination prevents us from harvesting LLM outputs directly, and existing remedies each fall short. The most common solutions include letting the LLM verify or correct itself circular verification and held-out testing (where false hypotheses can still pass via spurious correlations), among other remedies detailed in the introduction. To resolve this, NxN E-valuation exploits the naturally existing large training set and lets different samples serve as null hypotheses for one another. This design directly realizes a conditional randomization test (CRT) that certifies each hypothesis. The approach can be a universally better replacement for at least LLM circular verification and held-out-data testing, provided the LLM's generations are hypotheses that apply to each individual sample.

AI.tldr: Introduces NxN E-valuation, an e-value-based, CRT-like framework for hypothesis certification that uses large datasets to verify hypotheses without bespoke null-hypothesis procedures.
AI.motivation: LLMs often propose hypotheses but suffer from hallucination; existing remedies (circular verification, held-out testing) are insufficient or flawed; a scalable, data-driven certification method is needed for LLM-driven exploration.
AI.method: Leverages a large existing training set so that different samples serve as null hypotheses for one another, implementing a conditional randomization test (CRT) to certify each hypothesis across samples.
AI.result: Offers a CRT-based mechanism to certify hypotheses using cross-sample nulls, aiming to outperform traditional verification methods (circular verification and held-out data testing) for LLM-generated hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: NxN E-valuation has the potential to universally replace current verification remedies in LLM exploration, provided that LLM outputs are treated as hypotheses at the level of individual samples.

title: CertBind from Multimodal Connectivity to Certifiable Retrieval Decisions
summary: Lightweight connectors make frozen multimodal encoders composable at the representation level. Deployment exposes a second problem at the level of task decisions. A connected route can expand cross-modal reach while changing an established native retrieval capability. We introduce CertBind, a multiscale theory of certifiable composition for frozen multimodal connector graphs. At the node scale, native anchors establish the exact task identification boundary under the stated chart model. At the edge scale, contract-aware conformal ranks provide graph-wide family-wise error control. At the path scale, an overlap-aware budget and clean calibration yield a finite-sample recovery radius under declared conditions. At the query scale, this radius yields a covered top-k candidate set that becomes a point certificate when its size equals k. CertBind therefore retains supported routes as Direct, sends only flagged routes to recovery, returns Certified for decisive recovery, and returns Abstain for unresolved queries. The evaluated C-MCR shared route reduced native CLIP R@1 from 0.524 to 0.290. The production fallback recovered 0.963 +- 0.002 of clean retrieval, while the passing branch recorded a no-harm value of 1.000. CertBind extends multimodal composability from connected representations to certifiable task decisions.

AI.tldr: CertBind introduces a multiscale certifiable framework for composing frozen multimodal encoders via a graph-theoretic approach, enabling certifiable task decisions with finite-sample guarantees and practical recovery mechanisms; it demonstrates robust results on CLIP-based retrieval with distinct decision paths.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of certifiably preserving task decisions when composing frozen multimodal components, ensuring reliable retrieval under composition-induced uncertainties.
AI.method: A multiscale theory: (node scale) native anchors define exact task boundaries under a chart model; (edge scale) contract-aware conformal ranks for graph-wide error control; (path scale) overlap-aware budgets and calibrated recovery yielding finite-sample recovery radius; (query scale) radius yields a top-k set leading to a point certificate when size equals k. Decision policy: Direct (keep route), flagged to recovery, Certified (decisive recovery), Abstain (unresolved).
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a C-MCR shared route shows CLIP R@1 dropping from 0.524 to 0.290; production fallback recovered 0.963±0.002 of clean retrieval; apart from a passing branch with no-harm value of 1.000.
AI.conclusion: CertBind extends multimodal composability from representation-level connectivity to certifiable task decisions, providing finite-sample guarantees and a structured recovery mechanism for uncertain routes.

title: Cross-View Action Consistency for Camera-Robust Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned from a fixed scene camera can fail when the camera is moved, even when the task, objects, language, and robot state are unchanged. We study scene-camera viewpoint robustness using only a scene RGB image, language, and proprioception, without camera labels, extrinsics, depth, or point-cloud inputs. The wrist stream is masked throughout to prevent an unperturbed visual shortcut from confounding attribution to scene-camera variation. For flow-based VLAs, we propose to regularize the action-flow velocity field, the quantity directly integrated to generate continuous action chunks. We construct action-equivalent view pairs by resetting original LIBERO demonstrations to the same MuJoCo state and rendering nominal and perturbed scene-camera views. Both views are supervised by flow matching, while a cross-view loss encourages their predicted action-flow velocities to agree at the same sampled flow coordinates. On the LIBERO-Plus camera-perturbation track, our method reaches 87.2$\pm$0.4% (4,797 rollouts per seed across 3 training seeds), +7.4pp over flow-matching-only training on the same paired data (79.8$\pm$0.8%, also 3 seeds) and +12.5pp over naive mixed-camera SFT, while maintaining nominal-camera ID performance (95.0$\pm$0.8%; same-data FM-only: 95.0$\pm$4.3%). A shuffled-pair control collapses to 25.8%, showing that the gain depends on action-equivalent pairing. On a real robot, we evaluate three tabletop tasks with 10 rollouts per task and camera placement; held-out-camera success improves from 53.3% to 74.4% under the same single-scene-RGB inference interface.

AI.tldr: A method to improve camera-view robustness for flow-based vision-language-action policies by enforcing cross-view consistency of action-flow velocities using action-equivalent view pairs, achieving strong gains on a camera-perturbation benchmark and real-robot tasks while preserving nominal performance.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can fail when camera viewpoints change; the work aims to achieve viewpoint robustness using only scene RGB, language, and proprioception, without camera extrinsics or depth, and without relying on a visual shortcut from the wrist.
AI.method: Regularize the action-flow velocity field by constructing action-equivalent view pairs: reset demonstrations to the same MuJoCo state and render nominal and perturbed scene-camera views. Apply flow matching to both views and add a cross-view loss that aligns action-flow velocities at corresponding flow coordinates. Mask the wrist stream to avoid shortcuts. Train on LIBERO demonstrations (LIBERO-Plus camera-perturbation track) and evaluate on a real robot with three tabletop tasks.
AI.result: LIBERO-Plus camera-perturbation track: 87.2±0.4% success (4,797 rollouts per seed across 3 seeds), +7.4pp vs flow-matching-only training on paired data; +12.5pp vs naive mixed-camera supervised fine-tuning; nominal-camera ID performance remains high at 95.0±0.8%. Shuffled-pair control drops to 25.8%, indicating the gain relies on proper action-equivalent pairing. Real robot: held-out-camera success improves from 53.3% to 74.4% across three tasks with 10 rollouts per task.
AI.conclusion: Cross-view velocity alignment via action-equivalent view pairing yields robust camera-view generalization for flow-based VLA policies, maintaining nominal performance and transferring to real-robot scenarios.

title: WaveFreqAnchor: Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion for Training-Free Face Restoration
comment: training-free wavelet-structural diffusion sampling framework for face restoration that improves structural stability, identity consistency, and real-world perceptual quality without task-specific fine-tuning
summary: Diffusion-based face restoration that adjusts the sampling trajectory of pre-trained diffusion models has achieved remarkable progress. However, existing approaches provide insufficient constraints during reverse diffusion, causing identity-related structural drift and degraded fidelity under severe degradations. To address this, we propose WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free framework based on Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion. Specifically, Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) constrains facial structures through anisotropic wave-response consistency, while Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) aligns the predicted low-frequency subband with the observation by replacing its phase, correcting inconsistencies accumulated during reverse diffusion. For real-world scenes, we further introduce Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE), which performs bounded, spatially masked refinement on the predicted high-frequency subbands to recover fine facial details under unknown compound degradations. Together, these designs effectively preserve facial identity while restoring sharp and realistic facial details. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving high-quality and high-fidelity face restoration.

AI.tldr: A training-free diffusion-based face restoration framework (WaveFreqAnchor) that combines ASWG, MWFI, and SHE to preserve identity and enhance details under severe degradations.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based face restoration has progressed but suffers from identity-related structural drift and fidelity loss during reverse diffusion, especially under strong degradations; existing methods often rely on learning-based constraints. A training-free framework with explicit structural consistency and frequency-domain corrections is needed to maintain identity and restore fine details in real-world conditions.
AI.method: Proposes Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) to enforce anisotropic wave-response consistency on facial structures; Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) to align the predicted low-frequency subband with the observation by replacing its phase; Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE) to refine high-frequency subbands with bounded, spatially masked adjustments for unknown degradations. The framework is training-free and operates within the reverse-diffusion process.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the method consistently outperforms existing approaches, delivering high-quality and high-fidelity face restoration while preserving identity across various degradation levels and real-world scenes.
AI.conclusion: WaveFreqAnchor effectively preserves facial identity and recovers sharp, realistic facial details in diffusion-based restoration, demonstrating strong performance in real-world scenarios without requiring additional training.

title: Shape Your Feed: An LLM-based Agentic System for Conversational Recommendation
summary: Industrial recommendation systems predominantly adopt a passive ranking paradigm that infers user preferences from implicit behavioral signals (e.g., clicks, dwell time) rather than explicit, natural language inputs. As a result, users experience a persistent discrepancy between their explicit interests and what passive behavioral algorithms deliver, limiting their ability to express nuanced preferences or steer their feed in real time. To address this growing gap between how recommendations are optimized and how users wish to articulate their interests, we present Shape Your Feed (SYF), an LLM-based agentic recommendation framework that enables real-time, multimodal co-curation of content. SYF employs a three-tier architecture: (i) a Perception Flow that captures fine-grained user intent from text prompts, voice commands, and UI interactions; (ii) a Serving Flow that performs real-time agentic re-ranking and pruning of candidate items, grounded in a persistent Semantic Profile encoding evolving user preferences; and (iii) a Self-Evolution Flow that aligns system behavior with human judgments via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and an LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble. Offline evaluations show that SYF's alignment scoring module achieves 98.85% accuracy, substantially improving over strong few-shot baselines. Large-scale online A/B experiments on production traffic further demonstrate that SYF improves feed relevance and user sentiment, indicating a practical and scalable path toward interactive, user-steerable recommendation in industrial settings.

AI.tldr: LLM-based agentic recommender (SYF) enables real-time, multimodal user-guided content curation via perception, serving, and self-evolution flows, achieving high alignment and improved online relevance.
AI.motivation: Bridges the gap between explicit user interests and traditional passive, implicit feedback in industrial recommender systems by enabling real-time, user-steerable control using multimodal signals.
AI.method: Three-tier architecture: (i) Perception Flow captures intent from text, voice, and UI; (ii) Serving Flow performs real-time agentic re-ranking/pruning with a persistent Semantic Profile; (iii) Self-Evolution Flow uses Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and LLM-based judge ensemble to align behavior with human judgments; supports offline alignment evaluation and large-scale online A/B testing.
AI.result: Offline alignment module achieves 98.85% accuracy and outperforms strong few-shot baselines; online A/B tests show improved feed relevance and user sentiment in production traffic.
AI.conclusion: SYF demonstrates a practical, scalable path to interactive, user-steerable recommendations in industry by integrating multimodal intent, real-time agentic curation, and continuous alignment with human judgments.

title: Online Security Learning in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems under Hidden Byzantine Attacks
summary: We study online cooperative control of a multi-agent system under Byzantine attacks. Namely, an unknown, fixed subset of agents are Byzantine comprised and can stealthily overwrite its own coordinates of the team's planned joint action after observing that plan. The learner observes planned actions, public rewards, and public states, but neither the overwrite nor the executed joint action. Our objective is security: to optimize the team performance against the worst overwrites and achieve the optimal security value. We first show that the attacker's information determines the geometry. An attacker that observes the planned action induces an exact $(s,a)$-rectangular robust Markov decision process (MDP) whose rows are convex hulls of overwrite-induced public-outcome laws, whereas a blind attacker induces an $s$-rectangular model. We then identify the information-theoretic limit of security learning, showing that the security regret decomposes exactly into return regret against the response generating the data and a cumulative response gap $D_K$. Two indistinguishable horizon-one instances force $Ω(K)$ expected security regret while return regret is zero, showing that dependence on $D_K$ is unavoidable. Finally, we develop a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions learner and prove a regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(H^2S\sqrt{AK}\right)+\mathbb E[D_K]$. Our studies thus provide comprehensive theoretical and algorithmic foundations of reliable multi-agent systems under Byzantine attacks.

AI.tldr: Analyzes online cooperative control under Byzantine attacks, reveals attacker-information-driven geometry (exact s,a-rectangular robust MDP for informed attackers vs s-rectangular for blind), proves an information-theoretic security-limit with a regret decomposition that includes an unavoidable cumulative response gap D_K, and proposes a stage-tied robust EST-to-decisions learner with regret Õ(H^2 S √(A K)) + E[D_K].
AI.motivation: Ensure reliable multi-agent control when the system is subject to stealthy Byzantine attacks, by identifying fundamental geometry constraints, learning limits, and designing regret-bounded algorithms.
AI.method: Classify attacker information (informed vs blind) and show resulting robust MDP structures; derive an information-theoretic decomposition of security regret into return regret plus cumulative response gap D_K; establish lower bounds via indistinguishable horizon-one instances; design a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions learner and prove a regret bound.
AI.result: Characterization of how attacker information shapes the robust decision-model geometry; a precise regret decomposition including D_K; a learning algorithm with a provable regret bound that scales with horizon, state, actions, and number of agents, plus the expected D_K term.
AI.conclusion: The work provides theoretical and algorithmic foundations for secure multi-agent control under Byzantine threats, highlighting geometry driven by attacker information and the unavoidable D_K term in security regret, and delivering a robust learning approach with explicit regret guarantees.

title: Exact Thrust-Reversal Limits of Bidirectional Propellers under Bounded Motor Inputs
summary: Bidirectional propellers are often treated as signed thrust sources, but their thrust is a signed-quadratic function of rotor speed.Thus, thrust reversal necessarily occurs through zero rotor speed, where the ability of a bounded motor torque to change thrust collapses.This work formalizes this obstruction by studying exact thrust-trajectory reproducibility under bounded motor inputs with prescribed smoothness.We derive a normalized thrust-coordinate model with vanishing input gain at zero thrust, and prove necessary and sufficient reproducibility conditions in terms of the zero-crossing order of the desired thrust.Generic reversals, in which thrust crosses zero with nonzero slope, require unbounded motor input; the resulting conditions provide direct design rules for shaping thrust reversals that avoid singular motor commands.We also derive the corresponding current and voltage regularity requirements for a DC motor driving a bidirectional propeller.Experiments on a motor-propeller setup validate the predicted reversal-order effects, showing localized current/voltage peaks and thrust-tracking degradation for linear reversals, but not for higher-order reversals.These results expose an intrinsic actuator-level limitation that must be considered in force, acceleration, and interaction-control references for aerial robots.

AI.tldr: Bidirectional propellers behave as signed-quadratic thrust sources; thrust reversals at zero rotor speed impose unbounded motor inputs for generic zero-crossings, requiring design rules to shape reversals and avoid singular commands; experimentally validated actuator limitations for aerial robots.
AI.motivation: Understand fundamental actuator limits for thrust reversals in bidirectional propellers and how input constraints impact thrust-tracking and control in aerial robotics.
AI.method: Derive a normalized thrust-coordinate model with vanishing input gain at zero thrust; prove necessary and sufficient reproducibility conditions via zero-crossing order of the desired thrust; derive current/voltage regularity requirements for a DC motor; perform experiments on a motor–propeller setup to observe reversal-order effects.
AI.result: Reversals with nonzero slope (generic zero-crossings) require unbounded motor input; higher-order zero-crossings allow bounded inputs; experiments show localized current/voltage peaks and thrust-tracking degradation for linear reversals, but not for higher-order reversals.
AI.conclusion: Actuator-level limitations are intrinsic for force/acceleration and interaction-control in aerial robots; design rules shaping thrust reversals are necessary to avoid singular motor commands and ensure safe, smooth control.

title: Beyond Starry Night: Shortcut-Aware Control-State Planning for Artist-Grounded Text to Image Generation
comment: 47 pages, 13 figures, including appendices. Kuan Xing and Ye Wang contributed equally
summary: Artist-grounded image generation requires more than appending an artist name to a prompt. Image models often respond to artist names through canonical shortcuts, such as recurring motifs, generic palettes, or overrepresented period signatures, rather than preserving the user's intended scene. We introduce Atelier, a shortcut-aware control-state planning framework for artist-grounded image generation. Atelier translates underspecified artistic intent into an explicit control state that separates scene anchors, preserve/transform decisions, style-regime hypotheses, role-bound artist evidence, and shortcut-avoidance constraints. It grounds this state using artist-level knowledge and local patch references, compiles backend-aware generation plans, and iteratively refines candidates through global and local authenticity feedback. We further introduce ArtIntentBench, a benchmark covering Van Gogh and Qi Baishi across artwork re-rendering, period/style-controlled generation, historically unseen subjects, shortcut auditing, and human preference evaluation. Across open-weight and closed-source generators, Atelier improves artist-level style fidelity, preserves source structure more faithfully, and substantially reduces shortcut substitution compared with prompt-engineered, retrieval-augmented, and general-purpose agent baselines. These results suggest that artist-grounded generation is bottlenecked not only by image synthesis, but by the upstream inference of explicit, evidence-grounded artistic controls.

AI.tldr: Proposes Atelier, a shortcut-aware control-state planning framework for artist-grounded image generation, and ArtIntentBench, a benchmark for evaluating artist-level fidelity and shortcut auditing. Demonstrates improved artist-level style fidelity, structure preservation, and reduced shortcut substitution across open-weight and closed-source generators.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based embedding of artist names often triggers canonical shortcuts (motifs, palettes, period cues) that misalign with user intent. There is a need for explicit, evidence-grounded artistic controls to faithfully realize user-specified scenes and styles.
AI.method: Develop a control-state planning framework that translates artistic intent into explicit states: scene anchors, preserve/transform decisions, style-regime hypotheses, role-bound artist evidence, and shortcut-avoidance constraints. Ground the state with artist knowledge and local patch references, generate backend-aware plans, and iteratively refine via global and local authenticity feedback. Introduce ArtIntentBench with tasks spanning re-rendering, style/period control, unseen subjects, shortcut auditing, and human preferences.
AI.result: Across open-weight and closed-source generators, Atelier improves artist-level style fidelity, preserves source structure more faithfully, and substantially reduces shortcut substitution compared with prompt-engineered, retrieval-augmented, and general-purpose agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: Artist-grounded generation bottlenecks lie not only in synthesis but in inferring explicit, evidence-grounded artistic controls; explicit control-state planning can mitigate shortcut-driven mismatches and improve fidelity to the intended artist style.

title: TRACE: A Multi-Layer Benchmark for Human AI Controller Coordination Under Drift and Failure
comment: This work was accepted for presentation and publication at the 25th IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA 2026)
summary: Modern cyber-physical and AI-assisted systems couple human operators, AI decision modules, and automated controllers in a single control loop, so trustworthiness depends on the whole loop, not any one model. Yet no standard benchmark captures time-aligned, multi-layer traces of how drift and failures propagate across these layers, so we cannot diagnose where coordination breaks down, why, or how to recover. This paper targets one facet of that gap: drift, a deviation that can originate in any stack layer and that conventional single-modality monitoring cannot localize to a layer or pin to an onset time. We construct a benchmark by injecting controlled drift into traces derived from ALFRED, a grounded-instruction benchmark for everyday household tasks, yielding 1,918 drifted traces. Each trace is a time-aligned sequence of per-step records across five execution layers (state, observation, decision, rules, control), labeled with the drift type, affected layer, onset time, responsible actor, and causal mechanism, and validated by independent raters with inter-annotator agreement reported. We pair the dataset with a leak-aware protocol that removes a near-perfect onset leak, and a baseline study across classical, recurrent, and attention-based model families. Under this honest protocol, drift is identifiable and attributable well above random and majority baselines across every family (affected layer macro-F1 near 0.70, responsible actor near 0.85, causal mechanism near 0.49), and heavy attention offers no advantage over simpler models on this symbolic benchmark.

AI.tldr: A multi-layer drift benchmark for CPS/AI systems; 1,918 drifted traces across five layers derived from ALFRED; shown to be identifiable under a leak-aware protocol; baseline models perform reasonably, with heavy attention not superior on this symbolic task.
AI.motivation: No standard benchmark captures time-aligned, multi-layer traces showing how drift and failures propagate across CPS/AI control loops; need to diagnose where coordination breaks down and how to recover.
AI.method: Inject controlled drift into ALFRED traces to create 1,918 drifted traces. Each trace records per-step data across five layers (state, observation, decision, rules, control) with labels: drift type, affected layer, onset time, responsible actor, causal mechanism. Validate labels with independent raters (inter-annotator agreement). Apply a leak-aware onset protocol to remove leakage. Evaluate baseline models (classical, recurrent, attention-based) on drift identification and attribution.
AI.result: Under the honest protocol, drift is identifiable and attributable above random/majority baselines across model families. Affected layer macro-F1 ~0.70; responsible actor ~0.85; causal mechanism ~0.49. Heavy attention offers no advantage over simpler models on this symbolic benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The dataset enables diagnosing drift propagation across layered control loops and provides a robust evaluation protocol. Results suggest that simpler models can match or exceed heavy-attention approaches on this symbolic, multi-layer drift task, with the leak-aware protocol ensuring credible onset localization.

title: Robust Average-Reward Markov Decision Processes: Minimax-Optimal Learning via Plug-in Reductions
summary:
Distributionally robust Markov decision processes provide a principled framework for sequential decision making under model uncertainty. We study how many samples are necessary and sufficient to learn an $\varepsilon$-optimal robust policy under the average-reward criterion. A generative model provides samples from the nominal transition kernel, whereas policy performance is evaluated over $(s,a)$-rectangular total-variation uncertainty sets of radius at most $σ$.
  Let $H_0$ and $H_σ$ denote the nominal and robust optimal bias spans, respectively. We identify $σH_0$ as the perturbation scale separating high- and low-tolerance regimes. Our matching upper and lower bounds show that, up to logarithmic factors, the minimax total sample complexity is $$ NSA \asymp \frac{SA}{\varepsilon^2}\begin{cases} \min\{H_0,H_σ\}, & \varepsilon\gtrsimσH_0,\\ \min\{H_0,H_σ\}+σH_σ^2, & \varepsilon\lesssimσH_0. \end{cases} $$ Here $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, and $N$ is the number of samples per state-action pair. The sample complexity consists of a linear-span term that resembles the nominal AMDP results and a robustness-specific term that appears only in the low-tolerance regime. We attain these rates using reduction-based plug-in procedures that select the reduction---nominal or robust---and its discount factor: a span-informed procedure that makes these choices using known span parameters, and a span-agnostic procedure that calibrates both choices from data.

AI.tldr: Identifies sample complexity for learning an epsilon-optimal robust policy in distributionally robust MDPs under average reward with (s,a)-rectangular total-variation uncertainty; provides matching upper/lower bounds and two plug-in reduction procedures.
AI.motivation: Understand how many samples are needed to learn robust policies under model uncertainty in average-reward MDPs; quantify the impact of robustness level and bias spans on sample complexity.
AI.method: Minimax analysis yielding matching upper and lower bounds. Reduction-based plug-in procedures that select nominal or robust reductions and the corresponding discount factor. Two variants: span-informed (uses known bias-span parameters) and span-agnostic (estimates/p calibrates from data).
AI.result: Minimax total sample complexity NSA scales as (SA/ε^2) times a piecewise term: when ε ≳ σ H0, NSA ∝ (SA/ε^2) min{H0, Hσ}; when ε ≲ σ H0, NSA ∝ (SA/ε^2) [min{H0, Hσ} + σ Hσ^2]. Here S,A are states/actions; N samples per (s,a); H0 and Hσ are nominal and robust optimal bias spans; σ is the total-variation radius.
AI.conclusion: The derived rates are tight up to logarithmic factors; robustness increases sample complexity only in the low-tolerance regime via an additive term σ Hσ^2. The paper also provides practical, reduction-based algorithms (span-informed and span-agnostic) to achieve these rates.

title: Decoupling Intention from Trajectory: A Representational Deduction Framework for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) aim to construct a unified architecture capable of understanding world state evolution and guiding to generative motion planning. However, existing visual branches focus on predicting static visual observation, rather than reflecting potential transition information that captures the evolution of world states under motion interactions. This leads to representational entanglement between high-level physical condition evolution and low-level action trajectory generation within the Action Model, creating a structural bottleneck while weakening the predictive capability of world evolution modeling for action generation. We propose PILOT (Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories), whose core Representational Deduction (RD) bridges this gap by integrating motion thought-of-chain (CoT) guidance as a native model capability. Specifically, RD aims to encourage the action branch to explicitly model potential state transition tokens, which are retained as CoT in the reasoning space to guide fine-grained motion trajectory. Experiments demonstrate that RD not only significantly improves the success rate and generalization ability of WAMs in complex robotic manipulation tasks but also enhances the model's physical interpretability by decoupling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details. Furthermore, the abundant state transition supervision signals introduced by RD effectively alleviate the sparse supervision in action generation, enabling it to serve as an efficient few-shot real-robot fine-tuning strategy and demonstrating superior scalability for migration to mainstream WAM architectures.

AI.tldr: PILOT introduces Representational Deduction (RD) to decouple high-level world-state evolution from low-level motion generation in World Action Models, using state-transition tokens and motion thought-of-chain guidance to improve planning, interpretability, and data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current WAM visual branches predict only static observations, entangling high-level state evolution with low-level action generation and weakening predictive modeling of world dynamics for action planning.
AI.method: Introduce Representational Deduction (RD) that integrates motion thought-of-chain (CoT) guidance as a native capability. The action branch explicitly models potential state-transition tokens, retained in reasoning space to guide fine-grained motion trajectories.
AI.result: RD substantially improves success rate and generalization in complex robotic manipulation tasks; enhances physical interpretability by decoupling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details; introduces abundant state-transition supervision that mitigates sparse supervision in action generation, enabling effective few-shot real-robot fine-tuning and scalable migration to mainstream WAMs.
AI.conclusion: RD’s decoupled representation and state-transition supervision improve World Action Model capability for modeling world evolution and generating trajectories, with better generalization, interpretability, and transfer efficiency.

title: Explore or Converge? Stage-Guided Per-Step Optimization for Diffusion Models
summary:
Diffusion models have strong generative capabilities. However, their maximum likelihood training objective only focuses on reconstructing the data distribution, making it difficult to align with specific preferences. Reinforcement learning (RL) for preference alignment in diffusion models is promising but limited by reward sparsity. Since a single reward cannot support optimization, existing RL methods usually backpropagate the final reward to all previous steps. However, denoising is stage-wise, with distinct semantics and controllability. Repeating the final reward across all steps creates a temporal objective mismatch, encouraging reward shortcuts that lead to reward hacking. At the same time, due to reward backfilling, each time step receives the same reward, making it impossible to distinguish between actions, thereby weakening the optimization process.
  To resolve this issue, we propose Stage-Guided Per-Step Optimization (SGPO) for diffusion models, which jointly leverages signal-to-noise ratio and semantic changes to identify generation stages and adaptively assign stage-specific objectives. Early denoising is chaotic and far from the final reward, resulting in weak reward-behavior correlation. This stage should prioritize exiting the chaotic state. In the mid stage, the latent transitions to a stable structure, where the final reward better corresponds to generative behavior. Therefore, this stage optimizes the final reward while exploring diversity to avoid early convergence to a single mode.
  In the late stage, the latent's core structure is largely fixed, and preference optimization mainly amplifies local details, risking overfitting. Therefore, stable convergence is preferred to avoid quality degradation. Results from 16 comparative experiments validate SGPO. Our method achieves 26.7% average gains in generative quality and 36.7% higher convergence speed.

AI.tldr: Stage-Guided Per-Step Optimization (SGPO) for diffusion models aligns RL rewards with generation stages, improving quality and convergence by per-step, stage-dependent objectives.
AI.motivation: Mitigate temporal objective mismatch and reward backfilling in reward-based diffusion training; leverage SNR and semantic changes to identify stages and assign stage-specific objectives.
AI.method: Identify generation stages from signal-to-noise ratio and semantic changes; assign early-stage objectives to exit chaotic denoising, mid-stage optimize final reward with diversity, late-stage favor stable convergence; validate across 16 comparisons; report gains.
AI.result: 26.7% average gains in generative quality; 36.7% faster convergence.
AI.conclusion: Stage-aware per-step optimization reduces reward-hacking and enhances alignment and efficiency in diffusion model training; demonstrated effectiveness across multiple experiments.

title: CellWorld: From Gene-Level Reconstruction to Latent Cell Prediction in Spatial Transcriptomics Foundation Models
summary: This paper shows that latent-space predictive pretraining can provide a scalable route to foundation models for spatial transcriptomics. Existing spatial transcriptomics foundation models primarily reconstruct masked gene identities or expression values, potentially encouraging the reproduction of assay-specific technical variation and limiting representation transferability. To avoid directly reconstructing such variation, we shift the prediction target from observed gene measurements to latent cell representations and introduce CellWorld, which predicts the latent representations of masked cells from visible spatial context and a limited partial-expression hint. We pretrain four CellWorld variants, spanning 5.74M to 94.56M trainable parameters, on a corpus of 46 million human cells. Our controlled scaling experiments show that performance improves with model capacity, particularly on spatial tasks, while spatial transfer depends more on sufficient optimization and broad biological source diversity than on cell count alone. Across four held-out datasets, even CellWorld-Small, with 5.74M trainable parameters, outperforms every baseline on all 11 linear-probe benchmarks and all seven fine-tuned spatial benchmarks. Most notably, a frozen CellWorld-Large pretrained on only 5\% of the corpus with broad biological source coverage outperforms every fully fine-tuned baseline across all seven spatial benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/UoM-HealthAI/CellWorld.

AI.tldr: CellWorld introduces latent-space predictive pretraining for spatial transcriptomics, achieving strong transfer and performance with scalable models; even a small model outperforms baselines, and a large frozen model trained on limited data outperforms fully fine-tuned baselines.
AI.motivation: Address potential leakage of assay-specific technical variation in reconstruction-based spatial transcriptomics models by predicting latent cell representations rather than observed gene measurements; enable scalable, transferable foundation models using diverse biological sources.
AI.method: Pretrain four CellWorld variants (5.74M to 94.56M parameters) on 46M human cells; task is to predict latent representations of masked cells from visible spatial context and a limited partial-expression hint; evaluate on four held-out datasets using 11 linear-probe benchmarks and 7 fine-tuned spatial benchmarks.
AI.result: Model capacity improves performance, especially on spatial tasks; spatial transfer depends more on optimization and broad biological source diversity than on cell count alone; CellWorld-Small (5.74M params) outperforms all baselines on all 11 linear probes and all 7 fine-tuned spatial benchmarks; a frozen CellWorld-Large trained on only 5% of data with broad source coverage outperforms all fully fine-tuned baselines.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space predictive pretraining with broad biological diversity yields scalable, transferable spatial foundation models; supports strong performance even with partial data and small models; code available.

title: Newton-Schulz Retraction-Based Inference Enables Hidden Quantum Markov Models to Outperform Classical HMMs
summary: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are widely used probabilistic models for discrete sequential data but can be limited when hidden dynamics are complex. Hidden quantum Markov models (HQMMs) generalize HMMs by replacing probability vectors with density matrices and stochastic transitions with quantum operations, enabling richer latent representations. However, existing HQMM learning methods have not consistently outperformed Expectation--Maximization (EM)-trained HMMs on data not generated by quantum processes, limiting their practical applicability. We introduce NS-RIS, Newton--Schulz Retraction-based Inference on the Stiefel manifold, a scalable algorithm for learning trace-preserving HQMMs. NS-RIS uses Newton--Schulz orthogonalization to compute a polar-factor search direction while preserving Stiefel-manifold feasibility, avoiding costly matrix decompositions. We further establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee under standard assumptions on smoothness, stochastic gradients, and finite Newton--Schulz accuracy. Empirically, NS-RIS provides the first benchmark evidence that an HQMM can significantly outperform an EM-trained HMM on data not generated by a quantum model. On synthetic HMM-generated benchmarks, NS-RIS outperforms both EM and the state-of-the-art HQMM method COSM, improving the evaluation metric by an average of 38.5% and by up to 50.6%. On a synthetic HQMM benchmark, it improves the test metric over COSM by 18.9% while reducing runtime by 12.0%. On the real-world Splice classification benchmark, NS-RIS also surpasses both EM and COSM in higher-dimensional latent regimes, reducing mean classification error by 17.9% for latent dimension 6 and 14.9% for latent dimension 8 relative to COSM. These results move HQMMs beyond a theoretical generalization of HMMs and establish them as practical and expressive models for scientific sequence data.

AI.tldr: NS-RIS enables scalable learning of trace-preserving HQMMs; empirically beats EM-trained HMMs and prior HQMMs, making HQMMs practical for non-quantum data.
AI.motivation: HQMMs offer richer latent dynamics than HMMs but lack scalable training that consistently outperforms EM-trained HMMs on data not generated by quantum processes; address this gap.
AI.method: Newton–Schulz orthogonalization to compute a polar-factor direction on the Stiefel manifold, with RIS (retraction-based inference) to preserve feasibility and avoid costly matrix decompositions; provides finite-time stationarity guarantees under standard smoothness and gradient assumptions.
AI.result: First benchmark showing HQMMs outperform EM-trained HMMs on non-quantum data. On synthetic HMM benchmarks: NS-RIS outperforms EM and COSM by 38.5% on average (up to 50.6%). On synthetic HQMM benchmarks: 18.9% improvement over COSM with 12% runtime reduction. On Splice real-world benchmark: higher-dimensional latent regimes see 17.9% (dim 6) and 14.9% (dim 8) mean error reductions relative to COSM.
AI.conclusion: HQMMs can be practical and expressive for scientific sequence data, achieving superior accuracy and efficiency over prior methods and overcoming training limitations that previously hindered their adoption.

title: Automated Terminal-to-Housing Assembly System for Flat Ribbon Cable Harness
summary: This paper presents a sensor-minimal automated assembly system for bidirectional single-row flat ribbon cable harnesses (FRCHs). Unlike conventional peg-in-hole or single-terminal insertion tasks, FRCH assembly involves mechanically coupled multi-terminal insertion under flexible and dense geometric constraints. To address this problem, the proposed system performs the assembly through a purely mechanical sequence consisting of Cable Alignment, Lean & Slide, Weaving, and Clamping, without relying on active sensing or vision. Each mechanism is designed to progressively reduce correlated terminal misalignment, insertion interference, and instability before final locking. Experiments on bidirectional single-row FRCHs achieved an 83.75% end-to-end process success rate over 80 trials, with success rates of 85.0% and 82.5% in the first and second halves, respectively. The cycle time was 33 s under half-speed operation. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first automated prototype for FRCH terminal-to-housing assembly for multi-pin housings.

AI.tldr: Sensor-minimal automated FRCH assembly using a purely mechanical sequence (Cable Alignment, Lean & Slide, Weaving, Clamping) without active sensing/vision; achieves 83.75% end-to-end success over 80 trials with 33 s cycle time (half-speed). First automated prototype for multi-pin FRCH terminal-to-housing assembly.
AI.motivation: Frustration-free, reliable assembly of bidirectional single-row flat ribbon cable harnesses (FRCHs) under dense geometric constraints with mechanically coupled multi-terminal insertion, where conventional peg-in-hole or single-terminal methods rely on sensors/vision.
AI.method: A purely mechanical pipeline: Cable Alignment, Lean & Slide, Weaving, Clamping. Each stage progressively reduces terminal misalignment, insertion interference, and instability, without sensing or imaging. The design emphasizes sensor-minimal, mechanically-driven alignment and locking.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on bidirectional single-row FRCHs yielded 83.75% end-to-end success over 80 trials; first half 85.0%, second half 82.5%. Cycle time is 33 s under half-speed operation.
AI.conclusion: Presents the first automated prototype achieving FRCH terminal-to-housing assembly for multi-pin housings with a sensorless, purely mechanical process and demonstrates feasible performance, setting a baseline for sensor-free automation in complex multi-terminal insertions.

title: GraphVerse: A Comprehensive Visual Graph Reasoning Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across diverse vision-language tasks, creating an urgent need for more challenging benchmarks. Yet existing evaluations still provide limited insight into whether these models can truly reason over structured visual information. Visual Graph Reasoning (VGR) offers a compelling testbed for this challenge, requiring models to integrate perception, structural understanding, and multi-step reasoning over graph-based visual inputs. However, prior VGR benchmarks often reduce the task to visual perception followed by text-based reasoning, restrict evaluation to single-image settings, rely on answer-only metrics, and underrepresent realistic graph-centric scenarios. To bridge the gap, we introduce GraphVerse, a unified benchmark that jointly evaluates perception, visual reasoning, and text-based graph reasoning in MLLMs under both single-image and paired-image settings. At its core is a suite of Graph-centric Image Editing (GIE) strategies that modify graph images while preserving their semantics, turning them into active tests of visual reasoning. We further propose VGR-Score, a process-sensitive metric that evaluates reasoning quality beyond final-answer accuracy. Extensive experiments reveal several key limitations of current MLLMs in VGR, while also validating the effectiveness of GIE strategies and the transferability of GraphVerse to broader multimodal reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/sunyuanfu/GraphVerse.

AI.tldr: GraphVerse is a unified benchmark for Visual Graph Reasoning (VGR) in multimodal LLMs, introducing Graph-centric Image Editing (GIE) and the VGR-Score metric to evaluate both perception and multi-step graph reasoning in single- and paired-image settings; it reveals current MLLMs' limitations and validates the proposed methods, with code available.
AI.motivation: Current VGR benchmarks inadequately test true reasoning over structured visual graphs and often rely on perception-then-text reasoning, single-image setups, and final-answer accuracy. GraphVerse aims to jointly assess perception, visual reasoning, and text-based graph reasoning in both single- and paired-image contexts with process-aware evaluation.
AI.method: GraphVerse provides a unified benchmark for perception and reasoning over graph-based visuals. Central to the framework are Graph-centric Image Editing (GIE) strategies that modify graph images while preserving semantics to actively challenge visual reasoning. It also introduces VGR-Score, a process-sensitive metric that gauges reasoning quality beyond final answers. Evaluations are conducted on single-image and paired-image tasks to test transferability to broader multimodal reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments reveal notable limitations of current MLLMs in VGR tasks. The GIE strategies effectively test visual reasoning and improve the robustness of evaluation. GraphVerse shows transferability to broader multimodal reasoning capabilities beyond the proposed tasks, and the authors provide code for replication (GitHub).
AI.conclusion: GraphVerse offers a comprehensive, process-aware benchmark for evaluating VGR in multimodal LLMs, combining perception, visual reasoning, and graph-based reasoning in both single- and paired-image settings. The VGR-Score provides richer insights into reasoning quality, and Graph-centric Image Editing enables stronger, semantics-preserving perturbations to test models.

title: Vehicle routing problem using deep reinforcement learning - A case study about truck planning in the industry
summary: As an important component of the supply chain industry, transportation has experienced rapid development in the past decade with the assistance of digital platforms and intelligent algorithms. Within the field of transportation research, Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) has remained a persistent and enduring challenge. In the realm of management science, experts, and scholars from both the industrial and academic sectors have continuously explored optimization models and algorithms to effectively address routing problems, from the classical Traveling Salesman Problem to the more general Vehicle Routing Problem. These models and algorithms are applied in real-world industrial scenarios to achieve cost optimization and reduce carbon footprints. However, due to the complexity of real-world problems, numerous specific constraints are often added, and challenges such as information opacity, uncertainty, and irrational human behavior may arise. Therefore, deploying and optimizing mathematical models for VRP in practical scenarios while maintaining optimal results poses numerous challenges. This paper discusses and provides solutions for three different logistic use cases involving external truck network design. Through these industrial case study, the paper introduces how deep reinforcement learning-based vehicle routing optimization has been implemented. As a result, it can be observed that the routes optimized by reinforcement learning agent have over 10% total cost compared to baseline results. Furthermore, the paper proposes that in future research, DRL algorithms for vehicle routing problems could be generalized into more variations of VRP.

AI.tldr: DRL-based vehicle routing optimization is applied to three external truck network design use cases; results show DRL routes incur over 10% higher total cost than baselines, indicating feasibility and potential generalization for more VRP variations.
AI.motivation: VRP in real-world logistics is constrained by uncertainty, information opacity, and human behavior; advanced optimization via deep reinforcement learning is pursued to improve routing, reduce costs, and lower carbon footprint.
AI.method: Industrial case study with three logistic use cases focusing on external truck network design; implementation of deep reinforcement learning-based vehicle routing optimization.
AI.result: Routes optimized by the RL agent exhibit more than 10% higher total cost compared to baseline results; demonstrates feasibility of applying DRL to VRP but not yet superior to baselines.
AI.conclusion: DRL-based VRP methods could be generalized to additional VRP variations; future work needed to enhance performance and adapt to broader problem variants.

title: Bootstrap-Conditioned Action Selection with Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Contextual bandits offer a natural framework for sample-efficient personalization, but practical deployment remains difficult under sparse, biased interaction data, unreliable uncertainty estimates, and severe cold starts. We study whether pre-trained tabular foundation models with in-context learning can be turned into randomized policies for online decision making. We propose BC-ICL (Bootstrap-conditioned action selection using ICL), which at each round draws a bootstrap resample of the interaction history, conditions a frozen pre-trained ICL model on that resample, scores all actions, and selects the action with the highest sampled score. We further introduce an arm-context conditioning architecture that promotes shared statistical strength across actions and helps avoid common bootstrap failure modes of isolated-arm bandits. Empirically, this policy delivers strong early-round regret and regret performance on standard contextual bandit suites, outperforming established baselines under a strict online protocol.

AI.tldr: BC-ICL uses bootstrap resampling of interaction history and a frozen pre-trained in-context learning model to choose actions in contextual bandits; with an arm-context conditioning architecture to share information across actions, it achieves strong early regret and competitive regret on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address sample inefficiency, biased data, unreliable uncertainty estimates, and cold starts in contextual bandits by leveraging pre-trained tabular foundation models and in-context learning to produce randomized policies from bootstrap samples.
AI.method: Each round, draw a bootstrap resample of the interaction history, condition a frozen pre-trained ICL model on that resample, score actions, and select the action with the highest sampled score. Introduce an arm-context conditioning architecture to share statistical strength across actions and reduce bootstrap failure.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows strong early-round regret and competitive regret performance on standard contextual bandit suites, outperforming established baselines under a strict online protocol.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of bootstrapped ICL-based policies and arm-context conditioning for online decision making with sparse, biased data and cold starts; offers a practical path to sample-efficient personalization using pre-trained tabular foundation models.

title: A Haptic Robot Finger Designed for Guqin Instrument Playing
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Haptics
summary: With the rapid advancement of humanoid robotics and embodied intelligence technologies, numerous musical instrument-playing robots have emerged in recent years, such as pianos, chime bells, and taiko drums. These robots primarily employ open-loop positional control, rendering them incapable of operating instruments requiring dexterous hands and precise tactile perception, such as a violin, guitar, and guqin. This paper describes the design and validation of a high-precision tactile-sensing finger. By mimicking the shape of the fingertip and fingernail found on a human finger, we develop a biomimetic multimodal haptic fingertip and validate it on selected guqin string-contact tasks, including open-string and stopped-note comparisons, harmonic-tuning, and tactile-triggered bimanual coordination, using the guqin, a traditional Chinese musical instrument, as a challenging validation scenario rather than as a fully demonstrated robotic performance system. This research integrates tactile sensing with robotics technology, thereby contributing to applications in world heritage conservation and cultural dissemination.

AI.tldr: Biomimetic multimodal haptic fingertip for robotics; validated on guqin string-contact tasks to enable tactile sensing in dexterous instrument interaction, aiming to augment robotic play and heritage applications.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in robot dexterity for instrument playing due to reliance on open-loop control and lack of tactile feedback; explore tactile sensing to enhance manipulation of stringed instruments; contribute to heritage conservation and cultural dissemination.
AI.method: Design biomimetic fingertip and fingernail; integrate multimodal tactile sensing; validate on guqin tasks (open-string, stopped-note, harmonic tuning, tactile-triggered bimanual coordination) as challenging benchmarks rather than a full performance system.
AI.result: Demonstrated high-precision tactile sensing capabilities and meaningful validation in guqin contact tasks; shows viability of tactile sensing integration with robotics for complex instrument interactions.
AI.conclusion: Tactile sensing finger advances robotic dexterity and supports heritage-related applications; the approach provides a path toward more tactilely aware robotic performers and conservators.

title: AnyTrack: Unifying Visual Object Tracking with Any Modalities
comment: Accepted by ACM MM2026. More modifications may be performed
summary: Visual object tracking aims to continuously locate specific targets within sequential frames, evolving from single-modal methods to multi-modal ones. However, existing multi-modal trackers are typically designed for fixed modality combinations, requiring separate models for different inputs. This leads to a poor adaptability to missing or imperfect modalities, and limited generalization. To address these issues, we propose a novel unified framework called AnyTrack for object tracking with any modalities. Specifically, we design a Modality-aware Interaction Module (MIM) to facilitate dynamic interaction across diverse modalities. This module bridges modality discrepancies and aggregates temporal cues to maintain spatio-temporal consistency during cross-modal interaction. Furthermore, we introduce a Context Understanding Module (CUM) to establish spatial correspondence between visual features and target locations via global-local prompts. This module employs target-aware context modeling to enhance foreground-background discrimination for precise localization. Finally, to support the training and evaluation under diverse modalities, we extend existing multi-modal object tracking benchmarks by incorporating grayscale images, language descriptions, and audio clips. Extensive experiments with both complete and missing modality settings demonstrate that our AnyTrack achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating its effectiveness and flexibility. The source code is available at https://github.com/IdolLab/AnyTrack.

AI.tldr: AnyTrack offers a unified, modality-agnostic tracking framework with MIM for cross-modal interaction and CUM for context-aware localization, extended benchmarks, and SOTA results under complete and missing modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal trackers are fixed to specific modality combos and struggle with missing or imperfect modalities; a flexible framework is needed to generalize across arbitrary inputs while maintaining robust localization.
AI.method: Proposes Modality-aware Interaction Module (MIM) for dynamic cross-modal interaction and temporal cue aggregation; Context Understanding Module (CUM) for spatial correspondence via global-local prompts and target-aware context modeling; extends multi-modal tracking benchmarks to include grayscale, language, and audio; trains and evaluates under both complete and missing modality settings.
AI.result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across complete and missing modality settings; robust to modality absence and variations; code released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: AnyTrack provides a flexible and robust framework for tracking with any modalities, offering strong generalization to unseen modality combinations and modalities with missing data, supported by extended benchmarks and accessible code.

title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics of Polymers
summary: Coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics extends polymer simulation beyond the scales accessible to all-atom (AA) methods, but bottom-up CG modeling is laborious. The CG resolution is a design choice, so a transferable parameter set is generally not available and the potentials are derived anew for each polymer mapping. Here we present CGMas, a multi-agent framework that automates topology construction, equilibration, mapping, potential derivation, and validation from a natural-language specification of the polymer and target resolution. A large-language-model (LLM) reasoning agent infers the AA topology from polymer name, while layered self-correction resolves physical errors common to unsaturated, heteroatom-containing, and polar polymers. Downstream agents equilibrate the system, map it onto CG representation, derive potentials through Boltzmann inversion, and benchmark the model against its atomistic reference. CGMas completed all 27 homopolymer and copolymer tasks, matched the AA density to within 5% in 22, and reduced simulation from 38-88 min to 1 min, establishing agentic LLMs as a route to automated polymer coarse-graining.
