AI.motivation: Address poor generalization in LLM-ACP for complex combinatorial optimization by eliminating dependence on high-quality reference solutions for instance hardness and by increasing instance diversity through synthesized mutators.
AI.method: Define Potential Gain as a reference-free measure of generalization gain by perturbing generated algorithms and evaluating improvement on generated instances. Use LLMs to synthesize diverse instance mutators. Instantiate the framework on Greedy Constructive, Ant Colony Optimization, and Guided Local Search backbones. Evaluate on TSP and CVRP across six data distributions.
AI.result: PIAC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-ACP baselines across TSP and CVRP; notably, a 19.76% relative improvement for the TSP Greedy Constructive portfolio.
AI.conclusion: PIAC effectively enhances generalization in LLM-driven algorithm portfolios by removing dependence on reference solutions and by expanding instance diversity; the approach demonstrates robust gains across problem types and distributions.

title: Solver-Guided Reasoning for Mixed-Equilibrium Strategies
summary: Reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often grounded in human text, human demonstrations, and human-generated rationales. For equilibrium reasoning in complex games, however, relying on human data can be suboptimal. In fact, human play is often guided by intuition and heuristics and can deviate substantially from game equilibrium. This discrepancy is amplified in games with mixed-strategy equilibria, where human data is heavily biased toward pure strategies. Consequently, conditioning LLMs on this data yields weak game strategies. To grant LLMs the reasoning capacity in games, in this work, we study how to elicit equilibrium play using solver output. We propose Mixed-Strategy Decision Tree (MDT), which articulates the silent optimality of the equilibrium into sparse strategic rules that both humans and LLMs could understand. Using solver output rather than human annotation allows us to extend the input to arbitrarily new states and continuations. We instantiate this study on No-Limit Texas Hold'em by querying a solver oracle for over \textbf{250 million mixed-strategy decisions}; MDT together with other techniques \textbf{reduces the $\ell_1$ distance to the equilibrium by $52.6\%$} across $8$ different LLM configurations. A Route-only ablation tests the incremental contribution of the shadow-based contrast, while complete River-endgame and Liar's Dice experiments evaluate strategic fidelity and portability beyond the original NLH communication setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes Mixed-Strategy Decision Tree (MDT) to induce equilibrium play in LLMs by using solver-generated mixed-strategy decisions instead of human data; achieves a 52.6% reduction in L1 distance to equilibrium across 8 LLMs in No-Limit Hold'em and demonstrates transfer to endgame and Liar's Dice.
AI.motivation: Overcome bias and suboptimality of human data in mixed-strategy games by grounding LLM reasoning in solver output to enable robust equilibrium play and generalization to unseen states.
AI.method: Introduce MDT that encodes the silent optimality of equilibrium into sparse strategic rules; leverage a solver oracle to generate over 250 million mixed-strategy decisions; combine MDT with other techniques (shadow-based contrast); evaluate via Route-only ablation, complete river-endgame, and Liar's Dice to test strategic fidelity and portability beyond NLH.
AI.result: MDT plus auxiliary techniques reduce the L1 distance to the Nash equilibrium by 52.6% across eight LLM configurations; MTD demonstrates improved strategic fidelity and portability, extending beyond the NLH communication setting.
AI.conclusion: MDT provides a scalable, data-efficient means to elicit equilibrium reasoning in LLMs by grounding decisions in solver outputs, potentially generalizing to other games and complex decision tasks.

title: Synthetic LiDAR Data Generation and Deterministic Downsampling for Point Cloud Classification on the Edge
summary: Deploying three-dimensional deep learning frameworks to low-power embedded processors is bottlenecked by the unstructured nature of spatial data and the resource-intensive distance sorting algorithms often used before neural network inference. To address this gap, this paper presents a hardware-constrained workflow optimized for native execution on the Raspberry Pi 5. To account for the reality gap between noiseless, clean computer-aided design (CAD) datasets and real-world sensor data, we use physics-based simulation to construct a synthetic LiDAR dataset. Cross-dataset evaluations demonstrate a substantial drop in classification accuracy when networks trained on clean CAD data are evaluated on synthetic LiDAR sensor data, highlighting the critical need for sensor-aware training. To address the latency bottleneck of traditional geometric preprocessing on edge CPUs, we integrate an isolated, feature-driven Critical Points Layer (CPL) as a frontend filter. Our results show that the pretrained CPL deterministically compresses raw 1024-point clouds to a subset of 40 to 60 unique coordinates. When profiled on the ARM Cortex-A76 processor, the complete pipeline achieves an inference throughput of approximately 50 FPS while maintaining an instance classification accuracy of 88.36%, demonstrating the viability of deterministic real-time 3D perception at the edge.

AI.tldr: Hardware-aware 3D perception on edge devices using a Critical Points Layer to compress 3D point clouds; synthetic LiDAR data used to study sim-to-real gaps; achieves ~50 FPS and 88.36% accuracy on Cortex-A76; demonstrates feasibility of deterministic edge inference with sensor-aware training.
AI.motivation: Bottlenecks in unstructured 3D data processing on low-power embedded CPUs; distance-sorting and CAD-trained models underperform on real sensor data; need a hardware-conscious, real-time workflow for edge 3D perception.
AI.method: Develop hardware-constrained pipeline native to Raspberry Pi 5; generate physics-based synthetic LiDAR data; evaluate cross-dataset transfer from CAD to LiDAR; integrate a pretrained, feature-driven Critical Points Layer (CPL) as a frontend filter to deterministically compress 1024-point clouds to 40–60 points; run end-to-end inference on ARM Cortex-A76.
AI.result: CPL reduces 1024 points to 40–60 coordinates deterministically; end-to-end pipeline ~50 FPS with instance classification accuracy of 88.36%.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of deterministic real-time 3D perception at the edge with sensor-aware training; CPL front-end effectively reduces data and latency; underscores importance of sim-to-real alignment for embedded 3D DL.

title: MuST-VAD: Mutual Structured Learning for Video Anomaly Detection
summary: In this paper, we propose MuST-VAD, a mutual structured learning framework for weakly supervised video anomaly detection (VAD) in which an anomaly detector and a large vision-language model (LVLM) exchange their acquired knowledge. Detectors in weakly supervised VAD learn anomaly scores from features extracted by a fixed, task-agnostic backbone. These fixed features bound the achievable detection accuracy. Recent methods therefore transfer LVLM semantics into the detector as richer features. However, this transfer is one-way: what the detector learns about the target videos never returns to the LVLM. MuST-VAD extends the one-way transfer into a bidirectional learning loop. In this loop, the latest detector predictions supervise the LVLM adaptation, and the adapted LVLM returns updated representations that retrain the detector; the two models alternate these updates over small video groups. Both models train on detector-selected key clips, while confidence weighting and annotation-anchored question answering keep the exchanged supervision reliable. On UCF-Crime, our mutual learning improves the one-pass transfer baseline from 88.15% to 88.63% AUROC and from 37.25% to 42.46% average precision (AP), outperforming the state-of-the-art method in AP by 4.13 points.

AI.tldr: MuST-VAD enables bidirectional mutual learning between a weakly supervised anomaly detector and a large vision-language model (LVLM) for video anomaly detection, addressing fixed feature backbones and one-way LVLM transfer. It iteratively updates detector and LVLM representations via a mutual loop using detector-selected key clips, confidence weighting, and annotation-anchored QA.
AI.motivation: Overcome limited detection accuracy caused by fixed, task-agnostic features and one-way LVLM knowledge transfer in weakly supervised VAD by introducing a bidirectional mutual learning loop where the detector and LVLM continually refine each other.
AI.method: MuST-VAD sets up a bidirectional learning loop: (1) detector predictions supervise LVLM adaptation; (2) adapted LVLM provides updated representations that retrain the detector. Training occurs on detector-selected key clips with confidence weighting and annotation-anchored question answering to ensure reliable supervision. Updates alternate over small video groups.
AI.result: On UCF-Crime, the approach improves AUROC from 88.15% to 88.63% and AP from 37.25% to 42.46% (an AP gain of 4.13 points), outperforming the state-of-the-art in AP.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional mutual learning between a detector and an LVLM yields measurable gains in weakly supervised VAD, validating the effectiveness of exchanging supervision and dynamic feature adaptation for better anomaly detection.

title: Gated-BEPO: Confidence-Gated Bellman Credit Assignment for Large Language Model Agents
summary: Training large language model agents in long-horizon environments requires assigning credit from sparse terminal outcomes to individual actions. Existing critic-free methods propagate trajectory-level rewards uniformly across steps, while recent approaches construct step-level groups by matching repeated states and compare actions within each group. The former cannot distinguish useful actions in failed trajectories from ineffective actions in successful ones. The latter rely on step credit derived directly from individual trajectory outcomes and fixed-weight fusion with episode-level credit. We propose Gated-BEPO, which derives step-level credit from empirical rollout graphs. For each rollout group, Gated-BEPO constructs an empirical graph and estimates node values through a mean-backup Bellman fixed point that reflects the empirical action distribution of the current policy. We then accumulate these temporal-difference residuals along each sampled trajectory using generalized advantage estimation, yielding step-level Bellman advantages that capture both immediate and downstream effects. To adaptively fuse episode- and step-level credit, a confidence gate incorporates Bellman credit only at states with multiple observed successors and otherwise uses episode-level credit. Experiments on WebShop, ALFWorld, and visual Sokoban show consistent improvements across language and vision-language models, while diagnostic ablations support the effectiveness of Bellman fixed-point value estimation and show that step-level credit should be incorporated selectively rather than uniformly into the final advantage.

AI.tldr: Gated-BEPO introduces step-level credit via empirical rollout graphs to improve credit assignment in long-horizon RL for language and vision-language models, using a Bellman fixed-point for node values and a gating mechanism to selectively fuse step- and episode-level credit; it yields consistent performance gains across datasets.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment in long-horizon, sparse-terminal-reward scenarios is challenging. Existing critic-free methods blur trajectory-level rewards; step-level grouping methods either rely on outcome-derived credits or fixed fusion, failing to distinguish useful actions in failures or relying on fixed episode-level credit. A method capturing empirical action distributions and selective credit fusion could improve learning.
AI.method: For each rollout group, build an empirical graph and compute node values via a mean-backup Bellman fixed point reflecting the policy's empirical action distribution. Accumulate TD residuals along trajectories with generalized advantage estimation to obtain step-level Bellman advantages capturing immediate and downstream effects. Use a confidence gate to fuse episode- and step-level credit: apply Bellman credit only at states with multiple observed successors; otherwise rely on episode-level credit.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on WebShop, ALFWorld, and visual Sokoban shows consistent improvements for both language and vision-language models. Diagnostic ablations confirm the effectiveness of Bellman fixed-point value estimation and indicate step-level credit should be incorporated selectively rather than uniformly into the final advantage.
AI.conclusion: Gated-BEPO provides an adaptive, interpretable mechanism for credit assignment that combines step- and episode-level information only when warranted by the empirical rollout distribution, leading to improved performance across diverse tasks.

title: KReF: Training-Free Retrieval for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting and Predictive Uncertainty
summary: Probabilistic long-term time-series forecasting commonly relies on trained models. Training-free conformal methods typically construct intervals around a pre-existing point forecaster and do not natively represent a complete predictive distribution; sequential variants additionally suffer from increasingly delayed feedback at long horizons. We propose KReF, a training-free retrieval framework that treats retrieved historical futures as a querylocal empirical predictive distribution. After robust preprocessing, KReF embeds each lookback using handcrafted statistics or frozen random Fourier features and retrieves similar historical lookback-future pairs. Their similarity weights directly define predictive masses, quantiles, CRPS, and a weighted-mean point forecast. KReF further uses the observed query lookback to construct a probability-integral-transform map and applies validation-selected expansion and shrinkage rates to adapt interval boundaries. Across six LTSF benchmarks and four horizons, KReF obtains the lowest CRPS in all 12 dataset-embedding settings and the lowest IS90 in 9 settings. Without gradient-based fitting, its point forecasts also match or surpass trained baselines on two of six datasets. An archive-oracle analysis further reveals substantial headroom under finer horizon- and channel-wise routing. These results establish retrieval as a useful and underexplored inductive bias for LTSF.

AI.tldr: KReF introduces a training-free retrieval-based framework for long-term time-series forecasting that builds an empirical predictive distribution from retrieved historical futures. It yields probabilistic forecasts and interval estimates through weighted-similarity masses, with competitive CRPS/IS90 scores across benchmarks, without gradient-based fitting.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free conformal methods either rely on a pre-existing point forecaster or suffer from delayed feedback at long horizons; there is a need for native predictive distributions and effective inductive biases in long-term forecasting.
AI.method: Robust preprocessing; embed lookbacks with handcrafted statistics or frozen random Fourier features; retrieve similar historical lookback–future pairs; similarity weights define predictive masses, quantiles, CRPS, and a weighted-mean point forecast; use observed query lookback to build a probability-integral-transform (PIT) map and apply augmentation/shrinkage rates to interval boundaries.
AI.result: KReF achieves the lowest CRPS in all 12 dataset-embedding settings and the lowest IS90 in 9 of 12 settings across six LTSF benchmarks and four horizons; its point forecasts match or beat trained baselines on two of six datasets without gradient-based fitting; archive-oracle analysis indicates potential gains with finer horizon/channel routing.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval can serve as a strong, data-efficient inductive bias for long-term time-series forecasting, enabling probabilistic forecasting without training through an effective empirical predictive distribution and adaptive interval calibration.

title: WNM-3D: A World Navigation Model with 3D Scene Conditioning for Closed-Loop VLN
summary: Recent vision-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adapt pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) into vision-language-action (VLA) policies that map egocentric observations and language instructions directly to navigation actions. Although semantically capable, such action-centric training does not explicitly model how the agent's visual observations should evolve under its predicted motion. Generative world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, yet existing WAMs for continuous VLN do not condition joint future-view and action generation on geometry-aware representations inferred from the observed history. We present WNM-3D, a generative World Navigation Model with 3D scene conditioning for continuous VLN. To consolidate past observations into persistent scene context, a frozen feed-forward geometry encoder extracts geometry-aware representations from the monocular egocentric RGB history, and a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter converts them into a fixed-length prefix in the token space of the world-action Diffusion Transformer. Through block-causal attention, this prefix conditions every future video-action block, providing a shared geometric context for both future-view and action generation. We train WNM-3D through supervised world-action fine-tuning on A*-generated demonstrations, DAgger-style adaptation on policy-visited states, and DanceGRPO-based closed-loop policy optimization. Experiments on GN-Bench show that WNM-3D outperforms strong VLM-based navigation policies and its 2D-conditioned counterpart in closed-loop navigation. On a fixed near-goal evaluation set, WNM-3D also achieves higher flow-action consistency and lower visual-motion error.

AI.tldr: A 3D-scene conditioned generative World Navigation Model (WNM-3D) for continuous VLN that uses a frozen geometry encoder and a 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter to condition a world-action diffusion transformer, enabling joint future-view and action generation with geometry-aware context. Trained with A*-generated demonstrations, DAgger adaptation, and DanceGRPO optimization; outperforms VLM-based and 2D-conditioned baselines and improves flow-action consistency and visual-motion accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing action-centric VLN models do not explicitly model how visual observations evolve with motion, and current world-action models (WAMs) lack geometry-aware conditioning from observed history, limiting coherent perception-action generation in 3D environments.
AI.method: Extract geometry-aware history representations with a frozen monocular geometry encoder; convert them into a fixed-length token prefix via a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter; condition a world-action diffusion transformer through block-causal attention; train with supervised fine-tuning on A*-demonstrations, DAgger-style adaptation on policy-visited states, and DanceGRPO-based closed-loop optimization.
AI.result: In GN-Bench, WNM-3D surpasses strong VLM-based navigation policies and a 2D-conditioned variant in closed-loop navigation; on a fixed near-goal set, it exhibits higher flow-action consistency and lower visual-motion error.
AI.conclusion: 3D-scene conditioning enables coherent joint generation of future observations and actions in continuous VLN, yielding improved navigation performance and observation-action consistency.

title: RibAssist 3D: Biplanar Rib-Fracture Detection, Addressing, and Selective 3D Localization from CT-Derived Projections
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Code available at: https://github.com/kabJhai/RibAssist-3D
summary: Rib fractures are common, clinically significant, and time-consuming to localize on computed tomography (CT). We ask whether fractures detected in two orthogonal projections (anteroposterior, AP, and lateral) can be paired across views and triangulated into reliable 3D fracture points at a controlled rate of false 3D outputs. We answer this with a staged diagnostic study. Biplanar geometry is exact: detector-predicted centers reconstruct to median 4.0 mm 3D error when correspondence is correct. On the sealed cohort, dual-view availability reaches 61.1% and the candidate graph contains a correct pair for 58.4% of fractures. The binding limitation is not geometry or localization but confidence-limited cross-view correspondence. Lateral-detector retraining lifts dual-view availability (0.52 to 0.76 in development) and moves the frontier from 0% to 2.44% recall at 10 mm. When the policy commits a correct pair, the emitted point is geometrically accurate (sealed median 1.49 mm, rib-exact 93%). A pre-specified pass on the untouched 55-case cohort promotes 15 of 601 fractures to correct 3D localizations at 0.436 false 3D points per case, yielding 2.50% end-to-end commitment yield. The contribution is validated biplanar reconstruction geometry with high conditional localization fidelity, a staged identification of cross-view correspondence confidence as the effective bottleneck, and a selective assistive workflow that preserves uncertain findings rather than a standalone automatic reconstructor.

AI.tldr: A staged biplanar approach triangulates rib fracture 3D points from AP and lateral CT projections; cross-view correspondence is the bottleneck; detector retraining and a selective assistive workflow improve 3D localization fidelity, achieving high per-point accuracy but modest end-to-end yield (~2.5%).
AI.motivation: Rib fractures are common and time-consuming to localize on CT; accurate 3D localization from two orthogonal views is desirable but challenging due to cross-view correspondence; the study investigates feasibility, accuracy, and bottlenecks.
AI.method: Staged diagnostic study leveraging exact biplanar geometry: AP and lateral detector-predicted centers are paired into a candidate graph; evaluation on a sealed cohort; measure dual-view availability, correct cross-view pairs, and 3D localization accuracy; retrain lateral detector to improve dual-view availability; apply a policy to commit a correct pair; validate on an untouched 55-case cohort.
AI.result: Median 3D error of 4.0 mm when correspondence is correct; dual-view availability 61.1% with correct pair in 58.4% of fractures; lateral-detector retraining increases dual-view availability from 0.52 to 0.76 and recall at 10 mm from 0 to 2.44%; when a correct pair is committed, emitted 3D point median error 1.49 mm (rib-exact 93%); 55-case untouched cohort yields 15 of 601 fractures upgraded to correct 3D localizations at 0.436 false 3D points per case, 2.50% end-to-end yield.
AI.conclusion: Validates the feasibility of biplanar 3D reconstruction with high conditional localization fidelity; identifies cross-view correspondence confidence as the primary bottleneck; supports a selective assistive workflow that preserves uncertain findings rather than a fully automatic reconstructor.

title: CEDAR: Agent-Orchestrated Tree Search for Goal-Directed Optimization of Complex Systems
comment: Accepted as Talk in ALIFE 2026: The 2026 Conference on Artificial Life
summary: Complex systems, core objects of study in artificial life, model diverse phenomena through nonlinear, feedback-driven interactions that produce emergent behavior, with applications from population dynamics and biology to economic policy and strategic decision-making. Yet the difficulty of predicting how feedback structure gives rise to emergent behavior, a central open problem in artificial life, makes goal-directed design exceptionally challenging. In established practice, system structures are written in specialized modeling languages such as DYNAMO or STELLA, compounding the challenge with labor-intensive workflows that limit adoption and hinder timely decision-making. To address these challenges, we introduce CEDAR, an autonomous method that uses Large Language Model (LLM) agents to discover complex systems satisfying user-specified behavioral goals. Our key innovation is an LLM-driven Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) deeply coupled with complex systems: at each iteration, an LLM Judge evaluates emergent behavior against specified goals and an LLM Editor proposes improved variants, with the Judge acting as a fitness function and the Editor as a variation operator, akin to a generate-and-evaluate loop in evolutionary computation. We represent complex systems as a restricted, runnable subset of Python with domain-specific primitives, letting LLMs modify system dynamics directly. CEDAR formalizes this as an MCTS variant with an LLM-parameterized transition kernel and value function, enabling goal-directed discovery of complex system behaviors while preserving solution diversity, and its LLM-based interpretability reveals how structural changes drive emergent behavior. CEDAR reduces human effort while enabling capabilities difficult to achieve with existing approaches, facilitating broader adoption of complex systems across domains.

AI.tldr: An LLM-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search framework (CEDAR) autonomously discovers complex dynamical systems matching user goals by coupling an LLM Judge (fitness) and LLM Editor (variation) within a restricted Python model, enabling goal-directed design and interpretable insights.
AI.motivation: Emergent behavior in complex systems is hard to predict; traditional modeling languages are labor-intensive and hinder timely decision-making; there is a need for autonomous, goal-driven design that preserves diversity and interpretability.
AI.method: Represent systems in a runnable Python subset with domain-specific primitives; perform MCTS where transitions and value are parameterized by LLMs; use LLM Judge to evaluate emergent behavior against goals and LLM Editor to propose improvements; loop resembles generate-and-evaluate in evolutionary computation; focus on interpretability.
AI.result: CEDAR formalizes an LLM-driven MCTS variant that can discover system variants satisfying goals, reduces human effort, preserves diversity, and provides interpretable mappings from structural changes to behavior.
AI.conclusion: The approach broadens adoption of complex systems modeling by enabling autonomous, goal-directed design and delivering interpretability that clarifies how design choices drive emergent outcomes.

title: Sub-Quadratic Bisimulation Metrics via Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Coverage-Augmented Guarantees and Computable Two-Sided Certificates
summary: Bisimulation metrics quantify behavioral similarity in Markov decision processes, but their Wasserstein fixed-point operator updates every state pair and incurs quadratic pairwise work. We give a certificate-carrying sub-quadratic method for MDPs with bounded transition support and a useful low-dimensional indexing representation: an approximate-nearest-neighbor index selects the pairs updated by the exact restricted operator, while monotone lower and upper runs enclose the exact metric at every sweep. The main analytical result is a coverage-augmented anytime bound: local index quality alone cannot control global error, because uncovered pairs retain their initialization gap. The limiting error is at most $\max(ρ,\eop/(1-γ))$, and with exact covered backups the lower arm satisfies $\|\dann-d\|_\infty=ρ$. Because $ρ$ depends on the unknown exact metric, the algorithm returns the observable sandwich width instead; agreement of the induced lower and upper clusterings certifies exact recovery of the covered aggregation. A reward-oblivious lower bound shows sub-quadratic index-first coverage cannot remove the coverage term, while a separate adaptive lower bound requires $Ω(|\Scal|)$ pair evaluations. Exact-operator experiments verify the identity and enclosure in every seeded run, and timing experiments recover quadratic versus sub-quadratic scaling under both cheap and full Wasserstein backups. On the grouped $|\Scal|=64$ benchmark, exact restricted refinement reaches the exact-metric skyline once retrieval covers roughly half of all pairs, while independently trained MICo and DBC baselines stay $22$-$33\times$ above that skyline at every retrieval budget. Taxi shows the certificate abstaining under an uninformative embedding, while a $2500$-state gridworld improves over a reward-only metric by $28.6\%$ using $12.8\%$ of one quadratic sweep.

AI.tldr: Certificate-carrying, sub-quadratic bisimulation-metric updates for MDPs using approximate-nearest-neighbor indexing and monotone bounds, enabling exact metric recovery under partial coverage and offering sub-quadratic scaling with strong empirical gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Bisimulation metrics with Wasserstein fixed-point updates are powerful for quantifying behavioral similarity in MDPs but scale quadratically in the number of states due to pairwise state comparisons. A scalable, certificate-bearing method is needed for large MDPs.
AI.method: Introduce a low-dimensional, approximate-nearest-neighbor index to select the state pairs updated by the exact restricted operator. Use monotone lower and upper runs to enclose the exact metric at every sweep. Derive a coverage-augmented anytime bound where local index quality cannot alone bound global error because uncovered pairs retain initialization gaps. Report a certificate width (sandwich) that bounds the true metric and observe that, with exact covered backups, the lower bound matches the metric at the sup-norm. Prove both a reward-oblivious lower bound showing sub-quadratic index-first coverage cannot remove the coverage term and a separate adaptive lower bound requiring Ω(|S|) pair evaluations. Validate via exact-operator experiments, timing studies, and benchmarks (grouped 64-state, Taxi, 2500-state gridworld).
AI.result: The main analytic result bounds the limiting error by max(ρ, ε_op/(1-γ)); with exact covered backups the lower arm yields ||d_hat - d||_∞ = ρ. Since ρ depends on the unknown exact metric, the algorithm reports the observable sandwich width. Agreement between induced lower and upper clusterings certifies exact recovery of the covered aggregation. On benchmarks, exact restricted refinement reaches the exact-metric skyline once retrieval covers roughly half of all pairs; competing baselines (MICo, DBC) remain 22–33× above the skyline at every budget. In Taxi, the certificate abstains under an uninformative embedding; a 2500-state gridworld shows 28.6% improvement in reward metric using 12.8% of one quadratic sweep.
AI.conclusion: A certificate-carrying, sub-quadratic approach to Wasserstein-based bisimulation metrics is feasible for MDPs with bounded transition support. Exact recovery is guaranteed when coverage suffices, and sub-quadratic performance is demonstrated empirically. However, the error depends on an unknown ρ, prompting reporting the sandwich width, and there is an intrinsic coverage term that cannot be eliminated by index quality alone. The framework offers practical gains over strong baselines and points to future work on improving embedding quality and coverage strategies to reduce uncovered regions.

title: SkillEval: Decomposing Agent Skill Quality into Interpretable Signals
summary: Agent skills provide reusable procedural knowledge that helps agents solve specialized tasks. As their use expands, evaluating skill quality becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations often measure skill quality by testing whether a skill improves performance on specific downstream tasks. However, a reusable skill may apply to multiple task scenarios. Downstream evaluation mainly reflects the compatibility between a skill and the evaluated task, provides only a partial view of skill quality, and does not identify which aspect of the skill should be improved. We find that general properties of the \texttt{SKILL.md} document play an important role in skill quality. To evaluate these properties, we propose \textbf{SkillEval}, an interpretable framework for document-level skill evaluation. SkillEval evaluates each property using a fixed and inspectable scoring direction, producing interpretable scores. It further measures and reduces the influence of unrelated document features, such as length and formatting, so that each score captures its intended semantic property more specifically. Specifically, SkillEval learns an interpretable direction for each quality property from controlled positive--negative skill pairs in the hidden representation space of the model, and scores a new skill by projecting its representation onto these fixed directions. We use SkillEval to evaluate skills in controlled quality tests and show that SkillEval reliably distinguishes skills of different quality. In addition, SkillEval scores closely reflect downstream task performance, providing an early indication of whether a skill is likely to help an agent complete a task. We further explore SkillEval for diagnosing weaknesses in skill documents and guiding targeted revisions. The revised skills improve the targeted properties and achieve higher pass rates on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: SkillEval is an interpretable, document-level framework for evaluating reusable agent skills. It moves beyond downstream task performance by assessing fixed, interpretable quality properties of a SKILL.md document, using latent-space projections onto learned positive–negative directions. It reduces confounding features, correlates with downstream success, and supports diagnosing and revising skills to improve quality.
AI.motivation: Existing skill evaluations largely rely on downstream task performance, which only reveals task-specific compatibility and may miss other vital aspects of skill quality. A reusable skill should be evaluated on properties that generalize across tasks and be interpretable to guide improvement.
AI.method: Learn fixed, interpretable directions for each quality property from controlled positive–negative skill pairs in the model’s hidden representation space. For a new skill, project its representation onto these directions to obtain property-specific scores. Orthogonality and normalization help isolate properties and reduce influence from irrelevant features (e.g., length, formatting). Use the SKILL.md document as the basis and provide document-level property scores that are interpretable and inspectable.
AI.result: SkillEval reliably distinguishes between skills of different quality in controlled tests. The scores correlate with downstream task performance, offering an early signal of a skill’s usefulness. It also enables diagnosing weaknesses in skill documents and guiding targeted revisions, leading to improved property scores and higher pass rates on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: SkillEval delivers an interpretable, robust framework for evaluating and diagnosing skill quality at the document level, enabling targeted revisions and providing early indicators of downstream task utility.

title: CubicQuant: Parametric Non-Uniform Codebooks for High-Throughput LLM Inference with 1-8-Bit Weights
summary:
Weight quantization for large-language-model inference must balance adaptive reconstruction levels with representations regular enough for efficient GPU execution. Uniform integers constrain each group to a linear grid. Low-bit floating-point formats use a fixed exponent-mantissa structure, while learned codebooks gain flexibility at the cost of irregular decoding and additional metadata.
  We introduce CubicQuant, a parametric non-uniform scalar format that preserves a dense integer code stream while adapting reconstruction levels within each weight group. A monotonic cubic curve, specified by two shape parameters and one scale, maps uniformly spaced magnitude codes to non-uniform levels. The family spans 1-8-bit weight payloads, contains symmetric uniform integer quantization as an exact special case, and has effective width B + 64/G bits per weight for payload width B and group size G. We derive population distortion under Uniform, Gaussian, and Laplace distributions, formulate continuous and Dynamic-A8-carrier-aware fitting objectives, and describe direct packed-weight GPU execution.
  For finite groups of G=128 with 15,360 samples per distribution, W4 CubicQuant reduced reconstruction RMSE relative to optimally clipped four-bit uniform integer quantization by 3.90% on Uniform, 13.49% on Gaussian, and 28.14% on Laplace samples. Relative to the best enumerated four-bit finite floating-point format, the reductions were 3.90%, 9.44%, and 6.27%. Preliminary H200 kernel measurements show a workload-dependent crossover: model-dtype execution is faster for narrow GEMV, while Dynamic A8 becomes favorable as row count grows. The results establish the format's representational promise and direct executability; downstream model quality and cross-device end-to-end performance remain open evaluation questions.

AI.tldr: CubicQuant is a parametric non-uniform scalar quantizer for LLM weights using a monotonic cubic mapping per weight group, enabling 1–8 bit payloads with dense bitstreams, improving reconstruction RMSE versus uniform and fixed FP formats, and offering direct packed-weight GPU execution with a cross-over in kernel performance depending on problem size.
AI.motivation: To balance adaptive reconstruction levels with regular, GPU-friendly representations for large-language-model inference, overcoming rigidity of uniform quantization and the overheads of learned codebooks or fixed FP formats.
AI.method: Introduce a parametric non-uniform scalar quantization (CubicQuant) where a monotonic cubic curve (two shape parameters + scale) maps uniformly spaced magnitude codes to non-uniform reconstruction levels within each weight group. The family spans 1–8 bits, includes symmetric uniform integer quantization as a special case, derives population distortion for Uniform/Gaussian/Laplace, proposes continuous and Dynamic-A8-carrier-aware fitting objectives, and discusses direct packed-weight GPU execution. Payload width is B + 64/G bits per weight for payload width B and group size G.
AI.result: With finite groups G=128 and 15,360 samples per distribution: W4 CubicQuant reduces reconstruction RMSE versus optimally clipped 4-bit uniform quantization by 3.90% (Uniform), 13.49% (Gaussian), and 28.14% (Laplace); relative to the best 4-bit finite floating-point format, reductions are 3.90%, 9.44%, and 6.27%. H200 kernel measurements show a workload-dependent crossover: narrow GEMV favors model-dtype execution, while Dynamic A8 becomes favorable as row count grows.
AI.conclusion: CubicQuant demonstrates representational promise and direct executability for LLM weight quantization, but full model-quality and cross-device end-to-end performance require further evaluation.

title: MaskFlow: Precise, Consistent and Seamless Regional Image Editing
summary: Regional image editing has attracted considerable attention for its spatial controllability. Although instruction-based and mask-reference-based editing methods can achieve strong semantic alignment, reliable regional control remains challenging, where an edit must be accurately localized and naturally integrated with the preserved context. We propose \textbf{MaskFlow}, a training framework for precise localization, consistent background preservation, and seamless boundary transitions. MaskFlow incorporates the mask into the probability path and flow-matching objective, coordinating generation within the editable region with source preservation outside it. The proposed Soft-Poisson de-seaming module further refines the predicted vector field during both training and sampling to improve the smooth integration of the edited foreground with the preserved background. We also design a data synthesis pipeline to construct MEData, a mask-based image editing dataset for training regional image editing models and facilitating further research. Experiments on natural scenes and infographic images demonstrate consistent improvements over competing methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

AI.tldr: MaskFlow introduces a mask-aware training framework for regional image editing, achieving precise localization, preserved background, and seamless boundaries by integrating masks into the probability path and flow-matching objective, aided by a Soft-Poisson de-seaming module and a new MEData dataset.
AI.motivation: Regional editing requires accurate localization and natural integration with preserved context, which existing instruction- or mask-reference-based methods struggle to achieve reliably.
AI.method: Incorporates the mask into the generation probability path and a flow-matching objective to coordinate edits within the mask with source preservation outside; introduces a Soft-Poisson de-seaming module to refine the vector field during training and sampling; provides a data synthesis pipeline to create MEData for training and research.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on natural scenes and infographic images show consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over competing methods.
AI.conclusion: MaskFlow enables precise regional editing with strong localization, background preservation, and smooth boundary transitions, and the MEData dataset supports further research in this area.

title: From Points to Edges: Edge-Conditioned Spectral Operators for Physics-Sensitive PDE Learning
summary: Neural operators have become a central tool for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), with spectral operators offering efficient global mixing across spatial locations. However, many PDEs contain physics-sensitive local structures that are critical to the underlying physical behavior. For example, in Darcy flow, local material interfaces are often reflected by sharp changes in the permeability field and can strongly influence the solution. Existing spectral operators primarily adapt modal mixing based on center-point representations, making them insufficiently responsive to such localized structural variations. We propose the Edge-Conditioned Spectral Operator (ESO), a novel spectral operator framework that modulates global spectral mixing using local edge-wise variations. By incorporating the Pairwise-Variation Modal Mixer (PVMM) to inject local edge information into spectral mode selection, ESO preserves the global approximation capability of spectral neural operators while enabling the learned kernel to adapt to physics-sensitive local structures. Furthermore, we introduce a task-adaptive Physics-Aware Reweighting (PAR) that emphasizes physically important regions, identified by taskspecific physical quantities. Across nine PDE benchmarks, ESO consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Visual and region-wise analyses further demonstrate that ESO reduces solution errors near coefficient jumps, high-gradient flow structures, and other physically sensitive regions. The code is available at https://github.com/Tanpig-X/ESO.

AI.tldr: Introduces Edge-Conditioned Spectral Operator (ESO) with PVMM and PAR to incorporate local edge information into global spectral mixing, achieving state-of-the-art results on nine PDE benchmarks; code released.
AI.motivation: Spectral operators excel at global mixing but struggle with physics-sensitive local structures (e.g., interfaces, coefficient jumps). A mechanism is needed to adapt spectral kernels to local variations without sacrificing global approximation power.
AI.method: Propose ESO framework that modulates global spectral mixing using local edge-wise variations. Use Pairwise-Variation Modal Mixer (PVMM) to inject local edge information into spectral mode selection. Introduce Physics-Aware Reweighting (PAR) to emphasize physically important regions based on task-specific quantities.
AI.result: ESO achieves state-of-the-art performance across nine PDE benchmarks. Visual and region-wise analyses show reduced errors near coefficient jumps, high-gradient flow structures, and other sensitive regions.
AI.conclusion: ESO preserves the global approximation capability of spectral neural operators while enabling adaptation to physics-sensitive local structures through PVMM and PAR; demonstrates strong empirical gains and interpretability with region-focused analyses; code available.

title: Hidden Gauge Controls Feature Specialization in ReLU Networks
summary: Training changes a network's predictions while allocating task-relevant structure across its internal units. In an overparameterized ReLU network, several neurons can begin with exactly the same functional role, yet one may acquire a teacher feature while the others become redundant. We call the identity of that neuron feature ownership and ask whether it can be controlled by a parameter choice invisible to the initial predictor. In a tractable Gaussian teacher--student model, we fix the complete initial function and vary only a positive-homogeneous scaling gauge. Opposite gauges produce distinct feature trajectories and a sharp $Θ(D^2)$ separation in specialization time that no global change of clock can explain. Among any fixed number of initially duplicate students, assigning the favorable gauge to one neuron deterministically selects it as the owner and drives the remaining functional contribution to zero. An exact reaction--transport decomposition attributes the effect to different mobilities for changing a feature's coefficient and direction. We prove global selection and functional pruning, extend finite-time selection to visible perturbations and small-step full-batch gradient descent, and verify the predicted loss, alignment, pruning, and dissipation trajectories in population and finite-sample training. The initial predictor therefore determines neither when the feature is learned nor which neuron learns it.

AI.tldr: In overparameterized ReLU nets, among duplicate neurons sharing a feature, a positive-homogeneous gauge choice deterministically assigns feature ownership to one neuron, causing others to prune; this reveals a gauge-driven selection mechanism that cannot be explained by global clock changes. The Gaussian teacher–student model shows Θ(D^2) separation in specialization time, global selection and pruning, finite-time extension, and validation in training dynamics, implying the initial predictor does not fix when or which neuron learns a feature.
AI.motivation: Understand how parameterization, via gauge freedom, governs feature learning and neuron specialization beyond the initial predictor in overparameterized networks.
AI.method: Gaussian teacher–student model; fix the complete initial function; vary only a positive-homogeneous scaling gauge; derive reaction–transport decomposition; prove global selection and functional pruning; extend to finite-time selection with perturbations and small-step full-batch gradient descent; validate predictions in population and finite-sample settings.
AI.result: Distinct feature trajectories arise under different gauges with a sharp Θ(D^2) separation in specialization time; with an initially duplicate set of neurons, assigning the favorable gauge to one deterministically selects it as the owner and drives other functional contributions to zero; the reaction–transport decomposition attributes this to different mobilities of coefficient versus direction changes; global selection and functional pruning are proven, finite-time selection extended to perturbations and small-step GD, and loss/alignment/pruning/dissipation trajectories are verified in simulations.
AI.conclusion: The initial predictor does not determine when a feature is learned nor which neuron learns it; feature ownership is governed by an invisible parameterization gauge, highlighting gauge-driven, prune-then-learn dynamics in overparameterized networks.

title: AVCap: Reinforcing Audio-Video Joint Caption with Detail-Aware Reward
summary: Detailed audio-video joint captioning is essential for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior works are constrained by three main limitations: (1) the scarcity of high-quality public datasets with fine-grained audio-visual joint captions; (2) reinforcement-learning methods that rely on coarse reward signals; and (3) the lack of a benchmark and metric for evaluating detailed audiovisual captions at the atomic level. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVCap-100K, a high-quality dataset of 100K temporally aligned, detail-rich audio-video captions; (2) AVCap, a model optimized via Detail-Aware GRPO (Da-GRPO) that achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models and matches or surpasses proprietary models on several evaluations; and (3) AVCap-Bench and AVCap-Score, a specialized benchmark and metric for evaluating atomic-level details in audiovisual captions. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avcap.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive audiovisual captioning framework with AVCap dataset, Da-GRPO model, and AVCap-Bench/Score for atomic-level evaluation; claims state-of-the-art results for open-source models and competitive with proprietary models.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of high-quality fine-grained audio-visual captions, improve learning signals for captioning via detail-aware optimization, and establish a standard benchmark/metric for atomic-level audiovisual captions.
AI.method: (1) AVCap-100K: 100K temporally aligned, detail-rich audio-video captions. (2) AVCap: model optimized with Detail-Aware GRPO (Da-GRPO). (3) AVCap-Bench and AVCap-Score: benchmark and metric for atomic-level evaluation of captions.
AI.result: AVCap achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models and matches or surpasses proprietary models on several evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The work jointly addresses data, modeling, and evaluation gaps in detailed audiovisual captioning, enabling advances in multimodal video understanding and generation; reproducibility is supported by public code and datasets, though generalization to diverse domains remains to be fully validated.

title: Long-Horizon Agent Trajectory Attribution: A Unified Benchmark and Fine-Grained Annotation Framework
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate through long-horizon trajectories involving user instructions, tool use, external observations, and memory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate behavioral outcomes but provide limited support for fine-grained attribution analysis. We introduce trajectory attribution and develop a benchmark and annotation framework for this task. The benchmark organizes heterogeneous trajectories under a unified component schema and provides annotations of the primary attribution component, together with attack and execution chains where applicable. Instantiating the benchmark with trajectories from AgentDojo and the Stage and Canary settings of Agent3Sigma yields more than 1,300 annotated trajectories covering task-aligned actions, unsafe actions, and safety refusals. The benchmark defines two evaluation tasks, primary attribution localization and attribution-chain recovery, and provides reference baselines based on incremental trajectory contribution and component-level leave-one-out perturbation. It captures diverse attribution settings, including local and long-range attribution as well as structured attribution chains. Reference baseline results exhibit substantial performance differences across these settings, providing an initial characterization of the benchmark's attribution challenges. Beyond this initial instantiation, we release a reusable annotation skill that enables trajectories generated by new agent models to be standardized, annotated, and evaluated under the same framework. Project resources and future releases are available at https://github.com/chenjing-2024/agent-trajectory-attribution.

AI.tldr: Introduces a trajectory attribution benchmark and annotation framework for long-horizon LLM agent trajectories, with a unified component schema, two evaluation tasks, and reusable annotation tools, instantiated on AgentDojo and Agent3Sigma (Stage/Canary), yielding 1,300+ annotated trajectories and baseline results.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on behavioral outcomes and lack fine-grained attribution analysis across long-horizon agent trajectories; a structured attribution framework is needed to diagnose which components drive actions and safety outcomes.
AI.method: Develops a unified component schema for heterogeneous trajectories, provides annotations of the primary attribution component and where applicable attack/execution chains; instantiates the framework on AgentDojo trajectories and Stage/Canary settings from Agent3Sigma; defines two evaluation tasks (primary attribution localization and attribution-chain recovery); proposes baselines based on incremental trajectory contribution and component-level leave-one-out perturbations; releases a reusable annotation skill for standardizing new trajectories.
AI.result: Over 1,300 trajectories annotated, covering task-aligned actions, unsafe actions, and safety refusals; two evaluation tasks defined; baseline results show substantial performance differences across settings; resources available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Frames trajectory attribution as a tractable evaluation problem, enabling standardized annotation and benchmarking for long-horizon LLM agent behavior; provides reusable tooling and baseline methods, highlighting attribution challenges and inviting broader adoption and extension with new models.

title: ArchEGraph: A Large-Scale Graph Dataset for Geometry-Topology-Physics Aligned Building Energy Modeling
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, submitted to a conference
summary: Accurate estimation of building energy use is essential for achieving carbon neutral and sustainable buildings. To better understand the influence of design decisions on building energy use and calibrate machine learning models that can give architects and engineers rapid design feedback, large-scale datasets are needed that explicitly map building geometry to performance. We present ArchEGraph, a large-scale benchmark dataset that represents buildings as heterogeneous graphs with aligned geometry, topology, weather, and zone-level thermal loads. The dataset contains 5,481 buildings and 49,326 validated building-weather simulation cases. In total, it includes over 133,000 space nodes and 1.44 million face nodes, reflecting substantial geometric and topological complexity. Based on ArchEGraph, we define two benchmark tasks: (i) graph reconstruction from polygonal meshes, aiming to recover topological structure from geometric representations; and (ii) topology-informed load prediction, which leverages graph structure and temporal weather conditions to forecast zone-level response time series. We further introduce standardized evaluation protocols for both tasks and conduct cross-building and cross-climate generalization experiments to assess model robustness. ArchEGraph provides a unified testbed for studying geometry-topology-physics coupling in building energy modeling, enabling the development and evaluation of scalable and generalizable surrogate models.

AI.tldr: ArchEGraph is a large, graph-based benchmark linking building geometry, topology, weather, and zone-level loads; it defines two tasks—graph reconstruction from polygon meshes and topology-informed load prediction—with standardized protocols and cross-building/climate generalization to study geometry-topology-physics coupling in building energy modeling.
AI.motivation: To enable understanding of how design decisions affect energy use and to calibrate ML models for rapid design feedback, a large-scale, geometry-topology-physics aligned dataset is required.
AI.method: ArchEGraph represents buildings as heterogeneous graphs with aligned geometry, topology, weather, and thermal loads. It contains 5,481 buildings, 49,326 validated simulation cases, over 133,000 space nodes, and 1.44 million face nodes. Two benchmark tasks are defined: (i) graph reconstruction from polygonal meshes and (ii) topology-informed load prediction, aided by standardized evaluation protocols; cross-building and cross-climate experiments assess robustness.
AI.result: Defined two benchmark tasks and standardized evaluation protocols; created ArchEGraph as a unified testbed for studying geometry–topology–physics coupling in building energy modeling; demonstrated cross-building and cross-climate generalization experiments.
AI.conclusion: ArchEGraph enables scalable, generalizable surrogate models for building energy modeling and provides a comprehensive dataset and benchmarks for geometry-topology-physics coupling in building energy prediction and design optimization.

title: Debias in Text, Believe Your Eyes: Text-Anchored Cross-Modal Transfer for Visual Counter-Commonsense Reasoning
summary: The visual reasoning ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is crucial for downstream applications, particularly counter-commonsense reasoning, which requires models to reason beyond common assumptions. Recent studies mainly improve visual counter-commonsense reasoning by enhancing visual inputs, following the assumption that failures originate from insufficient visual grounding. However, our empirical analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not visual perception. MLLMs already capture the relevant visual evidence, and the correct answer exists in their decoding space. Instead, the shared language decoder resolves prior--evidence conflicts by favoring dominant language priors, especially for low-frequency factual scenarios. Motivated by this, we first propose a text-anchored data construction pipeline, whose core component, Fact-Frequency Distillation (FFD), estimates the prior strength of commonsense facts and distills verified counter-commonsense scenarios into a high-quality text corpus. Building upon this corpus, we introduce TACT, a text-anchored post-training framework that debiases the shared language decoder without requiring any visual training data. TACT routes evidence-following and prior-driven reasoning trajectories into different optimization stages, enabling the decoder to resolve prior--evidence conflicts. Across counter-commonsense visual benchmarks, TACT substantially improves visual reasoning while preserving general capabilities, demonstrating effective text-to-vision cross-modal transfer.

AI.tldr: Debias the shared language decoder of multimodal LLMs using a text-only post-training (TACT) guided by a Fact-Frequency Distillation (FFD) corpus to improve counter-commonsense visual reasoning without extra visual data.
AI.motivation: The bottleneck in counter-commonsense visual reasoning lies not in visual perception but in the decoder's priors, which favor dominant language facts and bias low-frequency counter-commonsense scenarios. A text-driven debiasing approach is needed to align reasoning with evidence.
AI.method: Introduce a text-anchored data construction pipeline using Fact-Frequency Distillation (FFD) to estimate prior strength of commonsense facts and distill verified counter-commonsense scenarios into a high-quality text corpus. Develop TACT, a text-anchored post-training framework that debiases the shared language decoder without using visual training data. TACT separates evidence-following and prior-driven reasoning trajectories into distinct optimization stages to resolve prior–evidence conflicts.
AI.result: Across counter-commonsense visual benchmarks, TACT substantially improves visual reasoning while preserving general capabilities, and demonstrates effective text-to-vision cross-modal transfer.
AI.conclusion: Text-driven debiasing of the decoder via FFD-guided corpus construction and TACT post-training effectively resolves prior–evidence conflicts in MLLMs, enhancing counter-commonsense visual reasoning without additional visual data.

title: Fast LapSum: Exact Differentiable Top-k at Million Scale
summary: The top-$k$ operation is a fundamental building block of modern sparse computation, enabling token routing, expert activation, memory selection, and attention pruning. Yet standard hard top-$k$ blocks gradients, while existing continuous (soft) relaxations remain too costly for large-scale models. We introduce Fast LapSum, an exact-budget soft top-$k$ primitive whose GPU solver runs in linear time after sorting. Unlike prior linear-time methods such as DFTopK, which relax the normalization constraint, Fast LapSum is, to our knowledge, the first method to preserve an exact selection mass of $k$ while remaining fully differentiable end-to-end. Our solver combines a linear-time threshold computation with an analytical vector--Jacobian product, and for extreme scales employs probabilistic bracketing to sort only the uncertain middle band of kernel-noised scores. The resulting overhead is almost negligible: the solver processes $10^6$, $10^7$, and $10^8$ scores in $0.41$, $1.15$, and $5.23$\,ms, respectively. This makes exact soft top-$k$ practical for sparse routing, retrieval, and large-scale optimization. We demonstrate Fast LapSum on two demanding applications operating over millions of coordinates inside the training loop: generating megapixel sparse adversarial examples with an exact soft budget of ${\sim}0.02\%$ of an image's pixels, achieving an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods, and training a fully differentiable sparse image coder from scratch.

AI.tldr: Fast LapSum delivers an exact-budget soft top-k with differentiable end-to-end training, achieving linear-time GPU performance after sort and enabling large-scale sparse routing and optimization.
AI.motivation: Standard hard top-k blocks gradients; soft relaxations are costly for large-scale models, hindering differentiable sparse operations in routing, retrieval, and attention pruning.
AI.method: An exact-budget soft top-k primitive with a GPU solver that sorts scores, computes a linear-time threshold, uses an analytical vector-Jacobian for backprop, and applies probabilistic bracketing to sort only the uncertain middle band of noisy scores for extreme scales.
AI.result: Demonstrates processing of 10^6–10^8 scores within sub-10 ms range (0.41–5.23 ms). Achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over prior methods on demanding applications, including exact soft budget sparse adversarial example generation and differentiable sparse image coding.
AI.conclusion: First method to preserve exact selection mass k while remaining fully differentiable; makes exact soft top-k practical for large-scale sparse routing, retrieval, and optimization.

title: Faster Query-Key Learning Sharpens Attention in Self-Attention Models
comment: Accepted to the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: A standard self-attention layer consists of two interacting circuits: the query-key circuit that governs attention allocation, and the output-value circuit that maps attended representations to predictions. Collapsed and factorized parameterizations of the query-key and output-value circuits lead to qualitatively different attention patterns. In particular, some parameterizations give sharper attention to task-relevant tokens, at a similar training loss. We analyze how the parameterizations of these circuits shape the parameter trajectories in single-layer self-attention models trained for next-token prediction. Through gradient-flow analysis, we show that factorization induces implicit rescaling of the two circuits' learning rates. We derive closed-form dynamics showing that output-value and query-key parameters move along a line, with relative speeds determined by their learning rates. Faster query-key learning relative to output-value learning thus produces sharper attention, as the model compensates for slower output-value learning by increasing attention mass on relevant tokens. Experiments show that differences in the relative learning rates of the two circuits govern attention concentration. This improves attention interpretability proxies while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

AI.tldr: Examines how collapsed vs factorized query-key and output-value parameterizations in one-layer self-attention alter attention patterns through implicit learning-rate rescaling; derives exact dynamics and shows faster query-key learning sharpens attention; validated empirically with comparable predictive performance and improved interpretability proxies.
AI.motivation: To understand how architectural parameterization shapes optimization dynamics and attention interpretability in self-attention, beyond mere training loss.
AI.method: Gradient-flow (continuous-time) analysis of single-layer self-attention; derive closed-form dynamics; compare factorized vs collapsed parameterizations; experiments with next-token prediction; quantify attention concentration and interpretability proxies.
AI.result: Factorization induces implicit rescaling of learning rates between circuits, causing parameters to move along a line; faster query-key learning relative to output-value produces sharper attention; empirical results show attention concentration modulated by relative learning rates; performance remains comparable; interpretability proxies improve.
AI.conclusion: Parameterization choice effectively controls attention sharpness via learning-rate coupling; improves interpretability without sacrificing performance; suggests design principles for attention mechanisms.

title: Degradation-Aware Prompt Learning with Cross-Modal Compensation for Adverse Weather Removal
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing. The code is available at: https://github.com/fanamber831/DCMPC-Net
summary: Adverse weather causes diverse and complex image degradations, severely compromising the reliability of computer vision systems. Existing all-in-one restoration models attempt to address multiple degradation types within a unified framework, but often lack explicit spatial and semantic modeling of degradation characteristics, limiting their adaptability to diverse weather conditions. To address this limitation, we propose a Degradation-Aware Cross-Modal Prompt Compensation Network (DCMPC-Net) that leverages cross-modal degradation cues from a pretrained vision-language model to condition restoration features within a unified backbone. Specifically, our DCMPC-Net mainly consists of the Cross-Modal Prompt Generator (CMPG), Prompt-Guided Attention Alignment Module (PGAAM), and Dual Feature Compensation Module (DFCM). The CMPG integrates textual embeddings with visual features to produce degradation-aware prompts that encode degradation-related semantic and contextual cues. These prompts are injected into the decoder via a PGAAM, which adaptively aligns semantic information with degraded regions to facilitate context-aware restoration. To further enhance structural fidelity, DFCM is introduced that disentangles degradation artifacts from scene structures, thereby improving the reconstruction of fine textures and detailed content. By integrating cross-modal semantic guidance with spatial alignment and structural enhancement, DCMPC-Net achieves robust and perceptually consistent restoration across diverse weather conditions. Extensive experiments show that DCMPC-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both task-specific and unified settings, achieving superior accuracy and visual fidelity.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal degradation-aware restoration network (DCMPC-Net) uses vision-language prompts and cross-modal alignment to improve weather-degraded image restoration, outperforming existing methods in diverse conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one restoration models lack explicit spatial and semantic modeling of degradation; leveraging cross-modal semantic cues from a pretrained vision-language model can adapt restoration to diverse weather conditions.
AI.method: Propose DCMPC-Net with CMPG, PGAAM, and DFCM. CMPG fuses textual embeddings with visual features to generate degradation-aware prompts; PGAAM injects prompts into the decoder and aligns semantic information with degraded regions; DFCM disentangles artifacts from scene structure to enhance textures and content.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both task-specific and unified restoration settings, with improved accuracy and perceptual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal semantic guidance combined with spatial alignment and structural enhancement yields robust, perceptually consistent restoration across diverse weather conditions and suggests a generalizable framework for degradation-aware restoration.

title: ReGraph: Learning to Generate Recipe Graphs from Food Images
summary: Recent Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have achieved impressive performance in recipe generation from food images.However, cooking is a structured transformation process in which ingredients undergo state changes through ordered actions,while free-form recipe language leaves the corresponding entities, intermediate states, and dependencies largely implicit and entangled.A graph representation makes this procedural knowledge explicit and compositional, providing a structured basis for assessing whether model outputs encode process-level knowledge rather than merely presenting plausible textual descriptions. To address this limitation, we present ReGraph, a large-scale recipe graph dataset that represents ingredients, cooking actions, and tools as entities, uses entity attributes to describe ingredient state changes, and employs typed relations to encode manipulation targets, destinations, and procedural ordering. ReGraph further incorporates explicit Recipe Reasoning Chain-of-Thought (RR-CoT) traces, providing auxiliary supervision for procedural decomposition and structured graph generation. Building on ReGraph, we propose Recipe Graph Learning (RGL), a two-stage framework that enables LMMs to generate a plausible fine-grained cooking workflow from a food image in the form of a structured recipe graph. Under a deterministic, schema-aware matching protocol, our experiments reveal a substantial gap between text-generation quality and recoverable procedural structure: recipes produced by existing approaches achieve competitive text-generation scores yet yield limited reference-aligned entity and relation structure under the ReGraph schema. In contrast, across two representative LMM backbones, RGL consistently improves the generation of cooking entities and procedural relations, while our analysis further shows that fine-grained ingredient-state capture remains the most challenging dimension.

AI.tldr: Proposes ReGraph: a large-scale recipe graph dataset encoding ingredients, actions, tools as entities with attributes and typed relations; includes RR-CoT traces. Introduces Recipe Graph Learning (RGL), a two-stage framework enabling LMMs to generate structured recipe graphs from food images. Finds a gap between text-generation quality and recoverable procedural structure; RGL improves entity and relation generation, while capturing ingredient-state changes remains hard.
AI.motivation: To move beyond free-form recipe text towards explicit, compositional procedural knowledge for cooking, enabling evaluation of whether LMM outputs encode process-level reasoning rather than plausible language alone.
AI.method: 1) Build ReGraph with entities (ingredients, actions, tools), attributes for state changes, and typed relations for manipulation targets/destinations/order; include RR-CoT traces for supervision. 2) Develop Recipe Graph Learning (RGL), a two-stage pipeline that maps food images to structured recipe graphs, with a deterministic, schema-aware matching protocol to assess alignment with the graph schema across two LMM backbones.
AI.result: There is a substantial gap between text-generation metrics and recoverable structural alignment to ReGraph; existing methods achieve competitive textual scores but poor entity/relation recovery. RGL consistently improves generation of cooking entities and procedural relations across backbones; fine-grained ingredient-state capture remains the most challenging dimension.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based procedural representations with RR-CoT supervision can improve structured output fidelity in LMMs for recipe generation; however, capturing fine-grained ingredient-state dynamics is still difficult and warrants further research.

title: Understanding Differentiable Embeddings Through Differential and Integral Geometry
comment: 19 pages in total, 12 for the main and 7 for the appendices. 9 figures in the main and 7 in the appendices
summary: How can an analyst decide whether a nonlinear dimensionality reduction embedding can be trusted? Existing diagnostics provide only partial answers: projection glyphs characterize local sensitivity, map-continuity scores measure local conditioning, and transport-based analyses reveal path-dependent inconsistencies. However, these methods appear unrelated and provide no common framework for understanding when they agree or not. We show that they are all derived from a single geometric object induced by every differentiable embedding, whether defined implicitly through optimization or explicitly by a learned mapping. This framework provides two complementary geometric views of an embedding. The differential view explains local behavior: its first-order term recovers projection glyphs, while its second-order curvature quantifies how far their linear approximation remains reliable. The integral view follows the same geometry along high dimensional paths and determines whether an embedding depends only on the current state or also on the path taken to reach it. We further show that map-continuity is a prerequisite for the other analyses. The framework is theoretically complete for diagnostics derived from the embedding geometry, and we prove the integral view irreducible: no amount of local measurement at any number of points, to any order of derivative, reproduces what it detects. Classical rank-based metrics form a complementary class based on finite-scale neighborhood relationships. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate theoretical predictions, demonstrate accurate curvature-based trust estimates on single-cell embeddings, and show that the integral analysis distinguishes single-valued embeddings from path-dependent optimization-based embeddings in ways that existing pointwise diagnostics cannot.

AI.tldr: Unifies diagnostics of nonlinear embedding trust under a single differentiable geometry, providing complementary differential and integral views that explain local and path-dependent behavior, with completeness results and empirical validation.
AI.motivation: Existing diagnostics (projection glyphs, map-continuity, transport analyses) are disparate and partial; a common geometric framework is needed to understand when they agree and to provide robust trust assessments for embeddings.
AI.method: Derive a single geometric object induced by any differentiable embedding (implicit via optimization or explicit mapping). Develop a differential view (first-order for local behavior, second-order for curvature) and an integral view (along high-dimensional paths) and establish that map-continuity is necessary for other analyses. Prove theoretical completeness for geometry-derived diagnostics and irreducibility of the integral view; position classical rank-based metrics as a complementary finite-scale approach. Validate on synthetic and real data, demonstrating curvature-based trust estimates and path-dependence distinctions.
AI.result: A unified geometric framework explains local and path-dependent diagnostics for embeddings. The differential view recovers projection glyphs and uses curvature to bound linear approximations; the integral view tracks geometry along paths to reveal path dependence that local measures cannot capture; map-continuity is a prerequisite; integral view is irreducible; rank-based metrics offer a complementary perspective. Empirical results confirm theoretical predictions and show practical trust estimation, particularly for single-cell embeddings, and distinguish path-dependent optimization-based embeddings.
AI.conclusion: The embedding geometry framework provides a complete, unified basis for diagnostics of nonlinear embeddings. It clarifies when different diagnostics agree, introduces two complementary views, and demonstrates irreducibility of the integral view. It also positions classical metrics as a related, finite-scale aid and validates the approach with experiments on synthetic and real data.

title: Dual-Space Modality Consistency Learning for Universal Cross-Modal Re-Identification
summary: Cross-modal Re-Identification (ReID) aims to retrieve the same identity across heterogeneous imaging modalities and has been widely studied in visible-infrared person ReID and cross-modal ship ReID. Existing methods have achieved promising performance by learning modality consistency in the spatial embedding space, yet often overlook frequency-domain modality discrepancy, particularly in high-frequency representations that are both highly discriminative and modality-sensitive. In addition, most approaches are tailored to specific modality settings, limiting their applicability across diverse cross-modal scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a Dual-Space Modality Consistency Learning (DSMCL) framework for universal cross-modal ReID. Specifically, DSMCL jointly models spatial feature distribution consistency and frequency-domain discriminative consistency. A Spatial Modality Consistency Learning (SMCL) branch performs Gaussian-based feature alignment, while a Frequency-aware Discriminative Consistency Learning (FDCL) strategy regularizes high-frequency representations through identity-aware cross-modal contrastive learning. By jointly capturing modality-specific characteristics and modality-shared identity cues, DSMCL learns robust representations and establishes a unified framework capable of accommodating diverse heterogeneous modality settings. Moreover, DSMCL is a plug-and-play framework that can be readily integrated into existing cross-modal ReID architectures. Extensive experiments on SYSU-MM01, RegDB, LLCM, HOSS-ReID, and CMShipReID across seventeen evaluation protocols show that DSMCL consistently improves multiple representative baselines.

AI.tldr: A dual-space framework (DSMCL) for universal cross-modal ReID that aligns spatial features and regu-larizes high-frequency cues via cross-modal contrastive learning, improving baselines across multiple datasets and protocols.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-modal ReID methods emphasize spatial consistency but neglect frequency-domain modality gaps and often target specific modality pairs, limiting generalization. A universal approach leveraging both spatial and high-frequency cues is needed.
AI.method: DSMCL comprises two branches: SMCL (Gaussian-based spatial feature distribution alignment) and FDCL (high-frequency discriminative consistency via identity-aware cross-modal contrastive learning). The framework is plug-and-play, designed to work with diverse cross-modal ReID architectures and modalities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SYSU-MM01, RegDB, LLCM, HOSS-ReID, CMShipReID across 17 evaluation protocols show DSMCL consistently improves representative baselines.
