This paper introduces a dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents, linking sidewalk-view imagery across urban, suburban, and regional Australian environments with individual rater attributes, and proposes the first user-conditioned multimodal deep learning framework for walkability perception, fusing visual features with respondent-level representations. A viewpoint-comparison study shows that sidewalk-view images receive significantly higher walkability ratings than matched street-view images, indicating that imagery source is a substantive design decision in perception surveys. The user-conditioned model improves rank agreement with observed ratings by 65% over an image-only baseline (quadratic weighted kappa 0.47 vs. 0.29), demonstrating that who is evaluating an environment carries predictive indication beyond image content alone. These findings support moving from aggregated, observer-independent walkability scores toward models that represent diverse users, enabling more inclusive assessment of pedestrian environments.

AI.tldr: Dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents linked to sidewalk-view imagery across Australian contexts; introduces a first user-conditioned multimodal framework fusing image features with respondent attributes; sidewalk-view yields higher perceived walkability; user-conditioned model improves rank agreement by 65% over image-only (kappa 0.47 vs 0.29).
AI.motivation: Current walkability research relies on aggregated, observer-independent scores and vehicle-mounted street-view imagery, which may misrepresent pedestrian perception. There is a need to account for perceptual heterogeneity and actual pedestrian visual experience by incorporating respondent attributes and sidewalk-level imagery.
AI.method: Assemble a dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents; collect sidewalk-view imagery across urban, suburban, and regional Australia; develop a multimodal deep learning framework that combines visual features with respondent-level representations (user-conditioned model); conduct a viewpoint-comparison study between sidewalk-view and matched street-view imagery; evaluate using rank agreement and quadratic weighted kappa, comparing against an image-only baseline.
AI.result: Sidewalk-view images receive significantly higher walkability ratings than matched street-view images, indicating imagery source influences perception. The user-conditioned model improves rank agreement with observed ratings by 65% over the image-only baseline, achieving a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.47 versus 0.29.
AI.conclusion: A shift from aggregated, observer-independent scores to models that represent diverse users is warranted for inclusive pedestrian environment assessment; incorporating respondent-level information improves prediction and reflects perceptual diversity across pedestrians.

title: YOLO-PEFT: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning on YOLO Family
summary: Generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods transferred from language models can fail silently on real-time detectors, whose heterogeneous operators and detection-specific components impose placement constraints absent from regular Transformer stacks. We propose YOLO-PEFT, a structure-aware framework that formulates adapter placement as an auditable constraint-planning problem. Given a detector graph, a PEFT request, and a resource budget, YOLO-PEFT assigns operator and semantic roles, evaluates explicit operator-validity, detector-semantic, graph-interface, and deployment predicates, records a reason code for each excluded module, and either emits a budgeted target-module plan or returns Refuse before training. Under the official VOC07+12 trainval-to-VOC07 test protocol, planner-selected RS-LoRA reaches 0.7138 and 0.7307 mAP50-95 on YOLO11s and YOLO12s, respectively, compared with 0.6428 and 0.6662 for Full-SFT. On RT-DETR-L, all seven evaluated LoRA-family configurations cross the predefined catastrophic threshold, supporting a calibrated Refuse-to-Full-SFT decision within the evaluated coverage. A controlled YOLO11 audit further shows that LoRA reduces peak training memory by 43.9 percent, although training takes 1.72 times longer. Within the evaluated detector families, placement policies, and calibration coverage, YOLO-PEFT replaces manual target-module trial and error with explicit, inspectable planning while preserving verified train-save-merge-export paths; refusal on unseen detector architectures remains an open validation problem. Project Page: github.com/Tencent/YOLO-Master

AI.tldr: YOLO-PEFT introduces a structure-aware, constraint-planning approach to PEFT for real-time detectors, delivering auditable adapter placement with budgeted target modules and demonstrated gains in mAP and memory-time trade-offs under VOC07+12, with limitations on unseen architectures.
AI.motivation: Current generic PEFT methods are not aware of detector-specific constraints, risking ineffective or unsafe adapter placement. There is a need for auditable, resource-bounded adapter deployment in heterogeneous detector graphs.
AI.method: Formulates placement as constraint-planning on a detector graph; assign operator and semantic roles; evaluate operator validity, detector semantics, graph interfaces, and deployment predicates; generate reason codes for excluded modules; output budgeted plan or Refuse.
AI.result: Planner-selected RS-LoRA improves mAP50-95 on YOLO11s/YOLO12s vs Full-SFT; on RT-DETR-L, all LoRA configs cross catastrophic threshold; LoRA reduces peak training memory by 43.9% with 1.72x longer training; planning provides explicit, inspectable decisions while preserving train-save-merge-export paths; refusal on unseen detectors remains open.
AI.conclusion: YOLO-PEFT enables auditable, constraint-aware PEFT deployment with explicit planning and safety guarantees within evaluated detector families; generalization to unseen architectures needs validation; project page available.

title: Finding Usable Weight Mechanisms with Tiled SVD
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Finding usable weight mechanisms via column-tiled SVD; pre-registered A/B/C eval on Gemma-2-2B (WikiText-2)
summary: The dominant approach to mechanistic interpretability trains proxy dictionaries such as sparse autoencoders and labels features from max-activating text. The best such atlases identify con- cepts, but that identity lives in the learned dictionary rather than in the network weights them- selves. We propose extracting mechanism mounts directly from linear sites by column-tiled SVD: each mount is a triple (v,u,σ) read as trigger, write, and strength. Identity is the weight rule. We evaluate mounts with a pre-registered suite judged on full-write energy lift rather than tile-local lift. On Gemma-2-2B with WikiText-2 (16,384-token subsample), all seven linear maps are scored: residual writes (mlp.down, attn.o) receive full A/B/C with steer after post-sublayer RMSNorm and pass 52/52 site-layers; other maps receive A/B only (mlp.gate/attn.q/attn.k/effective mlp.up/attn.v 26/26 each). Aggregate: 182/182 GO. We release library code, the corpus builder, the experiment entrypoint, and unit tests.

AI.tldr: Direct extraction of mechanism mounts from linear components using column-tiled SVD; all seven linear maps achieve full scores on a robust evaluation, enabling interpretation based on weight rules; code and data released.
AI.motivation: Improve mechanistic interpretability by aligning identified concepts directly with network weights and weight rules, rather than abstract dictionaries.
AI.method: Apply column-tiled SVD to linear sites to produce mounts (v, u, σ) interpreted as trigger, write, and strength. Identity corresponds to the weight rule. Evaluate using a pre-registered suite focused on full-write energy lift rather than tile-local lift, on Gemma-2-2B with WikiText-2 (16,384-token subsample). Assess seven linear maps (mlp.down, attn.o, mlp.gate, attn.q, attn.k, effective mlp.up, attn.v). Score with A/B/C and per-site-layer coverage (e.g., 52/52 or 26/26).
AI.result: All seven linear maps are scored: residual writes (mlp.down, attn.o) receive full A/B/C with steer after post-sublayer RMSNorm and pass 52/52 site-layers; other maps receive A/B only (mlp.gate/attn.q/attn.k/effective mlp.up/attn.v 26/26 each). Aggregate: 182/182 GO.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of extracting interpretable mechanism mounts directly from linear components; supports stronger alignment between interpretability artifacts and network weights; codebase, corpus builder, experiment entrypoint, and unit tests are released for replication and extension.

title: ELMZip: Onboard Satellite Image Compression via Extreme Learning Machines for Efficient Downlink
summary: The acquisition of multispectral imagery via small satellites (e.g., CubeSats) presents significant data downlink challenges due to high data volumes and restricted communication windows. While onboard image compression is critical to address this bottleneck, traditional methods often struggle to adapt to the nonlinear statistics of multi-band, multi-resolution data. To overcome these limitations, we propose ELMZip, a novel framework based on Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) and domain decomposition strategies for efficient, resolution-free onboard neural representation. ELMZip formulates the fitting process as a convex least-squares problem using random-feature single-layer networks, thereby eliminating the need for computationally expensive backpropagation. By adopting an asymmetric transmission protocol that sends only the compact output weights, the proposed method significantly reduces the downlink payload. Unlike previous neural representation approaches that rely on iterative optimization and require transmitting full network parameters, ELMZip achieves significant compression efficiency while maintaining high reconstruction fidelity. This capability enables immediate image reconstruction for analysis, allowing resource-constrained platforms to maximize data return and advancing real-time AI-powered Earth observation.

AI.tldr: ELMZip uses Extreme Learning Machines with random feature mappings and domain decomposition to build a resolution-free onboard neural representation for multispectral imagery. It reformulates fitting as a convex least-squares problem and transmits only compact output weights, enabling efficient downlink and immediate onboard reconstruction.
AI.motivation: CubeSat multispectral data face severe downlink bottlenecks due to high data volumes and limited communication windows; need adaptive, nonlinear compression that preserves fidelity while allowing real-time analysis on resource-constrained platforms.
AI.method: Employ random-feature single-layer networks to cast fitting as a convex least-squares problem, avoiding backpropagation; use domain decomposition for scalability; implement an asymmetric transmission protocol that sends only the output weights.
AI.result: Substantial reduction in downlink payload with high reconstruction fidelity; enables immediate image reconstruction on onboard platforms and supports real-time AI-powered Earth observation.
AI.conclusion: ELMZip offers a practical, efficient onboard neural representation approach that bypasses iterative optimization and full network parameter transmission, balancing compression gains with reconstruction accuracy.

title: KnifeHunter: Structured Local Representation Learning for Fine-Grained Knife Image Retrieval in Law Enforcement
summary: Knife-enabled violence presents a major public safety challenge, and law enforcement agencies require scalable tools for catalogue-level knife identification, intelligence analysis, and source attribution. Manual visual comparison is specialist, time-consuming, and difficult to scale under operational imaging conditions. We introduce KnifeHunter, an end-to-end forensic knife image retrieval system developed with UK law enforcement. The work contributes the KnifeHunter dataset, comprising 25,843 images across 543 knife classes from police evidence, retail catalogues, and border-force seizures, with structured metadata, Medium/Hard evaluation protocols, and large-scale distractor evaluation. We further propose CoRe-Net, a compact single-descriptor retrieval architecture that combines global context with spatially localised discriminative evidence. CoRe-Net introduces Structured Complementary Representation Learning (SCRL) to organise local evidence into complementary prototype-based representations, and Bi-Directional Reciprocal Fusion (BDRF) to integrate global and local evidence through residual projection and gated local-to-global injection. Using an EVA02-Base backbone and cosine-similarity retrieval, CoRe-Net achieves 88.0% mAP and 86.7% mP@10 on the Medium protocol, and 85.1% mAP and 83.8% mP@10 under distractor conditions. KnifeHunter was deployed by UK police forces during Operation Sceptre deployments from 2023 to 2025, achieving 99.2% mP@1 on field queries. These results demonstrate a practical and effective multimedia retrieval framework for fine-grained forensic knife matching in operational law-enforcement settings.

AI.tldr: Forensic knife image retrieval system KnifeHunter introduces a large dataset of 25,843 images across 543 knife classes and a compact retrieval model (CoRe-Net) with SCRL and BDRF, achieving strong mAP and mP@10 and deployed by UK police.
AI.motivation: Public safety demand for scalable, operational knife identification and attribution; manual visual matching is slow and not scalable under operational imaging conditions.
AI.method: End-to-end retrieval using a single-descriptor architecture; dataset creation; Structured Complementary Representation Learning (SCRL) for organizing local evidence into prototype-based representations; Bi-Directional Reciprocal Fusion (BDRF) integrating global and local evidence via residual projection and gated local-to-global injection; backbone EVA02-Base; cosine similarity; Medium/Hard and distractor evaluation; field deployment.
AI.result: 84-88% mAP and ~83-87% mP@10 on Medium; 85.1% mAP and 83.8% mP@10 under distractors; 99.2% mP@1 in field queries; practical effectiveness; deployed 2023-2025.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a practical and effective multimedia retrieval framework for fine-grained forensic knife matching in operational law-enforcement settings; large-scale dataset; real-world deployment.

title: FedLBW: A Loss-Based Weighting Strategy for Federated Learning on Non-IID Data in Wireless Networks
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative machine learning (ML) across distributed clients while preserving privacy. However, efficient model convergence in FL remains challenging, especially in wireless networks where non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data and frequent client dropouts are common. Traditional FL algorithms, such as FedAvg, rely solely on dataset size to weight client updates. This introduces biases towards clients with larger datasets and makes the process sensitive to non-IID data, outliers, and client dropouts. To address these challenges, we propose Federated Learning with Loss-Based Weighting (FedLBW), a novel aggregation method that assigns each client's update a weight proportional to the inverse of its validation loss, computed using a small proxy dataset on the server, rather than its dataset size. This ensures that lower-loss models exert greater influence during aggregation, prioritizing the most reliable updates and boosting overall performance. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets, including FashionMNIST (CNN), CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18), and CIFAR-100 (ResNet-34), we demonstrate that FedLBW achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to baseline algorithms such as FedAvg, FedAvgM, FedProx, FedNova, FedLAW and FedDkw, with notable improvements of up to 7.6 % higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 in extreme non-IID cases. Moreover, FedLBW showcases exceptional resilience to increasing dropout probabilities, consistently maintaining significantly higher accuracy even in challenging conditions. These results establish FedLBW as an effective and resilient solution for FL in wireless network environments, offering marked improvements in model accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness to non-IID data and client dropouts.

AI.tldr: FedLBW introduces loss-based weighting for FL aggregation by using a server-held proxy dataset to weight client updates by the inverse of their validation loss, mitigating biases from data size and non-IID data to improve accuracy and convergence, especially under client dropouts.
AI.motivation: Fix biases in FedAvg caused by using dataset size as the weight; address non-IID data and client dropouts in wireless FL to achieve faster convergence and higher accuracy.
AI.method: Compute each client's update validation loss on a small server proxy dataset; assign weight proportional to inverse loss (lower loss => higher weight); aggregate updates using these weights instead of dataset sizes; evaluate on FashionMNIST (CNN), CIFAR-10/100 (ResNet variants) under extreme non-IID and dropout conditions; compare to FedAvg, FedAvgM, FedProx, FedNova, FedLAW, FedDkw.
AI.result: FedLBW yields higher accuracy and faster convergence than baselines; improvements up to 7.6% on CIFAR-10 in extreme non-IID settings; maintains higher accuracy as dropout probability increases, demonstrating robustness to non-IID data and client dropouts.
AI.conclusion: Loss-based server-side weighting with a proxy dataset is an effective and resilient aggregation strategy for FL in wireless environments, boosting accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness to data heterogeneity and client churn.

title: A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums
summary: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine \cite{HannekeMoranWaknine2024} asked how the agnostic PAC learning curve of the direct sum $C^r$ depends on the single-instance learning curve $\epsagn(n\mid C)$ and on $r$. We show that the single-instance learning rate does not determine the direct-sum rate. Let $\F$ be the class of the two constant binary functions and let $\G$ consist of the zero function and the identity function. Both classes have agnostic learning curve of order $n^{-1/2}$.

AI.tldr: Direct-sum agnostic PAC learning rate is not determined by the single-instance learning rate; simple per-instance rates (n^{-1/2}) do not fix the multi-instance rate.
AI.motivation: Investigate how multitask/combined learning (direct sum) scales when only per-instance rates are known; test whether per-instance curves determine the direct-sum curve.
AI.method: Construct a minimal counterexample using two simple binary function classes F and G with matching agnostic learning curves, then analyze the agnostic PAC learning rate of their direct sum C^r to show independence from the single-instance rate.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the single-instance agnostic learning rate (order n^{-1/2} for F and G) does not control the direct-sum rate; the direct-sum rate can differ and is not implied by the per-instance curve.
AI.conclusion: One cannot infer direct-sum learning behavior from per-instance learning curves; direct-sum analysis requires separate derivation; the result highlights nontrivial interaction effects in multi-component learning even for simple base classes.

title: Explanation Stability of Test-Time Adaptation in Computational Pathology: A Large-Scale Benchmark
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has become a practical way to adapt deployed models to unlabeled target data, a setting that is especially relevant in computational pathology where staining, scanner, and cohort shifts are routine. While most TTA methods are evaluated by their effect on accuracy, clinical use also depends on whether the model's explanations remain reliable after adaptation. In this paper, we take a closer look at this largely unmeasured effect. We study explanation stability under TTA across two histopathology benchmarks, Camelyon17 and NCT CRC-HE, using five architectures ranging from convolutional networks to vision transformers and a pathology foundation model, seventeen TTA methods, and four attribution families. Across 2,958 adaptation runs, we observe a clear and systematic pattern: TTA methods differ sharply in how much they move model explanations, with frozen-backbone methods leaving attributions almost unchanged and continual methods such as CoTTA and RoTTA causing the largest drift. This effect is not uniform. Convolutional networks are substantially more sensitive than transformer and foundation-model backbones, and explanation drift increases with adaptation strength while remaining largely insensitive to batch size. Surprisingly, explanation stability is only weakly coupled to adaptation quality. Some methods preserve explanations almost perfectly while degrading calibration or accuracy, producing silent failures that would be missed by accuracy-only or explanation-only evaluation. These findings show that explanation stability is a distinct reliability axis for TTA in computational pathology. We release the metric, protocol, and full benchmark to support future work on adaptation methods that are not only accurate, but also stable and clinically auditable. Code: https://github.com/bahumanyarg11/tta-explanation-stability-pipeline

AI.tldr: Test-time adaptation (TTA) in computational pathology yields varying explanations stability across methods and architectures; frozen-backbone methods preserve attributions, while continual methods like CoTTA and RoTTA cause large explanation drift; convolutional nets are more sensitive than transformers or foundation models; explanation stability is a distinct reliability axis, not tightly tied to adaptation quality; a benchmark and code are released.
AI.motivation: To quantify how explanations behave under TTA in histopathology, where domain shifts and the reliability of explanations are critical for clinical trust.
AI.method: Comprehensive evaluation on Camelyon17 and NCT CRC-HE across five architectures (CNNs, ViTs, and a pathology foundation model), 17 TTA methods, and four attribution families. 2,958 adaptation runs were performed. The study analyzes explanation drift, adaptation strength, batch size effects, and the relationship between explanation stability and downstream metrics like calibration and accuracy.
AI.result: A clear pattern emerges: TTA methods differ in how much they move explanations. Frozen-backbone methods leave attributions almost unchanged; continual methods (e.g., CoTTA, RoTTA) induce the largest drift. Explanation drift is not uniform: CNNs are more sensitive than transformers and foundation-model backbones. Drift increases with adaptation strength and is largely insensitive to batch size. Explanation stability is only weakly coupled to adaptation quality; some methods preserve explanations but degrade calibration or accuracy, enabling silent failures. The authors provide a metric, protocol, and full benchmark, and release code for future work on stable, auditable adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Explanation stability constitutes a distinct reliability axis for TTA in computational pathology. The work provides a benchmark and tools to develop adaptation methods that are not only accurate but also explainable and clinically auditable.

title: ReQuant: Fixed-Grid Discrete Refinement for Post-Training Quantization
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used to reduce the memory and computational cost of large language models. Existing PTQ methods typically obtain an initial quantized model through heuristic rules or greedy optimization, and once quantization is completed the resulting integer assignments are usually treated as final. This observation motivates a complementary optimization stage within PTQ that keeps quantized weights improvable after an executable quantized model has been produced, while preserving the quantized format. We introduce ReQuant, a backpropagation-free fixed-grid refinement procedure for this stage. Agnostic to the PTQ initializer, ReQuant takes an existing quantized model as a feasible starting point and iteratively revisits its discrete weight assignments on the fixed quantization grid. Accepted updates strictly reduce the mean squared reconstruction error and remain on the original grid. In this way, ReQuant turns the initially fixed PTQ output into an iteratively optimizable discrete solution and serves as a plug-and-play post-processing stage for existing PTQ pipelines. Experiments across diverse model families, bit-widths, and downstream tasks show that ReQuant consistently improves quantized models from heterogeneous PTQ initializers, with especially large gains on simple initializers and lower bit-widths. Notably, ReQuant can refine a simple round-to-nearest initialization across multiple sweeps until it approaches or surpasses GPTAQ under the same quantization format. These results establish ReQuant as a practical complementary stage for further improving existing PTQ pipelines.

AI.tldr: ReQuant provides a backpropagation-free, fixed-grid weight refinement for post-training quantization (PTQ). Starting from an existing quantized model, it iteratively revisits discrete weight assignments on the fixed quantization grid to reduce mean squared reconstruction error, without changing the grid or using gradient updates.
AI.motivation: PTQ often yields suboptimal quantized weights due to greedy or heuristic initialization. A complementary, discretenvironment optimization stage can further improve accuracy without incurring full retraining or changing the quantization format.
AI.method: A grid-constrained, backpropagation-free optimization. Given a quantized model, ReQuant iteratively searches the discrete weight grid for updates that strictly decrease the mean squared error between full-precision and quantized representations, with updates constrained to the original fixed grid. It is agnostic to the initial PTQ method and acts as a plug-and-play post-processing stage.
AI.result: Across diverse model families, bit-widths, and downstream tasks, ReQuant consistently improves PTQ outputs from heterogeneous initializers. It yields especially large gains when starting from simple initializers and lower bit-widths, and can refine a simple round-to-nearest initialization to approach or surpass GPTQ under the same quantization format.
AI.conclusion: ReQuant is a practical, complementary stage that can be paired with existing PTQ pipelines to further refine quantized weights without introducing gradient-based optimization or changing the quantization grid.

title: How Molecular Generative Models Organize Molecular Identity
summary:
Generative models for matter are often evaluated as samplers over output representations, and their latent spaces are commonly used as proxies for navigating chemical space. Much less is known about how these models internally arrange discrete chemical identities within those representations. We study this arrangement by making molecular identity explicit and pulling it back through the generative process. Through these pullbacks we probe the regions that generate the same object, exposing the trained model's internal repertoire: a fixed partition that determines which objects (novel or not) the model can produce.
  Across three molecular generative architectures, we find that this repertoire is arranged into piecewise-constant regions separated by recurring coarse-to-fine boundaries. Its organization depends on the representation probed, the identity convention, decoder stochasticity, and the metric used to compare coordinates. During training, local chemical organization stabilizes while the number of distinct molecular identities represented within each neighborhood continues to change. Internal organization must therefore be characterized, rather than assumed, before a generative space can be treated as chemically navigable.

AI.tldr: Generative molecular models have a fixed, partitioned internal identity repertoire with piecewise-constant regions and recurring coarse-to-fine boundaries; organization depends on representation, identity convention, decoder stochasticity, and distance metric; local structure stabilizes during training while the diversity of identities per region keeps changing; thus internal organization must be characterized to treat the space as chemically navigable.
AI.motivation: To understand how discrete chemical identities are arranged inside latent or representation spaces of molecular generative models, not just how outputs are sampled.
AI.method: We pull back molecular identity through the generative process to identify regions that map to the same object, and compare across three generative architectures while varying representation, identity convention, decoder stochasticity, and the metric used to compare coordinates.
AI.result: The internal repertoire forms a fixed partition into piecewise-constant regions, separated by recurring coarse-to-fine boundaries. This organization stabilizes locally during training, but the number of distinct identities represented within each neighborhood continues to change. The observed structure depends on representation choice, identity convention, decoder randomness, and the distance metric.
AI.conclusion: Internal organization of the generative space cannot be assumed to be navigable; it must be characterized for each setup to reliably navigate chemical space and interpret generative trajectories.

title: RoRA: Role-Oriented Regional Allocation for Visual Token Pruning in MLLMs
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/LukieLuu/RoRA
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode images as long visual token sequences, making prefilling and KV-cache storage expensive. Existing training-free pruning methods select tokens by importance, diversity, or spatial coverage, but treat retained tokens as interchangeable and do not explicitly track which object-related regions are already covered. We present RoRA, a training-free framework that casts visual token pruning as role-oriented regional evidence allocation. Given a fixed budget, RoRA partitions tokens into a protected semantic core, complementary context, and fine-grained detail. It first calibrates text-conditioned attention with a positional prior and a prompt-calibrated object prior, then builds Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) from high-confidence anchors as lightweight proxies for covered object support. Context is explored mainly outside AARs, while a small AAR-guided budget restores local detail; pairwise similarity is used only for context-stage redundancy filtering. Under matched budgets, RoRA consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines across LLaVA and Qwen-VL families, retaining most of the unpruned accuracy even at aggressive pruning ratios, e.g., 96.5% of full performance at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5, and improving over D2Pruner by about 5% on Qwen3-VL at 75-90% pruning. At a 66.7% pruning ratio, RoRA requires only 0.7 ms for token selection and reduces end-to-end inference time by 24.6%, corresponding to a 1.33x speedup over unpruned inference on an NVIDIA H800.

AI.tldr: RoRA is a training-free visual token pruning framework for multimodal LLMs that allocates tokens into a semantic core, context, and detail. It calibrates attention with positional and object priors, builds Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) from high-confidence anchors to cover object regions, and largely explores context outside AARs with a small AAR-guided budget for local detail. It achieves strong performance retention and speedups under aggressive pruning across LLaVA and Qwen-VL, outperforming baselines such as D2Pruner.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs encode images as long visual token sequences, making prefilling and KV-cache storage expensive. Existing training-free pruning methods focus on token importance or diversity but treat retained tokens as interchangeable and lack explicit tracking of covered object-related regions, leading to inefficient pruning and potential loss of object-level information.
AI.method: RoRA partitions visual tokens into three roles under a fixed budget: protected semantic core, complementary context, and fine-grained detail. It calibrates text-conditioned attention using a positional prior and a prompt-calibrated object prior, then constructs Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) from high-confidence anchors as lightweight proxies for covered object support. The context is explored mainly outside AARs, while a small AAR-guided budget restores local detail. Pairwise similarity is used only for redundancy filtering in the context stage.
AI.result: Under matched budgets, RoRA consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines across LLaVA and Qwen-VL families, retaining most unpruned accuracy even at aggressive pruning. Examples: 96.5% of full performance at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5; ~5% improvement over D2Pruner on Qwen3-VL at 75-90% pruning. At 66.7% pruning, RoRA requires 0.7 ms for token selection and reduces end-to-end inference time by 24.6%, achieving 1.33x speedup over unpruned inference on an NVIDIA H800.
AI.conclusion: RoRA demonstrates the effectiveness of training-free, role-oriented regional evidence allocation for visual token pruning in MLLMs. By explicitly covering object-related regions with AARs and calibrating attention, it preserves accuracy while delivering substantial speedups and outperforming existing pruning baselines.

title: ZIPBrain: Can EEG Foundation Models Be Faster, Locally Deployable, but Accurate?
summary: This work investigates whether Electroencephalograph (EEG) foundation models (EFMs) can be made faster and locally deployable without sacrificing accuracy. EEG foundation models are a major trend, offering strong general-purpose representations. However, their computational burden grows quadratically with input length, hindering deployment on resource-constrained scenario, particularly for real-time clinical monitoring. EEG's low SNR further suggests many of these tokens are redundant and compressible with little accuracy cost. We propose ZIPBrain, a novel redundancy-aware EEG token pooling module that leverages this low-SNR characteristic to reduce token count. Given a token sequence, ZIPBrain partitions tokens into redundant and unique groups, then merges each redundant token with its most similar counterpart in the unique group. Furthermore, ZIPBrain serves as a training-free, plug-and-play module that seamlessly integrates into standard Transformer encoders with negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple EEG foundation models show ZIPBrain's strong versatility, achieving 1.3%-10.5% average improvement over baselines, while reducing wall-clock inference time by 32.7% (up to 41.8% with CUDA Graph) compared to the original EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: ZIPBrain is a training-free, plug-and-play token pooling module for EEG transformers that detects redundant tokens due to low-SNR signals and merges them with the most similar unique tokens, achieving faster inference with minimal accuracy loss across EEG foundation models.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models offer strong general-purpose representations but scale quadratically with input length, imposing computational burdens unsuitable for real-time, resource-constrained clinical monitoring. The low SNR in EEG signals implies substantial redundancy that can be compressed with little accuracy cost.
AI.method: ZIPBrain partitions the token sequence into redundant and unique groups, then merges each redundant token with its most similar unique token. It is training-free and integrates into standard Transformer encoders as a lightweight, plug-and-play module, introducing negligible computational overhead.
AI.result: Across multiple EEG foundation models, ZIPBrain yields 1.3%–10.5% average accuracy improvement over baselines and reduces wall-clock inference time by 32.7% (up to 41.8% with CUDA Graph) compared to the original EEG foundation models.
AI.conclusion: ZIPBrain provides versatile, fast, locally deployable EEG transformers with negligible overhead and improved efficiency/accuracy balance, addressing the practical deployment bottlenecks of EEG foundation models.

title: Density-aware Hierarchical Clustering Based on Element-Categorized Connection Subgraphs
summary: Clustering is a fundamental data mining technique for pattern recognition through unsupervised learning. Among various clustering methods, hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, and graph clustering stand out as representative approaches. For hierarchical clustering, it can be categorized into agglomerative and divisive modes to construct clusters in a recursive manner. The key aspect of both modes is the calculation of inter-cluster similarity, which determines whether to merge the sub-clusters into one cluster or divide a current cluster into sub-clusters. Traditionally, the similarity is derived from pairwise distances, often overlooking density variations and structural connectivity in graphs. To address this, we propose a density-aware hierarchical clustering method based on element-categorized connection subgraphs (DHC-ECS), which effectively integrates the hierarchical clustering, density-based clustering, and graph clustering. Particularly, a novel inter-cluster similarity metric is introduced that considers not only distances but also the element categorization in the KNN connection subgraphs, kernel density estimation, and local connectivity within sub-clusters. Extensive evaluations on heterogeneous benchmark datasets demonstrate that DHC-ECS exhibits superior overall performance in terms of clustering accuracy and parameter robustness compared with the baseline methods (including AChameleon, RNN-DBSCAN, McDPC, and G-RMS). The work indicates the great potential of the proposed clustering algorithm for low-dimensional datasets by leveraging local density and graph-structured connectivity (i.e., the duality of vertices and edges), as well as the possibility to determine an intrinsic threshold, reducing the reliance on manual parameter tuning.

AI.tldr: A density-aware hierarchical clustering method (DHC-ECS) that unifies hierarchical, density-based, and graph clustering by using element-categorized connection subgraphs and a novel inter-cluster similarity that accounts for distances, KNN subgraph categorization, kernel density, and local connectivity; shows superior accuracy and parameter robustness on diverse datasets, with intrinsic thresholding reducing manual tuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional hierarchical clustering relies on pairwise distances and often ignores density variations and graph connectivity. A unified approach that incorporates density information and graph structure can improve clustering quality and reduce dependence on manually chosen thresholds, especially for low-dimensional data.
AI.method: Introduce DHC-ECS, which uses element-categorized connection subgraphs. Develop a novel inter-cluster similarity that combines distance, element categorization in KNN connection subgraphs, kernel density estimation, and local sub-cluster connectivity. Integrates hierarchical, density-based, and graph clustering principles to form a density-aware hierarchical clustering framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on heterogeneous benchmark datasets show that DHC-ECS achieves superior clustering accuracy and parameter robustness compared with baseline methods (including AChameleon, RNN-DBSCAN, McDPC, G-RMS).
AI.conclusion: DHC-ECS demonstrates strong potential for low-dimensional datasets by leveraging local density and graph connectivity (vertices and edges duality) and can intrinsically determine thresholds, reducing manual parameter tuning.

title: International Transfer of Stochastic Cortical Self-Reconstruction
summary: Stochastic cortical self-reconstruction (SCSR) enables personalized mapping of gray matter atrophy, a hallmark of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), onto high-resolution cortical surfaces. Unlike conventional normative modeling approaches, which typically operate at a coarse regional level and remain inherently constrained by the covariates included during training, SCSR estimates an individualized healthy reference directly from the observed cortical thickness at the vertex level. This allows the detection of subtle, subject-specific deviations from healthy cortical shape. In this work, we investigate the generalization and transferability of SCSR, originally trained on UK Biobank (UKB) data, to an independent Chinese population dataset. Specifically, we evaluate the ability of SCSR-derived Z-scores to discriminate between healthy scans, individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and patients with AD, while also assessing model robustness across the lifespan. We compare four training strategies: direct application of the UKB-trained model, fine-tuning on Chinese data, training from scratch, and joint training on UKB and Chinese cohorts. As reconstruction backbones, we consider both a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Spherical UNet (SUNet). Our results demonstrate that SCSR provides robust detection of cortical atrophy in the Chinese population across all evaluated models. The highest discriminative performance was achieved by the fine-tuned SUNet model (average pairwise AUC = 0.848), followed closely by the UKB-trained SUNet. Moreover, reconstruction errors remained low across the lifespan, even when the training population exhibited a substantially narrower age distribution, indicating strong cross-population transferability.

AI.tldr: SCSR demonstrates cross-population transferability of individualized vertex-level cortical thinning mapping from UKB to a Chinese cohort, with SUNet-based fine-tuning yielding the best discrimination between HC, MCI, and AD (AUC ~0.848); reconstruction is robust across lifespan.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of coarse, covariate-driven normative models by deriving individualized healthy references at vertex level; assess generalizability and transferability of SCSR across populations to enhance early detection of neurodegenerative atrophy.
AI.method: Compare two backbones (MLP and SUNet) within SCSR, and four training strategies (direct UKB application, Chinese fine-tuning, training from scratch, joint UKB+Chinese). Evaluate performance on HC/MCI/AD discrimination via Z-scores derived from vertex-level reconstructions on UKB and Chinese datasets.
AI.result: SCSR robustly detects cortical atrophy in the Chinese cohort across all models. The top performance is achieved by fine-tuned SUNet with average pairwise AUC of 0.848; UKB-trained SUNet also performs well. Reconstruction errors remain low across lifespan, even with a narrower training age distribution, indicating strong cross-population transferability.
AI.conclusion: SCSR achieves cross-population generalization, especially with fine-tuned SUNet, suggesting that individualized, vertex-level healthy reference reconstruction can transfer across populations and remain sensitive to disease-related cortical thinning across ages.

title: Not All Problems Are Best Modeled as MILP: A DSL-Centric Framework for Flexible and Accurate Optimization Modeling
summary: Solving combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) requires not only efficient algorithms but also carefully crafted formulations. While recent works have leveraged LLMs to automate optimization modeling, current frameworks predominantly rely on a rigid mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) paradigm. In this paper, we argue that not all problems are best modeled as MILP, as forcing complex domains into linear constraints can induce prohibitive modeling complexity and severely restrict solver flexibility. To address this, we propose OptiDSL, a framework that shifts the focus from rigid MILP formulations to domain-specific language (DSL) representations. By utilizing LLMs to map natural language onto standardized, domain-accepted structures, OptiDSL decouples problem formulation from execution. This paradigm enables seamless integration with a diverse library of specialized solvers, ranging from traditional heuristics to modern learning-based methods. Experimental results on the comprehensive benchmark of 44 COP types show that OptiDSL significantly surpasses MILP-based pipelines, yielding a 51.66% gain in formulation accuracy and a 91.71% decrease in modeling time. Notably, it also outperforms MILP-based pipelines on the existing benchmark, achieving a 23.09% higher formulation accuracy. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OptiDSL.

AI.tldr: OptiDSL replaces rigid MILP formulations with a DSL-based framework guided by LLMs, enabling problem-to-solver decoupling and improved optimization modeling.
AI.motivation: Rigid MILP formulations can cause modeling complexity and limit solver flexibility when mapping complex COP domains; a domain-accepted DSL can streamline representation and leverage diverse solvers.
AI.method: Use LLMs to translate natural-language COP descriptions into standardized DSL representations; build a library of specialized solvers and decouple formulation from execution; evaluate across a 44 COP benchmark.
AI.result: Significant gains over MILP pipelines: 51.66% increase in formulation accuracy and 91.71% reduction in modeling time; also beats MILP baselines on the existing benchmark with 23.09% higher formulation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling formulation from execution via DSLs and leveraging domain-specific solvers yields substantial improvements in COP modeling and performance, as demonstrated by OptiDSL.

title: Beyond Foundation Models: Dimension-Aware Neural Architecture Search with Small-Data Representation Models for Cryocooler Lifetime Prediction
summary:
Large-scale pretrained time-series models achieve strong results through large-scale pretraining and task-agnostic representation learning, but they rely on abundant, diverse data that industrial and scientific domains often lack. We therefore propose the FSD-RM (Family of Small-Data Representation Models) paradigm as a practical alternative for limited, domain-specific telemetry. Rather than relying on large-scale pretraining, we focus on capacity-controlled representation learning using established encoder architectures (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer), selected for their suitability in small-data settings and interpretability.
  These encoders are trained unsupervised on multivariate telemetry data and integrated into a two-stage pipeline for downstream lifetime prediction. To systematically examine architectural trade-offs under data constraints, we employ \textbf{dimension-aware neural architecture search (NAS)} to jointly optimize model capacity and input dimensionality.
  Experiments on cryocooler telemetry show that the proposed approach achieves competitive predictive performance while reducing training cost and model complexity. The contribution lies in combining established representation learning techniques within a coherent, NAS-driven framework tailored to small-data regimes, with explicitly defined parameter settings and design choices. The results indicate that effective representation learning can be achieved without large-scale pretraining when appropriate inductive bias and capacity control are applied.

AI.tldr: A NAS-driven, small-data representation learning framework (FSD-RM) that uses capacity-controlled encoders trained unsupervised on limited multivariate telemetry to enable competitive lifetime prediction with lower training cost and model complexity.
AI.motivation: Industrial and scientific domains often lack abundant, diverse data required by large-scale pretrained time-series models. There is a need for practical, data-efficient representation learning tailored to small-data regimes.
AI.method: Use a family of established encoders (CNN1D, LSTM, GRU, Transformer) with capacity control, train them unsupervised on multivariate telemetry, and integrate into a two-stage pipeline for lifetime prediction. Employ dimension-aware neural architecture search (NAS) to jointly optimize model capacity and input dimensionality.
AI.result: On cryocooler telemetry, the approach achieves competitive predictive performance while reducing training cost and model complexity compared to baselines relying on large-scale pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Effective representation learning in small-data regimes is feasible by applying appropriate inductive biases and capacity control, with NAS-guided architecture and dimensionality choices guiding the trade-offs.

title: Geometry-Aware Camera Localization for Bronchoscopy
summary: Camera localization in bronchoscopy remains a challenging problem due to stringent accuracy requirements, real-time constraints, and limited training data. Compared to natural scenes, the confined anatomical structures demand millimeter-level precision, while intraoperative guidance necessitates low-latency inference. However, existing methods often fail to effectively exploit preoperative geometric priors, limiting their robustness and accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a unified geometry-aware bronchoscope localization framework (GABL) that effectively fuses preoperative structural priors with paired intraoperative video to estimate 6-DoF camera poses. Specifically, to address visual ambiguity in complex airways, we propose a graph-guided coarse-to-fine localization scheme that effectively leverages structural priors for precise pose estimation. Furthermore, to mitigate pose jitter and bridge the visual-structural gap, we integrate a Transformer-based tracking model with a novel RGB-depth matching objective, jointly enforcing spatio-temporal and geometric consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method yields remarkable reductions of 8.37% and 31.76% in translation and rotation errors over the prior state-of-the-art, alongside 4 times inference speedup (33.6 FPS) for robust real-time bronchoscope localization. Project website: https://paulili08.github.io/GABL/.

AI.tldr: GABL fuses preoperative priors with intraoperative video for 6-DoF bronchoscope localization using graph-guided coarse-to-fine localization and Transformer-based tracking with an RGB-depth matching objective, achieving real-time mm-scale accuracy improvements.
AI.motivation: Bronchoscope localization requires millimeter-level precision and low latency; existing methods underutilize geometric priors and struggle with robustness and real-time performance due to limited training data and challenging anatomical scenes.
AI.method: A unified geometry-aware framework that (1) uses a graph-guided coarse-to-fine localization leveraging structural priors for accurate pose estimation, and (2) employs a Transformer-based tracking model with a novel RGB-depth matching objective to enforce spatio-temporal and geometric consistency, integrating intraoperative video with preoperative priors.
AI.result: Significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art: 8.37% reduction in translation error and 31.76% reduction in rotation error, plus a fourfold increase in inference speed to 33.6 FPS, enabling robust real-time bronchoscope localization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GABL framework effectively combines structural priors with video data to achieve precise, real-time 6-DoF localization in bronchoscopy, addressing visual ambiguity and pose jitter while providing substantial accuracy and speed gains.

title: Unsupervised Adaptation of PDE Foundation Models
summary: Pretrained partial differential equation (PDE) foundation models can generalize across different equations, but adapting them to unseen PDE systems typically requires dense solution data, which is often expensive or unavailable. To address this limitation, we propose an unsupervised PDE-based finetuning framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth solutions. We first pretrain a neighborhood attention Transformer on diverse time-dependent PDEs spanning varying spatial scales, yielding transferable representations across heterogeneous equations. In the adaptation stage, we construct a physics-based objective using the PDE residual and boundary conditions, and finetune the model on unseen equations via low-rank adaptation (LoRA). To address the uneven learning across physical quantities in standard LoRA, we introduce NSLoRA, a Newton-Schulz orthogonalized variant that rebalances adaptation. Our method achieves performance comparable to supervised LoRA finetuning without requiring any ground-truth solutions, while consistently outperforming competitive neural operator baselines and recent PDE foundation models across heterogeneous PDE benchmarks spanning multiple spatial dimensions.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised finetuning of PDE foundation models via physics-based objectives and NSLoRA, enabling adaptation to unseen PDEs without ground-truth solutions and outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: PDE foundation models struggle to adapt to unseen equations without expensive labeled data (ground-truth solutions); offer a framework that leverages physics residuals to drive learning.
AI.method: Pretrain a neighborhood attention Transformer on diverse time-dependent PDEs across varying spatial scales. Adaptation uses a physics-based objective composed of PDE residuals and boundary conditions, finetuning unseen equations via LoRA. Introduce NSLoRA (Newton-Schulz orthogonalized LoRA) to rebalance adaptation across physical quantities.
AI.result: Achieves performance comparable to supervised LoRA finetuning without ground-truth data and consistently outperforms competitive neural operator baselines and recent PDE foundation models across heterogeneous PDE benchmarks spanning multiple spatial dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised PDE-based fine-tuning is viable for cross-domain PDE generalization; NSLoRA mitigates uneven gains across physical quantities and enables robust adaptation without labeled solutions.

title: Every Cache Entry Earns Its Place: Global Allocation of Resolution and Coverage for KV Cache Compression
summary: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long contexts, KV cache storage and repeated access have become a major bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage. Therefore, we propose GraceKV, a global approach for the allocation of resolution and coverage in KV cache compression, and formulate the compression process as a global resource allocation problem under a fixed cache budget. GraceKV treats each layer-KV head-slot combination as an atomic unit and builds a prototype tree. Leaf nodes correspond to token-level KV entries, while each internal node uses a single prototype to compress the KV space covered by its children. A set of non-overlapping nodes in the tree forms the representation of an atomic unit. Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache budget. Finally, the nodes retained across all trees form the compressed KV cache. This process adaptively determines the allocation of cache resources among atomic units globally and the balance between resolution and coverage. GraceKV requires no additional training, and the entire compression and inference process is performed on the GPU. Systematic experiments across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show that GraceKV ranks first in 24 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128-fold compression. These results validate the effectiveness of global budget allocation in coordinating information coverage and local resolution.

AI.tldr: GraceKV is a global budget-aware KV-cache compression framework for LLMs. It treats layer-head-slot groups as atomic units, builds a prototype tree to compress token KV space, and allocates a shared cache budget globally to balance local resolution and information coverage. No extra training is required; compression/inference runs on GPU. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across long-context tasks and remains robust under up to 128× compression.
AI.motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods rely on fixed rules and operate locally (eviction/merging), preventing flexible, cross-layer/head/slot resource flow and joint optimization of resolution and coverage. A global budgeting approach could coordinate resources to improve long-context performance.
AI.method: Model the KV cache as atomic units (layer-head-slot). Build a prototype tree where leaf nodes are token-level KV entries; internal nodes summarize the KV space of their children with a single prototype. A set of non-overlapping nodes forms an atomic unit. Operations: expanding by adding a root expands coverage; splitting nodes improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a fixed cache budget. The final cache is the union of nodes retained across trees. No training is required; compression/inference runs entirely on GPU.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show GraceKV achieves top performance in 24 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128× compression, validating the efficacy of global budget allocation for balancing resolution and coverage.
AI.conclusion: Global budget-aware KV-cache compression without additional training enables effective, GPU-based inference for long-context LLMs. GraceKV coordinately allocates resources across all atomic units, improving information coverage and local resolution under a fixed cache budget.

title: Beyond Fluency: A Clinical Benchmark and Anomaly-Enhanced Baseline for Spine MRI Report Generation
comment: Maria Monzon and Catherine R. Jutzeler contributed equally as shared last authors. Accepted at the CV4Clinic Workshop, CVPR 2026
summary: Radiology reporting is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability, making automated report generation an attractive clinical application for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). We benchmark state-of-the-art VLMs on lumbar spine MRI with a focus on diagnostic accuracy and demonstrate that standard lexical and semantic metrics poorly reflect clinical correctness: fluent, well-structured reports can score highly while containing clinically meaningful diagnostic errors. To address this failure mode, we propose an architecture-agnostic framework that augments VLM inputs with spatially localized, disc-level anomaly heatmaps generated by a semi-supervised U-Net++ model. These heatmaps both improve anatomical sensitivity through explicit visual grounding and provide an independent interpretability output for clinical oversight, moving us closer to diagnostically reliable, visually grounded VLMs for lumbar spine MRI interpretation.

AI.tldr: VLMs for lumbar spine MRI can generate fluent reports, but standard metrics miss critical diagnostic errors; introducing disc-level anomaly heatmaps from a semi-supervised U-Net++ to ground VLM outputs improves anatomical sensitivity and provides independent interpretability, aiming for more reliable, visually grounded diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Radiology report automation using VLMs is hampered by misalignment between linguistic metrics and clinically correct diagnoses; there is a need for explicit visual grounding and interpretable outputs to ensure diagnostic reliability.
AI.method: An architecture-agnostic framework augments VLM inputs with spatially localized, disc-level anomaly heatmaps generated by a semi-supervised U-Net++; heatmaps serve as explicit visual grounding and an independent interpretability channel.
AI.result: The heatmaps improve anatomical sensitivity and provide an interpretable output for clinical oversight, addressing the mismatch between fluency and clinical correctness.
AI.conclusion: Visually grounded, interpretable VLMs with disc-level heatmaps move toward diagnostically reliable lumbar spine MRI interpretation, independent of the underlying VLM architecture.

title: BONSAI: Evolvability-Guided Tree Search over Skills
summary: A skill is a naturallanguage document that steers a frozen agent whose weights cannot be updated so any capability the agent lacks must be supplied in prose Optimising a skill is therefore optimising text against a score and the standard recipe which keeps any edit that raises a heldout score is blind in a specific way a single score cannot tell a document perched on a narrow overfit spike from one resting on a broad plateau even though only the second can still be improved We introduce BONSAI a novel skilloptimisation framework that steers instead by evolvability the capacity of a region of documentspace to keep producing viable variation under further mutation a property biology treats as separate from present fitness BONSAI grows skills as a MonteCarlo search tree in which every child document is a mutation of its parent and descends it under an upperconfidence selection rule whose exploitation term blends a skills own fitness with the fitness of its mutational neighbourhood Because every child is a mutation the mean score recorded beneath a node estimates that neighbourhoods evolvability at no extra cost so the rule concentrates budget on regions that keep improving while its exploration term keeps a currently weak branch in contention BONSAI ships the single bestscoring document it finds at no cost beyond the acceptifbetter loop it replaces With a frozen 30B agent and averaged over three benchmarks BONSAI lifts heldout accuracy over the skillfree agent by 2313 points and improves on two budgetmatched baselines GEPA and SkillOpt by 387 and 397 points respectively

AI.tldr: BONSAI: an evolvability-guided skill optimization that uses a Monte Carlo search tree over mutated natural-language skills to steer a frozen 30B agent; reports large heldout accuracy gains compared with a skill-free baseline and two budget-matched baselines across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Single-score optimization is brittle and can overfit to narrow spikes; optimizing evolvability—the ability of a region of the skill space to yield viable future mutations—can sustain progress as the document space is explored.
AI.method: Construct a Monte Carlo tree where each node is a skill (natural-language document). Each child is a mutation of the parent. Selection uses an upper-confidence bound that blends the node's own fitness with the fitness of its mutational neighbourhood. The node mean estimates evolvability. Budget concentrates on regions that improve while exploration maintains weak branches. The best-scoring document is shipped with a freeze-and-deploy loop. Evaluation uses a frozen 30B agent across three benchmarks, comparing to a skill-free agent and two baselines (GEPA, SkillOpt).
AI.result: BONSAI reports heldout accuracy gains over the skill-free agent by 2313 points and improvements over GEPA and SkillOpt by 387 and 397 points respectively across three benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Evolvability-guided skill optimization can outperform traditional single-score optimization for frozen-weight agents, offering a principled approach to exploring the space of prompt-like skills and identifying high-evolvability regions.

title: Hyperbolic Graph Embedders for Link Prediction and Topology Reconstruction
summary: Hyperbolic embeddings provide compact geometric representations of complex networks in hyperbolic spaces, but systematic comparisons of methods developed in machine learning, network science, and algorithmics remain rare. We benchmark 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedders under a unified protocol for link prediction and topology reconstruction on synthetic and empirical networks. The protocol captures both missing-link recovery and the preservation of local and global network structure. Maximum-likelihood and representation-learning-based approaches, including hybrid variants, achieve the strongest overall performance, although no method dominates across all tasks and structural regimes. Performance is more strongly associated with embedding paradigm than with disciplinary origin. We identify the network regimes in which different paradigms succeed or fail and provide practical guidance for method selection in downstream applications.

AI.tldr: 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedders benchmarked for link prediction and topology reconstruction; no universal winner; performance correlates with embedding paradigm; max-likelihood and representation learning (incl. hybrids) perform best overall; guidelines provided for method selection.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of systematic, cross-disciplinary benchmarking of hyperbolic graph embedding methods; compare ML, network science, and algorithmic approaches under a unified protocol.
AI.method: Unified benchmarking protocol on synthetic and real networks; evaluate 13 unsupervised hyperbolic graph embedders on (i) missing-link recovery (link prediction) and (ii) topology reconstruction (local/global structure preservation); assess performance across regimes and hybrids.
AI.result: Max-likelihood and representation-learning-based approaches (including hybrids) yield strongest overall performance; no single method dominates all tasks or structural regimes; performance aligns more with embedding paradigm than disciplinary origin.
AI.conclusion: Different paradigms excel in different regimes; provide practical guidance for method selection in downstream applications based on task and network regime.

title: Multiple Hypothesis Flow Estimation for Video Frame Interpolation under Matching Ambiguity
summary: Many flow-based video frame interpolation (VFI) methods synthesize an intermediate frame by estimating optical flow fields, warping the two input frames, and blending the warped observations. These latent flow fields are typically learned through image-level reconstruction supervision without direct flow annotations. In ambiguous regions containing repetitive or stochastic textures, rotating symmetric structures, or fast motion with blur, the matching evidence for a single query may contain multiple comparable and spatially separated peaks. Although the ground-truth intermediate frame provides indirect supervision, it may not uniquely identify the latent correspondence in ambiguous regions.When several locations provide multiple plausible matches, a single-flow estimator can retain only one displacement and discard the remaining candidates. If the selected match is incorrect or inconsistent with those of neighboring pixels, warping samples content from mismatched locations, producing ghosting, structural distortion, or blur.To address this limitation, we propose a multiple hypothesis flow estimation framework that preserves top-K candidate correspondences and selects one per location through a reliability-guided router. Each hypothesis is initialized from a coarse matching anchor and refined separately through anchor-centered local attention. Frame synthesis is thus conditioned on one selected flow-appearance hypothesis rather than a soft combination of candidate motions.Experiments on the proposed MA-HD benchmark and public VFI benchmarks show that our method achieves the best LPIPS and DISTS among the compared methods.

AI.tldr: Introduces a multiple-hypothesis flow estimation framework for video frame interpolation that preserves top-K motion candidates per pixel and selects one via a reliability-guided router, avoiding ghosting from single-flow estimates.
AI.motivation: Single-flow VFI struggles in ambiguous regions (repetitive textures, symmetry, fast motion with blur) where multiple plausible matches exist; standard image-level supervision may not uniquely identify true correspondences, causing artifacts.
AI.method: Generate multiple motion hypotheses per pixel initialized from coarse anchors; refine each hypothesis with anchor-centered local attention; use a reliability-guided router to pick one hypothesis per pixel; synthesize the intermediate frame conditioned on the selected flow-appearance hypothesis rather than blending candidates.
AI.result: On the proposed MA-HD benchmark and public VFI benchmarks, the method achieves the best LPIPS and DISTS scores among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining multiple plausible correspondences and selecting the most reliable one per pixel mitigates ghosting and distortion in ambiguous regions, yielding improved perceptual quality in frame interpolation.

title: PTQ4SNN: Membrane-Aware Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) enable sparse and event-driven computation, but their low-bit deployment remains incomplete because recurrent membrane states are commonly retained in floating point even after weight quantization. Quantizing these states is challenging because their distributions differ across channels and from the preceding weights, while small perturbations near the firing threshold may alter spike decisions and accumulate over time. We propose PTQ4SNN, a membrane-aware post-training quantization framework that jointly quantizes weights and recurrent membrane states using only a small calibration set. First, a channel-wise Unified Scale Bridge constrains the membrane scale as s_mem,c = s_w,c * 2^k_c, adapting to membrane distributions while enabling shift-compatible scale conversion. Second, Mixed-Precision Bit Allocation assigns 2/4/8-bit precision to membrane channels according to firing activity and quantization sensitivity under an average-bit budget. The framework operates on reusable projection-LIF pairs and supports both convolutional SNNs and spike-driven Transformers without backbone retraining. Experiments on static and event-based classification and semantic segmentation show that PTQ4SNN effectively preserves model accuracy under W4 quantization and approximately 4-bit membrane precision.

AI.tldr: A membrane-aware post-training quantization method for SNNs that jointly quantizes weights and recurrent membrane states with minimal calibration, enabling low-bit deployment without retraining.
AI.motivation: Quantizing recurrent membrane states in SNNs is hard due to channel-dependent distributions and perturbation sensitivity near firing thresholds; existing quantization methods struggle to preserve spike decisions and temporal dynamics across channels.
AI.method: Propose Unified Scale Bridge to relate membrane scale to weight scale via s_mem,c = s_w,c * 2^k_c; employ mixed-precision bit allocation (2/4/8-bit) across membrane channels under an average-bit budget; reuse projection-LIF pairs; supports both convolutional SNNs and spike-driven Transformers; requires only a small calibration set and no backbone retraining.
AI.result: Experiments on static and event-based classification and semantic segmentation show accurate retention under W4 quantization with approximately 4-bit membrane precision across tested backbones.
AI.conclusion: PTQ4SNN delivers effective membrane-aware quantization with minimal calibration data, enabling robust, low-bit deployment of SNNs on various architectures; the approach is scalable via channel-wise scaling and mixed-precision allocation.

title: Accounting Graph Transformer for Short-History Multi-KPI Forecasting in Small Businesses
summary: Small businesses often have only 12-24 months of accounting history, yet planning and risk workflows require coordinated forecasts across financial statements. We study joint 12-month forecasting of 13 income-statement, balance-sheet, cash-flow, and working-capital key performance indicators (KPIs) from 71 monthly ledger series. We introduce the Accounting Graph Transformer (AGT), which represents each ledger series as a masked token, exchanges information through typed attention on a fixed accounting-relation graph, pools target-specific context, and fuses it with a gated three-month recency path. Across 11,993 forecast origins from 1,060 unseen companies, AGT achieves sample-weighted KPI-macro mean absolute error (MAE) $0.6990 \pm 0.0013$ over three independent seeds, compared with $0.7378 \pm 0.0014$ for the strongest baseline, LightGBM. At the pre-specified seed 42, a paired company-clustered bootstrap gives a LightGBM-minus-AGT difference of 0.0395 with 95% confidence interval (CI) $[0.0350,0.0439]$. AGT is best on all 13 KPIs against LightGBM, TimeMixer, and SOFTS in the matched seed-42 comparison, while final-architecture ablations show that relational attention, accounting topology, and the recency path each improve validation and test accuracy. On 7,094 additional unseen companies with origins sampled from January-May 2025, AGT obtains 0.7548 MAE versus 0.7694 for SOFTS. A single 5.3M-parameter model produces 156 aligned forecasts without company-specific fitting, providing one forecasting layer for integrated planning, liquidity, and working-capital analysis.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Accounting Graph Transformer (AGT) to jointly forecast 12 months of 13 KPIs across income statement, balance sheet, cash flow, and working capital for 71 ledger series. AGT outperforms baselines (e.g., LightGBM) on KPI-MAE across multiple seeds and unseen companies, using a single 5.3M-parameter model to produce 156 forecasts without per-company fitting for integrated planning.
AI.motivation: Small businesses often have limited accounting history (12-24 months) yet require coordinated, multi-KPI forecasts for planning, liquidity, and risk management. The paper aims to enable joint, 12-month forecasting across financial statements by modeling ledger series and their interrelations.
AI.method: Represent each ledger series as a masked token. Use typed attention on a fixed accounting-relation graph to exchange information between series, then pool target-specific context and fuse with a gated recency path (three months). Train on 11,993 forecast origins from 1,060 unseen companies. Compare against baselines (LightGBM, TimeMixer, SOFTS) and perform ablations (relational attention, topology, recency path). Evaluate with KPI-macro MAE. Include bootstrap comparisons at seed 42 and additional evaluations on 7,094 unseen companies (Jan–May 2025).
AI.result: AGT achieves KPI-macro MAE 0.6990 ± 0.0013 (three seeds) versus LightGBM 0.7378 ± 0.0014. Seed-42 bootstrap difference LightGBM–AGT = 0.0395 (CI [0.0350,0.0439]). AGT tops all 13 KPIs against LightGBM, TimeMixer, and SOFTS in seed-42 comparison. On 7,094 unseen companies, AGT 0.7548 MAE vs 0.7694 for SOFTS. A 5.3M-parameter model forecasts 156 aligned horizon forecasts without per-company fitting.
AI.conclusion: Relational attention, accounting topology, and the recency path collectively improve forecast accuracy. The architecture offers a single forecasting layer suitable for integrated planning, liquidity, and working-capital analysis across multiple KPIs.

title: Human-AI Perceptual Alignment by Playing Hues and Cues
summary: Evaluating the perceptual alignment between Contrastive Vision-Language Models (CVLMs) and humans is typically constrained by traditional benchmarks that overlook fine-grained semantic and cultural nuances. In this work, we propose a novel evaluation framework that leverages the gamified, discrete color space of the board game Hues and Cues. By mapping the board's 480 color cells to the CIE xy chromaticity diagram, we calculate empirical perceptual distances across a carefully curated 100-word vocabulary spanning seven semantic categories. To properly contextualize model performance, we establish an empirical lower bound of expected error-the Human Consistency baseline-calculated via Leave-One-Out (LOO) cross-validation on a dense dataset of color associations collected from 325 human observers through a custom digital interface. We evaluate 162 models across multiple architectural families and pre-training datasets to assess their semantic color grounding. Our results demonstrate that while CVLMs successfully replicate human cognitive biases, such as idealized memory colors for concrete physical referents (e.g., food and plants), they systematically diverge from the human baseline in abstract, subjective, and pop-culture domains. We identify two distinct failure modes in severely misaligned concepts: semantic misclassification and a systematic uncertainty collapse into a default blue coordinate. Furthermore, we reveal that highly curated pre-training datasets are significantly more effective than massive, uncurated corpora in mitigating these severe misalignments. Ultimately, this work highlights that despite their broad categorization capabilities, current CVLMs still fail to capture the nuanced, localized consensus of human color memory, emphasizing the value of gamified tasks in exposing underlying model biases. The data and code are publicly available to test other metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a gamified, color-space evaluation for CVLMs using Hues and Cues to assess perceptual alignment with humans; finds CVLMs mimic some human biases for concrete referents but diverge in abstract/cultural domains; curated pretraining helps mitigate misalignment; 162 models evaluated; 325 human participants; data and code released.
AI.motivation: Traditional CVLM benchmarks overlook fine-grained semantic and cultural nuances in color memory. A gamified, perceptual task is proposed to reveal biases and local consensus, providing a stringent test of grounding beyond surface-level category accuracy.
AI.method: Map 480-color Hues and Cues board to CIE xy; compute empirical perceptual distances across a curated 100-word, seven-category vocabulary. Establish a human baseline via Leave-One-Out cross-validation on color-association data from 325 observers. Evaluate 162 CVLMs across architectures and pretraining datasets. Analyze failure modes and the impact of curated versus uncurated pretraining.
AI.result: CVLMs reproduce certain human biases for concrete referents (e.g., foods, plants) but deviate from human baselines in abstract/subjective/pop-culture domains. Two failure modes in misalignment: semantic misclassification and uncertainty collapse to a default blue. Highly curated pretraining datasets mitigate misalignment more effectively than massive uncurated corpora.
AI.conclusion: Gamified color-grounding evaluation reveals nuanced divergences between CVLMs and human color memory. Current models struggle to capture localized human color consensus; curated pretraining improves alignment. Data and code are publicly available for further benchmarking.

title: DocMemo: Dynamic Evidence Discovery via Probabilistic Memory-Guided Retrieval for Multi-Modal Document Understanding
comment: DocMemo is a memory-guided framework for long-document reasoning that uses tri-level memory and dynamic Bayesian belief updating to overcome static retrieval limits and improve evidence tracking. 16 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables
summary: Long-document understanding requires locating sparse and heterogeneous evidence across hundreds of pages, yet existing systems remain limited by static retrieval and fragile cross-round memory.
