Mainstream single-round methods commit to a fixed top-$k$ page set at the outset and struggle to recover from early retrieval errors; recent iterative approaches allow multi-round evidence acquisition, but they do not investigate the propagation mechanism of cross-round states, making it difficult to track the dynamic changes in page relevance. To address these limitations, we propose DocMemo, a memory-guided framework that formulates long-document reasoning as dynamic evidence exploration. DocMemo maintains a tri-level retrieval state consisting of Document Schema Memory, Page Belief Memory, and Question Episodic Memory, which respectively capture structural priors, dynamic relevance estimation, and query-specific reasoning trajectories. During reasoning, DocMemo continuously refines cross-round page selection through Bayesian page belief updating with Thompson sampling, spatial proximity propagation, and structure-aware adaptive-granularity evidence access, while supplementing page-level evidence with fine-grained visual regions. Experiments on 3 benchmarks show that DocMemo achieves state-of-the-art performance and validate the efficacy of structured memory and dynamic page belief updating. Code is available at https://github.com/Harrygof/DocMemo.

AI.tldr: DocMemo introduces a memory-guided, multi-level retrieval framework for long documents, using tri-level memory and Bayesian evidence updating to dynamically explore evidence across pages.
AI.motivation: Long documents contain sparse, heterogeneous evidence scattered across hundreds of pages. Static top-k retrieval and single-round methods fail to adapt to retrieval errors or capture cross-round changes in page relevance; there is a need for dynamic, memory-informed evidence exploration.
AI.method: DocMemo maintains a tri-level retrieval state: Document Schema Memory (structural priors), Page Belief Memory (dynamic relevance), and Question Episodic Memory (query-specific reasoning). It updates page beliefs with Bayesian updating and Thompson sampling, propagates spatial proximity signals, applies structure-aware adaptive-granularity evidence access, and augments page evidence with fine-grained visual regions.
AI.result: On three benchmarks, DocMemo achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the benefits of structured memory and dynamic page belief updating; code is released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory and dynamic cross-round updating enable effective long-document reasoning, allowing continuous refinement of evidence selection and improved performance over static or non-memory-based approaches.

title: Beyond Isolation: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning Component Synergy for Sample-Efficient Continuous Control
summary: Reinforcement learning systems are significantly more complex than other machine learning paradigms due to inherent properties, causing RL system design to jointly account for many tightly coupled factors. Despite advances in individual algorithmic components, their functional interdependencies remain underexplored: do they exhibit mutual synergy or counterproductive interference? To bridge this gap, we conduct a systematic investigation and find that the efficacy of different components exhibits significant task-dependency, and naively stacking state-of-the-art techniques does not necessarily yield performance gains; instead, it often triggers emergent challenges, such as compounded non-stationarity. Building upon these findings, we distill a suite of actionable insights into the principled coordination of these components. Guided by these insights, we propose ROSER, an RL framework that coordinates three critical dimensions: Model-based Representation, Optimization Stability, and Experience Replay. Across diverse continuous-control benchmarks, ROSER consistently outperforms vanilla baselines and achieves 17.60% gains over naive stack. Our findings underscore the necessity of a holistic perspective in RL system design and paves the way for developing sample-efficient agents.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates interdependencies among RL system components, showing task-dependent efficacy and that naive stacking of techniques can cause non-stationarity; it proposes ROSER, a framework coordinating Model-based Representation, Optimization Stability, and Experience Replay, achieving consistent improvements (17.60% over naive stacking) across continuous-control tasks.
AI.motivation: To address the neglected issue of functional interdependencies among RL components and the non-stationarity that arises from layering algorithms, by developing a holistic design principle for RL systems.
AI.method: Systematic empirical analysis of component interactions in RL, followed by the design and evaluation of ROSER, a framework coordinating three dimensions: Model-based Representation, Optimization Stability, and Experience Replay, across diverse continuous-control benchmarks.
AI.result: ROSER consistently outperforms vanilla baselines and yields 17.60% gains over naïve stacking, indicating meaningful gains from principled coordination rather than naive component aggregation.
AI.conclusion: A holistic RL-system design is crucial; coordinated management of representation, optimization stability, and experience replay can improve sample efficiency and performance, guiding future development of RL agents.

title: InstanceSplat: Instance-Aware Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scene Understanding
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables efficient and generalizable 3D reconstruction, but current feed-forward 3DGS methods for scene understanding remain largely category-oriented. In contrast, instance-aware 3DGS methods typically rely on per-scene optimization and often decouple reconstruction from instance and semantic learning, limiting reciprocal interactions among them. We present InstanceSplat, a unified feed-forward 3DGS framework for generalizable 3D reconstruction and instance-aware scene understanding from pose-free multi-view images. In a single forward pass, InstanceSplat constructs an instance-aware Gaussian representation that jointly encodes appearance, geometry, instance identity, and language-aligned semantics. Shared 3D Gaussians ground instance identities across views, producing renderable and cross-view-consistent instance features. To allow reconstruction and scene understanding to benefit from each other, we further design an instance-centric learning strategy that connects reconstruction, instance learning, and semantic learning through shared instance structure. Specifically, instance cues guide reconstruction, language-aligned semantics strengthen the discrimination of confusing same-category instances, and instance regions aggregate semantic evidence into coherent object-level predictions. Experiments on novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic understanding under varying input-view settings and on an unseen dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, practical efficiency, and strong generalization.

AI.tldr: Unified feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (InstanceSplat) for generalizable instance-aware 3D reconstruction from pose-free multi-view images, bridging reconstruction, instance, and language-aligned semantics with shared 3D Gaussians; state-of-the-art across novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, open-vocabulary semantics.
AI.motivation: Current feed-forward 3DGS methods are largely category-oriented and often decouple reconstruction from instance and semantic learning, limiting cross-task interactions and generalization; per-scene optimization in instance methods hinders efficiency and scalability.
AI.method: Propose InstanceSplat: a unified feed-forward 3DGS framework that builds an instance-aware Gaussian representation encoding appearance, geometry, instance identity, and language-aligned semantics. Shared 3D Gaussians ground identities across views to produce renderable, cross-view-consistent instance features. An instance-centric learning strategy links reconstruction, instance learning, and semantic learning via shared instance structure: instance cues guide reconstruction; language-aligned semantics discriminate confusing same-category instances; instance regions aggregate semantic evidence into object-level predictions.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic understanding under varying input-view settings and on an unseen dataset, with practical efficiency and strong generalization.
AI.conclusion: A unified, generalizable framework that enables reciprocal benefits between 3D reconstruction and scene understanding through instance-aware Gaussian representations and instance-centric learning, scalable to open-vocabulary semantics and multi-view inputs.

title: MemOPD: On-Policy Distillation through Memory State Alignment for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agents accumulate growing contexts during interaction, impairing performance and stability. Compact memory mitigates this problem by compressing and rewriting the history retained between model invocations. Learning what to retain typically relies on proximal policy optimization (PPO) with final task rewards, but sparse rewards provide little guidance for individual memory updates. This limitation motivates on-policy distillation (OPD), which supplies dense teacher supervision on student rollouts. For such supervision to be valid, the teacher must evaluate each sampled action under the same state in which it was generated. However, the context rewriting performed during memory compression can break this alignment. When sampled responses are retained and re-encoded for later invocations, flattening the interaction into a persistent history may cause the teacher to score the action under a state that the student never visited during rollout. The action therefore remains on-policy by provenance, but not necessarily by state. We therefore propose Memory-Aligned On-Policy Distillation (MemOPD). MemOPD records the inputs and sampled outputs of each model invocation, restores its original token positions and causal visibility, and packs the reconstructed invocations for efficient teacher scoring. The teacher provides full-vocabulary supervision at the sampled action positions, while PPO preserves the final task objective. Experiments verify state alignment across several context updates and show that it improves F1 by 7.0% over persistent-history teacher scoring in a matched control. Overall, MemOPD-3B improves F1 over PPO by up to 416.2%, while packing yields up to a 1.63x speedup in actor computation during training. The code for this work is publicly available at: https://github.com/TPssp/MemOPD.

AI.tldr: MemOPD aligns on-policy distillation by reconstructing and aligning memory invocations, enabling state-consistent teacher supervision and yielding large F1 gains and speedups.
AI.motivation: Addresses growth of context in long-horizon agents and misalignment between teacher scoring and student state due to memory rewriting; dense supervision required.
AI.method: MemOPD records inputs/outputs of model invocations, restores original token positions and causal visibility, packs reconstructed invocations for efficient teacher scoring; teacher provides full-vocabulary supervision at sampled positions while PPO preserves final objective.
AI.result: State alignment across context updates verified; F1 improves by 7.0% over persistent-history teacher scoring in a matched control; MemOPD-3B improves F1 over PPO by up to 416.2%; packing yields up to 1.63x speedup in actor computation during training.
AI.conclusion: MemOPD demonstrates effective memory-state alignment for on-policy distillation, delivering substantial accuracy and efficiency gains; code available at the provided URL.

authors: Rixta A. H. van Eijck van Heslinga
title: Representation-driven Endoscopic Visual Embedding Alignment for Latent Generation
summary: Developing foundation generative models for endoscopy is limited by the gap between natural and clinical images and the computational cost of training large Diffusion Transformers. Although representation alignment has improved efficiency in general computer vision, its role within the highly specialized endoscopic image space remains unclear. We introduce REVEAL (Representation-driven Endoscopic Visual Embedding Alignment), the largest generative foundation model for endoscopy to date, trained on GastroNet-5M (GN-5M), a multicenter dataset of 5 million endoscopic frames. Instead of depending on out-of-domain priors, REVEAL employs encoders pretrained directly on the endoscopic distribution to align diffusion latents with domain-specific visual features, preserving fine textures and intricate anatomical structures. Beyond image generation, REVEAL also serves as a powerful feature extractor; in multiple benchmarks, it delivers performance that is competitive with, and in several cases exceeds, endoscopic foundation models such as EndoViT and Endo-FM, specifically tuned for classification tasks, while demonstrating strong representation robustness under realistic imaging corruptions. REVEAL produces high-fidelity images and maintains robust structural coherence in latent-space edits such as inpainting and outpainting. This high-capacity backbone lowers the computational threshold for building specialized clinical tools, offering an open, versatile foundation for conditional synthesis, segmentation, and out-of-distribution detection in future intelligent gastroenterology systems.

AI.tldr: REVEAL is a large endoscopy-specific foundation model trained on GN-5M that aligns diffusion latents with endoscopic features via encoders pretrained on endoscopy, enabling high-fidelity generation, strong classification performance, robustness to corruptions, and latent-space editing, with open potential for conditional synthesis, segmentation, and OOD detection.
AI.motivation: To close the gap between natural and clinical endoscopic imagery and reduce training cost for diffusion-based models by using domain-specific representations rather than relying on out-of-domain priors.
AI.method: REVEAL uses encoders pretrained directly on the endoscopic distribution to align diffusion latents with domain-specific visual features, preserving fine textures and anatomical structures. Trained on GastroNet-5M (GN-5M), a multicenter 5-million-frame endoscopic dataset. Functions as a generative backbone and feature extractor, enabling conditional synthesis and downstream tasks.
AI.result: REVEAL achieves competitive or superior performance compared with specialized endoscopic foundation models (e.g., EndoViT, Endo-FM) on classification benchmarks and demonstrates strong robustness to realistic imaging corruptions. It produces high-fidelity images, maintains structural coherence in latent-space edits (inpainting/outpainting), and lowers the computational threshold for building clinical tools.
AI.conclusion: REVEAL establishes a versatile, domain-aligned, open backbone for endoscopy that supports conditional synthesis, segmentation, and OOD detection, accelerating the development of intelligent gastroenterology systems.

title: Transformers Struggle to Use Their Emergent World Models: Revisiting the Tower of Hanoi, and the Illusion of Thinking
summary: The Tower of Hanoi is a simple planning puzzle that in prior work has proven challenging for large reasoning models (LRMs). Current models solve the standard formulation of the puzzle, but still struggle with the flat-to-flat variant (where initial and goal states are not restricted to have all rings on a single peg). This paper presents an in-depth study of how both small, in-house Transformers and large, third-party LRMs solve this task. To understand the failures mechanistically, we first train small Transformers from scratch on precomputed solution traces. Using a variety of interpretability techniques, we show that these Transformers develop an emergent world model: a linearly decodable, geometrically faithful representation of the puzzle's state space (the Sierpinski triangle), that is causally involved in solving the puzzles. Second, we return to the large LLMs and apply our techniques to two frontier reasoning models, Qwen3.6-27B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, that attempt to solve the task through extended chain-of-thought. Surprisingly, we find that both models encode the Sierpinski world model near-perfectly at the end of the prompt, and yet fail at the majority of tasks when there are more than 3 rings. We locate the source of this failure in the decaying representation of the world model. We probe for the representation at different stages during planning, and establish causality by showing that performance can be improved by injecting the prompt-time representation at inference. The failure of the models is thus one of maintenance of the required representations, not their absence, and performance is at least partially recoverable. These results thus reframe the reported collapse in performance from prior work: current Large Reasoning Models build a world model, and then lose it.

AI.tldr: Small transformers develop a linearly decodable world model of the Tower of Hanoi state space (the Sierpinski triangle) that is causally involved in solving; large LRMs encode this model but fail for >3 rings due to decay in maintenance, which can be mitigated by injecting the representation during inference.
AI.motivation: Understand whether and how emergent world models underlie planning on the Tower of Hanoi, and why large reasoning models exhibit performance collapses on extended planning prompts.
AI.method: Train small Transformers from scratch on precomputed solution traces; apply interpretability methods to reveal emergent world models; analyze frontier large LLMs (Qwen3.6-27B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) under extended chain-of-thought; probe representations across planning stages; test causality by injecting prompt-time representations at inference.
AI.result: Small transformers form a linearly decodable, geometrically faithful world model (the Sierpinski triangle) that is causally linked to solving the puzzles. Large LLMs encode this world model near-perfectly by the end of the prompt but fail when more than 3 rings are involved due to decay of the representation during planning; injecting the prompt-time representation at inference improves performance, indicating the issue is maintenance, not absence of the world model.
AI.conclusion: The work reframes prior findings by showing that current large reasoning models can build a world model but must maintain it; improving representational maintenance can recover performance and is key to robust long-horizon planning.

title: Modular TTT: Rethinking Test-Time Training as Composable Modules
summary: Test-time training (TTT) views sequence modeling as an online learning problem in which fast weights are updated by an internal learning rule. Despite the growing number of TTT variants, existing approaches typically hard-code each variant separately, which makes it difficult to design new TTT methods and to isolate the role of each component. To address this, we propose Modular TTT, a framework that represents the inner learner as a directed acyclic graph and exposes the fast-weight network, loss function, learning rate, weight decay, and normalization as explicit design dimensions. Modular TTT automatically composes primitive-level train-view forward, train-view backward, and causal query-view rules into the full graph-level TTT computation, including the fast-weight state transition. Using Modular TTT, we systematically ablate the components of TTT and find that small learning-rate initialization, weight decay, and a single-layer nonlinearity improve performance, while MSE and inner-product losses perform similarly. Deeper fast-weight networks and normalization tend to hurt performance because they induce excessively large activations, while residual connections and gating provide little measurable benefit. Guided by these findings, we train the best resulting variant as 410M- and 1.45B-parameter models on 100B tokens, and observe training loss and benchmark performance comparable to Gated DeltaNet.

AI.tldr: Modular TTT frames test-time training as a composable DAG that exposes inner-learner components (fast weights, loss, LR, weight decay, normalization) as design dimensions, enabling automatic construction of train-view and query-view rules and systematic ablations; findings favor small LR init, weight decay, and single-layer nonlinearity, while deeper networks and normalization can hurt due to large activations.
AI.motivation: To reduce heterogeneity across TTT variants and isolate component contributions, enabling systematic design, ablation, and scalable training of large-fast-weight models.
AI.method: Represent inner learner as a directed acyclic graph; explicitly parameterize fast-weight state transitions and design dimensions; automatically compose primitive train-view and query-view rules into a full graph-level TTT computation; perform ablations on learning-rate initialization, weight decay, and nonlinearity; train best variant to 410M and 1.45B parameters on 100B tokens.
AI.result: Ablations show small learning-rate initialization, weight decay, and a single-layer nonlinearity improve performance; MSE and inner-product losses are similar; deeper fast-weight networks and normalization can hurt due to large activations; residual connections and gating offer little benefit; the best variant achieves comparable training loss and benchmarks to Gated DeltaNet at scale.
AI.conclusion: Modular TTT provides a unified framework to compare TTT variants, identifies robust design choices (low LR init, weight decay, simple nonlinearity), and demonstrates competitive performance at large scale with a strong, if not superior, baseline relative to existing TTT methods.

title: Flow-Corrected Shape Optimization: Taming Manifold Drift in High-Dimensional 3D Models
summary: Optimizing 3D shapes within the latent spaces of deep generative models is fundamental to computer assisted engineering, yet remains prone to a critical failure mode we term manifold drift: the tendency of gradient-based optimization to move latent vectors away from the manifold of valid shapes. This problem is exacerbated in state-of-the-art 3D shape generative models that operate in increasingly high-dimensional latent spaces where valid shapes occupy a vanishingly small fraction of the full space. Existing mitigation strategies, including latent regularization and flow-matching approaches, either sacrifice expressiveness, demand a difficult trade-off between objective guidance and generative fidelity that remains prone to manifold drift, or are computationally infeasible to scale to modern, large-capacity 3D shape models. We introduce a novel optimizer-corrector framework that alternates between gradient steps for objective minimization and guided flow matching to drive the latent state back to the valid shape manifold. By decoupling objective minimization from flow-based correction, optimizing freely and correcting strictly, this alternating design avoids inherent trade-offs, preserving geometric validity without sacrificing expressiveness while remaining computationally feasible on modern 3D shape models. We demonstrate its effectiveness across generative priors of varying complexity, from simple vector latent spaces to large-scale architectures across a variety of downstream optimization tasks, including aerodynamic drag reduction and object compliance optimization.

AI.tldr: An optimizer-corrector framework alternates gradient-based objective minimization with guided flow matching to keep latent vectors on the valid 3D-shape manifold, addressing manifold drift in high-dimensional generative priors.
AI.motivation: Manifold drift: gradient-based optimization tends to leave the manifold of valid shapes in high-dimensional latent spaces. Existing mitigations trade expressiveness or scalability. A scalable, expressive method is needed for modern 3D priors.
AI.method: An alternating scheme: perform objective-minimizing gradient steps and, in between or afterwards, apply guided flow matching to push the latent state back onto the valid shape manifold. By decoupling objective optimization from flow-based correction, the approach preserves expressiveness while enforcing validity.
AI.result: Demonstrated across varying priors from simple vector spaces to large-scale architectures. Improves downstream tasks such as aerodynamic drag reduction and object compliance optimization, with a computationally feasible workflow on modern 3D models.
AI.conclusion: The optimizer-corrector framework preserves geometric validity without sacrificing expressiveness and scales to large 3D generative models, offering a general solution to manifold drift across diverse generative priors and optimization objectives.

title: MemWM: Memory-Augmented Text-Based World Model
summary: World models are increasingly used to support planning in agents by predicting how environment states evolve in response to agent actions. Yet fluent next-state predictions can still omit task-critical facts, corrupt product attributes, or apply incorrect transition rules. To address such systematic prediction errors, we introduce MemWM, a memory-augmented text-based world model. MemWM uses world memory, a curated memory bank of transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts, to condition next-state imagination. We evaluate factual state preservation with Structured State Fidelity (SSF), which scores predicted states through benchmark-specific facts and fields. Compared with SFT, memory-augmented training improves SSF by up to 206.3%. In the full planning setting, we keep the policy model frozen and provide policy-side world skill: retrieved task-level skills and step-wise corrective guidance for action selection. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, memory-augmented agents improve downstream success over an SFT-trained world-model agent, with up to a 65.4% relative gain. Sensitivity analyses further show that retrieved memory improves task success and efficiency under different memory and action-budget settings.

AI.tldr: MemWM: a memory-augmented text-based world model that uses a world memory to improve factual state fidelity and planning performance, outperforming SFT across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Mitigate systematic next-state prediction errors (omitted facts, wrong transitions) in world models used for planning by incorporating curated memory of rules, facts, and state caches.
AI.method: Introduce MemWM with a world memory that conditions next-state imagination on curated transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts. Evaluate using Structured State Fidelity (SSF); in full planning, freeze the policy and supply policy-side world skills (task-level skills and corrective guidance). Assess across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld.
AI.result: SSF improvements up to 206.3% over SFT; downstream task success gains up to 65.4% relative; memory retrieval improves task success and efficiency across memory and action-budget settings; robust sensitivity analyses.
AI.conclusion: Memory-augmented world models yield substantial gains in factual state retention and planning effectiveness, suggesting broad applicability across domains with different memory and action budgets.

title: Online Conformal Prediction Beyond Feedback
summary: Uncertainty quantification is essential when deploying machine learning models in safety-critical applications. Online conformal prediction (OCP) provides theoretically principled uncertainty quantification for arbitrary black-box classifiers and non-i.i.d. data streams by constructing prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the true label at a user-specified frequency. OCP usually updates prediction sets using feedback from previously deployed predictions. We instead study an OCP setting beyond feedback: on each round, the learner can either output a prediction set or query the correct label, but not both. Thus, no deployed prediction is ever evaluated directly. We reduce this problem to a partial monitoring game in which prediction actions return no observation and a separate query action reveals the label. The reward function is constructed in a way that encourages the learner to output small prediction sets while ensuring that the correct label is covered with a sufficiently high probability. To solve this game, we develop OCP with queries (OCPQ) by adapting the label efficient forecaster of Cesa-Bianchi, Lugosi, and Stoltz (2004) to our setting. For any black box classifier and any (non-i.i.d.) oblivious data stream of length $T$, OCPQ has $O(T^{2/3})$ expected regret and expected coverage at least $β-O(T^{-1/3})$ for a user-defined $β$, while querying only an expected $T^{-1/3}$ fraction of rounds. This provides coverage comparable to bandit-based OCP methods while requiring no feedback from deployed prediction sets. Experiments on real-world datasets further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: OCPQ: online conformal prediction with label queries reducing feedback, achieving O(T^{2/3}) regret and β-coverage with sublinear query rate.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification in safety-critical ML under limited feedback; desire to avoid evaluating deployed predictions; handle non-i.i.d. data streams; adapt conformal prediction to partial monitoring.
AI.method: Reduce to partial monitoring where prediction actions produce no observation and a separate query reveals the label; construct reward to promote small prediction sets while maintaining coverage; adapt label-efficient forecaster (Cesa-Bianchi et al. 2004) to OCPQ.
AI.result: For any black-box classifier and non-i.i.d. oblivious data stream of length T, OCPQ achieves expected regret O(T^{2/3}) and expected coverage at least β - O(T^{-1/3}); queries requested are O(T^{-1/3}); coverage comparable to bandit-based OCP; experimental validation on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: OCPQ provides principled, low-feedback uncertainty quantification with sublinear regret and low query cost in non-i.i.d. settings; practical effectiveness demonstrated.

title: CANIS: Generation-Assisted 3D Canonicalization via an Image-Semantic Bridge
summary: Canonicalizing 3D object orientation is fundamental to 3D understanding and analysis. Existing approaches often rely on geometric cues, although 3D canonicalization ultimately requires a semantically meaningful orientation. To address this gap, we propose CANIS, a category-agnostic, generation-assisted framework that introduces the semantic orientation prior of a frozen image-to-3D generative model into 3D canonicalization, without canonicalization-specific training or category-specific templates. Specifically, CANIS first renders the input object from candidate viewpoints, selects an informative view, and generates a proxy in a canonical orientation. During generation, a sparse structural latent encoded from the input guides the proxy to preserve the geometry of an object. CANIS then uses the selected image as a semantic bridge between the input and the proxy. Image patches identify semantic regions on the proxy, and depth back-projection locates the corresponding regions on the input. The resulting semantic anchors constrain geometric matching, from which we estimate the rigid transformation that canonicalizes the input. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks validate CANIS and its key components, while qualitative results on partial observations and OmniObject3D suggest its applicability to incomplete and real-world scans. CANIS also improves downstream 3D classification, part segmentation, and dense correspondence under arbitrary rotations. Project page: https://kenkenzaii.github.io/Canis.

AI.tldr: CANIS is a category-agnostic, generation-assisted framework that injects semantic orientation priors from a frozen image-to-3D generator into 3D canonicalization, avoiding category-specific training or templates and improving downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Canonical orientation requires semantic (not just geometric) cues; existing approaches rely on geometry or category templates and struggle with incomplete scans. A category-agnostic method that leverages semantic priors from a frozen generative model can robustly canonicalize object orientation.
AI.method: Render the input object from candidate viewpoints, select an informative view, and generate a proxy in canonical orientation using a frozen image-to-3D generator. A sparse latent from the input preserves geometry during generation. The generated proxy serves as a semantic bridge to the input: image patches identify semantic regions on the proxy, and depth back-projection locates the corresponding regions on the input. Semantic anchors constrain geometric matching to estimate a rigid transformation that canonicalizes the input.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic benchmarks validate CANIS and its components; qualitative results on partial observations and OmniObject3D demonstrate applicability to incomplete and real-world scans. CANIS also improves downstream 3D classification, part segmentation, and dense correspondence under arbitrary rotations.
AI.conclusion: CANIS shows that semantic orientation priors from a frozen image-to-3D model can enable category-agnostic 3D canonicalization without specialized training or templates, enabling robust orientation alignment and improvements in downstream 3D tasks.

title: How Much, Then Where: Credit-Conserving Action-to-Token Allocation for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Credit assignment in multi-turn agent reinforcement learning operates at two levels: assigning trajectory-level credit to actions and distributing each action's credit across its tokens. In this paper, we introduce FACTOR, which separates these decisions. FACTOR uses checkpoint-calibrated TD residuals to assign per-action credits that telescope to the trajectory advantage, and feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps to allocate each credit across the realized action tokens. Per-action normalization preserves the action-average coefficient and prevents token-level sign flips. We pair this construction with an action-mean reduction, removing the implicit dependence of an action's scalar surrogate weight on its token length. At the behavior policy and before clipping, each action's inner action-mean surrogate equals its TD credit. FACTOR consistently improves over competitive baselines across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with every environment-seed comparison favoring FACTOR and the largest gains emerging on the longest-horizon environment. The same hyperparameters transfer without retuning to a larger backbone and to a different model family. Ablations identify TD action credit as the dominant driver of the improvement, with hindsight token allocation contributing complementary gains.

AI.tldr: FACTOR decouples trajectory-level credit from per-token credit in multi-turn RL, using TD residuals to assign per-action credit that telescopes to the trajectory advantage and feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps to allocate across action tokens. Per-action normalization and an action-mean reduction stabilize credits and remove token-length biases. At the behavior policy, the inner action-mean surrogate equals the TD credit. Empirically, FACTOR yields robust improvements across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with the largest gains on longer horizons; hyperparameters transfer across backbones/model families; ablations show TD action credit as the dominant driver, with hindsight token allocation providing extra gains.
AI.motivation: Two-level credit assignment is a core challenge in long-horizon, multi-turn RL: (i) allocating credit to actions over a trajectory (trajectory-level credit) and (ii) distributing each action's credit across the realized tokens that constitute the action. Existing methods often couple these levels, leading to unstable or inefficient learning. The work proposes a decoupled approach (FACTOR) to improve credit signaling and sample efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce FACTOR: (1) checkpoint-calibrated TD residuals assign per-action credit that telescopes to the trajectory advantage; (2) feedback-conditioned teacher-student likelihood gaps allocate per-action credit across realized action tokens. Per-action normalization preserves the action-average coefficient and prevents token-length sign flips. An action-mean reduction removes implicit dependence of an action's scalar surrogate weight on token length. At the behavior policy and before clipping, the inner action-mean surrogate equals the TD credit.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, FACTOR consistently outperforms competitive baselines across environment seeds; largest gains occur on the longest-horizon environment. Hyperparameters transfer without retuning to a larger backbone and to a different model family. Ablations show TD action credit as the dominant driver of improvement, with hindsight token allocation providing complementary gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling trajectory-level and token-level credit with FACTOR yields robust, scalable improvements in long-horizon multi-turn RL. The TD action credit component is the primary driver, while token-level allocation adds extra gains; the method generalizes across environments and architectures with minimal retuning.

title: Interpretable reinforcement learning with decision-tree pruning
summary: Reinforcement learning policies are difficult to inspect, but interpreting them is a prerequisite for trustworthiness. Converting a trained policy into explicit decision-tree rules improves transparency and the resulting artifacts often remain too complex for human understanding. We present a pruning process that simplifies such rule-based policies while preserving task performance and making edits to the policy auditable. The process defines a small set of structural and usage-aware operators and evaluates candidate edits by re-executing the policy to measure return and interpretability proxies. This exposes an transformation process from complex to compact policy structures. We investigate this approach on classic control and MuJoCo benchmarks, where pruning traces reveal consistent interpretability improvements while maintaining high performance.

AI.tldr: Pruning RL policies into compact, interpretable rule-based forms by structural and usage-aware edits, validated by re-executing for return and interpretability proxies; achieves interpretability gains with little performance loss on classic control and MuJoCo tasks.
AI.motivation: Enable trust and auditability in RL by transforming opaque policies into transparent, auditable rule-based representations without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Introduce a small set of operators (structural and usage-aware) to edit the policy; iteratively evaluate candidate edits by re-running the policy to measure return and interpretability proxies; prune to produce a concise rule-based policy; test on classic control and MuJoCo benchmarks.
AI.result: Consistent interpretability improvements observed with preserved high task performance; pruning reveals interpretable traces while maintaining performance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a viable transformation from complex to compact policy structures, enabling auditable, interpretable RL policies without significant degradation in performance.

title: Foundation Models Adaptation for Multi-View Multi-modal Cardiac MRI Segmentation and Direct Ejection Fraction Estimation
summary: Foundation models have shown strong transferability in cardiac MRI (CMR), but their effectiveness for heterogeneous multi-view and multi-sequence CMR analysis remains unclear. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of fine-tuning and combining different CMR foundation models for the Universal Multi-Sequence, Multi-Center and Multi-View CMR Segmentation (CMR-Multi) Challenge. CineMA was fine-tuned for cine and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) segmentation across short-axis and long-axis views. For direct left-ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) estimation, we used two recent frozen CMR foundation models to extract embedding vectors that were then combined using attention-based multiple-instance learning for LVEF regression. In the challenge validation set, cine segmentation achieved Dice scores of 0.862, 0.883, and 0.902 for short-axis, two-chamber and four-chamber cine MRI, respectively. LGE segmentation achieved Dice scores between 0.621 and 0.846 across views. The direct LVEF regression model achieved an MAE of 4.96 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of 0.91. These results indicate that foundation models can be effectively adapted and combined for multi-view CMR analysis, while accurate LGE scar segmentation remains a challenging task.

AI.tldr: Foundation models are effectively adapted via fine-tuning and fusion for multi-view, multi-sequence CMR: strong cine segmentation across views, variable LGE segmentation performance, and high-accuracy LVEF regression when combining embeddings from frozen models with attention-based MIL.
AI.motivation: Assess how fine-tuning and combining different CMR foundation models performs on a heterogeneous multi-view, multi-sequence CMR challenge, addressing transferability, view-sequence diversity, and LVEF estimation without full supervision.
AI.method: Fine-tune CineMA for cine and LGE segmentation across short-axis and long-axis views. For LVEF, extract embeddings from two frozen CMR foundation models and fuse them via attention-based multiple-instance learning for regression.
AI.result: Cine segmentation Dice: 0.862 (SAX), 0.883 (2-chamber), 0.902 (4-chamber). LGE segmentation Dice: 0.621–0.846 across views. LVEF regression MAE: 4.96 percentage points; Pearson r = 0.91.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models can be effectively adapted and combined for multi-view CMR analysis; however, accurate LGE scar segmentation remains challenging.

title: DiDPO: Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization for Coding Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training coding agents, where the execution feedback from compilation and tests provides objective verification. However, unlike agent tasks, coding agents face a unique and finer-grained credit assignment challenge: at each step, coding actions simultaneously pack varying changes into different regions of a code version, which makes the contribution of independent change indistinguishable. Existing RLVR methods mostly leverage the outcome reward or step-level reward, which fails to dive into a code diff and makes unique properties of coding actions invisible to training. In this paper, we propose Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization (DiDPO), a critic-free RL method that constructs fine-grained credit units directly from the structure of code diffs. DiDPO organizes multi-turn coding interactions into multiple thought--action steps and discovers code diffs across sampled trajectories. It then selects anchors by aggregating highly similar sub-diffs split from each whole diff by our ``groupability score'', which provides the splitting schema that optimally balances the semantic scope of anchors and the group mass they may form. Finally these anchors form advantage groups and project the diff-level advantage back to individual response tokens. Experiments on long-horizon coding and reasoning benchmarks show that DiDPO significantly outperforms strong agentic RL baselines. On Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, DiDPO exceeds comparable methods by over 10\% and narrows the gap with far larger models, offering a principled framework for fine-grained credit assignment in coding agent training. We also open-source verl-code, an agentic rl codebase that supports various RL methods and coding benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DiDPO is a critic-free RL method for coding agents that uses diff-level credit assignment via anchors derived from code diffs to propagate advantages to tokens, improving long-horizon coding benchmarks and narrowing gaps to larger models; codebase verl-code is open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Coding agents face fine-grained credit assignment: at each step, actions modify multiple code regions, making independent contributions indistinguishable. Existing RLVR methods rely on outcome or step rewards and overlook diff-level semantics. A diff-aware credit mechanism can enable more accurate credit assignment and better learning.
AI.method: Diff-in-Diff Policy Optimization (DiDPO) constructs multi-turn coding interactions as thought–action steps, samples trajectories to discover code diffs, and groups sub-diffs into anchors using a groupability score to split diffs optimally. Anchors form advantage groups, enabling diffusion of diff-level advantages back to individual response tokens; the approach is critic-free and uses policy optimization.
AI.result: Empirical results on long-horizon coding and reasoning benchmarks show strong gains over agentic RL baselines. On Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, DiDPO outperforms comparable methods by over 10% and narrows the gap with larger models.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a principled, fine-grained credit-assignment framework for coding agent training via diff-level anchors and groupability-based diff splitting; demonstrates effectiveness and provides the open-source verl-code RL codebase supporting various methods and benchmarks.

title: Machine Learning-Based Inter-Crystal Scatter Recovery for Ultra-High Resolution PET Imaging
comment: 19 pages, to b published in Physic in Medecine and Biology
summary: Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events pose a significant challenge in ultrahigh- resolution positron emission tomography (UHR-PET), especially as detector crystals become smaller and their readouts increasingly segmented. Current approaches either reject these events, reducing sensitivity, or accept them with suboptimal positioning algorithms, degrading image resolution. We present a feed forward neural network to optimize ICS event recovery by inferring the line-of-response belonging to the first Compton interaction. Our approach was validated using both Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data from the fully pixelated LabPET-IIbased preclinical and brain UHR-PET scanners.Results demonstrate a 70% to 106% increase in sensitivity while preserving sub-millimeter spatial resolvability (down to 1.6 mm) compared to conventional methods. This ICS recovery approach is an effective solution that compensates for the lower detection efficiency of small, pixelated detectors in UHR-PET, enabling reduced scan times and lower radiation doses while largely preserving image quality.

AI.tldr: A feed-forward neural network recovers inter-crystal scatter events in UHR-PET to improve sensitivity by 70–106% while preserving spatial resolution (~1.6 mm) and enabling shorter scans.
AI.motivation: ICS events degrade image quality and sensitivity in ultrahigh-resolution PET with small, segmented crystals; recovering these events can boost sensitivity without sacrificing resolution.
AI.method: Train/validate a feed-forward neural network to infer the line-of-response of the first Compton interaction, using Monte Carlo simulations and experimental LabPET-II-based data; compare against conventional ICS handling methods.
AI.result: Sensitivity increases by ~70–106% relative to conventional methods; spatial resolvability preserved at ~1.6 mm (note potential inconsistency with 'sub-millimeter'); approach suggests reduced scan times and lower dose with maintained image quality.
AI.conclusion: ICS recovery via neural-network-based inference effectively mitigates detector granularity limitations in UHR-PET, enabling higher sensitivity without sacrificing resolution or requiring larger detectors.

title: EliSeg: Verified Target Construction for Report-Grounded Abnormality Segmentation
summary: Radiology reports describe clinical observations but do not specify executable segmentation targets. They may contain present, negated, prior,uncertain, or irrelevant findings, while multiple valid abnormalities may coexist. Existing segmentation methods largely bypass this ambiguity by receiving a target identity or spatial prompt before inference, which acts as a hidden target oracle. We study report-grounded abnormality segmentation, where a model must determine target eligibility, cardinality, and finding-to-mask correspondence directly from an unfiltered report before delineating the corresponding regions. We propose \textbf{EliSeg}, an atcor--verify--revise framework that integrates target construction with mask generation. A grammar-constrained Actor proposes target slots and masks, an independent text-only Verifier reconstructs the eligible finding inventory, and Revision selectively re-executes the shared Actor when their target structures disagree. EliSeg requires no predefined target identity, finding prompt, point, or bounding box. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR-ILS show that EliSeg consistently outperforms direct segmentation methods and extract-then-segment cascades across findings, while effectively suppressing masks for ineligible report mentions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of verification and revision, and evaluation on CheXlocalize demonstrates effective transfer of the EliSeg to an external dataset.Code is available at https://github.com/Maybach-dream/EliSeg.

AI.tldr: EliSeg is a target-agnostic framework for report-grounded abnormality segmentation that constructs and revises target-masks from unfiltered radiology reports using an Actor-Verifier-Revision loop, outperforming direct segmentation and extract-then-segment baselines and transferring to new datasets.
AI.motivation: Radiology reports contain diverse, ambiguous mentions (present, negated, prior, uncertain, irrelevant) and multiple abnormalities; existing segmentation relies on predefined targets, causing suboptimal handling of ambiguity and coexisting findings.
AI.method: An atcor--verify--revise framework: a grammar-constrained Actor proposes target slots and masks without predefined identities; a text-only Verifier reconstructs the eligible finding inventory from the report; a Revision step re-executes the Actor when target structures disagree; no predefined target identity or prompts required.
AI.result: EliSeg consistently outperforms direct segmentation methods and extract-then-segment cascades across findings on MIMIC-CXR-ILS, while suppressing masks for ineligible report mentions; ablation confirms roles of verification and revision; shows effective transfer to CheXlocalize on external data.
AI.conclusion: A target-agnostic, end-to-end segmentation framework that handles report ambiguity and coexisting findings, with robust transferability to external datasets; code available for reproducibility.

title: A MARL Centered Reference Architecture for Large Language Model Augmentation in Smart Manufacturing
summary: Modern manufacturing imposes six coupled demands on adaptive control: local decisions with global consequences, partial observability, nonstationarity, reflex speed response with long horizon effects, delayed and diffuse outcomes, and dynamics that resist explicit modeling. Cooperative multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL), posed as a Dec-POMDP under centralized training with decentralized execution, is a particularly natural formalism for these demands. This paper adopts a MARL centered scope and asks where large language models (LLMs) should augment, interface with, train, or, in the strongest competitive case, replace that coordination core. A taxonomy organizes the literature through four LLM attachment points: policy, reward design, communication between agents, and hierarchical planning. A conditional capability profile separates native mechanism, reported performance, formal guarantee, and engineering maturity, and a deployment readiness analysis identifies the evidence behind each role. These stages yield the principal contribution: a three layer MARL centered reference architecture, grounded in evidence, for semantic reasoning, adaptive cooperative control, and independently assured execution. The LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP is a descriptive comparative notation for that architecture, recording four attachment choices without introducing a new decision process class or algorithm. Under the reviewed evidence, conventional MARL is better suited to frequent, structured, decentralized coordination after task specific training, whereas LLM components are promising for semantic interpretation, reward drafting, human interaction, and slower supervisory planning. Current LLM only manufacturing controllers do not yet establish equivalence for strict real time, decentralized, safety critical control; this conclusion is bounded by the available evidence and does not assert impossibility.

AI.tldr: A structured MARL-centric framework with LLM augmentation for Dec-POMDPs; taxonomy of attachment points; evidence-based architecture; current LLM controllers not yet proven for real-time safety-critical control.
AI.motivation: Modern manufacturing imposes coupled, partially observable, nonstationary control demands; MARL under Dec-POMDP with centralized training and decentralized execution is a natural fit. The paper seeks to position where LLMs should augment or replace coordination core.
AI.method: Taxonomy of four attachment points (policy, reward design, inter-agent communication, hierarchical planning); conditional capability profile (native mechanism, reported performance, formal guarantees, engineering maturity); deployment readiness analysis; proposes a three-layer MARL-centered reference architecture; introduces LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP as a descriptive notation without new decision processes.
AI.result: Conventional MARL is better for frequent, structured decentralized coordination after task-specific training. LLM components show promise for semantic interpretation, reward drafting, human interaction, and slower supervisory planning. Current LLM-only manufacturing controllers do not yet achieve equivalence for strict real-time, decentralized, safety-critical control; conclusions are bounded by available evidence.
AI.conclusion: Provides an evidence-grounded, three-layer MARL-centered reference architecture for semantic reasoning, adaptive cooperative control, and independently assured execution. The LLM-Augmented Dec-POMDP notation records attachment choices without introducing new algorithms; emphasizes preserving MARL core while leveraging LLMs for specific roles.

title: Capacity Confounds and Coverage Guarantees in Adaptive Sub-model Federated Learning
summary: Sub-model federated learning lets resource-constrained clients train width-reduced versions of a global model, but existing methods allocate capacity by device resources alone. A natural next step, allocating capacity by each client's data heterogeneity as estimated from the updates the server already observes, has been repeatedly suggested. We ask whether that step is possible, using HAS-FL, an adaptive capacity-allocation framework, as a test case. Our findings are threefold. First, validated against ground-truth label-distribution divergence on reproducible partitions, update-divergence estimates of client heterogeneity are dominated by capacity rather than data: across two corrected estimators, multiple datasets, and all seeds, the estimates correlate strongly and negatively with device capacity, and no data signal remains once capacity is controlled for. This previously undocumented confound affects any method estimating client statistics from sub-model updates. Second, adaptive allocation has a hidden failure mode: when every client is capped below full width, the uncovered parameters stay at random initialization and progressively corrupt the global model. A simple coverage guarantee removes the failure and explains why uniform allocation collapses. Third, a matched-budget control settles what adaptivity contributes: random allocation to the same average budget performs no differently on both image benchmarks, and on the naturally partitioned text benchmark the adaptive policy is the weakest of the three strategies while consuming the most capacity. Sub-model training remains valuable because it admits constrained clients at quadratically reduced cost, but what protects accuracy is parameter coverage rather than allocation intelligence. Its apparent benefits come from capacity budgeting and coverage, and future designs need heterogeneity signals separable from capacity effects.

AI.tldr: Adaptive capacity allocation in sub-model federated learning is not aided by estimating heterogeneity from updates; capacity effects dominate, causing update-based signals to be misleading. A simple coverage guarantee prevents a failure mode where under-capped clients leave uncovered parameters randomized and corrupt the global model; randomized and uniform allocations perform comparably, suggesting benefits stem from capacity budgeting and coverage rather than data-driven adaptivity.
AI.motivation: To test whether client data heterogeneity signals can be inferred from sub-model updates to drive adaptive capacity allocation in HAS-FL, and whether such adaptivity improves global model quality under resource constraints.
AI.method: Empirically compare update-divergence estimates (two corrected estimators) of client heterogeneity against ground-truth label-distribution divergence across reproducible partitions. Evaluate across multiple datasets, seeds, and two image benchmarks plus a text benchmark. Compare allocation strategies: uniform, adaptive (HAS-FL), and matched-budget random controls. Introduce a simple coverage guarantee to mitigate under-coverage failures.
AI.result: Update-divergence estimates are dominated by device capacity; data signals vanish when capacity is controlled. Adaptive allocation has a hidden failure: under partial width capping, uncovered parameters stay at random initialization and corrupt the global model; the coverage guarantee fixes this. In matched-budget tests, random allocation with the same average budget yields no performance difference; on text, adaptive policy underperforms relative to other strategies. Overall, sub-model training remains attractive for efficiency, but accuracy relies on parameter coverage rather than intelligent allocation; heterogeneity signals must be separable from capacity effects.
AI.conclusion: The claimed benefits of heterogeneity-driven adaptivity are illusory within HAS-FL; capacity budgeting and complete parameter coverage drive performance. Future designs should isolate true data heterogeneity signals from capacity effects to enable meaningful adaptive allocation.

title: Same Attention, Different Truths: Put Logit-Lens over Visual Attention to Detect and Mitigate LVLM Object Hallucination
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often suffer from object hallucination, generating objects that are absent from the image. Prior work largely attributes this to insufficient visual attention. However, we find that both real and hallucinated objects receive equally strong visual attention in the model's mid-to-late layers, suggesting that the key issue may not be how much the model attends, but what it attends to and why. To this end, we decode the visual features of high-attention regions using Logit Lens, and observe that regions corresponding to real objects can be correctly decoded to the target object tokens, whereas those for hallucinated objects cannot. Building on this, we identify two hallucination mechanisms: (i) visual uncertainty, triggered by semantically similar or confusable regions; masking these regions eliminates the hallucination. (ii) contextual prior, triggered by strong co-occurrence priors; even when the initially attended region is masked, the hallucination persists and attention drifts to other regions. Based on these findings, we propose a simple yet effective training-free Detect-Mitigate framework comprising a Logit-Lens Consistency Check to detect hallucination and targeted remedies: High-Attention Regions Masking (HARM) for visual uncertainty hallucination, and Visual Evidence Enhanced Decoding (VEED) for contextual prior hallucination. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple hallucination benchmarks. Code will be available.

AI.tldr: A training-free Detect-Mitigate framework using Logit-Lens to diagnose and mitigate object hallucination in LVLMs: high-attention regions reveal real objects via Logit-Lens; two causes are visual uncertainty and contextual priors; remedies HARM and VEED yield state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Object hallucination in LVLMs remains unresolved; existing explanations focus on attention magnitude rather than what is attended. Understanding the qualitative nature of attended regions and decoding capabilities can reveal underlying causes and guide mitigation.
AI.method: 1) Use Logit-Lens to decode high-attention regions; compare decoded tokens for real vs. hallucinated objects. 2) Identify two mechanisms: (a) visual uncertainty; masked confusable regions to reduce hallucination; (b) contextual priors; masking may not suffice due to co-occurrence priors and attention drifting. 3) Propose a training-free Detect-Mitigate framework: Logit-Lens Consistency Check to detect hallucinations; HARM to mask high-attention regions; VEED to enhance decoding with visual evidence. 4) Evaluate on multiple hallucination benchmarks; claim state-of-the-art results.
AI.result: Real object regions can be decoded to target tokens with Logit-Lens; hallucinated object regions fail decoding. Masking high-attention regions reduces visual-uncertainty-induced hallucinations; addressing contextual priors via VEED improves decoding of attended regions and reduces hallucinations. The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on several hallucination benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hallucinations stem from visual uncertainty and contextual priors rather than mere attention magnitude. A training-free Detect-Mitigate pipeline (Logit-Lens Consistency Check, HARM, VEED) effectively detects and mitigates LVLMs object hallucinations, achieving SOTA on benchmarks; code will be released.

title: NiyamAI - An Intent-Bound AI Agent with Cryptographically Verifiable Guardrails using Zero-Knowledge Proofs
summary:
Giving an AI agent the ability to send emails, query databases, or execute commands is useful--until the agent is tricked into doing something it shouldn't. Prompt injection, hallucinated reasoning, and unsafe tool calls form the primary attack surface for autonomous LLM agents. Existing defenses rely on software checks like system prompts or policy filters running on the same machine the attacker targets, offering no verifiable proof of execution. We introduce Niyam-AI, a framework that makes safety enforcement provable. At session start, permitted tools and constraints are locked into an Intent Contract committed via SHA-256. Every tool call is intercepted and validated by an isolated Judge model; upon passing, a zk-SNARK proof is generated via EZKL.
  The tool executes only after proof verification, allowing third parties to confirm enforcement without accessing Judge model weights. Evaluating Niyam-AI on 2,000 real-world scenarios from Agent-SafetyBench against NeMo Guardrails, Meta's Llama Prompt Guard 2, and OpenAI's GPT-OSS-Safeguard using 5-fold stratified cross-validation yields an F1 score of 88.5% with a 1.1% false-positive rate (bootstrap 95% CI: [85.19%, 91.88%], N=1000). McNemar's exact paired test confirms significant improvement: Niyam-AI wins 390 discordant scenarios against NeMo (vs 20 losses), 115 against Prompt Guard 2 (vs 13), and 384 against GPT-OSS-Safeguard (vs 19) with p < 0.0001 in all cases.
  Proof generation adds 2260.6 +/- 218.4 ms per approved action, while verification takes 53.1 +/- 11.8 ms. Niyam-AI provides a guardrail that is both highly accurate and mathematically verifiable--though this reflects a classifier adapted to Agent-SafetyBench evaluated against zero-shot baselines, a distinction discussed in Section IV.C.

AI.tldr: Niyam-AI introduces a provably enforceable safety framework for autonomous agents using an Intent Contract, an isolated Judge model, and zk-SNARK proofs to gate tool calls; demonstrates strong empirical performance against leading baselines with verifiable proofs.
AI.motivation: Address the primary attack surface of autonomous LLM agents (prompt injection, hallucinated reasoning, unsafe tool calls) and the lack of verifiable proof of enforcement in existing defenses.
AI.method: At session start, permitted tools and constraints are locked into an Intent Contract committed via SHA-256. Each tool call is intercepted and validated by an isolated Judge model; upon passing, a zk-SNARK proof is generated via EZKL. The tool executes only after proof verification, enabling third parties to confirm enforcement without accessing Judge weights. Evaluation on 2,000 real-world Agent-SafetyBench scenarios, compared against NeMo Guardrails, Meta's Llama Prompt Guard 2, and OpenAI's GPT-OSS-Safeguard using 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
AI.result: F1 score of 88.5% with a 1.1% false-positive rate (bootstrap 95% CI: [85.19%, 91.88%], N=1000). McNemar's test shows significant improvement: Niyam-AI beats NeMo (390 discordant vs 20), Prompt Guard 2 (115 vs 13), GPT-OSS-Safeguard (384 vs 19), p<0.0001. Proof generation adds 2260.6±218.4 ms per approved action; verification takes 53.1±11.8 ms.
AI.conclusion: Niyam-AI provides a highly accurate and mathematically verifiable safety guardrail for autonomous agents. The results are based on a classifier adapted to Agent-SafetyBench evaluated against zero-shot baselines; discussed in Section IV.C.

title: Edge Sparsification via Temporal Forman-Ricci Curvature for Dynamic Graph Learning
summary:
Temporal graph learning has become essential for analyzing real-world systems whose interactions continuously evolve over time, including financial transaction networks, communication systems, and online social platforms. However, learning from large-scale temporal graphs remains computationally challenging when networks are dense and rapidly changing. To address this limitation, we propose a network-curvature-inspired edge sparsification framework for dynamic graph learning. Our proposed method, TRicci, extends classical Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs by capturing structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition.
  Experiments on 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework preserves predictive performance across multiple graph-level prediction tasks. The results show that TRicci sparsifies temporal graphs by approximately 80% while reducing end-to-end downstream training and inference time by an average of 55.94%, without substantial degradation in predictive performance. Our findings suggest that temporal curvature can serve as a principled basis for scalable temporal graph learning by preserving predictive temporal-structural information under substantial sparsification.

AI.tldr: A curvature-inspired edge sparsification method (TRicci) for directed weighted temporal graphs that extends Forman-Ricci curvature to capture structural support, recency, and competition, enabling ~80% sparsification with minimal loss in predictive performance and ~56% speedup in training/inference.
AI.motivation: To address computational challenges of learning from dense, rapidly evolving temporal graphs by sparsifying the graph while preserving predictive temporal-structural information.
AI.method: Extend Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs and build a sparsification framework (TRicci) that leverages structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition to select edges for retention.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmarks shows TRicci preserves predictive performance across various graph-level tasks while sparsifying edges by ~80% and reducing end-to-end training/inference time by ~55.94% on average.
AI.conclusion: Temporal curvature is a principled basis for scalable temporal graph learning, enabling substantial sparsification without substantial degradation in predictive performance by maintaining essential temporal-structural information.

title: H2AL: Hyperbolic Hierarchy-aware Aggregative Learning for Registration-based Few-shot Medical Image Segmentation
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26)
summary: Registration-based Few-shot medical image segmentation (RFMIS) aims to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled images by warping a labeled image through registration. However, existing methods primarily perform pixel-level optimization and inference in Euclidean space, treating anatomical structures as flat and disjoint. This neglect of inherent hierarchies degrades pseudo-label quality and weakens the discrimination of ambiguous regions, limiting the segmentation performance. To overcome this challenge, we propose a Hyperbolic Hierarchy-aware Aggregative Learning framework for RFMIS, termed H2AL, that enhances both deformation plausibility and anatomical discrimination for dual-task learning. Specifically, we introduce a Hyperbolic Hierarchy-aware Infusion (H2I) module, which leverages the hierarchical modeling capability of hyperbolic space to learn precise hierarchy-aware representations via transformation-guided supervised hyperbolic contrastive learning, and injects such hierarchical priors into Euclidean space through a gated infusion block while preserving semantic richness. Furthermore, we propose an end-to-end joint optimization algorithm by gradient aggregation, where the gradients from the registration and segmentation decoders, embedding semantic and hierarchical cues, are aggregated to update the shared encoder to promote collaborative learning across tasks. Extensive experiments on two anatomical regions, with five experimental settings, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method in both registration and segmentation. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/JiamingCai469/H2AL.

AI.tldr: H2AL is a hyperbolic hierarchy-aware framework for registration-based few-shot medical image segmentation that models anatomical hierarchies in hyperbolic space and fuses them into Euclidean space, with gradient-aggregated dual-task optimization for improved pseudo-labels and segmentation.
AI.motivation: Existing RFMIS methods optimize in Euclidean space, treating anatomy as flat/disjoint, which impairs pseudo-label quality and ambiguity discrimination. Exploiting hierarchical structure via hyperbolic geometry can improve representation learning and segmentation performance.
AI.method: Introduces H2I (Hyperbolic Hierarchy-aware Infusion) to learn hierarchy-aware representations in hyperbolic space through transformation-guided supervised hyperbolic contrastive learning, and injects these priors into Euclidean space via a gated infusion block. Proposes end-to-end joint optimization by gradient aggregation across registration and segmentation decoders to train a shared encoder under dual-task constraints.
AI.result: Reported extensive experiments on two anatomical regions with five settings, showing effectiveness and efficiency in both registration and segmentation; code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic hierarchy modeling coupled with gradient-aggregated dual-task learning improves deformation plausibility and anatomical discrimination in RFMIS, offering a principled approach to leverage anatomical hierarchies for better pseudo-labels and segmentation.

title: Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory
summary: Memory systems have shown promise for improving agent performance, but their potential remains largely unexplored for small language models, which struggle to generate sufficient successful trajectories on their own. We propose Agent Memory Distillation (AMD), a training-free framework that transfers structured knowledge from a large teacher agent to a small student agent through hierarchical memory. AMD constructs three complementary memory types from successful teacher trajectories: Workflow memory encodes task-level strategies, Subtask memory provides concrete behavioral examples at an intermediate granularity, and Function memory captures per-function calling conventions and common pitfalls. Workflow and Subtask memories are injected proactively at the start of each task, while Function memory is retrieved reactively upon tool-calling errors. We evaluate AMD on three tool-use benchmarks using four student models (4B-8B parameters) with GPT-5-mini as the teacher, achieving average accuracy gains of 27.2%p, 11.2%p, and 3.4%p on AppWorld, BFCL V3, and ToolSandbox, while consistently outperforming existing memory-based baselines. Further analysis shows that Subtask memory contributes the largest gains, teacher effectiveness depends on both teacher capability and student compatibility, and 4B-sized students benefit most from AMD.

AI.tldr: Agent Memory Distillation (AMD) enables small language models to achieve higher tool-use performance by distilling three hierarchical memories from a large teacher without training.
AI.motivation: Small LMs struggle to generate sufficient successful trajectories; memory augmentation is promising but underexplored for tiny models; AMD aims to transfer structured knowledge from a high-capacity teacher in a training-free way.
AI.method: Construct three complementary memories from successful teacher trajectories: Workflow memory (task-level strategies), Subtask memory (intermediate-granularity behavioral examples), Function memory (per-function calling conventions and pitfalls). Proactively inject Workflow and Subtask memories at task start; retrieve Function memory reactively on tool-calling errors; evaluate on three tool-use benchmarks with four 4B–8B student models using GPT-5-mini as teacher.
AI.result: On AppWorld, BFCL V3, and ToolSandbox, AMD yields average accuracy gains of 27.2, 11.2, and 3.4 percentage points respectively over baselines; 4B-sized students benefit most; Subtask memory provides the largest gains; teacher effectiveness depends on teacher capability and student compatibility.
AI.conclusion: AMD offers a training-free, hierarchical memory distillation framework that substantially boosts small LMs on tool-use tasks; structured memories (especially Subtask memory) are effective conduits for transferring teacher knowledge; effectiveness scales with student size and teacher–student compatibility.

title: Fluid-DiT: Graph-Free Diffusion Transformers for Fluid Flow Simulations Learning
summary: Simulating complex fluid flows requires capturing full equilibrium distributions rather than just mean trajectories, yet high-fidelity solvers remain computationally prohibitive. Recent advances, such as Diffusion Graph Networks (DGNs), have combined diffusion models with graph neural networks to sample equilibrium states directly from unstructured meshes, enabling distributional accuracy even from short simulations. However, graph-based diffusion approaches suffer from hand-crafted architectural constraints, limited receptive fields in message passing, and costly multi-scale designs, which restrict scalability to larger and more complex domains. We propose Fluid-DiT, a Graph-Free Diffusion Transformer that replaces graph message passing with attention-based denoising, eliminating explicit graph design while preserving the ability to model distributions of chaotic flows. Our framework introduces a latent-space formulation that disentangles geometric fidelity from distributional learning, reducing high-frequency artifacts and accelerating sampling. By leveraging the transformer's global receptive field, Fluid-DiT naturally captures both local flow structures and long-range correlations without requiring hierarchical graph coarsening. On canonical benchmarks including laminar cylinder wakes, ellipse-flow systems, and turbulent 3D wing experiments, Fluid-DiT consistently outperforms graph-based diffusion baselines in both sample quality and distributional accuracy, achieving higher $R^2$ correlations and lower Wasserstein distances. Moreover, it generalizes robustly from short, incomplete trajectories to unseen Reynolds numbers and geometries, demonstrating strong scalability.

AI.tldr: Fluid-DiT introduces a graph-free diffusion transformer for sampling equilibrium flows from unstructured domains, outperforming graph-based diffusion methods in quality and distributional accuracy, with robust generalization and scalability.
AI.motivation: Need accurate distributional representations for complex fluid flows. Graph-based diffusion approaches have restrictive architectures, limited receptive fields, and costly multi-scale designs that hinder scalability to larger, more complex domains.
AI.method: Replace graph message passing with attention-based denoising in a latent-space formulation that decouples geometric fidelity from distributional learning. Use a transformer with a global receptive field to capture both local structures and long-range correlations, avoiding explicit graph coarsening.
AI.result: Fluid-DiT outperforms graph-based diffusion baselines on laminar cylinder wakes, ellipse flows, and turbulent 3D wing simulations, with higher R^2 correlations and lower Wasserstein distances; demonstrates robust generalization from short/incomplete trajectories to unseen Reynolds numbers and geometries, indicating strong scalability.
AI.conclusion: A graph-free diffusion transformer achieves accurate distributional learning for complex flows, simplifying architecture, improving scalability, and maintaining distributional fidelity across diverse benchmarks.

title: SkySeaLand: A Wide-Format Satellite Transportation Benchmark with an Ultra-Lightweight Detection Baseline
summary: Satellite object detection is challenged by small targets and wide-format scenes that lose detail under standard square-input resizing. We introduce SkySeaLand, a public dataset of 1,307 high-resolution satellite images and 19,101 verified bounding boxes across airplane, boat, car, and ship classes in terrestrial and maritime scenes. Native COCO and YOLO annotations are provided. The collection is dominated by large source images and wide scene geometry: 84.5 percent exceed 3,836 pixels on the longest side and 73.1 percent are near a 3:1 aspect ratio. We evaluate twelve detectors from the YOLO, RT-DETR, DETR, and Faster R-CNN families using a common split and COCO metrics. The tested YOLO and RT-DETR variants obtain 84.4--88.2 mAP50, with no consistent accuracy gain from larger parameter counts under the reported model-specific recipes. We also report SkyDet, a 1.22 M parameter anchor-free baseline that obtains 60.5 mAP50 and 24.32 mAP50-95 in a 4.90 MB footprint, with 13.74 ms latency (72.8 FPS) on a Tesla T4. SkySeaLand provides a compact benchmark for mixed land--maritime transportation detection, while SkyDet establishes a documented low-footprint reference rather than a state-of-the-art accuracy claim.
