AI.tldr: Public high-resolution satellite dataset SkySeaLand (1,307 images, 19,101 boxes) for mixed land–maritime detection; baseline SkyDet; extensive evaluation of 12 detectors showing limited gains with larger models; SkySeaLand as compact benchmark and SkyDet as low-footprint reference.
AI.motivation: Address small-target detection and detail loss in wide-format satellite imagery due to standard resizing; provide a publicly available, COCO/YOLO-annotated dataset and a lightweight baseline for edge deployment.
AI.method: Assemble SkySeaLand with native COCO and YOLO annotations; evaluate twelve detectors from YOLO, RT-DETR, DETR, and Faster R-CNN using a common split and COCO metrics; introduce SkyDet, a 1.22M-parameter anchor-free baseline with compact footprint.
AI.result: Detectors (YOLO and RT-DETR variants) reach 84.4–88.2 mAP50; no consistent accuracy gains with larger parameter counts under the reported recipes; SkyDet achieves 60.5 mAP50 and 24.32 mAP50-95 with a 4.90 MB footprint and 13.74 ms latency (72.8 FPS) on a Tesla T4; dataset characteristics show 84.5% exceed 3,836 px on the longest side and 73.1% near 3:1 aspect ratio.
AI.conclusion: SkySeaLand provides a compact benchmark for mixed land–maritime detection, while SkyDet offers a documented low-footprint reference rather than a state-of-the-art accuracy claim; dataset is public.

title: SetEasy: A Multi-Modal Classroom Engagement Assessment and Seating Optimization Framework
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Published in the Proceedings of ASCAAD 2025
summary: SetEasy optimizes classroom engagement in fixed seating grids. It fuses multimodal sensing (wristband physiology, 4K video, environmental data) and trains a v-Gage model grounded in a revised ISEQ. Each week, two-week engagement forecasts are mapped to a student-seat utility matrix, and CP-SAT generates seating plans under visual-access and social-dynamics constraints. In a four-week deployment (23 students, 331 classes), v-Gage converged across affective, behavioral, cognitive, and overall dimensions, cutting RMSE from 0.75 to 0.53. Optimization raised mean engagement from 0.30 to 0.70, with over two-thirds of seats reaching high engagement and back-row low-activity patterns markedly reduced. These results show that, without hardware changes, interpretable, data-driven seating strategies can substantially enhance engagement. The multimodal "assessment + optimization" paradigm offers a transferable, sustainable path to culturally responsive, differentiated spatial design amid global homogenization.

AI.tldr: Multimodal sensing and optimization (SetEasy) improve classroom engagement via seat assignment, with notable RMSE reduction and engagement gains in a four-week study.
AI.motivation: To enhance classroom engagement and deliver culturally responsive, differentiated spatial design by combining data-driven assessment with optimization in fixed seating grids.
AI.method: Collect multimodal signals (wristband physiology, 4K video, environment), train a v-Gage model on revised ISEQ; forecast two weeks ahead; map forecasts to a student-seat utility matrix; solve seating with CP-SAT under visual-access and social-dynamics constraints; deploy over four weeks (23 students, 331 classes).
AI.result: v-Gage converged across affective, behavioral, cognitive, and overall dimensions; RMSE dropped 0.75→0.53; mean engagement rose 0.30→0.70; >2/3 seats achieved high engagement; back-row low-activity patterns reduced; no hardware changes required; demonstrates transferability of the assessment+optimization paradigm.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven seating optimization can substantially boost engagement and offers a transferable, sustainable approach to culturally responsive classroom design in standardized environments.

title: Momba: Network Modernization Improves Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have shown that improving neural network architectures can yield substantial gains in sample efficiency and asymptotic performance without altering the underlying algorithms. In contrast, work on multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which aims to discover a set of policies that balance trade-offs among conflicting objectives, has predominantly focused on algorithmic innovations, leaving the area of architectures underexplored. While the optimal policies and value functions can differ significantly depending on the trade-offs, MORL algorithms commonly represent them with simple feedforward networks conditioned on the trade-off. This raises the question of whether the performance of the algorithms could be improved with more expressive function approximators. In this paper, we integrate recent advances in neural network design: (i) observation and feature normalization, (ii) weight normalization, and (iii) modeling of distributional returns with an entropy-regularized MORL algorithm. The empirical results across standard continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that these changes substantially improve the quality of the produced solution sets without requiring major changes to the underlying algorithm.

AI.tldr: Architectural enhancements (normalization, weight normalization, distributional returns via entropy-regularized MORL) significantly improve MORL solution sets in continuous control tasks with minimal changes to the underlying algorithms.
AI.motivation: MORL has focused on algorithmic innovations rather than network architectures; exploring expressive function approximators could yield better trade-off policies.
AI.method: Integrate three neural-design advances into MORL: (i) observation/feature normalization, (ii) weight normalization, and (iii) distributional returns with entropy-regularization; evaluate on standard continuous control benchmarks.
AI.result: Substantial improvements in the quality of the produced solution sets across benchmarks, with improved sample efficiency and asymptotic performance, achieved without major changes to the MORL algorithm.
AI.conclusion: Neural architecture choices materially influence MORL performance; incorporating normalization and distributional returns is an effective, low-friction way to enhance MORL without altering core algorithms.

title: GeoDistill-Refine: Silhouette-First Geometry Distillation for Annotation-Free Spacecraft Segmentation
summary: Foundation segmentation models can provide supervision for spacecraft imagery without manual training masks, but their predictions vary with textual prompts and may contain geometric errors that are amplified during distillation. This paper presents GeoDistill-Refine, a two-stage framework that transfers offline SAM 3 pseudo-masks to a compact segmentation network. Six fixed prompts are fused by an unweighted 50% vote to stabilize the teacher output. The student first learns the foreground silhouette and is then refined with signed-distance-field, skeleton, and area objectives derived from the pseudo-mask. A sample-level gate, computed from prompt agreement, the valid-prompt ratio, and pseudo-mask area plausibility, reduces the influence of unreliable pseudo-geometry. On the SpaceSense-Bench HJM lockbox set, GeoDistill-Refine improves Image IoU and Boundary F1 by 0.0456 and 0.1380, respectively, over a plain pseudo-label student. External evaluations on the SPEED+ Lightbox and Sunlamp domains and on TANGO show competitive regional overlap together with gains in boundary quality or foreground precision. The deployed TinyUNet contains 0.263 M parameters and requires approximately 1.1 ms per image on an RTX 4090; SAM 3 pseudo-mask construction and the auxiliary geometry branches are used only during training.

AI.tldr: GeoDistill-Refine is a two-stage distillation framework that transfers offline SAM-generated pseudo-masks to a compact segmentation network (TinyUNet) for spacecraft imagery. It mitigates prompt-induced geometry errors via six-prompt fusion (50% unweighted vote) and a sample-level gating mechanism, then refines the student with signed-distance-field, skeleton, and area losses. The approach yields modest but consistent gains in IoU and Boundary F1 across multiple domains while keeping the student model ultra-light during inference.
AI.motivation: To stabilize teacher outputs from foundation models (SAM) when used for pseudo-labeling in domain-specific segmentation (space imagery), reducing geometric errors and prompt sensitivity while producing a compact, fast student model suitable for deployment.
AI.method: Two-stage knowledge distillation: (1) pseudo-label generation by six fixed prompts fused through a 50% unweighted vote to produce robust teacher masks; (2) a TinyUNet student trained to predict foreground silhouette, followed by geometry-aware refinement using signed-distance-field (SDF) losses, skeleton constraints, and area-based objectives derived from pseudo-masks; a sample-level gate—based on prompt agreement, valid-prompt ratio, and pseudo-mask area plausibility—reduces influence of unreliable pseudo-geometry; during training only.
AI.result: On SpaceSense-Bench HJM lockbox: Image IoU and Boundary F1 improve by 0.0456 and 0.1380 over a plain pseudo-label student. External evaluations (SPEED+ Lightbox, Sunlamp, TANGO) show competitive regional overlap with improvements in boundary quality or foreground precision. Deployed TinyUNet has 0.263M params and ~1.1 ms per image on RTX 4090; SAM pseudo-mask construction and geometry branches used only in training.
AI.conclusion: GeoDistill-Refine demonstrates that combining multi-prompt fusion, a gating mechanism, and geometry-aware refinement can produce a compact, fast segmentation model with robust boundary and foreground performance when distilling from foundation models, with demonstrated generalization across several spacecraft-imagery domains.

title: EMAS: Stabilizing Multi-Agent System Evolution through Evidence-Guided Revision
summary: Many methods for automated multi-agent system design optimize prompts and topologies during an initial design stage and then deploy the resulting system unchanged on subsequent samples. Experience from these samples is rarely consolidated into reusable system updates, while accuracy-oriented designs may incur high token costs. We introduce EMAS (Evolving Multi-Agent System), which uses this experience to revise MAS topology and prompts without updating LLM parameters, either to improve accuracy or to reduce cost. EMAS converts traces into structured diagnoses that specify a revision operation and target. It generates a candidate revision only when the same diagnosis recurs across samples and applies it only if paired validation against the current MAS meets the corresponding acceptance criterion. Across four benchmarks and two LLMs, EMAS attains the highest task-weighted overall accuracy for both backbones and is best or tied in six of eight model--benchmark settings. Within two evolution epochs, EMAS achieves relative gains of 6.30% and 20.10% in task-weighted accuracy on Kimi-K2-6 and Qwen3.6-27B, respectively. On MBPP with Qwen3.6-27B, EMAS raises accuracy from 55.09% to 89.12% while reducing token use per task by 62.2%. These results show that EMAS can turn experience from new samples into reusable updates to MAS topology and prompts.

AI.tldr: EMAS updates MAS topology and prompts from accumulated experience without updating LLM parameters, improving accuracy and reducing cost.
AI.motivation: Current MAS design often optimizes prompts/topologies only during an initial stage and fails to consolidate ongoing experience from new samples into reusable updates; accuracy-focused designs incur high token costs. EMAS seeks reusable, low-cost improvements by exploiting observed recurrence of issues.
AI.method: EMAS converts interaction traces into structured diagnoses that specify a revision operation and a target. A candidate revision is generated only when the same diagnosis recurs across samples and is applied only if paired validation against the current MAS meets the acceptance criterion. No LLM parameter updates are performed. Evaluation spans four benchmarks and two LLMs, across two evolution epochs.
AI.result: EMAS achieves the highest task-weighted accuracy across baselines in six of eight model–benchmark settings, with gains of 6.30% (Kimi-K2-6) and 20.10% (Qwen3.6-27B). On MBPP with Qwen3.6-27B, accuracy rises from 55.09% to 89.12%, while token use per task decreases by 62.2%. Overall, EMAS demonstrates that experience from new samples can be transformed into reusable topology‑and‑prompt updates without LLM fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: EMAS demonstrates that accumulated experience can be converted into validated, reusable updates to MAS topology and prompts, achieving higher accuracy and lower token cost without updating LLM parameters.

title: Conformal Fusion Under Missing Modalities
summary: Multimodal fusion architectures typically assume all modalities are available at inference, yet sensor failures, acquisition variability, and cost constraints routinely produce incomplete observations. Existing work treats modality absence as a prediction-accuracy problem, leaving a more basic question unanswered: whether a model's confidence estimates remain calibrated when an entire input stream is removed. We argue that missing-modality robustness and calibrated uncertainty are a single coupled property, and introduce Modality-Conditioned Conformal Fusion (MCCF), an architecture that addresses both at once. MCCF combines a multimodal bottleneck fusion backbone trained with modality dropout, per-modality evidential heads producing modality-decomposed Dirichlet distributions, and a Dempster-Shafer combination rule that fuses the per-modality evidence into a joint predictive distribution; an absent modality contributes vacuous evidence that is structurally ignored, so the fused uncertainty automatically reflects the reduced information without test-time imputation. A Mondrian conformal calibration module keyed on the modality-presence mask then provides finite-sample group-conditional coverage for every non-empty modality subset. MCCF is, to our knowledge, the first method with formal coverage guarantees under arbitrary modality availability through architectural integration rather than post-hoc recalibration, and the evidential decomposition yields per-modality vacuity scores that localise uncertainty to the absent modality responsible. Across a synthetic problem and three real multimodal benchmarks, MCCF holds its target coverage on every modality-presence subset, substantially narrows the coverage gap between full and partial modalities relative to a marginal split-conformal baseline, and imposes no measurable accuracy cost relative to temperature-scaled and evidential baselines.

AI.tldr: MCCF unifies missing-modality robustness with calibrated uncertainty using modality-conditioned evidences and a DS fusion, with Mondrian conformal calibration guaranteeing coverage for any subset of available modalities.
AI.motivation: Address the coupled challenge of robustness to absent modalities and calibrated uncertainty, moving beyond post-hoc recalibration to a principled architectural solution.
AI.method: A multimodal backbone trained with modality dropout; per-modality evidential heads output Dirichlet distributions; Dempster-Shafer fusion of per-modality evidence into a joint predictive distribution; absent modalities contribute vacuous evidence; Mondrian conformal calibration conditioned on the modality-presence mask yields finite-sample, group-conditional coverage for every non-empty modality subset.
AI.result: Empirically maintains target coverage for all modality subsets, reduces the coverage gap between full and partial modalities compared to a marginal split-conformal baseline, and incurs no measurable accuracy loss relative to baselines.
AI.conclusion: MCCF represents, as claimed, the first approach to provide formal coverage guarantees under arbitrary modality availability via architectural integration; its evidential decomposition also yields per-modality vacuity to localize uncertainty to the missing modality.

title: Addressable Memory for Video World Models
summary: We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) offsets then fall outside the range seen during training and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space corrupts memory by averaging together incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this addressable cache, we study two memory compression approaches: WorldTrace-Field compresses history for temporal coherence, while WorldTrace-Landmark stores verbatim scene traces at detected transitions for episodic recall. We further introduce LoopBench, a benchmark evaluating whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. WorldTrace-Field improves temporal consistency by +15.5%, and WorldTrace-Landmark improves episodic recall by +19.5% on LoopBench, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.

AI.tldr: WorldTrace introduces a training-free memory framework to enable long-horizon visual persistence in interactive video world models by making memory slots addressable and using two compression modes, improving temporal coherence and episodic recall without retraining (LoopBench benchmark).
AI.motivation: Visual persistence deteriorates when rollout horizons exceed the training horizon due to RoPE offset misalignment and memory compression artifacts. A training-free memory mechanism that preserves and retrieves stored visual content over long horizons is needed to extend persistent generation.
AI.method: Propose WorldTrace: a memory framework with a growing KV cache where each summary slot is assigned a distinct virtual position to keep memory addressable in-distribution. Study two compression strategies within this addressable cache: WorldTrace-Field (temporal coherence by history compression) and WorldTrace-Landmark (verbatim scene traces at transitions for episodic recall). Introduce LoopBench as a benchmark to test reconstruction after long detours. Compare baselines to show improvements.
AI.result: WorldTrace-Field improves temporal consistency by 15.5%; WorldTrace-Landmark improves episodic recall by 19.5% on LoopBench, enabling visually persistent generation for long horizons without retraining.
AI.conclusion: A training-free memory framework that enables robust long-horizon visual persistence in interactive video world models by making compressed memory addressable and using specialized retention strategies. The approach yields substantial gains in both temporal coherence and episodic recall without retraining.

title: Authoring and Management of Transparent Research Integrity Assessments of Randomised Clinical Trial Publications Using LLM-assisted Tools and Provenance Knowledge Graphs
summary: Systematic reviews of Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) are routinely used as evidence for clinical care guidelines. Such evidence has to meet high research integrity standards to prevent low quality or false research outputs influencing the clinical care. However, assessing research integrity of published RCTs is a complex process requiring manual effort, and potentially resulting in diverse opinions of the human assessors. This paper describes INSPECT-AI, an LLM-based interactive tool that assists human reviewers with research integrity assessments of published RCTs based on the community approved INSPECT-SR framework, and the Research Integrity Provenance and Evidence ontology (RIPE-O) for documenting the provenance of the assessment process. In addition, we present the Research Integrity Provenance and Evidence knowledge graph (RIPE-KG), an initial set of 140 expert research integrity assessments of 95 RCT publications generated by INSPECT-AI and described using RIPE-O.

AI.tldr: Introduces INSPECT-AI, an LLM-based interactive tool to assist human reviewers in research integrity assessments of published RCTs using the INSPECT-SR framework; documents provenance via RIPE-O and builds RIPE-KG with 140 expert assessments across 95 RCTs.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews rely on high-integrity RCTs; integrity assessment is labor-intensive, prone to subjectivity and disagreements among reviewers; a standardized, provenance-aware tool could reduce manual load and improve consistency.
AI.method: Developed INSPECT-AI, an LLM-driven interactive assistant aligned with the INSPECT-SR framework; uses RIPE-O to document assessment provenance; RIPE-KG stores assessments as a knowledge graph. Reported an initial set of 140 expert integrity assessments of 95 RCT publications produced by INSPECT-AI and described with RIPE-O.
AI.result: Feasibility demonstrated: creation of RIPE-KG comprising 140 expert integrity assessments of 95 RCTs generated by INSPECT-AI and described using RIPE-O.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a provenance-backed framework (RIPE-O/RIPE-KG) and an LLM-assisted workflow (INSPECT-AI) to enable scalable, standardized research integrity assessments of RCTs for systematic reviews.

title: MAUPITI: On-Device Prototype-Based Learning on a Smart Infrared Sensor
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Embedded Systems Letters
summary: Low-resolution infrared (IR) array sensors represent an interesting solution for privacy-preserving human sensing in embedded systems. In this letter, we describe a smart multi-pixel IR sensor integrating a 16$\times$16 thermal MOSFET (TMOS) array and a RISC-V microcontroller extended with low-precision SIMD instructions, capable of on-device learning and continual adaptation for pose and gesture recognition tasks under tight memory and power constraints ($<$32kB on-chip memory, $\approx$1.5mW). To avoid the memory overheads of backpropagation and replay buffers, we adopt a prototype-based Nearest Class Mean (NCM) classifier in which a simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) encoder is trained and quantized offline, while class prototypes are stored and updated on the device in streaming mode. With experiments on two datasets, we show that this approach yields accuracy on par with a conventional classifier, with negligible latency overheads in both the classification and the prototype update ($<$0.29% considering both phases), effectively enabling online adaptation of the perception framework.

AI.tldr: Prototype-based on-device learning for privacy-preserving pose/gesture recognition using a 16x16 TMOS infrared sensor and streaming prototype updates, achieving near-classifier accuracy with minimal latency under tight memory/power limits.
AI.motivation: Enable privacy-preserving human sensing on resource-constrained embedded devices by combining low-resolution thermal sensing with online adaptation, avoiding backpropagation and large replay buffers.
AI.method: Hardware: a 16x16 thermal MOSFET (TMOS) array with a RISC-V MCU and low-precision SIMD. Software: an offline-trained, quantized CNN encoder paired with a Nearest Class Mean (NCM) classifier that stores and updates class prototypes on-device in streaming mode, eliminating backpropagation and replay buffers.
AI.result: Achieves accuracy comparable to a conventional classifier on two datasets, with negligible additional latency (<0.29%) for both classification and prototype updates, while staying within memory (<32 kB) and power (~1.5 mW) constraints, enabling online adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of private, on-device pose/gesture recognition under stringent resource constraints using a prototype-based NCM classifier with streaming prototype updates and an offline-trained CNN encoder.

title: UniJEPA: A Unified Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Task-Agnostic Visual World Modeling
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a principled framework for self-supervised learning of world models in compact latent spaces, yet existing methods are fragmented: some predict masked parts of a single image in latent space (I-JEPA), others learn to predict global photometric transformations (Image World Models), while video-scale JEPAs predict future temporal states and are post-trained for action-conditioned planning (V-JEPA~2, DINO-World, DINO-WM). These objectives are treated as distinct recipes with separate encoders, predictors, and anti-collapse regularizers, hindering a single model from unifying image-level and video-level world modeling. We present UniJEPA, a unified JEPA that jointly learns photometric prediction (image-level transformations) and temporal prediction (video-level next-state dynamics) in one shared latent space. A single end-to-end objective, composed of a next-embedding prediction loss and a Gaussian regularizer, yields a provably anti-collapse encoder-predictor pair trainable from raw pixels without EMA, stop-gradient, or pre-trained encoders. We show that the same latent space supports controllable abstraction: photometric prediction learns invariant structure while temporal prediction learns equivariant dynamics. After action-conditioned post-training on offline trajectories, UniJEPA enables zero-shot planning by treating goal features as prediction targets. On image, video, and control benchmarks, UniJEPA matches or surpasses task-specific JEPAs while requiring a single loss hyperparameter, and plans up to tens of times faster than generative world models at comparable accuracy.

AI.tldr: UniJEPA: a unified JEPA that jointly learns image-level photometric predictions and video-level temporal dynamics in one shared latent space, enabling zero-shot planning with a single loss and anti-collapse guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing JEPAs are fragmented across image-level and video-level objectives, requiring separate encoders, predictors, and regularizers, hindering unified world modeling and efficient planning.
AI.method: Train a single end-to-end JEPA with a next-embedding prediction loss and a Gaussian regularizer on raw pixels, without EMA, stop-gradient, or pre-trained encoders; learn a shared latent space supporting both photometric and temporal predictions.
AI.result: Matches or surpasses task-specific JEPAs on image, video, and control benchmarks; zero-shot planning after offline action-conditioned post-training; faster planning (tens of times) than generative world models at comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A single-loss, unified JEPA yields controllable abstraction where photometric prediction enforces invariant structure and temporal prediction enforces equivariant dynamics; effective for unified image/video/world modeling and planning without per-task customization.

title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretable Models of Human Randomisation Failures
summary: Mixed strategy equilibrium predicts i.i.d play: past actions should not help predict future decisions. Human players, however, systematically depart from this benchmark, and in O'Neill's zero sum card game, these departures can be predicted by black box sequence models such as LSTMs. This paper asks whether that predictive power can be achieved by transparent alternatives that also reveal the behavioural structure behind it. Using 84,060 decisions from 2,802 pairs, the analysis first benchmarks naive and behavioral models against interpretable machine learning and deep learning models, then evaluates the modified EWA specifications of prior work against these benchmarks and uses the LASSO diagnostics to motivate a further nested frequency tracking extension. The results show that repeat or avoid behavior, especially players' management of their own recent action histories, accounts for most of the interpretable and strategically exploitable signal, while frequency tracking adds little out of sample.

AI.tldr: Transparent models with interpretable features largely match the predictive power of LSTM-style models in predicting deviations from mixed-strategy play in O’Neill’s zero-sum game, with repeat/avoid behavior and self-history driving most of the signal; frequency tracking adds little out-of-sample.
AI.motivation: Assess whether the predictive power of black-box sequence models can be matched by transparent alternatives and to reveal the behavioral structure behind predictability in O’Neill’s zero-sum card game; compare naive, behavioral, interpretable ML, and deep learning models, along with modified EWA specs and LASSO-guided extensions.
AI.method: Use 84,060 decisions from 2,802 player pairs; benchmark naive, behavioral, interpretable ML, and deep learning models; evaluate modified EWA specifications; apply LASSO diagnostics; introduce a nested frequency tracking extension; perform out-of-sample evaluation.
AI.result: Repeat or avoid behavior, especially management of players’ own recent action histories, account for most of the interpretable and strategically exploitable signal; frequency tracking adds little out of sample; LASSO diagnostics motivate the behavioral features.
AI.conclusion: Transparent, interpretable models capturing action history and repeat/avoid behavior can largely reproduce the predictive power of black-box models in this setting, offering clearer insight into the underlying behavioral structure and suggesting limited value from complex frequency-tracking features outside in-sample fit.

title: An AI4AI Framework for Visual Token Pruning
summary: Visual-token pruning can substantially reduce the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods largely rely on fixed, handcrafted heuristics and costly expert trial and error. As pruning objectives, budgets, and model architectures diversify, manually navigating the expanding design space becomes increasingly difficult. This paper aims to build an AI4AI framework for visual-token pruning by addressing a natural question: Can large language models automatically design effective visual-token reduction algorithms? Although LLMs possess broad algorithmic knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, translating such general knowledge into effective solutions for a specialized task remains nontrivial. We argue that the key lies in designing an appropriate search-state representation that connects the internal knowledge of LLMs with the structural requirements and constraints of visual-token pruning. Based on this insight, we propose AutoPrune, a training-free framework for LLM-driven visual-token pruning policy design. At its core, AutoPrune introduces a Token Pruning Domain-Specific Language (TPDSL) comprising 131 reusable atoms for budget control, token scoring, selection constraints, and token reassembly. A key property of TPDSL is that it represents each search state as a residual modification of a strong base policy. This residual formulation narrows the search space and directs the LLM's attention toward the policy components that are most consequential for performance. Experiments on 14 multimodal benchmarks and three MLLM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability of AutoPrune. Even when removing 94.4% of visual tokens, AutoPrune preserves more than 99% of full-token performance while reducing FLOPs by 9.9x and prefill latency by 6.4x.

AI.tldr: AutoPrune is a training-free AI4AI framework that lets LLMs design visual-token pruning policies for multimodal LLMs using a domain-specific language (TPDSL) with 131 atoms. It uses a residual search-state representation to efficiently explore policy components, achieving substantial token pruning with minimal accuracy loss and large speedups across 14 benchmarks and 3 backbones.
AI.motivation: Visual-token pruning can greatly reduce inference costs for multimodal LLMs, but existing methods rely on handcrafted heuristics and trial-and-error. The design space is expanding with diverse budgets and architectures, making manual design impractical. An AI4AI approach aims to leverage LLMs to automatically design effective pruning policies.
AI.method: Introduce AutoPrune, a training-free framework that uses a Token Pruning Domain-Specific Language (TPDSL) consisting of 131 reusable atoms for budget control, token scoring, selection constraints, and token reassembly. The search state is represented as a residual modification of a strong base policy, narrowing the search space. The LLM is guided to design policy components, which are then evaluated without additional training across multiple benchmarks.
AI.result: AutoPrune achieves aggressive token pruning (up to 94.4% visual tokens removed) while preserving over 99% of full-token accuracy. It also reduces FLOPs by 9.9x and prefill latency by 6.4x. The approach shows effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability across 14 multimodal benchmarks and three MLLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven visual-token pruning with a residual search-state framework and TPDSL enables effective, training-free design of pruning policies. The approach offers a scalable AI4AI solution for reducing inference costs in multimodal models with strong empirical validation.

title: I Seek You in Videos: Identity-Conditioned Queries for Person-Centric Video Reasoning
comment: Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26). 6 figures, 5 tables
summary: Real-world video reasoning often involves multimodal, multi-source inputs, whereas existing video reasoning tasks typically assume a simplified video-text setting, limiting identity matching and person-centric reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Identity-conditioned Queries (ICQ) task, in which models are required to jointly associate and interpret an input video and a reference image of a person, and leverage this conditioning to address identity grounding, behavior understanding, and temporal reasoning, among other challenges. Building on ICQ, we present ISYV (I Seek You in Videos), a systematic solution comprising three components: (1) ISYV-Bench, a challenging evaluation benchmark with 1,377 real-world complex videos and 1,377 question-answer pairs, organized into six difficulty levels spanning capabilities from identity recognition to causal reasoning; (2) ISYV-75K, a large-scale training set of 75K high-quality samples constructed via automated annotation, multi-stage verification, and manual review; and (3) ISYV-Framework, containing an ICQ-oriented model and training strategy for learning to exploit informative video shots without additional shot-level annotations. Extensive experiments show that both mainstream closed-source and open-source MLLMs struggle on ISYV-Bench, especially in cross-domain identity matching and long-horizon tracking. ISYV-Model outperforms strong baselines and in some aspects approaches closed-source performance. Overall, ISYV provides a unified task definition, scalable datasets/benchmarks, and modeling insights for person-centric video reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces Identity-conditioned Queries (ICQ) for joint video and reference image identity grounding, and ISYV—a benchmark (ISYV-Bench), a training set (ISYV-75K), and a framework (ISYV-Framework) for person-centric video reasoning; results show current MLLMs struggle on cross-domain identity matching and long-horizon tracking, with ISYV-Model achieving competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Real-world video reasoning requires integrated identity grounding, behavior understanding, and temporal reasoning across multimodal inputs; existing video QA tasks rely on simplified video-text settings and lack robust identity matching and long-horizon tracking.
AI.method: Proposes Identity-conditioned Queries (ICQ) as a joint video-image conditioning task. Builds ISYV-Bench (1,377 real videos and QA pairs across six difficulty levels), ISYV-75K (75k training samples via automated annotation, multi-stage verification, and manual review), and ISYV-Framework with an ICQ-oriented model and training strategy that exploits informative video shots without shot-level annotations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show mainstream MLLMs (closed- and open-source) struggle on ISYV-Bench, especially for cross-domain identity matching and long-horizon tracking; ISYV-Model surpasses strong baselines in several aspects and approaches closed-source performance on some tasks.
AI.conclusion: ISYV offers a unified task definition, scalable datasets/benchmarks, and modeling insights to advance person-centric video reasoning, highlighting the gap in current models and the need for targeted architectures and training strategies.

title: From probability to causality in probabilistic logic programming
summary: Probabilistic logic programming is a formalism of statistical relational artificial intelligence that supports causal queries, including interventions from outside the system. When the structure of a probabilistic logic program is learned from data, however, only probabilistic information is used, and a single probability distribution may be compatible with several causal orders. This leads to ambiguity in interventional reasoning, raising the question of when the causal order is uniquely determined by the distribution. Exploiting the relationship between acyclic probabilistic logic programs and Bayesian networks, we derive conditions under which the probabilistic information encoded in a program determines a unique causal order. We also incorporate constraints arising from relational structure by taking into account prescribed sets of causal symmetries induced by the underlying relational vocabulary. The result is a method for verifying when a learned probabilistic logic program supports well-defined intervention semantics.

AI.tldr: A study of when a learned probabilistic logic program implies a unique causal order for interventions, by linking acyclic PLP to Bayesian networks and incorporating relational symmetry constraints to verify well-defined intervention semantics.
AI.motivation: Interventional reasoning in probabilistic logic programs is ambiguous when multiple causal orders fit the learned probabilistic distribution; there is a need to determine when the causal order is uniquely determined and semantically well-defined.
AI.method: Derive conditions that map the probabilistic information in an acyclic probabilistic logic program to a unique causal order, leveraging the PLP–Bayesian network correspondence and imposing relational symmetry constraints induced by the vocabulary. Present a verification method to assess well-defined intervention semantics.
AI.result: A set of criteria that determine when a learned PLP yields a unique causal order and a practical method to verify that the program supports well-defined interventional semantics, accounting for relational structure via symmetry constraints.
AI.conclusion: Under the established conditions, learned probabilistic logic programs can support unambiguous intervention semantics; relational symmetries strengthen the linkage between PLPs and causal order, enabling verifiable well-defined interventions.

title: Stochastic Autoregressive Learning
summary:
Motivated by LLMs, which generate outputs by iteratively sampling from next-token distributions, we introduce a PAC-learning model for binary stochastic autoregressive learning. This generalizes the deterministic autoregressive learning framework of Joshi et al., COLT 2025. In our model, one fixed generator assigns a Bernoulli next-token distribution to every prompt string. Starting from an input prompt, a token is sampled and appended to the prompt; the same generator is then applied again to this expanded prompt; this procedure is repeated for $M$ steps. Three forms of supervision are considered: base one-step samples, chain-of-thought (CoT) samples that reveal full random trajectories of length $M$, and end-to-end (e2e) samples that reveal only the final token of length $M$ trajectories. For a generator class, we study the minimum number of samples $m_{base}(\varepsilon),m_{CoT}(\varepsilon), m_{e2e}(\varepsilon)$, resp., required to learn the one-step probabilities in the base model, and the final-token probability in the CoT and e2e models, under squared loss error~$\varepsilon$.
  We show that stochastic autoregressive learning fundamentally differs from the deterministic theory. At scale $\varepsilon$, there is no universal comparison between the three learning tasks: both $m_{CoT}/m_{base}$ and $m_{e2e}/m_{CoT}$ can be made simultaneously arbitrarily larger than $M/\varepsilon$, the natural analogue for the existing deterministic results. Nevertheless, after altering scales, for every class, CoT learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded by base learning at scale $\varepsilon/M^2$, whereas e2e learning at scale $\varepsilon$ is upper-bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by $(M/\varepsilon) m_{CoT}(Θ(\varepsilon))$. These dependencies and scales are essentially tight. We complement these bounds by studying dimension $d$ logistic functions in our model.

AI.tldr: Introduces a PAC-learning framework for binary stochastic autoregressive models inspired by LLMs, with one fixed Bernoulli next-token generator and three supervision modes (base one-step, CoT, e2e). Analyzes sample complexity m_base(ε), m_CoT(ε), m_e2e(ε) for learning implied probabilities, reveals fundamental differences from deterministic cases, derives scaling-based upper bounds linking the tasks (CoT ≤ base at ε/M^2, e2e ≤ (M/ε)·m_CoT(Θ(ε))) and shows these dependencies are tight; also investigates dimension-d logistic functions.
AI.motivation: To understand how stochastic autoregressive learning behaves under different supervision schemes and to resolve how sample complexity compares to the deterministic autoregressive setting, particularly in the regime relevant to large language models.
AI.method: Model: a fixed generator assigns a Bernoulli distribution to each next token given a prompt. From a prompt, repeatedly sample a token to extend the prompt for M steps. Consider three supervision regimes: (1) base one-step samples, (2) chain-of-thought (CoT) revealing full random trajectories of length M, (3) end-to-end (e2e) revealing only the final token after M steps. For a hypothesis class of generators, bound the minimum sample counts m_base(ε), m_CoT(ε), m_e2e(ε) needed to learn one-step probabilities (base) and final-token probabilities (CoT/e2e) under squared loss ε. Also analyze dimension d logistic functions.
AI.result: Foundational differences from deterministic learning: no universal ordering among the three tasks at scale ε; both m_CoT/m_base and m_e2e/m_CoT can be made arbitrarily large relative to M/ε. After rescaling, for any class, CoT learning at scale ε is upper-bounded by base learning at scale ε/M^2, while e2e learning at scale ε is upper-bounded up to log factors by (M/ε)·m_CoT(Θ(ε)). These relationships are essentially tight. The paper also analyzes dimension-d logistic functions within this framework.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic autoregressive learning exhibits distinct sample-complexity behavior from deterministic settings; with appropriate scaling, one can relate the difficulties across supervision regimes, and the bounds are tight up to logarithmic factors. The results are complemented by a study of dimension-d logistic functions.

title: Conformal Coverage Guarantees for Any Video Temporal Grounder
summary: Event boundaries in continuous video are ambiguous: re-annotate the same query-video pair and independent annotators mark moments that overlap by less than half on a large fraction of samples. The ground truth for video temporal grounding is therefore a distribution over intervals, yet every grounder returns a single interval with no statement of reliability, so at deployment a wrong interval is indistinguishable from a right one. COVER changes the output object: a post-hoc, model-agnostic wrapper that turns any grounder, a trained localizer or a black-box video--language model, into one that emits a temporal region containing the true moment with probability at least $1-α$, by calibrating the quantile of a temporal nonconformity score on held-out labels and widening the base prediction by that amount. The guarantee is finite-sample and distribution-free under exchangeability, and requires neither retraining nor white-box access. We give two score families, a two-sided boundary-widening score for grounders that emit an interval and a super-level-set score for grounders that emit a relevance signal, and develop theory specific to grounding that bounds how large the certified region becomes, when coverage survives conditioning on event length, and how it degrades when moments from one video break exchangeability. Across three benchmarks and five grounders, realized coverage tracks the target, and calibration exposes what point metrics hide.

AI.tldr: COVER is a post-hoc, model-agnostic wrapper for video temporal grounding that provides finite-sample, distribution-free probabilistic guarantees: it outputs a temporal region containing the true moment with probability at least 1-α by calibrating a nonconformity score on held-out labels, with two score families for different grounder types and is validated across benchmarks and grounders.
AI.motivation: Ground truth for video temporal grounding is inherently ambiguous due to annotator disagreement, making ground-truth intervals a distribution. Existing grounders return a single interval without reliability statements, risking incorrect localization at deployment. A calibrated, reliable output region is needed that is model-agnostic and does not require retraining.
AI.method: A post-hoc wrapper (COVER) that wraps any grounder/localizer/black-box model to emit a temporal region containing the true moment with probability at least 1-α. It uses calibration of a temporal nonconformity score on held-out labels and widens the base prediction by the derived quantile. Two score families are proposed: a two-sided boundary-widening score for interval emitters and a super-level-set score for relevance-signal emitters. The approach is finite-sample and distribution-free under exchangeability and requires no retraining or white-box access. Theoretical results bound region size under event-length conditioning and degradation under non-exchangeable moments.
AI.result: Empirically, across three benchmarks and five grounders, the method achieves realized coverage that tracks the target coverage. Calibrated regions reveal limitations of point metrics, and the approach demonstrates practical, reliable uncertainty quantification for video grounding without model access to internals.
AI.conclusion: COVER provides a practical, model-agnostic, finite-sample, distribution-free uncertainty quantification framework for video temporal grounding. It delivers probabilistic guarantees on containing the true moment, exposes hidden deficiencies of point-based metrics through calibration, and is applicable to a variety of grounders without retraining.

title: Recipes for Creativity: Iterative Generation and Evaluation in Large Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Short paper accepted at ICCC'26
summary: Generative models are often evaluated through singular artifacts, whereas human creativity typically emerges through iterative generation, appraisal, and refinement. This pilot study examines whether iterative search improves LLM creativity by adapting FunSearch to recipe generation for the 2024 Pillsbury Bake-Off and evaluating outputs against human benchmarks using TTCT-based LLM evaluation. Across two experiments, we test iteration count, generator temperature, and in-loop selection-scorer model size. Results show that iterative generation-selection can produce recipes with creativity scores comparable to human benchmarks, but additional iterations alone do not improve creativity. The in-loop evaluator matters most: a smaller selection scorer yields significantly higher scores across most TTCT dimensions, while temperature has limited effects except for originality. These findings suggest that evaluator design is a first-order design variable in subjective creative search.

AI.tldr: Iterative generation with selection can match human-creative benchmarks in recipe tasks, but adding more iterations alone does not boost creativity; the in-loop evaluator design (smaller scorer) is the dominant factor, with limited influence from temperature except on originality.
AI.motivation: To assess whether iterative search improves LLM creativity in a real-world task by adapting FunSearch to recipe generation and evaluating with TTCT-based LLM metrics against human benchmarks.
AI.method: Two experiments testing: (1) iteration count, (2) generator temperature, (3) in-loop selection-scorer model size. Outputs (recipes) were generated for the 2024 Pillsbury Bake-Off and evaluated against human benchmarks using TTCT-based metrics.
AI.result: Iterative generation with selection can yield recipes with TTCT creativity scores comparable to human benchmarks. Additional iterations beyond the initial one do not increase creativity. The in-loop evaluator is the primary driver; a smaller selection scorer yields significantly higher TTCT scores across most dimensions, while temperature has limited effects except for originality.
AI.conclusion: Evaluator design is a first-order design variable in subjective creative search. Prioritizing a smaller, perhaps more stringent selection-scorer within the loop can boost perceived creativity more than increasing iteration depth or adjusting temperature.

title: Learning Suffers More Than the Policy Class Under Partial Observability: A Closed-Form Analysis
summary:
When a reinforcement learning agent cannot observe the full state, we usually blame its policies: it cannot see enough to represent a good one. We show that in a solvable case the bigger problem lies elsewhere. Even when a good policy is available and the agent's value function is expressive enough to describe it exactly, learning still ends up somewhere far worse.
  We study a partially observed linear-quadratic problem in which a standard actor-critic learner can be solved in closed form. At our default setting the best policy the agent can represent is already close to optimal, costing 10.4% more than the ideal controller that observes everything. Learning does not find it. The algorithm instead comes to rest at a policy that is 35% worse than the best one available to it, and we can say exactly where and why.
  The cause is a bias in what the critic learns rather than a limit on what the actor can express. Because the agent cannot attribute what it sees to the part of the state it cannot observe, the critic misreads that unexplained variation as sharp curvature in its own value estimates, and the actor follows that error away from the optimum. We derive closed-form expressions for the resulting policy, for its cost, and for the one design choice that removes the problem, which is how far the learner looks ahead before trusting its own value estimates. Deep reinforcement learning experiments follow these predictions closely. Notably, giving the agent memory of past observations does not help, while changing how far it looks ahead does.

AI.tldr: In a partially observed linear-quadratic setting, an actor-critic learner can be solved in closed form, revealing that even with a near-optimal policy and expressive value function, learning fails due to critic bias caused by unobserved state. The best policy available to the agent is 10.4% worse than the fully observed ideal, yet learning converges to a policy 35% worse. The bias stems from misattributing unexplained variation to value curvature; the remedy is to adjust how far ahead the learner looks before trusting its value estimates. Memory of past observations does not help; horizon tuning is the decisive fix.
AI.motivation: To understand why policy learning can be fundamentally biased under partial observability even when the policy class and value function are rich enough, and to identify a concrete design choice (look-ahead horizon) that eliminates the bias.
AI.method: The authors analyze a partially observed linear-quadratic (LQ) control problem and solve a standard actor-critic learner in closed form. They derive exact expressions for the resulting policy and its cost, plus the design choice for the look-ahead horizon that removes the bias. They corroborate predictions with deep RL experiments, noting that memory does not improve outcomes and only horizon adjustment does.
AI.result: The learned policy is biased due to critic misinterpretation of unobserved state variation as value curvature, leading to a 35% worse performance than the best information-bounded policy. The best policy within the agent’s information is 10.4% worse than the fully observable optimum. A single design change—how far the learner looks ahead before trusting its value estimates—remedies the bias; deeper experiments align with the theory.
AI.conclusion: Critic bias, not limited expressivity, accounts for poor learning under partial observability. Adjusting the look-ahead horizon removes the bias, while simply adding memory does not help. Theoretical closed-form results align with deep RL experiments, underscoring horizon-aware actor-critic design as the key fix.

title: SABRE: Scalable and Automated Benchmarking of VLMs under Stress
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures. Code and resources will be available at https://zesearch.github.io/vlm-SABRE/
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are improving rapidly, but benchmark development lags behind, making weaknesses hard to identify. Building stress tests is costly: samples must satisfy controlled conditions, remain answerable, and challenge current models. We present SABRE, a scalable, automated pipeline that converts a Test Primer (a Markdown Task Design with Data Schema) into structured specifications, generated or edited images, and question-answer pairs. Automated filtering removes candidates solved by a Filtering VLM, while human review verifies candidate validity and supports annotation correction and localized image repair. We instantiate SABRE-Prior to test whether VLMs follow visual evidence instead of relying on world priors -- learned expectations about familiar objects and scenes. Its 600 images and 1,000 questions span Context (unexpected entities in familiar scenes), Texture (counterfactual materials), Attribute (noncanonical component counts), and Language Elicitation (answers suggested by language but unsupported by the image). Across six VLMs, macro-average accuracy ranges from 17.8% to 31.3% (22.6% mean). A real-image Attribute control is comparably difficult for the Filtering VLM. SABRE-Counting and SABRE-Spatial pilots show that the workflow supports other stress-test settings. These results establish SABRE as a reusable framework for constructing and refreshing VLM stress tests rather than a single fixed benchmark.

AI.tldr: A scalable, automated stress-testing pipeline (SABRE) converts a Test Primer into structured specs, generated or edited images, and QA pairs, with automated Filtering and human validation. It reveals VLMs' reliance on world priors over visual evidence, using a 600-image, 1000-question evaluation across Context, Texture, Attribute, and Language Elicitation; six VLMs score only 17.8–31.3% (mean 22.6%), and SABRE is proposed as a reusable framework for constructing and refreshing VLM stress tests rather than a fixed benchmark.
AI.motivation: As VLMs improve rapidly, benchmark development lags, making weaknesses hard to identify. Building stress tests is costly due to the need for controlled conditions, answerability, and challenge. SABRE aims to automate stress-test construction and validation to systematically expose failures tied to visual evidence vs. prior world knowledge.
AI.method: SABRE pipeline: (1) Convert a Test Primer (Markdown Task Design with Data Schema) into structured specifications, generated/edited images, and question–answer pairs. (2) Automated Filtering uses a Filtering VLM to discard candidates solvable without genuine stress testing. (3) Human review validates candidate viability and supports annotation correction and localized image repair. (4) Instantiate SABRE-Prior to test whether VLMs follow visual evidence rather than world priors. (5) Dataset comprised of 600 images and 1,000 questions spanning Context (unexpected entities in familiar scenes), Texture (counterfactual materials), Attribute (noncanonical component counts), Language Elicitation (answers suggested by language but unsupported by the image). (6) Evaluate six VLMs; report macro-average accuracy 17.8%–31.3% (22.6% mean). (7) Use real-image Attribute control for a comparably difficult baseline for the Filtering VLM. (8) SABRE-Counting and SABRE-Spatial pilots demonstrate workflow adaptability to other stress-test settings.
AI.result: Across six VLMs, macro-average accuracy ranges from 17.8% to 31.3% (mean 22.6%). The real-image Attribute control remains comparably difficult for the Filtering VLM. The SABRE workflow is extensible via SABRE-Counting and SABRE-Spatial, supporting additional stress-test configurations.
AI.conclusion: SABRE provides a reusable framework for constructing and refreshing VLM stress tests rather than a single fixed benchmark, enabling scalable, automated stress-test generation with human validation to diagnose weaknesses tied to visual evidence rather than world priors.

title: TOFD: Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling against Poisoning Attacks in Split Federated Learning
summary: Split Federated Learning (SFL) facilitates privacy-preserving collaborative training with reduced client-side overhead. However, its split architecture introduces unique attack surfaces, rendering it vulnerable to diverse poisoning attacks. Most existing defenses fail to exploit the split paradigm, limiting their ability to detect and contain malicious behaviors at an early stage. To bridge this gap, we propose Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling (TOFD), a unified framework that jointly enables proactive detection and robust optimization against a wide range of poisoning attacks. TOFD operates in three stages: (1) Target Inference, which identifies potential attack targets by refining class-wise safe zones via class-specific Margin Perturbation (MP); (2) Sample Purification, which adaptively filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated through cross-class min-max normalization of MP; and (3) Decoupling Optimization, which leverages an adversarial guidance model to capture attack-induced patterns and decouple their influence during optimization, thereby suppressing residual adversarial effects. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of TOFD. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses under diverse attack scenarios, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.

AI.tldr: TOFD offers a three-stage defense for Split Federated Learning against poisoning: Target Inference, Sample Purification, and Decoupling Optimization. It provides convergence guarantees and achieves strong robustness with low overhead, outperforming state-of-the-art defenses across multiple datasets and attack scenarios.
AI.motivation: Split Federated Learning introduces unique attack surfaces and existing defenses underexploit the split paradigm, hindering early detection and containment of malicious behavior. A unified, proactive defense tailored to the split setting is needed.
AI.method: Stage 1 Target Inference uses class-specific Margin Perturbation to refine class-wise safe zones and identify potential attack targets. Stage 2 Sample Purification adaptively filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated via cross-class min-max normalization of Margin Perturbation. Stage 3 Decoupling Optimization employs an adversarial guidance model to capture attack-induced patterns and decouple their influence during optimization, suppressing residual adversarial effects. The authors also provide theoretical convergence guarantees for TOFD.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five datasets show TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses under diverse poisoning attacks, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.
AI.conclusion: TOFD delivers a unified, proactive defense for Split Federated Learning against poisoning by combining target inference, sample purification, and decoupled optimization, with proven convergence and strong empirical robustness.

title: MirrorWorld: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Mirror Reflection Generation
summary: Recent advances in video diffusion models (VDMs) have enabled high-fidelity video synthesis. However, generating mirror reflections remains challenging because the content within a mirror must remain consistent with the surrounding scene. Existing VDMs are not specifically designed to model scene-to-mirror relationships, which can lead to reflections with incorrect content or inconsistent spatial arrangements. We observe that mirror reflection generation involves two complementary challenges: determining what scene content should be reflected and how the reflected content should be spatially arranged within the mirror region. Motivated by this observation, we propose MirrorWorld, a reflection-aware video inpainting framework that models scene-to-mirror relationships during generation. Specifically, we introduce Semantic Relation Distillation (SRD), which transfers relational information from a frozen visual foundation model to encourage semantic associations between visible scene content and mirror regions. We further propose Geometric Transformation Alignment (GTA), which learns a transformation that guides the spatial arrangement of reflected content. The two components play complementary roles, with SRD modeling what should be reflected and GTA modeling how it should be arranged. To facilitate research on this problem, we construct a benchmark for video mirror reflection generation by repurposing four existing video mirror datasets into a unified reflection reconstruction task. Experimental results show that MirrorWorld achieves improved reflection reconstruction quality over representative image-based reflection generation methods and strong video inpainting baselines.

AI.tldr: MirrorWorld introduces a reflection-aware video inpainting framework with SRD and GTA to model what to reflect and how to arrange reflections, plus a repurposed video mirror benchmark; it outperforms image-based reflection generation and strong video inpainting baselines in reflection reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Mirror reflections must be content-consistent with the surrounding scene and spatially coherent within the mirror region. Existing video diffusion models lack explicit modeling of scene-to-mirror relationships, leading to content and layout inconsistencies.
AI.method: Semantic Relation Distillation (SRD) transfers relational information from a frozen visual foundation model to enforce semantic links between visible scene content and mirror regions. Geometric Transformation Alignment (GTA) learns a transformation to guide the spatial arrangement of reflected content. A benchmark is built by repurposing four existing video mirror datasets into a unified reflection reconstruction task.
AI.result: MirrorWorld achieves improved reflection reconstruction quality over representative image-based reflection generation methods and strong video inpainting baselines.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both what to reflect (semantic relations via SRD) and how to arrange it (geometric alignment via GTA) yields more faithful mirror reflections; the constructed benchmark will facilitate further research in video mirror reflection generation.

title: Winning by Peeking: Unenforced Budgets and Test-Set Selection Inflate Short-Budget AutoML Comparisons
summary: Comparisons between AutoML systems at short time budgets -- tens of seconds rather than hours -- are common in tool READMEs and workshop papers, and they are easy to get wrong. We report a case study in which a simple AutoML engine, Orcetra, appeared to beat FLAML and AutoGluon on 513 OpenML datasets, winning 57.1% of them at a nominal 60-second budget and 78.4% of datasets against FLAML alone at 30 seconds. Both margins came from protocol defects that a results table cannot show. The search loop scored every candidate on the test split and reported the best, making the headline metric a maximum over dozens of noisy estimates while the baselines selected on training data and touched the test set once; and the budget was checked before launching a candidate but never enforced during one, so the system consumed a median of 120 s against a 60-second budget, 2.24x the wall-clock AutoGluon used. Re-running with selection moved to a validation split, the deadline enforced externally and every framework pinned to an equal share of the machine, Orcetra's win rate on the re-run subset falls from 59.4% to 34.3% and no pairwise difference against either competitor remains significant. Recording both estimands inside a single search lets us attribute the collapse: the selection rule accounts for 4.8 percentage points and unequal compute for most of the rest. The same traces give the selection bias as a function of budget, measured rather than assumed: it grows with $K$ but reaches only 0.27 accuracy points, about five times below the $σ\sqrt{2\ln K}$ bound a marginal-standard-error argument predicts, because candidates scored on shared test rows cancel most of the noise. We close with a checklist for short-budget comparisons. Code, per-dataset results and the scripts that regenerate every number and figure in the paper are released with it.

AI.tldr: Short-budget AutoML comparisons are fragile and prone to protocol bias; a case study showed Orcetra appeared to beat FLAML and AutoGluon due to defects, but corrected experiments reduced or eliminated the advantage; highlights need for robust, preregistered evaluation and provides a checklist and open-code to reproduce results.
AI.motivation: Expose and quantify biases in rapid, budget-constrained AutoML benchmarks and provide guidelines to ensure fair comparisons.
AI.method: Case study comparing Orcetra, FLAML, and AutoGluon on 513 OpenML datasets with nominal 30–60s budgets. Identified protocol defects: test-set leakage via selecting best candidate on test data, un-enforced budget during search, and unequal compute. Re-ran with validation-based selection, external deadline enforcement, and equal share of compute; analyzed traces to attribute observed differences to selection bias and compute disparity. Quantified bias as a function of budget and assessed noise cancellation due to overlapping test splits.
AI.result: Initial results claimed Orcetra wins on 57.1% of datasets at 60s and 78.4% at 30s. Re-run with corrected protocol reduced Orcetra’s win rate to 34.3%, with no significant pairwise differences against either competitor. Selection bias accounted for 4.8 percentage points; compute inequality explained most of the remainder. Bias grew with budget but remained small (0.27 accuracy points) compared to a theoretical bound, due to cancellation of noise from shared test rows.
AI.conclusion: Short-budget benchmarks can be misleading without strict controls. The paper offers a practical checklist for fair comparisons and provides reproducible code and data to audit results.

title: A foundation-model approach to pediatric headache classification from rs-fMRI
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures. In Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 340, 2026 (Machine Learning for Healthcare Conference)
summary: Headache is the most common neurological disorder in children and substantially affects quality of life. We investigated whether resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) can support pediatric headache classification using machine learning. We encoded rs-fMRI data using NeuroSTORM, a recent foundation model, and fine-tuned it to distinguish healthy controls from children with headache and subsequently classify headache subtypes. We compared NeuroSTORM with a standard neuroscience approach using functional-connectivity (FC) matrices derived from brain activity as predictors. Using 189 rs-fMRI scans from 110 individuals collected across two visits (prevalence of any headache: 74%), NeuroSTORM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.82-0.82) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for discriminating headache from non-headache. In contrast, models trained on FC matrices showed lower performance (AUROC, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.67-0.67]; AUPRC, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.85-0.85]). In multiclass classification of healthy controls, chronic migraine, and non-chronic headaches (e.g., post-viral headache, new daily persistent headache, post-traumatic headache), NeuroSTORM achieved a macro-AUROC of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.68-0.69). Results suggest that the approach can distinguish chronic migraine but has difficulty differentiating other headache subtypes from chronic migraine. Overall, under limited-data conditions, NeuroSTORM appears to capture latent rs-fMRI representations that transfer to headache-related tasks without relying on FC features. These findings provide proof of concept for fMRI-based prediction of pediatric headache and highlight potential future utility for subtype identification and individualized treatment strategies.

AI.tldr: NeuroSTORM fine-tuned on rs-fMRI outperforms FC-based models for pediatric headache detection and shows potential for subtype differentiation; results are promising but limited by sample size and data scarcity.
AI.motivation: Evaluate ML-based pediatric headache classification using rs-fMRI and compare a foundation-model representation (NeuroSTORM) with traditional functional-connectivity (FC) features.
AI.method: 187 rs-fMRI scans from 110 individuals across two visits; fine-tune NeuroSTORM to distinguish headache from non-headache and to classify headache subtypes; compare with FC-matrix-based predictors; tasks include binary discrimination and multiclass classification (healthy controls, chronic migraine, non-chronic headaches); evaluation via AUROC and AUPRC.
AI.result: NeuroSTORM achieved AUROC 0.82 (95% CI 0.82–0.82) and AUPRC 0.93 (95% CI 0.93–0.94) for headache vs non-headache; FC-based models yielded AUROC 0.67 and AUPRC 0.85; for multiclass (HC, chronic migraine, non-chronic headaches) NeuroSTORM macro-AUROC = 0.69 (95% CI 0.68–0.69).
AI.conclusion: Under limited-data conditions, NeuroSTORM captures latent rs-fMRI representations transferable to headache-related tasks without relying on FC features, providing proof of concept for fMRI-based pediatric headache prediction and potential for future subtype identification and individualized treatment; performance is better for distinguishing chronic migraine but limited for other subtypes.

title: SimWAM: A Simple World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/SimWAM/
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) improve end-to-end autonomous driving by transferring video dynamics priors to action prediction, but existing methods require costly future generation at inference. We present SimWAM, a simple yet effective WAM that uses video generation purely as a training signal. It co-trains a pretrained video expert and a lightweight action expert with joint flow matching. An isolated attention mask keeps action prediction independent of future frames, allowing the video branch to be discarded after training and leaving a self-contained planner that directly predicts trajectories. Since the two experts share no parameters and interact only through a unified attention interface, the video backbone could be replaced and the action expert scaled independently without modifying the learning objective or inference pipeline. We further apply reinforcement learning to optimize a compositional driving reward beyond trajectory imitation. Our SimWAM achieves $91.5$ PDMS on NAVSIM, surpasses state-of-the-art WAM-based planners with substantially lower latency, and transfers zero-shot to nuScenes. These results position SimWAM as a simple yet solid baseline that could readily benefit from advances in video generation for efficient autonomous driving. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/SimWAM/

AI.tldr: SimWAM is a training-time–only video-guided World-Action Model for autonomous driving, decoupling video dynamics learning from action prediction via joint flow matching of a video expert and a lightweight action expert; at inference, a self-contained planner predicts trajectories with low latency, and the video branch is discarded.
AI.motivation: Reduce inference-time cost and rigidity of prior World-Action Models by making video generation a training signal and enabling modular, scalable architectures with independent video-backbone and action-head components.
AI.method: Co-train a pretrained video expert and a lightweight action expert using joint flow matching. Use an isolated attention mask so action prediction remains independent of future frames. Discard the video branch after training; keep a modular, attention-based interface for interaction. Allow replacing the video backbone and scaling the action expert independently without changing the objective. Apply reinforcement learning to optimize a compositional driving reward beyond imitation.
AI.result: Achieves 91.5 PDMS on NAVSIM, surpassing state-of-the-art WAM-based planners with substantially lower latency, and transfers zero-shot to nuScenes.
AI.conclusion: SimWAM provides a simple, effective baseline that leverages video-generation advances for efficient autonomous driving, offering a modular, train-time-only video signal approach with potential for further improvements via video priors.

title: An End-to-End Agent Auditing Engine
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), harnesses have become essential infrastructure for deploying agents across a wide range of domains. The fast-evolving harness ecosystem has also made rigorous capability evaluation increasingly important. However, efficiently building an end-to-end, systematic, and comprehensive evaluation pipeline remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce $A^2E$ (Agent Auditing Engine), an end-to-end evaluation engine designed for agent harnesses. $A^2E$ leverages our newly proposed Agent Task Protocol (ATP) to enable the rapid integration of evaluation tasks with different harnesses. Through an automatically instrumented Monitor, it captures and generates standardized execution traces during experiments. In the Evaluation stage, $A^2E$ systematically assesses harness capabilities using a suite of multidimensional metrics. Compared with correctness alone, these metrics provide a more fine-grained characterization of differences among harnesses in execution efficiency, tool use, task planning, and error recovery. Experiments conducted with $A^2E$ further reveal that model-harness combinations exhibit substantial performance variation across different types of tasks, and that no single combination consistently outperforms all others across every task. These findings not only demonstrate the necessity of systematic evaluation but also provide useful guidance for the co-evolving of models and harnesses. Our code is available at https://github.com/datamllab/A2E.

AI.tldr: A^2E is an end-to-end evaluation engine for agent harnesses, introducing the Agent Task Protocol (ATP) and an instrumented Monitor to enable multidimensional, standardized evaluation of harness capabilities; results show significant variability across model-harness pairs and tasks, underscoring the need for systematic evaluation and guiding co-evolution of models and harnesses.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of the LLM harness ecosystem demands scalable, rigorous evaluation beyond correctness, as different harnesses and tasks exhibit diverse behaviors that are not captured by traditional single-metric assessments.
AI.method: Proposes A^2E architecture with an Agent Task Protocol (ATP) enabling quick integration of evaluation tasks with various harnesses, and an instrumented Monitor that automatically collects standardized execution traces. The Evaluation stage uses multidimensional metrics (beyond correctness) to assess execution efficiency, tool use, task planning, and error recovery.
AI.result: Empirical experiments reveal substantial performance variation across model-harness combinations and task types, with no single pairing outperforming others universally. This highlights the importance of systematic evaluation for guiding co-evolution of models and harnesses.
AI.conclusion: Systematic evaluation of agent harnesses is essential; A^2E and ATP provide a practical framework for rapid, standardized assessment, and the findings offer guidance for selecting or combining models and harnesses across tasks. Code is available at the project repository.

title: FUSE: Feature-Wise Unified Specialization with Cross-Column Exchange for Mixed-Type Tabular Flow Matching
summary: Generating mixed-type tabular data requires jointly modeling diverse feature distributions and their complex cross-column dependencies. Variational flow matching handles distinct endpoints via factorized distributions, yet leaves feature-specific processing and cross-column interactions implicit within a shared backbone. We introduce Feature-wise Unified Specialization with cross-column Exchange (FUSE) to explicitly separate these roles. FUSE applies separate adaptive mixture modules to numerical and categorical features, allowing each feature to combine shared specialized subnetworks, while joint attention preserves information exchange across all columns. We also characterize the excess population risk from restricted conditioning contexts and bound the continuous Wasserstein generation error by endpoint-prediction risk. Comprehensive experiments on eight tabular datasets demonstrate that FUSE achieves strong and consistent performance across distributional fidelity and downstream utility metrics.

AI.tldr: FUSE introduces a feature-wise architecture for mixed-type tabular data generation that explicitly separates feature-specific processing from cross-column information exchange. It uses separate adaptive mixtures for numerical and categorical features plus joint attention, improves fidelity and downstream utility, and provides theoretical bounds.
AI.motivation: To jointly model diverse feature distributions and cross-column dependencies in tabular data generation, addressing limitations of variational flow matching where per-feature processing is implicit within a shared backbone.
