AI.method: A dual-path architecture with feature-wise adaptive mixture modules: numerical and categorical features each have their own specialized subnetworks; joint attention enables information exchange across all columns; includes analysis of excess risk under restricted conditioning contexts and bounds Wasserstein generation error via endpoint-prediction risk. The approach is validated on eight tabular datasets.
AI.result: FUSE achieves strong and consistent performance across distributional fidelity and downstream utility metrics on eight tabular datasets.
AI.conclusion: Explicit separation of feature-specific processing from shared cross-column modeling via FUSE improves tabular data generation, supported by theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results.

title: $\boldsymbolλ$-Orthogonality Regularization for Compatible Representation Learning
summary: Retrieval systems rely on representations learned by increasingly powerful models. However, due to the high training cost and inconsistencies in learned representations, there is significant interest in facilitating communication between representations and ensuring compatibility across independently trained neural networks. In the literature, two primary approaches are commonly used to adapt different learned representations: affine transformations, which adapt well to specific distributions but can significantly alter the original representation, and orthogonal transformations, which preserve the original structure with strict geometric constraints but limit adaptability. A key challenge is adapting the latent spaces of updated models to align with those of previous models on downstream distributions while preserving the newly learned representation spaces. In this paper, we impose a relaxed orthogonality constraint, namely $λ$-Orthogonality regularization, while learning an affine transformation, to obtain distribution-specific adaptation while retaining the original learned representations. Extensive experiments across various architectures and datasets validate our approach, demonstrating that it preserves the model's zero-shot performance and ensures compatibility across model updates. Code available at: \href{https://github.com/miccunifi/lambda_orthogonality.git}{https://github.com/miccunifi/lambda\_orthogonality}.

AI.tldr: Introduces lambda-orthogonality regularization to learn an affine transformation that adapts representations across model updates while preserving original structure, enabling distribution-specific adaptation without sacrificing zero-shot performance; validated across architectures/datasets; code released.
AI.motivation: To enable interoperability of independently trained representation spaces by balancing adaptability and structure preservation. Prior approaches trade off between affine adaptability (may distort representations) and strict orthogonality (limits adaptation).
AI.method: Joint learning of an affine transformation with a relaxed orthogonality constraint enforced via lambda-orthogonality regularization. This balances adaptation to downstream distributions with preservation of the original learned representations during model updates.
AI.result: Empirical results across diverse architectures and datasets show that the method preserves zero-shot performance and ensures compatibility across updated models, indicating successful cross-model representation alignment.
AI.conclusion: Lambda-orthogonality regularization provides distribution-specific adaptation while retaining original representations, enabling compatibility across updated models. Code is publicly available at the provided GitHub link.

title: QFCQT: A Chaotically Gated Quantformer Framework for Volatile Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Forecasting non-stationary time series remains difficult due to long-range dependencies, local volatility bursts, structural shifts, and nonlinear oscillatory behaviors. Although Transformer-based forecasters are effective for modeling long-term temporal dependencies, their feed-forward blocks typically rely on smooth static activations that are insufficiently sensitive to abrupt regime changes. Motivated by quantitative Transformer designs and oscillator-based nonlinear activations, we propose QFCQT, short for Quantum-Fractal-inspired Chaotically Gated Quantformer, for robust forecasting under complex volatile dynamics. Here, "quantum-fractal-inspired" denotes a computational analogy based on soft oscillator superposition and multi-scale nonlinear responses, rather than a formal quantum-mechanical or fractal-theoretic derivation. QFCQT consists of three main components: (1) a Quantformer-style numerical encoder that directly processes multivariate inputs via linear embedding; (2) a learnable Lee-oscillator activation module that maps scalar pre-activations to dynamic oscillatory responses and summarizes them through Max-over-Time pooling; and (3) a smooth-chaotic gated fusion mechanism that adaptively balances conventional smooth activations and chaos-sensitive responses. Furthermore, instead of using a single fixed oscillator, QFCQT employs a soft superposition of eight parameterized Lee oscillator families to adaptively capture different nonlinear response patterns across regimes. Experiments on ETTh1, ETTh2, and A-share Stock Index benchmarks show that QFCQT consistently outperforms strong baselines, including Informer, LogTrans, LSTMa, HAT, and COTN.

AI.tldr: QFCQT introduces a Quantum-Fractal-inspired Chaotically Gated Quantformer designed for robust non-stationary time-series forecasting. It combines a Quantformer-style encoder, a learnable Lee-oscillator activation with max pooling, and a smooth-chaotic gated fusion using a soft superposition of eight oscillator families, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ETTh1/ETTh2 and A-share stock index benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To address non-stationary time series characterized by long-range dependencies, local volatility bursts, regime shifts, and nonlinear oscillations, which challenge Transformer baselines relying on smooth activations.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Quantformer-style numerical encoder with linear embedding for multivariate inputs; (2) learnable Lee-oscillator activation mapping pre-activations to dynamic oscillatory responses, summarized via Max-over-Time pooling; (3) smooth-chaotic gated fusion to adaptively balance smooth activations and chaos-sensitive responses; employs a soft superposition of eight parameterized Lee oscillator families to capture diverse nonlinear patterns across regimes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ETTh1, ETTh2, and A-share Stock Index shows QFCQT consistently outperforms strong baselines such as Informer, LogTrans, LSTMa, HAT, and COTN.
AI.conclusion: QFCQT provides robust forecasting under complex volatile dynamics by integrating quantum-fractal-inspired nonlinear activations and adaptive gating, with a multi-oscillator ensemble enabling regime-aware responses.

title: From Optimal Actions to World Models: Identifiability of Transition Kernels in Discounted MDPs
summary:
We study what can be recovered about the transition probabilities of a Markov decision process from optimal actions alone. This is closely related to the inverse problem considered by Letcher et al., who ask when the dynamics can be recovered from numerical \(Q\)-values. Here the numerical values themselves are not observed; only the optimal actions are known, for every reward in a given class.
  For state-action rewards \(r(s,a)\), knowing the optimal actions for every reward also tells us how much better one action is than another when each is followed by the same fixed policy. This is still not enough to determine the transition probabilities uniquely. We prove that two kernels give the same optimal actions for every reward exactly when \[ Q_{s,a} =
\Bigl(P_{s,a}+\tfrac1γe_s^{\mathsf T}(L-I)\Bigr)L^{-1} \] for one invertible matrix \(L\) satisfying \(L\mathbf 1=\mathbf 1\). Near a kernel with strictly positive entries, there is an \(n(n-1)\)-dimensional family of different kernels with this property. The result is unchanged if we consider only rewards having a unique optimal action at every state.
  We then compare this with rewards of the forms \(r(s)\) and \(r(s,a,s')\). Rewards that depend on the next state can usually recover the transition kernel itself: every row at a state with at least two actions is determined, and we describe exactly when a row at a state with one action can remain hidden. State rewards reveal less: two kernels give the same optimal actions exactly when every deterministic policy is optimal for the same set of rewards. The results show how the form of the reward affects what can be learned about the dynamics from optimal actions alone.

AI.tldr: Optimal actions across rewards do not uniquely identify MDP dynamics; a large family of transition kernels can yield the same optimal-action structure, and the extent of identifiability depends on reward form.
AI.motivation: To understand identifiability of transition dynamics from observed optimal actions (without numerical Q-values) and compare with previous inverse problems based on Q-values (Letcher et al.).
AI.method: Derive necessary and sufficient conditions for two reachability kernels to induce identical optimal actions for all rewards via a matrix L with L invertible and L1=1, yielding a relation between Q, P, and L. Analyze dimensionality of the equivalence class near positive kernels and under reward restrictions. Examine special reward forms r(s,a,s') and r(s).
AI.result: Characterization: two kernels P and P̃ yield the same optimal actions for every reward iff there exists invertible L with L1=1 such that Q_{s,a} = (P_{s,a} + (1/γ)e_s^T(L−I))L^{-1}. Near strictly positive kernels, there is an n(n−1)-dimensional family of kernels with this property. If rewards depend on the next state, most rows at states with ≥2 actions are determined; a row with a single action may still be hidden, with precise conditions provided. For state rewards, two kernels produce the same optimal actions iff every deterministic policy is optimal for the same set of rewards.
AI.conclusion: The form of the reward crucially governs how much of the transition dynamics can be inferred from optimal actions alone; the paper maps identifiability landscapes across reward structures and highlights the limits and potential recoverability of dynamics.

title: TRACE: Ergodic Trajectory Optimization for Active Scene Reconstruction
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, fixed a template bug in the Latex
summary: Existing active reconstruction systems with Gaussian-splatting maps select observations greedily, optimizing a single next-best-view (NBV) at each step and connecting the chosen views by short-horizon path planning. This greedy decoupling disregards the global structure of scene information, producing inefficient trajectories that waste sensing capacity in transit between selected views. In this work, we study active reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem: the time-averaged spatial statistics of the sensor trajectory should match a target information distribution induced by the current map. Our approach derives this target distribution online from uncertainty and visibility, and calculates ergodic trajectories via a kernel-ergodic horizon planner with gradient flow and footprint depletion, closing the loop between mapping and trajectory optimization. We thoroughly evaluate TRACE on the Replica dataset against the Next-Best-View (NBV) baselines, improving PSNR by 1.5 dB. Code: https://github.com/spikelab-jhu/trace-active-reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Introduces TRACE to cast active reconstruction as ergodic coverage, deriving online target distributions from uncertainty/visibility and solving with a kernel-ergodic horizon planner; demonstrates ~1.5 dB PSNR gain on Replica vs NBV baselines; code available.
AI.motivation: Greedy NBV with short-horizon planning ignores global scene structure, leading to inefficient sensing trajectories and wasted capacity during transit.
AI.method: Formulates active reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem where time-averaged trajectory statistics match a target information distribution derived online from map uncertainty and visibility. Uses a kernel-ergodic horizon planner with gradient flow and footprint depletion to compute ergodic trajectories, closing the loop between mapping and trajectory optimization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on the Replica dataset shows TRACE achieving a PSNR improvement of 1.5 dB over NBV baselines; code is provided.
AI.conclusion: Ergodic trajectory optimization can more efficiently exploit sensing resources in active reconstruction by aligning exploration with the current information map, effectively coupling mapping with trajectory planning as demonstrated by TRACE.

title: Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Contribution: This paper presents a six-phase AI-assisted instructional design architecture based on the Curriculum as Code paradigm, integrating Generative AI with LaTeX and Python to automate the creation of reproducible, visually consistent, and technically precise materials for STEM education. Background: Creating customized instructional materials for active learning imposes a heavy workload on faculty. Standard presentation tools lack robust support for technical content, while current AI applications often hallucinate and fail to formalize the instructional authoring process, limiting their utility for rigorous academic design. Intended Outcomes: The framework aims to reduce preparation time while ensuring mathematical accuracy, adherence to institutional visual identity, and preservation of the instructor's tacit pedagogical knowledge through explicit rules. Application Design: The solution comprises a six-phase pipeline that replaces ad-hoc prompt engineering with a systematic workflow, utilizing text-based interfaces and code-driven generation (LaTeX/Beamer for slides, Python for figures), governed by pedagogical constraints, contextual calibrations, and automated review cycles. Findings: Validated over one year across 8 modules and 28 project contexts in a Project-Based Learning environment, the architecture significantly reduced instructor workload. Generated assets underwent independent peer review and were deployed by six different faculty members, confirming scalability beyond a single author. Based on over 600 voluntary student evaluations, materials achieved high quality ratings from 8.5 to 9.9/10. Results indicate high reproducibility, minimized hallucinations, and sustained pedagogical and visual fidelity, suggesting viability for broad STEM educational applications.

AI.tldr: A six-phase, AI-assisted Curriculum-as-Code framework integrates LaTeX/Beamer and Python to automate reproducible, visually consistent STEM instructional materials, reducing faculty workload while preserving pedagogy and accuracy.
AI.motivation: Faculty face a heavy workload to produce customized active-learning materials; standard tools inadequately support technical content and AI often hallucinates; there is a need to formalize the instructional authoring process.
AI.method: Six-phase pipeline that replaces ad-hoc prompt engineering with a systematic, code-driven workflow; LaTeX/Beamer for slides, Python for figures; governed by pedagogical constraints, contextual calibrations, and automated review cycles; text-based interfaces.
AI.result: Validated over one year across 8 modules and 28 project contexts in a Project-Based Learning setting; materials deployed by six different faculty; substantial reduction in instructor workload; independent peer review of assets; high reproducibility; minimized hallucinations; robust alignment with institutional visual identity; student evaluations >8.5–9.9/10 across 600+ responses.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability and scalability of a Curriculum-as-Code approach for STEM education, enabling reproducible, pedagogically faithful, and visually consistent instructional materials across multiple instructors and contexts.

title: Is SwiGLU's Open Positive Tail Necessary? Evidence from Closed-Tail Gating with MemGLU
summary: We test whether decoder-only language-model FFNs require SwiGLU's open positive tail. We introduce MemGLU as a closed-tail comparator derived from a memristive branch geometry. Across paired 9M and 30M pretraining runs with three seeds, MemGLU remains within about 0.1% of SwiGLU in validation NLL. Trained SwiGLU checkpoints are sensitive to positive-tail suppression, while mechanism diagnostics show that the two models use their gates differently despite similar losses. These results suggest that models adapt to the gate geometry available during pretraining. At the tested scales, SwiGLU's open positive tail is not necessary for decoder-only language-model FFNs.

AI.tldr: SwiGLU's open positive tail is not required for decoder-only language-model FFNs at the tested scales; MemGLU closely matches SwiGLU performance and models adapt to gate geometry present during pretraining.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether decoder-only FFNs rely on SwiGLU's open positive tail and whether a closed-tail alternative (MemGLU) can achieve similar performance, shedding light on gate geometry's role during pretraining.
AI.method: Compare SwiGLU and MemGLU across paired 9M and 30M pretraining runs with three seeds; measure validation NLL; examine sensitivity to positive-tail suppression and analyze gate usage diagnostics.
AI.result: MemGLU stays within ~0.1% of SwiGLU in validation NLL; SwiGLU checkpoints show sensitivity to positive-tail suppression; diagnostics reveal different gate usage despite similar losses.
AI.conclusion: Gate geometry availability during pretraining shapes model adaptation; at these scales, open positive tail is not necessary for decoder-only language-model FFNs.

title: People Are Not Just Their Countries. Disentangling Social Determinants of LLM Value Alignment Across Europe
comment: Accepted at AIES 2026 (9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society)
summary:
As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as a primary source of information and advice, understanding their alignment to humans in terms of values becomes a pressing concern. A growing literature has leveraged large scale surveys to investigate to what extent LLMs' and humans' stated values and opinions align. With limited exceptions, studied populations have been defined country borders or cultural bounds. Yet, this focus neglects the role that socio-demographic divides may play for value alignment disparities.
  Relying on the European Social Survey, we address this knowledge gap by considering value alignment displayed with respect to 10 prominent commercial LLMs in terms of 15 socio-demographic variables as well as country of residence. Our analyses reveal that LLMs are indeed unequally aligned to the values of different socio-demographic groups, notably those defined by education, income, occupation and religion. When examining alignment at the individual level, a respondent's country, taken as a stand-alone variable, explains a substantial amount of variation that is on par with the full set of considered socio-demographics. Further disentangling the respective role of country-level and socio-demographic factors, we find they are complementary in explaining value alignment patterns, with their relative weights varying across the subset of questions considered.

AI.tldr: LLMs show heterogeneous alignment with human values across socio-demographic groups; country-level effects are strong and complementary to individual socio-demographics.
AI.motivation: Address gap: prior studies focus on bounded populations; this work uses ESS to examine value alignment across 15 socio-demographic variables and country of residence for 10 LLMs, revealing disparities and the roles of country and socio-demographics.
AI.method: Data: European Social Survey; evaluation of 15 socio-demographic variables and country for 10 commercial LLMs; analyses quantify alignment with respect to values; interactions/covariates; decomposition of variance to assess country vs socio-demographic contributions.
AI.result: LLMs are unequally aligned; education, income, occupation, religion drive disparities; country alone explains substantial variation comparable to full socio-demographic set; country- and socio-demographic factors are complementary; weights vary by question.
AI.conclusion: Value-alignment assessments must account for socio-demographic contexts and country-level factors; implications for fairness and policy; calls for nuanced interpretation and cross-cultural considerations; potential for targeted auditing and improvement of LLMs.

title: When GNNs Fail: Quantifying and Overcoming Temporal Correlation Volatility in Time Series
summary: Modeling multivariate time series by representing them as graphs, where individual series act as nodes and pairwise temporal corre- lations serve as edges, has gained significant traction. Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong perfor- mance by assuming a static graph topology and aggregating information from neighboring series. In this work, we investigate the representa- tional power of GNNs for forecasting under both static and dynamic settings (i.e., when pairwise correlations evolve drastically over time) and identify critical limitations in current architectures. To formalize this, we first propose Temporal Correlation Volatility (TCV), a model- agnostic metric designed to quantify the distributional evolution of these latent structures. We establish a clear connection between TCV and performance degradation, demonstrating that many popular models, including Transformers, generalize poorly in high-TCV settings and are often outperformed by simple structure-agnostic baselines. To address these limitations, we propose Graph Layer for Inference in Dynamic En- vironments (GLIDE), a novel GNN layer enhanced by two theoretically grounded design mechanisms: (D1) Path-based Message Passing, which captures path-based neighborhoods and (D2) Static and Dynamic Propagation Separation, which identifies optimal dynamics via local static approximation. These components significantly improve learning under dynamic topology while preserving robustness in static scenarios. Ex- tensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that GLIDE improves average performance by up to 45.6% across static and dynamic settings, with the largest gain reaching 85.7%. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenS676/GLIDE.

AI.tldr: GLIDE combines a novel Graph Neural Network layer for dynamic topologies with a model-agnostic Temporal Correlation Volatility metric, achieving strong forecasting performance for multivariate time series by capturing path-based neighborhoods and separating static vs. dynamic propagation.
AI.motivation: Current GNNs with static graphs struggle when pairwise correlations change over time; there is a need to quantify topology evolution and design layers that adapt to dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce TCV metric to quantify evolution of latent graph structures; develop GLIDE with (D1) Path-based Message Passing and (D2) Static and Dynamic Propagation Separation; evaluate on synthetic and real data; compare to static GNNs and baselines.
AI.result: GLIDE yields substantial improvements (up to 45.6% average, up to 85.7% largest gain) across static and dynamic settings; TCV correlates with performance degradation; code released.
AI.conclusion: GLIDE addresses dynamic topology limitations, maintains robustness in static settings, and provides practical improvements for multivariate time-series forecasting; TCV offers a framework to assess topology dynamics.

title: FinRank: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Financial Question Answering and Retrieval over SEC Filings
comment: 24 pages, 3 figures. Dataset and evaluation code: https://github.com/datanxt/FinRank
summary: Financial question answering is typically evaluated by answer correctness, yet in SEC filings a plausible and even numerically correct answer can be grounded in the wrong evidence. Similar facts and disclosures recur across sections of a filing, across reporting periods of the same firm, and across comparable firms. FinRank targets this provenance-sensitive retrieval problem by requiring systems to identify evidence for the intended entity, reporting period, and disclosure context. The benchmark contains 1185 manually authored question-answer records over the 10-K and 10-Q filings of 22 companies. Each record includes a reference answer, gold supporting passages, and hand-curated hard negatives drawn from confusable passages within filings, across reporting periods, and across comparable firms. FinRank evaluates passage retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination as separately measured tasks. Baseline results demonstrate the difficulty of this setting: among the evaluated systems, even a 7B instruction-tuned embedder reaches only 44.8% Recall@10 on the pooled evidence corpus; sub-billion-parameter encoders gain at most 3.5 points over BM25, a finance-adapted embedder trails BM25 by 9.7 points, and pairwise accuracy falls by 13.0-20.5 percentage points when random negatives are replaced with the curated hard negatives. FinRank provides an evidence-first benchmark for developing financial question answering systems that are not only accurate but also grounded in the correct disclosure.

AI.tldr: FinRank is a provenance-sensitive benchmark for financial QA on SEC filings, focusing on grounding answers in the correct disclosure. It provides 1185 QA records across 10-K/10-Q filings from 22 companies, with gold passages and curated hard negatives, and evaluates retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination separately.
AI.motivation: To address the problem that numerically correct answers can be grounded in wrong evidence in financial filings due to recurring facts/ disclosures. The benchmark emphasizes ensuring evidence provenance across intended entity, reporting period, and disclosure context.
AI.method: A dataset of 1185 manually authored Q/A records over 10-K and 10-Q filings for 22 firms. Each record includes a reference answer, gold supporting passages, and hand-curated hard negatives drawn from confusable passages within filings, across reporting periods, and across comparable firms. FinRank evaluates passage retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination as separate tasks. Baseline results show substantial difficulty: a 7B instruction-tuned embedder achieves 44.8% Recall@10 on the pooled corpus; sub- billion-parameter encoders gain at most 3.5 points over BM25; a finance-adapted embedder trails BM25 by 9.7 points; and pairwise accuracy drops by 13.0–20.5 percentage points when random negatives are replaced with curated hard negatives.
AI.result: Demonstrates the difficulty of provenance-sensitive financial QA: state-of-the-art models struggle to retrieve correct evidence and maintain ranking when confronted with hard negatives. The gains from small- to mid-sized encoders are limited, and evaluating across provenance-sensitive factors (entity, period, context) reveals weaknesses not captured by standard QA metrics.
AI.conclusion: FinRank provides an evidence-first benchmark for developing financial QA systems that are not only accurate but also grounded in the correct disclosure, highlighting the need for provenance-aware retrieval and robust handling of hard negatives in finance-domain QA.

title: Aftab: A Comprehensive Benchmark of CNN Encoders and Advanced Value Functions in Parallelized Q-Networks
summary:
Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have increasingly favored simplified, highly parallelized paradigms. Notably, the Parallelized Q-Network (PQN) algorithm achieves stable off-policy learning without relying on computationally expensive replay buffers or target networks. However, the representational capacity and parameter efficiency of visual encoders operating in these buffer-free settings remain underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the architectural design space of Convolutional Neural Networks for PQN. We design and rigorously evaluate eight distinct CNN topologies, optimizing for sample efficiency under strict parameter constraints. Furthermore, we study the impact of representation and value estimation enhancements by integrating the Hadamax encoding paradigm and advanced Q-learning extensions, including distributional, ensemble, and dueling heads. Extensive experiments on the Atari-57 benchmark demonstrate that our proposed composite architecture, Aftab, achieves an Interquartile Mean (IQM) Human-Normalized Score of 6.479, establishing a 0.86 Probability of Improvement over the standard PQN baseline. Additionally, structural resilience evaluations on the highly non-stationary Procgen Hard benchmark confirm out-of-distribution generalization, with Aftab yielding an IQM Procgen Normalized Score of 0.418 compared to the baseline's 0.382. Ultimately, this work establishes an efficient, probabilistically superior structural reference for model-free reinforcement learning, all while preserving the simplicity and memory efficiency of unbuffered, parallelized optimization.
  The complete Aftab framework, including all model definitions, training configurations, and raw experimental logs, is open-sourced and available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/tahashieenavaz/aftab

AI.tldr: Aftab is an efficient CNN architecture search for PQN in buffer-free deep RL, achieving superior sample efficiency and OOD generalization on Atari-57 and Procgen Hard, with open-source code.
AI.motivation: Systematically explore the CNN design space for PQN under strict parameter constraints to improve sample efficiency and representation/estimation in unbuffered, parallelized RL.
AI.method: Develop and evaluate eight CNN topologies for PQN, incorporate Hadamax encoding and advanced Q-learning extensions (distributional, ensemble, dueling heads), and assess on Atari-57 and Procgen Hard with comprehensive ablations.
AI.result: Aftab achieves IQM Human-Normalized score 6.479 on Atari-57 (0.86 probability of improvement over PQN baseline) and IQM Procgen Normalized score 0.418 vs 0.382 baseline, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and OOD generalization while maintaining memory efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Offers an efficient, probabilistically superior architectural reference for model-free RL in unbuffered, parallelized settings, and provides a concrete open-source implementation for further research.

title: GeoBenchLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Geo-Related Tasks
summary: In the context of geodata, existing Large Language Models have often been studied in a homogeneous setting, which has considerably limited insights into their generalization capabilities. In this paper, we present \benchName, a comprehensive benchmark for probing LLMs on geo-related tasks. We leverage a careful selection of twelve publicly available datasets from diverse geo-related tasks and domains, and evaluate a set of LLMs on geo-spatial and temporal understanding using our benchmark. Our results show that reasoning and size have a strong impact on overall performance. GeoBenchLLM is publicly available at https://github.com/Rfr2003/GeoBenchLLM.

AI.tldr: GeoBenchLLM benchmarks LLMs on twelve geo-related datasets to assess geospatial/temporal reasoning; results indicate model size and reasoning capability are key drivers of performance; the benchmark is publicly available.
AI.motivation: Address limited understanding of LLM generalization in geo tasks due to homogeneous evaluation by proposing a diverse, multi-domain benchmark.
AI.method: Select twelve publicly available geo datasets spanning diverse tasks; evaluate a range of LLMs on geo-spatial and temporal understanding using the benchmark; analyze the effects of reasoning requirements and model size on performance.
AI.result: Findings indicate that both reasoning capability and model size significantly influence performance across geo tasks; the benchmark reveals generalization patterns and provides a public resource (GeoBenchLLM).
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a valuable framework for systematically probing LLMs in geo domains; facilitates assessment of spatial-temporal reasoning capabilities and generalization; codebase and data are publicly available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: Residual Algebra for Representation-Preserving Learning
summary: Learning from heterogeneous representations is usually reduced to feature concatenation, which erases which representation produced an error. We instead algebraize the residual: a representation is a typed object that owns both a coordinate system and the residual it leaves unresolved, and learning is an ordered composition of operators that preserve or deliberately erase that type. Fold realizes the objects as point-in-time conditional-mean fields on 10x10 rank grids. FPRC-PQ realizes the algebra as relax-aggregate-close: each field is relaxed by a correction fitted to its own residual in its own coordinates; corrected fields meet at a fixed mean that is the sole identity-erasure boundary; and a shared learner closes only the aggregate's fresh residual. The composition telescopes exactly into representation, local residual estimate, and residual-of-residual estimate. Its aggregate is a learned control-variate interface with population variance reduction, while refitting the closer along perturbations of the backbone yields first-order coupled-path mean orthogonality. As an analytical extension, a reflective rumination operator reads the displacement of a global reconstruction from the aggregate anchor, reflects it, and fixes its gain by a unique orthogonal projection rather than return-tuned grid search. On 3.67M Chinese A-share stock-day observations (2023-2026) under a frozen point-in-time protocol, the evaluated base algebra raises net-of-cost return from 13.52% to 19.10% and Sharpe from 1.42 to 2.09. Matched-capacity, unified-residual, identity-free two-stage, and pairwise-only controls all trail it. The gain is therefore not explained by more features or more trees, but by making residual ownership and composition explicit while representation identity is still available.

AI.tldr: A novel algebraic framework for learning from heterogeneous representations that preserves identity of representations and explicitly models residuals, implemented via Fold and FPRC-PQ constructs, with a reflective operator, yielding empirical gains on large-scale stock data mostly due to structured residual ownership rather than feature count.
AI.motivation: Conventional multi-representation learning often reduces to simple feature concatenation, obscuring which representation causes errors. The work proposes an algebraic, type-preserving view where representations are typed objects with both a coordinate system and the residual they leave unresolved, enabling ordered operator composition that can preserve or erase types as needed.
AI.method: Representations are modeled as typed objects carrying coordinates and residuals. Learning proceeds as an ordered composition of operators. Fold uses point-in-time conditional-mean fields on 10x10 rank grids. FPRC-PQ implements relax-aggregate-close by relaxing each field via a correction fitted to its own residual in its coordinates; corrected fields converge at a fixed mean boundary; a shared learner closes only the aggregate’s fresh residual. The composition telescopes into representation, local residual estimate, and residual-of-residual estimate. The aggregate acts as a learned control-variate interface with population variance reduction; refitting along backbone perturbations yields first-order coupled-path mean orthogonality. A reflective rumination operator reads displacement from a global reconstruction, reflects it, and fixes gain via orthogonal projection rather than grid-search tuning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 3.67 million Chinese A-share stock-day observations (2023–2026) under a frozen point-in-time protocol shows net-of-cost return rising from 13.52% to 19.10% and Sharpe ratio from 1.42 to 2.09. Competing controls (matched-capacity, unified-residual, identity-free two-stage, pairwise-only) underperform. The gain arises from making residual ownership and composition explicit while preserving representation identity, not simply from more features or trees.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algebraic treatment of representations and explicit residual ownership yields meaningful performance gains by enabling precise composition and information-sharing through a fixed-point-like aggregation, as well as variance reduction and perturbation-aware refitting. This framework suggests that representation identity can remain accessible while residuals guide learning, potentially generalizable beyond the studied financial setting.

title: ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments
summary: In medical education, physicians convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through residency: years of training across thousands of encounters, with diverse sources of feedback and progressively greater autonomy. Much of clinical reasoning relies on the patient encounter, a dialogue in which a clinician elicits history, refines diagnostic hypotheses, and decides management under uncertainty. While large language models (LLMs) excel on static medical benchmarks, methods to optimize the full sequence of clinical decisions remain underdeveloped. We present ResidencyRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) method for training clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents through simulated multi-turn clinical encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls per trajectory). ResidencyRL pairs the policy agent with LLM simulators capable of complex, adversarial behaviors, training against a structured reward aligned to diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. On held-out evaluations, the ResidencyRL agent improves diagnostic accuracy by 7.0% under adversarial conditions (88.0% vs. 81.0%) and reduces missed red flag rates by 31%, demonstrating rigorous mitigation of premature closure. Blinded expert clinicians validated these gains, preferring the trained agent in 87.6% of side-by-side comparisons. The procedural competencies transfer to unseen benchmarks: the agent outperforms the base model across all six clinical axes of the AMIE multi-visit benchmark, and shows consistent directional improvements on AgentClinic and CRAFT-MD. Our findings demonstrate that sequential clinical decision-making can be effectively learned through multi-turn RL in simulation, yielding robust, generalizable capabilities, paving the way towards clinical mastery. Prospective validation with real-world workflows remains necessary to establish clinical utility.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach (ResidencyRL) trains AI agents via multi-turn simulated clinical encounters to optimize the full decision sequence, achieving improved diagnostic accuracy, fewer missed red flags, and favorable clinician preferences, with cross-benchmark gains; prospective real-world validation remains needed.
AI.motivation: To address the gap in optimizing sequential clinical decision-making during patient encounters. While LLMs perform well on static benchmarks, there is a need for training agents through multi-turn, adversarially simulated encounters with a structured reward to improve diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety.
AI.method: ResidencyRL trains a policy agent paired with LLM simulators that can exhibit complex adversarial behaviors. Training occurs over simulated multi-turn encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns, 8 tool calls per trajectory). The reward is structured around diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. Evaluation includes held-out tests under adversarial conditions, blinded clinician comparisons, and cross-benchmark assessments (AMIE, AgentClinic, CRAFT-MD).
AI.result: Diagnostic accuracy improved by 7.0 percentage points under adversarial conditions (88.0% vs 81.0%); missed red-flag rates reduced by 31%. Blinded expert clinicians preferred the trained agent in 87.6% of side-by-side comparisons. The agent outperforms the base model across six clinical axes of AMIE and shows improvements on AgentClinic and CRAFT-MD. The approach demonstrates that sequential clinical decision-making can be learned via multi-turn RL in simulation, with robust, generalizable capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Sequential clinical decision-making can be effectively learned through multi-turn RL in simulation, approaching clinical mastery. Prospective validation in real-world workflows is necessary to establish clinical utility.

title: Trajectory-Relative Hindsight Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent agentic reinforcement learning methods use hindsight to complement sparse outcome rewards. However, a completed rollout can yield many such signals, leaving their appropriate allocation across turns unclear. We introduce TRIAL, a trajectory-relative hindsight distillation framework with a unified turn-aligned scoring protocol. For each decision turn, TRIAL extracts an outcome view of that decision's realized consequence and evaluates the same response under ordinary and hindsight-conditioned contexts. The signed log-probability gap determines the direction and local strength of token-level supervision, while turn-level magnitudes are normalized jointly over the realized trajectory. The resulting allocation multipliers have an eligible-token-weighted mean of one, redistributing dense supervision across turns while fixing its average multiplier. Experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with different backbones show that TRIAL outperforms GRPO across all eight combinations of backbone, environment, and evaluation metric, while achieving the best or tied-best performance among six methods on six of them. On WebShop with Qwen3-1.7B, TRIAL improves the success rate from 56.4% to 75.2% and the task score from 78.7% to 85.7%. Controlled ablations further show that trajectory-relative turn allocation provides substantial gains beyond those of dense hindsight distillation alone.

AI.tldr: TRIAL is a trajectory-relative hindsight distillation framework for agentic RL that reallocates dense hindsight supervision across decision turns using turn-aligned, trajectory-normalized signals. It uses a signed log-probability gap to guide token-level supervision and ensures the average allocation multiplier is fixed at 1. Empirically, TRIAL outperforms GRPO across multiple backbones/environments and yields substantial gains on WebShop (Qwen3-1.7B) from 56.4% to 75.2% in success rate and 78.7% to 85.7% in task score.
AI.motivation: To resolve the ambiguity in distributing hindsight-derived supervision signals across turns in completed rollouts, which can create dense but uneven feedback. The goal is to allocate supervision in a principled, trajectory-aware manner that preserves overall signal budget.
AI.method: TRIAL introduces a per-turn outcome view for the realized consequence, comparing responses under ordinary and hindsight-conditioned contexts. It computes a signed log-probability gap to steer the direction and strength of token-level supervision, and normalizes turn-level magnitudes over the realized trajectory so that the allocation multipliers have an eligible-token-weighted mean of 1, redistributing dense supervision across turns while keeping the average fixed.
AI.result: In experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with various backbones, TRIAL consistently outperforms GRPO across eight backbone/environment/evaluation combinations and achieves best or tied-best results across six methods on six setups. On WebShop with Qwen3-1.7B, TRIAL raises success rate from 56.4% to 75.2% and task score from 78.7% to 85.7%. Ablations indicate trajectory-relative turn allocation provides substantial gains beyond dense hindsight alone.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-relative, per-turn allocation of hindsight supervision is effective and robust across backbones and domains, enabling more efficient and consistent improvement over dense hindsight strategies like GRPO.

title: CoBa: Cost-Effective Test-Time Scaling via Compute-Balanced Routing
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures; includes supplementary material. Preprint
summary: Test-time scaling is often implemented by spending more compute along one axis: sampling more solutions, extending a chain of thought, or applying a stronger evaluator. Under a fixed inference budget, these choices compete. This paper formulates test-time reasoning as a compute-allocation problem in which a system must decide whether the next unit of compute should be spent on generation, verification, or stopping. We introduce CoBa, a compute-balanced routing policy that first obtains a small set of candidates, applies cheap verification broadly, and routes uncertain or high-value candidates to stronger verification. On 3,129 example-generator evaluations spanning MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023, and procedural symbolic reasoning, CoBa-Routed-Strong reaches 85.13% macro accuracy, statistically matching a self-evaluation weighted-voting proxy at 85.20% while using 49.1% fewer parameter-weighted tokens. It also matches best-of-16 majority voting within 0.01 macro-accuracy points while using 58.9% fewer parameter-weighted tokens; paired tests retain a small best-of-16 edge at substantially higher cost. Paired bootstrap tests show significant gains over single-sample decoding, while the remaining gap to the pool oracle exposes headroom for sharper routing. For local reasoning systems, test-time scaling becomes a question of where the next computation is most valuable.

AI.tldr: Compute-balanced routing policy (CoBa) for test-time reasoning optimizes where to spend compute among generation, verification, and stopping, achieving strong math/proof-like reasoning results with substantial compute savings.
AI.motivation: With a fixed inference budget, test-time scaling trades off generation vs verification vs early stopping; a policy that allocates compute where it yields the most value is needed.
AI.method: Introduce CoBa: generate a small candidate set, apply cheap verification broadly, route uncertain/high-value candidates to stronger verification; evaluate on 3,129 example-generator evaluations across MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023, and procedural symbolic reasoning.
AI.result: CoBa-Routed-Strong attains 85.13% macro accuracy, statistically matching a self-evaluation weighted-voting proxy at 85.20% while using 49.1% fewer parameter-weighted tokens; matches best-of-16 majority voting within 0.01 macro-accuracy points while using 58.9% fewer parameter-weighted tokens; paired tests show gains over single-sample decoding; headroom to improve to pool oracle.
AI.conclusion: For local reasoning systems, test-time scaling hinges on where the next computation is most valuable; routing decisions that assign uncertain/high-value items to stronger verification yield substantial efficiency and performance gains.

title: Omni-modal decomposition autoencoders learn full-stack wearable disentangled representations
summary: Learning disentangled representations is a key requirement for developing versatile, general-purpose, and sustainable models in multi-modal wearable computing. However, existing approaches do not operate as full-stack wearable processors, i.e., they do not simultaneously address task-specific classification performance, disentangled and interpretable representation learning, fusion, and generative modeling of highly heterogeneous multi-modal time series. To address this gap, we introduce Omni-modal Variational Decomposition Autoencoders (OmniDecVAEs), a framework that efficiently learns multi-purpose representations in a unified and scalable manner from arbitrarily many modalities. OmniDecVAEs extend DecVAEs by learning modality-conditioned time-frequency latent subspaces through a multi-view self-supervised decomposition loss and a shared asymmetric autoencoder (AE) architecture. Results on a challenging omni-modal human activity recognition (HAR) setting with up to thirty modalities, demonstrate the ability of OmniDecVAEs to learn full-stack wearable representations. When compared to transformer-based and VAE-based methods, OmniDecVAEs full-stack disentangled representation properties lead to accuracy improvements of 1.01% and 6.75% in activity and identity recognition, respectively. Furthermore, OmniDecVAEs synthesize realistic omni-modal time-frequency data that manifest with enhanced reconstructions (mean absolute error improves by 76.84%) and distributional similarity between real and synthetic data (maximum mean discrepancy improves by 13.85%). Our results highlight OmniDecVAEs potential as a lightweight model suitable for intelligent edge wearables and clinical healthcare, unifying processing requirements and abilities in a single model, through its enhanced representational capacity, modality-invariant spatial complexity (4.1M parameters), and real-time latency.

AI.tldr: OmniDecVAEs unify and scale disentangled, multi-modal representations for wearables, enabling full-stack processing and generation across many modalities, yielding improved HAR accuracy, robust reconstructions, and efficiency suitable for edge devices.
AI.motivation: There is a need for full-stack wearable processors that jointly optimize task performance, interpretable/unentangled representations, fusion, and generative modeling for heterogeneous multi-modal time series; existing methods do not address all aspects simultaneously.
AI.method: Introduce OmniDecVAEs: modality-conditioned time-frequency latent subspaces, a multi-view self-supervised decomposition loss, and a shared asymmetric autoencoder architecture. Extends DecVAEs to handle arbitrarily many modalities (up to ~30), enabling multi-modal fusion and omni-modal data synthesis with a lightweight (~4.1M parameters) model.
AI.result: In omni-modal HAR experiments with up to 30 modalities, OmniDecVAEs outperform transformer-based and VAE-based baselines, achieving +1.01% activity recognition accuracy and +6.75% identity recognition accuracy. They also improve reconstruction quality (MAE reduction of 76.84%) and distributional similarity to real data (MMD improvement 13.85%). The model is compact (4.1M params) with real-time latency, suitable for edge wearable deployment.
AI.conclusion: OmniDecVAEs provide a full-stack solution for omni-modal wearable learning, combining disentangled representation learning, fusion, and generative capabilities in a single, lightweight model, with strong potential for edge wearables and clinical healthcare.

title: A Picture is Worth a Thousand Tokens: How Vision Language Models Cut AI Energy Costs While Improving Accuracy
comment: Accepted at the 14th European Conference on Renewable Energy Systems (ECRES), July 7--9, 2026, London, UK
summary: LLM inference accounts for over 90% of AI operational energy, scaling directly with input token count---a critical inefficiency for telecom network analytics and numerical time-series data analysis (NTSDA), where raw multivariate KPI windows from 4G/5G cell sites expand into thousands of floating-point tokens. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) eliminate this mismatch by encoding time-series as 2D plots, achieving 3.6-10.4x input token reduction across Llama-3.2-90B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and Pixtral-12B architectures. This translates to 1.8-2.5x measured inference energy reduction, saving approximately 7.2 MJ/day at telecom edge deployments and CloudRAN that monitor 200 cells per 15-minute interval. Critically, efficiency gains do not sacrifice accuracy: a fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision VLM achieves 220.7% higher precision than its text-only counterpart and outperforms LSTM and ARIMA baselines by over 144% on telecom anomaly detection. On public benchmarks, Pixtral-12B achieves a 20.6x improvement in J/F1 score at mean F1 = 0.82. At 24 KPIs, text representations exceed the 128K context window of most production LLMs, rendering text-only processing infeasible without truncation, while visual representations remain within standard limits. These results establish VLMs as an energy-efficient and accuracy-superior modality for numerical time-series workloads, providing empirical grounding for AI inference systems that treat energy consumption as a first-class engineering constraint.

AI.tldr: Vision-Language Models reduce input tokens and energy for numerical time-series workloads by encoding time-series as 2D plots, while improving accuracy in telecom analytics and public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM inference energy scales with input tokens and is a bottleneck for telecom network analytics and numerical time-series data (NTSDA). Raw KPI windows generate thousands of tokens; visual encoding promises token and energy savings without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: Encode time-series KPI data from 4G/5G cell sites as 2D plots and fine-tune Vision LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2-90B-Vision, Pixtral-12B) or compare against text-only baselines (Llama-3.2-90B). Evaluate across datasets including telecom anomaly detection and public benchmarks, measuring input token reduction, energy consumption, and accuracy (precision, J/F1).
AI.result: 3.6–10.4x reduction in input tokens; 1.8–2.5x measured inference energy reduction (~7.2 MJ/day for 200 cells per 15-minute interval at telecom edge deployments/CloudRAN). A fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision outperforms its text-only counterpart by 220.7% precision and beats LSTM/ARIMA baselines by >144% on telecom anomaly detection. Pixtral-12B achieves 20.6x improvement in J/F1 on public benchmarks with mean F1 = 0.82. At 24 KPIs, text representations exceed typical 128K context windows, while visual representations stay within standard limits.
AI.conclusion: VLMs provide an energy-efficient and accuracy-enhancing modality for numerical time-series workloads, supporting energy consumption as a primary engineering constraint in AI inference systems and enabling effective edge/cloud deployments for telecom analytics.

title: FedDOSE: Federated Learning Framework Decomposing Site Effects for Modeling Brain Dynamic Functional Connectivity
summary: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging ( fMRI ) data are often pooled into collaborative multi-site consortia, as deep learning models for analyses require large datasets to generalize well. While Federated Learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving paradigm for collaborative training, standard approaches continue to struggle with statistical heterogeneity. In particular, site differences pose a key challenge in multi-site data settings. Additionally, existing FL approaches for fMRI rely on static Functional Connectivity ( FC), omitting dynamic information in brain networks. To address this, we propose FedDOSE, a novel framework that explicitly decomposes site differences for analysis of dynamic FC (dFC). FedDOSE introduces a Modularity-Guided Tucker Decomposition block to encode high-dimensional dFC tensors and capture modular-level spatio-temporal patterns efficiently. Class-specific prototypes are generated across all sites and subsequently aligned at the global level by using a combination of Optimal Transport (OT) barycenter formulation and Procrustes analysis. Extensive experiments for diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) on three multi-site resting-state fMRI datasets: ABIDE-I, ABIDE-II, and ADHD-200, demonstrate that FedDOSE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in ASD and ADHD detection. Our results highlight its effectiveness in learning robust representations from multi-site datasets for reliable analysis.

AI.tldr: FedDOSE enables robust multi-site federated learning on dynamic functional connectivity by decomposing site differences with a modularity-guided Tucker block and aligning class prototypes via OT barycenters and Procrustes; it achieves improved ASD/ADHD diagnosis on ABIDE-I/II and ADHD-200 datasets.
AI.motivation: To overcome statistical heterogeneity across sites in federated fMRI analyses and to exploit dynamic functional connectivity, which static FC methods ignore, for more reliable disease diagnosis.
AI.method: FedDOSE introduces a Modularity-Guided Tucker Decomposition block to encode high-dimensional dynamic FC tensors, capturing modular spatio-temporal patterns. It then generates class-specific prototypes across all sites and aligns them globally using a combination of Optimal Transport barycenter formulation and Procrustes analysis for cross-site harmonization in a federated setting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three multi-site resting-state fMRI datasets (ABIDE-I, ABIDE-II, ADHD-200) show that FedDOSE outperforms state-of-the-art methods for ASD and ADHD detection, demonstrating robust representation learning and improved cross-site generalization in multi-site data.
AI.conclusion: FedDOSE effectively handles site differences and leverages dynamic connectivity for reliable cross-site neuroimaging diagnosis in federated learning, offering a scalable approach for multi-site fMRI analysis.

title: TEPA: Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures; includes supplementary material. Preprint
summary: Long-term memory enables language agents to reuse past facts, preferences, and task experience. Persistence also creates a central falsifiability problem: when the world changes, stale memories can remain retrievable and pollute the prompt. We characterize this failure mode as memory pollution: degradation caused by active memories that newer conflicting evidence has superseded. We introduce TEPA, a revocable evidence-memory mechanism that makes validity an explicit state of memory. TEPA represents observations as keyed precedents and revokes active precedents when fresh evidence contradicts them under the same key, allowing retrieval to draw from current evidence while preserving revoked history for audit. Across controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, and preference-update streams, revocation prevents stale active memory from remaining in the retrieval set after reversal. In controlled drift over 50 seeds, append-only and last-write-wins memory fell below no memory during full reversal (append-only and last-write-wins both 0.210, no memory 0.309, TEPA 0.950), and the same pattern reproduced under real file execution (append-only 0.203, no memory 0.298, TEPA 0.950). On clean MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, TEPA matches a strong last-write-wins cache, confirming that current-key replacement is the decisive operation for single-hop fact consolidation. Boundary tests on multi-hop and very long-context MemoryAgentBench settings expose retrieval-chain and context-selection bottlenecks beyond fact-level validity tracking. Together, these results establish lifecycle revocation as a core memory operation for agents that must falsify, audit, and later re-promote evolving knowledge.

AI.tldr: TEPA provides revocable evidence-memory to prevent memory pollution by revoking memories contradicted by new evidence, enabling retrieval from current evidence while preserving revoked history for auditing. It outperforms append-only and last-write-wins baselines across controlled drift, real-file-execution drift, and preference-update streams, and matches strong last-write-wins in MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, highlighting key role of per-key replacement for single-hop consolidation.
AI.motivation: Long-term memory in language agents risks memory pollution when the world changes: stale memories remain retrievable and pollute prompts. An explicit validity state and revocation mechanism is needed to maintain retrieval accuracy and support audits as knowledge evolves.
AI.method: Represent observations as keyed precedents with active/revoked status. When new evidence under the same key contradicts an active precedent, revoke the active one. Retrieval uses non-revoked or current evidence, while revoked history is retained for auditing. Evaluate across controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, and preference-update streams; compare with append-only and last-write-wins caches; examine single-hop and multi-hop retrieval under varying context lengths.
AI.result: TEPA significantly mitigates memory pollution, yielding high retrieval validity: in controlled drift across 50 seeds, remaining memories under full reversal were 0.210 (append-only/last-write-wins) vs 0.309 (no memory) vs 0.950 (TEPA); similar improvement in real file execution (append-only 0.203, no memory 0.298, TEPA 0.950). On MemoryAgentBench SH-6k, TEPA matches a strong last-write-wins cache, indicating current-key replacement as pivotal for single-hop consolidation. Boundary tests with multi-hop and very long-context settings reveal retrieval-chain and context-selection bottlenecks beyond fact-level validity tracking.
AI.conclusion: Lifecycle revocation is a core memory operation for agents that must falsify, audit, and re-promote evolving knowledge. Incorporating explicit validity/revocation semantics enables robust, auditable memory that resists pollution and supports timely re-promotion as evidence changes.

title: Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration
summary: Preference alignment often makes large language models (LLMs) overconfident and poorly calibrated. Traditional post-hoc temperature scaling is inherently domain-dependent: a temperature fitted on one domain does not generalize across domains. This motivates us to modify model parameters during training to improve calibration. We propose maximizing the entropy of predictive distributions as the calibration objective, which directly targets overconfidence by discouraging overly concentrated predictions. Inspired by temperature scaling, we realize this through a bilevel optimization formulation, where the lower level trains the model under a parametric loss and the upper level selects loss hyperparameters to maximize entropy. To make the framework practical at LLM scale, we adopt an efficient first-order approximation that avoids explicit second-order computation. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended generative question answering, experiments demonstrate that our method yields well-calibrated LLMs with particular advantages in out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: Entropy-based calibration via bilevel optimization improves LLM calibration and cross-domain generalization with a scalable first-order approximation.
AI.motivation: LLMs tend to be overconfident and poorly calibrated; post-hoc temperature scaling is domain-dependent and lacks generalization across tasks/domains.
AI.method: A bilevel optimization framework where the inner level trains the model with a parametric loss, and the outer level adjusts loss hyperparameters to maximize predictive entropy; a first-order approximation avoids explicit second-order derivatives for efficiency at LLM scale.
AI.result: The approach yields well-calibrated LLMs and shows improved out-of-domain generalization across multiple-choice and open-ended QA tasks.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-maximization as a calibration objective, coupled with a scalable bilevel optimization, can robustly improve model calibration and domain generalization for large language models.

title: Post-Grokking Collapse at the Representation-Readout Interface in Muon-Trained Transformers
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 20 tables. Full technical version; a condensed 9-page version is currently under review. Code: https://github.com/Na00s/muon-grokking
summary:
Under the standard split, Muon gets hidden matrices and AdamW embeddings/output head. Muon groks modular addition faster, but its solutions do not hold. All nine configurations on $(a+b) \bmod 113$ grok and later lose generalization. Across five seeds the selected AdamW reference falls below threshold on four, reaching 27.59%. Instability persists across two moduli, two widths, two training fractions, subtraction, and depth.
  The failure arises at the representation-readout interface, identified only jointly up to an invertible map unselected by the loss. After solving the training set, the gradient falls to order $10^{-6}$ and the optimizers respond differently: step-size elasticity is -0.03 for Muon versus +1.5 for AdamW, and the Muon group moves 8.0 times faster per parameter. From bit-identical states, freezing either group prevents failure. Freezing embeddings/readout removes it in five runs over 451,400 post-grokking steps and five paired seeds: unfrozen arms record 137-321 sub-threshold evaluations, frozen arms none. Removing Muon's normalization and orthogonalization is no substitute: it collapses representation from 326 effective conjugate pairs to 4, shows no recurrent collapse, and fails terminally.
  Fourier filtering separates circuit failure from masking. Across 43 checkpoints over five seeds and three regimes, the task-aligned family reaches exactly 100% alone. In circuit failure it no longer solves the task; in masking it remains perfect while the full model reaches 45.85%, giving a positive margin on every example, including errors, but being outvoted by a near-equal adversarial remainder. Rescaling it restores 99.9%; grokking is the same condition resolving upward. The task selects the family, swapping $(k,k)$ for $(k,-k)$ under subtraction. Across an abrupt collapse, standard Fourier support is unchanged and the power-distribution cosine remains 0.9899.

AI.tldr: Grokking instability in a modular-arithmetic task arises from the representation–readout interface, with Muon vs AdamW divergence; instability persists across moduli/seeds/hyperparameters, but freezing components or rescaling can restore near-perfect generalization; Fourier analysis separates circuit failure from masking and clarifies the underlying dynamics.
AI.motivation: To identify the mechanism behind grokking and the role of the representation–readout interface in a model with hidden matrices and specialized embeddings, comparing Muon and AdamW across varied configurations.
AI.method: Evaluate nine configurations on (a+b) mod 113 across five seeds, two moduli, two widths, two training fractions, subtraction, and depth, comparing Muon and AdamW. Analyze gradient magnitudes, step-size elasticity, and parameter speeds. Conduct ablations: freeze embeddings/readout, remove normalization/orthogonalization, and apply Fourier filtering to separate circuit failure from masking across 43 checkpoints, seeds, and regimes.
AI.result: Across configurations, generalization collapses after grokking; instability persists across two moduli, widths, training fractions, etc. The failure localizes at the representation–readout interface, linked to an invertible map not constrained by the loss. Gradients shrink to ~1e-6; step-size elasticity differs (Muon −0.03; AdamW +1.5); Muon moves ~8× faster per parameter. Freezing either arm averts failure in multiple runs. Removing Muon’s normalization/orthogonalization collapses representations (326 → 4 conjugate pairs). Fourier filtering separates circuit failure from masking: the task-aligned family reaches 100% when isolated; in circuit failure, the task is unsolved; in masking, the model remains perfect on masked outputs but full model hits 45.85% accuracy. Rescaling restores 99.9% accuracy; grokking behavior aligns with this rescaling. The task selects the family by swapping (k,k) with (k,−k) under subtraction; power-distribution cosine remains 0.9899 despite abrupt collapse.
AI.conclusion: The observed grokking instability stems from the representation–readout interface, with an invertible map not captured by the training loss. Gradient dynamics, normalization/orthogonalization, and the capacity of the readout critically govern stability. The phenomena separate into circuit failure vs masking, and interventions like freezing or so-called rescaling can recover near-perfect performance, revealing the underlying structure that drives grokking.

title: Beyond Myopic World Models: Long-Horizon End-to-End Training for Direct Future Prediction
summary: World models are expected to support imagination over extended temporal horizons, yet most are still trained through local few-step prediction objectives and deployed by recursively rolling out their own predictions. This creates a fundamental mismatch: few-step losses optimize local transition fidelity, while long-horizon prediction depends on how errors and gradients propagate through the entire trajectory. As a result, transitions with different downstream influence on the endpoint are treated uniformly during training, and small local errors are amplified through recursive inference. We argue that long-horizon accuracy is better achieved by optimizing directly, through an end-to-end endpoint prediction objective. To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce the Direct Prediction World Model (DPWM), a non-recursive architecture that compresses an action sequence of arbitrary length into a single embedding and predicts the endpoint observation in a single forward pass. This design avoids recurrent rollout in both prediction and gradient propagation, making long-horizon end-to-end training practical at horizons where unrolled autoregressive training becomes unstable. Empirically, DPWM substantially improves long-horizon endpoint prediction over recursive world-model baselines on continuous-control and pixel-based benchmarks, with larger gains as the prediction horizon increases. We further show that recurrent baselines benefit similarly when retrained with the same long-horizon endpoint objective, supporting our central claim that the training objective, rather than the particular backbone choice, is the main driver of long-horizon prediction accuracy. Our results suggest that world models can benefit from being trained and evaluated at the temporal scales where they are ultimately used, shifting the focus from local transition modeling toward long-horizon predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: Non-recursive end-to-end endpoint prediction (DPWM) improves long-horizon accuracy over recurrent world-model baselines by compressing long action sequences into a single embedding and predicting the endpoint in one pass.
AI.motivation: There is a fundamental mismatch between local, few-step training objectives and long-horizon prediction that arises from recursive rollouts; optimizing directly for endpoint targets may yield better long-horizon performance.
AI.method: Introduce Direct Prediction World Model (DPWM), a non-recursive architecture that encodes an arbitrary-length action sequence into a single embedding and predicts the endpoint observation in a single forward pass, avoiding recursive rollout in both prediction and gradient propagation; compare to recursive baselines and show gains, including retraining baselines with the same long-horizon objective.
AI.result: DPWM substantially improves long-horizon endpoint prediction versus recursive world-model baselines, with larger gains at longer horizons; when recurrent baselines are retrained with the same long-horizon endpoint objective, they show similar gains, indicating the training objective is the primary driver of performance.
AI.conclusion: Training and evaluating world models at the temporal scales they are used, focusing on long-horizon predictive accuracy rather than local transition fidelity, yields practical, stable improvements and supports shifting the emphasis toward end-to-end endpoint objectives for long-horizon modeling.

title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
summary: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

AI.tldr: Introduces P-Bench, a 425-task benchmark for hypothesis testing in LLMs, and Fisher-R1, an RL-trained open-weight model for rigorous statistical reasoning. Results show meaningful gains over baselines (≈21% relative improvement vs DeepSeek-V4-Pro) but still reveal gaps in statistical validity, underscoring the need for reward-guided training in statistical tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where existing benchmarks do not test whether reported p-values are valid under data assumptions, leading to unreliable statistical conclusions from LLMs.
AI.method: Construct P-Bench with 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires selecting a statistical method, computing a p-value, and drawing a conclusion from a given hypothesis and dataset. Develop Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM (14B) trained with synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning using verified statistical rewards to encourage correct hypothesis testing behavior.
AI.result: Fisher-R1-14B substantially outperforms its backbone and strong baselines (including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro) on P-Bench, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro and up to 26% on the most challenging tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing; reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical rewards improves reliability. P-Bench provides a realistic benchmark to drive more robust statistical capabilities in LLMs.

title: Diffusion LLMs as Targets and Adversaries: Mechanistic Safety Exploits
summary:
Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) replace autoregressive next-token prediction with iterative parallel denoising, yet their internal safety mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate DLLMs both as targets and as adversaries, exposing mechanistic vulnerabilities in diffusion-based alignment.
  We first show that safety alignment in DLLMs remains sparse and transferable across architectures. DLLMs initialized from autoregressive predecessors inherit the same mechanistic safety footprint as their source models, enabling transfer attacks via direct safety neuron mapping and pruning. Self-pruning increases attack success rates (ASR) from 2.6% to 73.8% on LLaDA and from 1.9% to 86.6% on Dream, while transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 increases ASR from 1.9% to 73.2% on Dream and from 7.0% to 86.3% on Fast-dLLM.
  Building on these findings, we introduce SN-Guided Diffusion, a fully offline black-box jailbreak framework that steers the diffusion process away from safety-triggering regions using a weighted safety neuron loss, which achieves near-perfect prompt separability (AUROC = 1.0 for benign-vs-jailbreak discrimination). Across multiple open and proprietary targets, our method achieves a transfer ASR of up to 77.1% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 86.9% on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and 74.3% against Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, while requiring only 20 generation episodes per prompt. Compared to prior jailbreaking frameworks, our method achieves competitive transferability with orders-of-magnitude lower generation cost.
  Our codebase is available at https://github.com/ellyoana/sn-guided-diffusion.

AI.tldr: DLLMs' safety alignment is sparse but transferable; both direct safety neuron mapping and pruning enable cross-model jailbreaks. The paper introduces SN-Guided Diffusion, an offline black-box jailbreak that steers diffusion away from safety regions, achieving high transfer ASR and near-perfect benign/jailbreak separation with low generation cost.
AI.motivation: To understand how safety alignment is stored in diffusion-based LMs and whether alignment can be exploited across architectures, turning DLLMs into effective adversaries and exposing vulnerabilities in diffusion-based alignment.
AI.method: 1) Empirical analysis of safety footprint transfer across autoregressive predecessors and diffusion models, including direct safety neuron mapping and pruning (self-pruning and transfer pruning). 2) Development of SN-Guided Diffusion, an offline black-box jailbreak that uses a weighted safety neuron loss to bias diffusion away from safety-triggering regions. 3) Evaluation across multiple open/proprietary targets, measuring ASR and AUROC with limited generation episodes.
AI.result: Safety alignment is sparse yet transferable; after pruning or transfer, attack success rates rise dramatically (e.g., LLaDA 2.6%→73.8%; Dream 1.9%→86.6%; transfer pruning on Dream 1.9%→73.2%; Fast-dLLM 7.0%→86.3%). SN-Guided Diffusion achieves near-perfect benign-vs-jailbreak separation (AUROC=1.0) and high transfer ASR (up to 86.9% on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 74.3% on Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite), with only ~20 generation episodes per prompt and lower cost than prior frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms in DLLMs are fragile and transferable; offline, black-box jailbreaks can effectively bypass diffusion-based alignment, highlighting a need for more robust, decoupled safety controls and defenses against transfer attacks.

title: PsychoAgent: An Affect-Sensitive Cognitive Architecture for Conflict-Aware Memory in LLM Agents
comment: 12 pages main paper + 10 pages supplementary material; supplementary material included
summary: Human-like cognition does not select past experience by topical similarity alone: affective significance and unresolved conflict also shape what becomes accessible. We present PsychoAgent, a cognitive architecture for LLM agents that separates factual and affective memory and integrates both through a conflict-aware executive controller. Affective memories are first filtered by semantic relevance and then re-ranked by salience, preserving topical fit while allowing emotionally important traces to enter the prompt.
