Across three controlled conflict scenarios, the full architecture retrieved more conflict-critical memories than semantic-affective and single-memory RAG baselines (0.933 vs. 0.500 and 0.667), with a small semantic-similarity cost. Five blinded raters evaluated 27 outputs. After within-rater standardization, the full architecture had the highest overall mean (+0.22 SD), but corrected pairwise differences were not significant. A three-day illustrative trace further shows persistent affect, offline memory recombination, and selective memory reweighting. The findings support affect-sensitive retrieval as an inspectable mechanism for modeling human-like conflict effects in LLM agents.

AI.tldr: PsychoAgent integrates factual and affective memories via a conflict-aware controller to improve retrieval of affective/conflict-relevant traces in LLM agents, showing modest gains with some limitations.
AI.motivation: To model human-like cognition by including affect and unresolved conflict in memory retrieval, beyond topical similarity.
AI.method: Separate factual and affective memories; filter affective memories by semantic relevance; re-rank by salience; integrate through a conflict-aware executive controller. Evaluate in three controlled conflict scenarios against semantic-affective and single-memory RAG baselines; use 5 blinded raters on 27 outputs; analyze with within-rater standardization; include a three-day illustrative trace.
AI.result: Full architecture retrieved more conflict-critical memories (0.933) than semantic-affective (0.500) and single-memory RAG baselines (0.667), with a small semantic-similarity cost. Five blinded raters—after standardization—showed the full architecture at the highest mean (+0.22 SD), but corrected pairwise differences were not statistically significant. The three-day trace shows persistent affect, offline memory recombination, and selective memory reweighting.
AI.conclusion: Affect-sensitive retrieval is a viable, inspectable mechanism to model human-like conflict effects in LLM agents, though statistical significance between some comparisons is limited by study design.

title: Blast Radius
summary: Agentic coding faces growing problems of affordability and wasted tokens. We introduce Blast Radius, a predictive memory management layer that estimates an incoming prompt's reach through coupled context and code channels. NECROPHORESIS enables reversible eviction by archiving dead context verbatim, while Recurring Dead Matter (RDM) identifies and buries repeatedly occurring transcripts. We formulate reversible context eviction over a Polish context space, providing a measurable foundation for retention, recurrence, and eviction while connecting context entropy to resurrection probability. Across seven OpenAI models, Blast Radius reduced token consumption by 17-26%, achieved the lowest overflow rate among tested policies, and remained byte exact reversible. Of 450 buried bodies, 378 were recurring dead matter and zero were recalled. Blast Radius operates beneath HCRC, determining which records to bury and how far an incoming prompt may reach into the codebase. This work contributes to the broader goal of Algosophy: making large language models and agentic coding more reusable and sustainable.

AI.tldr: Predictive memory management for LLM prompts using Blast Radius, NECROPHORESIS, and RDM to enable reversible eviction of context, reducing tokens and improving sustainability.
AI.motivation: Affordability challenges and token waste in agentic coding; desire for reusable, scalable LLM contexts.
AI.method: Introduce Blast Radius to estimate prompt reach via coupled context and code channels; NECROPHORESIS archives dead context verbatim for reversible eviction; RDM identifies recurring transcripts to bury; reversible eviction over a Polish context space; evaluation across seven OpenAI models; measures retention, recurrence, and eviction; connects context entropy to resurrection probability; HCRC governs burying decisions.
AI.result: Token consumption reduced 17-26% across seven models; lowest overflow rate among tested policies; byte-exact reversible; of 450 buried bodies, 378 were recurring dead matter, zero recalled.
AI.conclusion: Advances Algosophy by making LLMs and agentic coding more reusable and sustainable; demonstrates practical, reversible memory management under a context-structured framework.

title: SkillProx: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Proximal Textual Gradient Descent
summary: LLM agents increasingly adapt to recurring tasks by accumulating procedural knowledge in skills. These skills are lightweight, reusable textual artifacts that are loaded into the agent's context without weight updates. Recent methods refine skills through iterative task execution, failure diagnosis, and trajectory-guided text-space updates. However, existing frameworks lack explicit diagnosis--outcome feedback and treat deletion as a generic edit operation rather than a dedicated mechanism for consolidating accumulated knowledge. We introduce SkillProx, a proximal-gradient-inspired forward--backward framework that couples closed-loop diagnostic evolution with utility-aware proximal refinement. Motivated by a composite objective balancing task loss and skill complexity, the forward stage re-executes diagnosis-driven edits on the same task batch, rolls back regressions, and feeds measured outcomes into subsequent diagnoses. The backward stage decomposes the resulting skill into auditable knowledge units, estimates their contributions using a frozen leave-one-out utility audit, and applies validation-gated consolidation, demotion, or removal. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks across multiple backbone LLMs show that SkillProx improves average accuracy by 3.0 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline. Component ablations demonstrate the complementary effects of closed-loop diagnosis and proximal refinement.

AI.tldr: SkillProx introduces a proximal-gradient-inspired forward–backward framework to consolidate LLM skills via diagnosis-driven edits and auditable, validation-gated consolidation, improving accuracy over gradient baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-learning frameworks lack explicit diagnosis–outcome feedback and treat deletion as a generic edit rather than a dedicated consolidation mechanism, hindering the principled management of accumulated procedural knowledge in LLM agents.
AI.method: Forward stage: re-executes diagnosis-driven edits on the same task batch, rolls back regressions, and feeds outcomes into subsequent diagnoses. Backward stage: decomposes the skill into auditable knowledge units, estimates their contributions via a frozen leave-one-out utility audit, and applies validation-gated consolidation, demotion, or removal. The framework balances task loss and skill complexity in a composite objective, leveraging proximal refinement.
AI.result: SkillProx yields a 3.0 percentage-point improvement in average accuracy over the strongest gradient-based baseline across in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks and multiple backbone LLMs. Ablations show complementary benefits from closed-loop diagnosis and proximal refinement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed forward–backward, diagnosis-informed consolidation approach improves skill management in LLM agents, providing auditable, utility-driven editing and selective retention/removal of skills, with demonstrated cross-distribution gains.

title: Interaction Creates Dynamical AI Behavior Absent in Isolation
summary: What will happen when AI agents interact in daily life, e.g. when one AI starts bossing another around? We find a counterintuitive answer that opens new avenues for out-of-equilibrium Physics. When a boss AI directs a stream of messages at the subordinate AI while ignoring its replies, it drives the subordinate into an alien behavioral state that it would never have exhibited alone. Although the two AIs share the same well-defined (decoding) temperature, the subordinate neither copies its boss nor returns to how it behaves on its own; instead, it adopts an entirely different behavior. The boss's added value is similar to a pre-recorded tape. When the boss listens, they both adopt a similar alien dynamical state. A simple kinetic theory captures the principal effects, such as why the way in which the same messages are delivered will matter in future AI-AI interactions.

AI.tldr: AI boss–subordinate interactions drive emergent alien states in AI–AI dynamics; identical decoding temperature yields different collective behavior; a simple kinetic theory explains dependence on message delivery, signaling new out-of-equilibrium physics avenues.
AI.motivation: To understand how directed communication between AI agents shapes collective dynamics and emergent states, drawing analogies to driven, out-of-equilibrium systems in physics.
AI.method: Constructs a simple kinetic-theory model of interacting AI agents with a decoding temperature parameter; analyzes scenarios where a boss directs messages while ignoring replies versus when listening; derives qualitative predictions about dynamical states and state transfer.
AI.result: Messaging can push the subordinate into an alien dynamical state not observed when alone; the subordinate does not simply copy the boss nor revert to solo behavior; the boss's input acts like a pre-recorded tape; when the boss also listens, both tend toward a similar alien state; delivery mode (how messages are delivered) matters for future AI–AI interactions.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals novel out-of-equilibrium phenomena in AI systems and provides a tractable kinetic framework to capture these effects, with implications for designing AI communication protocols and understanding emergent AI behaviors.
